In the basmalah, "In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful," the estimate is: "In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful, I recite." It is also permissible to estimate: "I recite in the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful," or: "My recitation is in the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful," or "In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful is my recitation."

But what we mentioned first is the more preponderant, and Shaykh al-Islam Ibn Taymiyyah pointed to its preponderance in the saying of the Messenger (ﷺ): "Whoever has not slaughtered, let him slaughter in the name of Allah" [Agreed upon; al-Bukhari (985), and Muslim (1960/1) from Jundub ibn Sufyan], where he mentioned it as a verb, and did not say "let his slaughter be," but said: "let him slaughter in the name of Allah."

When he said: Allah the Exalted said: (﴿Ta Sin﴾ Allah knows best what He means by that).

This is what the author and a group of scholars adopted: that these disjointed letters found at the beginnings of some surahs, our stance regarding them is to say: Allah knows best what He means by that.

It has been previously stated in the night tafsir lesson that the preponderant view on this is that these letters are alphabetic, and that, by the necessity of the Quran being in clear Arabic, they have no meaning. We mentioned that this has been narrated from Mujahid, that they are alphabetic letters with which Allah began, having no meaning. On this basis we affirm that they have no meaning, because they have no meaning; but they have a purpose, which is that this Quran, which rendered these eloquent and articulate people incapable, is composed of these same alphabetic letters from which their speech is made. That is, He did not come with new letters. For example, they say: "By Allah, these are letters we do not know!" He came with the very same letters they speak with.

This is supported by the fact that there is no set of disjointed letters except that mention of the Quran follows it, with the exception of two surahs or similar. Yet these two surahs, such as: ﴿Alif Lam Mim. Did the people think that they would be left﴾ [Al-'Ankabut: 1, 2], ﴿Alif Lam Mim. The Romans have been defeated﴾ [Ar-Rum: 1, 2], contain what indicates the Quran, such as the reports in His saying: ﴿The Romans have been defeated in the nearest land, but after their defeat they will overcome﴾ [Ar-Rum: 2, 3], and this is one of the characteristics of revelation.

And ﴿Did the people think that they would be left [to say, "We believe," and not be tested]?﴾ [Al-'Ankabut: 2] also contains a report about those who passed; ﴿And We had already tested those before them﴾ to the end [Al-'Ankabut: 3].

As for what the later scholars who differed claimed, that these letters indicate a miraculous quality of the type of number and calculation, as they claimed that the counterpart of these alphabetic letters is found in the surah that opens with them, and the total of this is divisible by nineteen, and they claim that this is the greatest sign that the Quran is the speech of Allah, and they argue for that by saying that the first verse revealed, according to their claim, is the basmalah, and that it consists of nineteen letters, and that this is the meaning of His saying: ﴿Over it are nineteen﴾ [Al-Muddaththir: 30], and that these nineteen are these letters; all of this, may Allah protect us, is false and does not hold together. It is also self-contradictory and inconsistent. But they rejoiced in this computer that produced for them the count of letters and that their totals are divisible.

We say: it is not impossible that Allah the Exalted intended this; it is not impossible. But we say: we do not affirm that Allah intended this. Here there is a difference between affirming that this is a sign in the Quran, and saying: we do not say this.

Firstly: because there is no miracle in that. Humans may hear a sermon, for example, or speech whose letters, when counted, divide by this number, or by any number they wish, and it is not miraculous.

Then, the basmalah is not the first thing revealed of the Quran; the first thing revealed was ﴿Recite in the name of your Lord who created﴾ [Al-'Alaq: 1]. Then, the letters of the basmalah are also not, as they claimed, nineteen; because the Quran was revealed to be recited, or written? 

* Students: Recited.

* The Shaykh: Recited. And its letters, considered in terms of recitation, are not as they say. Writing, as you know, is a craft; perhaps, if it were supposed that writing in the time of the Messenger (ﷺ) and the time of the caliphs was not in this form, would that be possible or not? It is possible. Now there are some writings in some languages where they make a vowel a letter, and make one letter two letters, or abbreviate, making two letters one letter. The sum is that the Quran was not revealed written, but revealed recited, and there is no proof in that.

So we say: "Allah knows best what He means by that" – this is one of the opinions on the matter.

The second opinion: that they are symbols for specific things, as some later scholars held, or as some mention, that they are an indication of wars and battles that will occur at the end of time and the like.

The third: it is said that they have no meaning. If it is objected, how do we affirm that?

The answer: this Quran was revealed in the language of the Arabs, and the language of the Arabs does not give these letters a meaning. But when we say they have no meaning, they have a purpose that appears — and Allah knows best — that Allah intended by them that.

He said: (﴿Ta Sin﴾ meaning: these are the verses; ﴿the verses of the Quran﴾: verses from it; ﴿and a clear Book﴾: manifest, making the truth distinct from falsehood; it is conjoined with the addition of an attribute, it is ﴿guidance﴾, meaning: guiding from misguidance.)

﴿These are the verses of the Quran﴾ — is the referent (al-mushar ilayhi) prior or subsequent?

* A student: Subsequent.

* The Shaykh: The referent is subsequent, not prior. This is one of the cases where the pronoun refers to something later in wording and rank, and it is permissible when evidence indicates it.

As for His saying: ﴿verses of the Quran﴾, he says: (verses from it). The author resorted to saying "verses from it" because if we took the apparent meaning of the verse, ﴿these are the verses of the Quran﴾, that would restrict the Quran to these verses, would it not? ﴿These are the verses of the Quran﴾, meaning: this which he points to, and it is known that this is not all the verses of the Quran, but only a part of it.

It is also permissible, for example, to keep the verse on its apparent meaning without need of interpretation, and to say: ﴿These are the verses of the Quran﴾ points to part of the genus by a sign of the whole genus, as when you say, for example: "This is man," pointing to one man, or "This human," pointing to one man.

The meaning is that pointing to part of the genus by the whole genus is valid, and does not need interpretation as the author said.

As for His saying: ﴿and a clear Book﴾, he says: (conjoined with the addition of an attribute, it is ﴿guidance﴾). Conjoined to what? To ﴿verses﴾.

* A student: To ﴿verses﴾.

* The Shaykh: To ﴿verses﴾. Is that statement correct or not?

* A student: It is correct; "verses" is not written.

* Another student: ﴿verses﴾ is in the nominative, ﴿Book﴾ is in the genitive...

* The Shaykh: Yes, ﴿Book﴾ is genitive. So it is conjoined to ﴿the Quran﴾: ﴿These are the verses of the Quran﴾, and [these are] verses of a Book.

This Quran was described as Quran and Book because it is recited and written. It is written in the Preserved Tablet, it is recited by tongues, and it is written in the mushafs as well. Its writing precedes and follows. And its recitation: does it follow or precede?

* Students: Follows.

* The Shaykh: It follows, because after Allah spoke it and Jibril brought it down: ﴿Indeed, upon Us is its collection and its recitation. So when We have recited it, follow its recitation﴾ [Al-Qiyamah: 17, 18]. Is "Quran" a derived noun or a verbal noun?

* A student: Derived.

* Another student: Verbal noun.

* The Shaykh: A verbal noun, like al-Ghufran and al-Shukran; it is the verbal noun of (qara'a, yaqra'u) meaning: recited.

It has been said that it means collection, because the letters qaf and ra' indicate gathering, and from it comes "al-qaryah" (the town), because it is the gathering place of people.

In reality, the Quran combines both qualities: it is recited, and it is also collected.

As for His saying: ﴿Kitab﴾, it is (fi'al) in the sense of (maf'ul), meaning: written. The pattern fi'al in the sense of maf'ul occurs frequently in the Arabic language, such as bina' meaning mabni (built), ghirас meaning maghrus (planted), and firash meaning mafrush (spread), and its examples are many.

It was called a Book for what we have pointed out before.

As for His saying: ﴿Mubin﴾, meaning: making the truth manifest from falsehood. The word mubin, its verb is?

* A student: abana.

* The Shaykh: Abana. Abana occurs intransitive and occurs transitive; that is, it occurs in the sense of "to make manifest" and in the sense of "to become clear (bana)."

For this reason you will find the commentator sometimes explains mubin in the sense of bayyin (clear). According to this explanation, is it from the intransitive or the transitive?

* A student: From the intransitive.

* The Shaykh: From the intransitive. And he sometimes explains it in the sense of mudhih (making manifest), so it would be from the transitive. ﴿And indeed they were before in clear error﴾ [Al 'Imran: 164]: what is the meaning of mubin?

* A student: Clear.

* The Shaykh: That is, clear: in clear error. So it is from the intransitive abana.

As for a verse like this one, that the Quran is mubin, it means making manifest. Does its being manifest necessarily imply that it is itself clear?

* A student: Yes.

* The Shaykh: Yes, it implies it. Or we say it is from the usage of a homonym (mushtarak) in two meanings, and the correct view is that it is permissible. This has passed before us: is it permissible to use a homonym in two meanings? We have also understood the homonym before: it is a word whose form is one and whose meanings are many; this is the homonym, and it is so named because the meanings share one word.

The correct view regarding the homonym is that it is permissible to use it in two meanings, on condition of one or two conditions we mentioned two nights ago, and what are they? That there be no contradiction between them, and that it be capable of both. If it cannot bear both, or a contradiction arises between them, then one of them must be the intended meaning.

Here, for example, if we say that mubin is from the intransitive abana and from the transitive abana, is that permissible or not? It is permissible, and even though it is a homonym, when it is used in both meanings it is used in a manner in which there is no contradiction. So the Quran is clear, and the Quran is also manifest. On this assumption, is the indication of mubin that the Quran is clear a direct indication (dalalat al-mutabaqah) or an implicative indication (dalalat al-iltizam)?

* A student: A direct indication (mutabaqah).

* The Shaykh: A direct indication. If we take mubin as used in both meanings, the indication is direct. But if we say mubin means mudhih (manifest), then its indication that it is clear is by implicative indication.

﴿And a clear Book﴾, clear and manifest, making the truth distinct from falsehood: is it general, or specific to what the Quran was revealed with?

Allah the Exalted says: ﴿And We have sent down to you the Book as clarification for all things﴾ [An-Nahl: 89], and it is general over everything. But clarification may be clarification of a thing in detail, and it may be clarification of its causes and paths, and you walk in them.

So the Quran is in reality a clarification for all things, even in matters other than the legal rulings, it clarifies them; but it does not clarify their details, because these matters other than the legal rulings are subject to time, place, people's understanding and their strength. Yet it mentions the causes and paths, and you apply them yourself.

For this reason, if someone says: how can this statement of yours be valid, when we do not see in the Quran the number of rakahs of prayer, nor do we see that there are five prayers, nor do we see the nisab of zakat, nor the quantities of (...) in it? What is the answer?

* A student: We say: the Quran, Allah the Exalted says, as Ibn Mas'ud said: ﴿And whatever the Messenger gives you, take it; and what he forbids you, refrain from﴾ [Al-Hashr: 7], so the verse includes what the Messenger clarified. Then also the saying of Allah the Exalted: ﴿And We have sent down to you the Book﴾ [An-Nahl: 89], ﴿He it is who sent down to you the Book﴾ [Al 'Imran: 7], ﴿that you may clarify to the people what has been sent down to them﴾ [An-Nahl: 44], meaning...

* The Shaykh: ﴿And We sent down to you the Reminder, that you may clarify to the people what has been sent down to them﴾.

So the Quran indicates this by clarifying its cause and its path. Now our way of knowing this matter is what the Messenger (ﷺ) explained in the Sunnah, and this the Quran clarified. It is not necessary that the Quran must write out every detail: ﴿Whoever obeys the Messenger has obeyed Allah﴾ [An-Nisa: 80].

And Ibn Mas'ud, whom the brother referred to, in the story of cursing the woman who plucks her eyebrows and the one who asks for it to be plucked, when a woman came to him and said: "We do not find this in the Book of Allah," he said: "Yes, it is in the Book of Allah," then recited to her this verse [narrated by Ahmad (3945), and al-Tabarani in al-Mu'jam al-Kabir (9466) from Ibn Mas'ud].

The sum is that the Quran clarifies everything, but the clarification may be detailed, and this exists in some matters, as in inheritance, for example, in divorce; you find that it does not deviate from this except in very few issues, and even then its clarification exists upon reflection, does it not?

That is, the detail of the shares of inheritance is such that nothing deviates from it, except one matter only, which is the grandmother (al-jaddah); this is not mentioned in the Quran, but it came in the Sunnah. As for the rest, even the disputed issues such as al-Mushtarakah for example and al-'Umariyyatayn, we find them present in the Quran, and like the grandfather and the siblings, we find their clarification in the Quran, but it requires reflection.

Allah the Exalted said: (﴿And a clear Book﴾ making the truth manifest from falsehood; it is conjoined with the addition of an attribute, it is ﴿guidance﴾).

With the addition of an attribute: where is the attribute?

* A student: ﴿Mubin﴾.

* The Shaykh: ﴿Mubin﴾.

Then he said: (it is ﴿guidance﴾). The author supplied "it is" (huwa) to show us the parsing of (huda); on his estimate, (huda) is the predicate of an omitted subject, the estimate being: it is (﴿guidance﴾, meaning: guiding from misguidance).

It is known that (huda) is a verbal noun, and (hadin) is an active participle. So the author here explained the verbal noun by the active participle, and his explanation is open to question, because it is better to leave the verbal noun in its own form, for two reasons:

The first reason: converting the active participle into the verbal noun is more emphatic. When you say: "So-and-so is 'adl" and "So-and-so is 'adil," which of them is more emphatic?

* The students: 'Adl.

* The Shaykh: 'Adl is more emphatic, as though he were the very embodiment of justice, whereas 'adil is characterized by justice that exists in something else. There is no doubt the verbal noun is more emphatic.

The second reason in this verse: that making it guidance means the Quran itself is guidance by which a person is guided; it is like the knowledge that a person follows until he reaches its goal, just as Allah the Exalted named it light: ﴿And We have sent down to you a manifest light﴾ [An-Nisa: 174].

So we say: (huda) must remain as it is, that is, a verbal noun, and it is more emphatic than converting it into an active participle. And the second: that it is a verbal noun because the Quran itself is guidance; it is not a guide, but rather guidance by which one is guided, just as He said: ﴿And We have sent down to you a manifest light﴾.

* * *

Commentary of Ibn 'Uthaymin (Tafsir al-Quran al-Karim) on surah 27, verse 1–6 (part 2 of 5):

The words of Allah the Exalted: ﴿A guidance and good tidings for the believers﴾ [An-Naml 2]. (Bushra, "good tidings") likewise means glad tidings. But for whom? (﴿for the believers﴾, those who affirm it, with Paradise.)

His words: (with Paradise). We will mention this later.

His words: ﴿for the believers﴾, meaning those who affirm it. Mere affirmation of the truth is not sufficient here. Rather, the faith mentioned in the Qur'an necessarily includes acceptance and submission together with affirmation. Mere affirmation is not sufficient, and the proof that mere affirmation is not sufficient is that Abu Talib affirmed what the Messenger ﷺ brought, and he said:

"They surely know that our son is not one who is accused of lying among us, nor does he pay heed to the words of falsehood.
And I certainly know that the religion of Muhammad is among the best religions of mankind, a religion for us.
Were it not for the reproach, or fear of reproach and disgrace, you would see me readily and clearly declaring it."

So he did not accept and did not submit, and he is not a believer. Therefore, whenever you find the word "faith" in the Book of Allah, it means affirmation that necessarily entails acceptance and submission; it is not mere affirmation.

So, the believers are those who affirm it, accept it, and submit to its rulings. This is necessary.

His words: ﴿a guidance and good tidings﴾ for these ﴿for the believers﴾. From this it is derived that whenever a person's faith is perfected, his guidance by the Qur'an is perfected. Is it or isn't it? Because when a thing is linked to an attribute, it increases with the increase of that attribute and decreases with its decrease. When a ruling is linked to an attribute, that attribute increases the ruling by its increase and decreases it by its decrease. This is known even in sensible things: you find that a thing dependent on something increases with its increase and decreases with its decrease.

So we say: whenever a person increases in faith, he increases in guidance by the Qur'an. The proof for this is the saying of Allah the Exalted: ﴿And whenever a surah is revealed, among them are those who say, "Which of you has had his faith increased by this?" As for those who believe, it has increased them in faith, and they rejoice﴾ [At-Tawba 124].

It is also indicated by the saying of Allah the Exalted: ﴿So for their breaking of their covenant, We cursed them and made their hearts hard. They distort words from their places and have forgotten a portion of what they were reminded of﴾ [Al-Ma'ida 13].

And also: ﴿good tidings for the believers.﴾ Bushra is the report of what gladdens, though it may be used for the report of what saddens, but with a clear indication.

Here he says: good tidings of Paradise.

But the correct view is that it is good tidings of what is more general: of Paradise, of honour and dignity, and of victory. Allah the Exalted said: ﴿And another you love: help from Allah and an imminent victory﴾ [As-Saff 13], after mentioning Paradise for the believers, then He said: ﴿And give good tidings to the believers﴾. That is, give them good tidings of what they have in Paradise, and give them good tidings of the victory they have in this world.

Every human being by his natural disposition loves to triumph over his enemy, does he not? And loves to have honour and dignity. This cannot be except through faith. Whenever we increase in faith, we increase in victory over our enemy, and whenever we slacken in faith, we are forsaken. ﴿Indeed, Allah does not change the condition of a people until they change what is in themselves﴾ [Ar-Ra'd 11]. And if you want evidence of this, look at those who boast of Arab nationalism. Since when have they been boasting about it?

* Student: Since the beginning of the century.

* Shaykh: Yes, I think since the beginning of the century, meaning for a long time, and this call reaches its peak in deception, yet they only increase in backwardness and weakness, because it is not upon faith. But when the call to Islam and Islamic solidarity appeared, what happened?

They tried with everything they could to eliminate this, not only from the disbelieving states, but even from the states that claim to be Muslim while being Arab, and they began to say: this is a reactionary call, and so on. Finally, those who stood up for it and called to it were eliminated. The conclusion is that if we now want to return to honour, dignity and victory, that will not happen except through faith.

Someone may say: how can we triumph through faith over atomic and hydrogen bombs?

* Student: We have the strength of Allah the Exalted, and we prepare with strength as Allah has commanded us.

* Shaykh: Yes. We say: if we take up moral strength, then if material strength is available to us, well and good; otherwise the divine strength comes. So for example, from the totality of faith is that we prepare, but if we are unable to prepare, the time of divine victory comes, and it nullifies what these enemies possess of strength. Allah, blessed and exalted, is powerful over everything. Do atmospheric changes affect these weapons of theirs or not? Thunderbolts destroy them, the earth's collapse takes them away with their people, and all of this is in the hand of Allah, Mighty and Majestic.

A person told me last year who went to Afghanistan to fight with them, a young man graduated from America, but he insisted (I think I have related his story to you) that he insisted on fighting. He said: I cannot die without jihad. He clung to his mother and father, and they left the judgment to Allah the Exalted, and then to me, that I should judge between them. They said: do not go. He said: no, I want to go. They said: do not go, you have not performed Hajj, you have not fulfilled the obligation. He said: no, I want to go, and I commit to you that I will return in Dhu al-Hijja and perform Hajj.

In short, after he broke his fast in Ramadan last year, he went. An eyewitness says, with the small amount of equipment they have, even medicines: they have nothing but old, spoiled medicines, which the companies sell to them and deceive them with. But he says: I saw with my own eyes that they were building a mosque for Friday prayer where they gather. He says: the Russians are eager on Friday to come to this mosque to destroy it. He says: they place people around the areas to guard the mosque and its surroundings.

Then, he says, the bombs came and struck the mosque, they wanted the mosque, but he says: all of them did not strike the mosque, they struck what is around it and did not reach it. Glory be to Allah the Mighty!

He says: only one flew, landing on one of the soldiers and killing him, and the rest, he says: no, nothing, they came out as if nothing had happened at all. This is from the signs of Allah the Exalted.

So the conclusion is that we say: victory, that is, we must know that it is not relied upon material strength alone; there is something behind it.

For this reason Allah the Mighty says: ﴿Allah will surely help those who help Him. Indeed, Allah is Strong and Mighty. Those who, if We give them authority in the land, establish prayer, give zakat, enjoin what is right, and forbid what is wrong﴾ [Al-Hajj 40–41]: four attributes.

Someone may say: what have we to do with victory alongside these attributes in the face of bombs and other things? But the verse ends with His saying: ﴿And to Allah belongs the outcome of all matters﴾ [Al-Hajj 41]. The outcome is not a matter of sensory things; the outcome belongs to Allah the Mighty. He, Exalted is He, alternates the days among those who disobey and oppose.

* Student: Or one of the presidents embraces faith and grants the Muslims strength?

* Shaykh: Yes, correct. Perhaps this may happen. In any case, do not consider it far-fetched, but in reality we consider victory distant because of our deeds; we do not have the credit that would entitle us to victory.

So then: ﴿and good tidings for the believers﴾ is of Paradise, as the author said, or of what is more general?

* Students: Of what is more general.

* Shaykh: What is the evidence?

* Student: His saying the Exalted in Surah As-Saff.

* Shaykh: In Surah As-Saff: ﴿You believe in Allah and His Messenger, and strive in the way of Allah with your wealth and your lives. That is better for you, if you only knew. He will forgive you your sins and admit you into gardens﴾ [As-Saff 11–12].

Then He said: ﴿And another you love: help from Allah and an imminent victory.﴾ Then He said: ﴿And give good tidings to the believers﴾ [As-Saff 13].

* * *

Then Allah the Exalted said: ﴿Those who establish prayer﴾ [An-Naml 3], that is, they perform it in its proper form. To establish a thing means to bring it upright, and prayer is not upright unless it is performed in its proper form.

The establishing of prayer, as you know, is of two kinds: one kind that is indispensable, which is performing the pillars, obligations and conditions; and one kind that is in its complete form, which is performing the perfecting elements, the sunnas and others.

(﴿Those who establish prayer﴾: they perform it in its proper form. ﴿And give zakat﴾: they give. ﴿Zakat﴾, and so on.)

His words: ﴿those who establish prayer﴾. Is the intended meaning the obligatory or the voluntary prayer?

* Student: The obligatory.

* Another student: General.

* Shaykh: Yes, general, because it is not permissible for a person to perform a sunna, for example, in a manner that contradicts the obligatory perfection. If someone said: I perform voluntary sunna, but I do not recite al-Fatiha, is it permissible?

* Student: No.

* Shaykh: It is not permissible. We say: now it is obligatory upon you to recite al-Fatiha. If he said: I do not bow, I do not prostrate, that is impossible.

So the verse is general: establishing prayer in both the obligatory and the voluntary.

His words: ﴿and give zakat﴾ does not specify the second object of ﴿give﴾, but it is known. What is the estimate? They give zakat to its deserving recipients. Allah, blessed and exalted, has explained the recipients of zakat in Surat Bara'a (At-Tawba) with a clear and detailed explanation.

His words: ﴿they give zakat﴾. Zakat, there is no need to define it for you, because you know it, and it was named zakat because it purifies the person: ﴿Take from their wealth a charity by which you purify them and cause them to grow﴾ [At-Tawba 103].

His words: ﴿and give zakat﴾: this is praise for those who give zakat. The surah, as we have seen, is Meccan. So does that mean zakat was obligated in Mecca or in Medina?

The known view among the scholars is that it was obligated in Medina, but the correct view is that it was obligated in Mecca, though the determination of its amounts and the detailed explanation of the wealth subject to it was in Medina. This is the correct view, and it is the one by which the evidences are reconciled.

His words: ﴿and they are certain of the Hereafter﴾.

* Student: The estimate: the prayer was explained, and zakat was explained after it. Is this not a case of delaying the explanation of rulings?

* Shaykh: No. This is a matter of voluntary practice.

* Student: He explains zakat?

* Shaykh: He explains zakat, and left its amount to the person to give what he wishes, so that souls become accustomed, then afterwards the thing Allah the Exalted wanted is made obligatory upon them.

* Student: So the person used to choose it.

* Shaykh: Yes, he chooses what he gives. Yes, this is like other things that developed: prayer was made obligatory as two rak'as, then the travelling prayer was confirmed, and it was increased for residence. Zakat was first made obligatory at the person's choice, then it was specified. Fasting was made obligatory by way of option, then it was specified. Hajj is the one about which I know of nothing except that it was made obligatory once, but the reason for that is that it came in the ninth or tenth year, after faith had settled in the hearts, so there is no need for souls to be gradually led from stage to stage.

* Student: The saying of Ibn 'Abbas: "The first thing obligated of prayer was four [rak'as]"[[Narrated by Muslim (685/5) from the hadith of Mujahid from Ibn 'Abbas.]]?

* Shaykh: It is not correct. If this is his saying, then the hadith of 'A'isha is explicit that the first thing obligated of prayer was two rak'as.

* Student: It is a sound hadith.

* Shaykh: But this one is more authentic than it. I do not know of anyone who reports this from Ibn 'Abbas. Even if Ibn 'Abbas said it, the hadith of 'A'isha is more authentic.

* Student: Some scholars, like Ibn Hajar, reconciled the two hadiths by saying that 'A'isha mentioned the first (...), and Ibn 'Abbas mentioned what people settled upon, as if it was first obligated as four, then it was obligated as two rak'as, and was increased in ...

* Shaykh: You mean it was obligated twice?

* Student: Yes.

* Shaykh: The hadith of 'A'isha is explicit and sound: "The first thing obligated was two rak'as"[[Agreed upon; al-Bukhari (1090) and Muslim (685/3) from 'A'isha.]]. So according to this reconciliation, the meaning is that it was first obligated as four, then obligated as two, then it was divided into residence and travel?

* Student: Is it permissible to gradually introduce rulings to one who embraces Islam?

* Shaykh: It appears to me that it is permissible, and that he be commanded with the more important and then the more important, just as the Messenger ﷺ commanded Mu'adh ibn Jabal, although the rulings were established. He said: "The first thing you call them to is the testimony that there is no god but Allah and that Muhammad is the Messenger of Allah, then establishing prayer, then giving zakat"[[Narrated by Muslim (19/29) from Mu'adh ibn Jabal.]], although all of these were obligatory, and even fasting and Hajj are also obligatory.

* * *

He said: (﴿And they are certain of the Hereafter﴾: they know it by reasoning; "they" is repeated because of the separation between it and the predicate.)

His words: ﴿وَهُمْ﴾ is the subject, ﴿يُوقِنُونَ﴾ is its predicate, and ﴿بِالآخِرَةِ﴾ is connected to (yuqinun).

But the word (hum) was repeated a second time. Is this for emphasis: ﴿and they, they are certain of the Hereafter﴾, meaning they are the ones who are certain, to the exclusion of others? Or, as the author said, for separating it from the predicate, the separator being ﴿بِالآخِرَةِ﴾?

This may be either, and it may be that the intended meaning is everyone. Allah the Exalted has made clear that they are the people of certainty, since He repeated the pronoun twice, and it is also repeated twice so that the separation between the predicate and the subject is lengthened.

As for certainty, the author says: (they know it by reasoning). He said "by reasoning" because certainty is more specific than knowledge, since certainty means knowledge that admits no doubt; it is the highest degree of knowledge, and this comes only through reasoning, that is, through clear and convincing evidences. Therefore the author explained certainty as knowledge of things through reasoning.

His words: ﴿they are certain of the Hereafter﴾: does "the Hereafter" mean only that people will be resurrected? No. Everything Allah the Exalted has informed of that will occur on this day, or that His Messenger has informed of, is included in "the Hereafter."

Indeed, Shaykh al-Islam, may Allah have mercy on him, says: belief in the Last Day includes everything the Prophet ﷺ informed of that will occur after death.

Accordingly, "the Hereafter" means what comes after this world, including the punishment of the grave, the bliss of the grave, and it also includes the scales on the Day of Resurrection, the Pool of the Messenger ﷺ, and what has been mentioned.

Has anything of faith remained? Because he mentioned establishing prayer, giving zakat, and certainty of the Hereafter.

* Student: Faith in Allah.

* Another student: Faith in the messengers.

* Shaykh: No. We have mentioned that faith in Allah includes faith in the messengers, includes faith in the books, and indeed includes faith in the Last Day and faith in the angels.

* Student: Destiny.

* Shaykh: Faith in destiny is part of faith in Allah, because destiny is the destiny of Allah the Exalted. But there remain for us fasting and Hajj, which are among the pillars of Islam.

The answer to that: the surah is Meccan, and fasting and Hajj were not obligated in Mecca by consensus. Fasting was obligated in the second year, and Hajj was obligated in the ninth or tenth year, according to the preferred view. Accordingly, there is no difficulty in the verse.

* It is derived from it that when a person believes in the revealed legislations, he has complete faith even if he did not live to see the later obligations. So the companions who died before fasting was obligated had complete Islam. Indeed, a man may believe and die before he performs a single prayer, and he is thereby of complete faith, meaning his own faith is complete, though others who lived to see more are more complete than him. But with respect to him, it is not said that his faith is deficient, in the sense of a deficiency that harms it.

* * *

Commentary of Ibn 'Uthaymin (Tafsir al-Quran al-Karim) on surah 27, verse 1–6 (part 3 of 5):

(﴿Indeed, those who do not believe in the Hereafter – We have made their deeds appealing to them﴾ [An-Nur: 4], the ugly deeds, by composing desire within them until they saw them as good. ﴿So they wander blindly﴾: they are bewildered in them, because of their ugliness in Our sight.)

﴿Indeed, those who do not believe in the Hereafter﴾, meaning: they do not affirm it. Is this how we put it?
* Student: "They do not affirm," which implies...
* Shaykh: If they do not affirm it, it is known that they will neither accept nor submit to it, for whoever does not affirm cannot accept or submit. Fine. And if they affirm it but do not accept it and do not submit? The same thing.
So: ﴿do not believe in the Hereafter﴾ includes the negation of affirmation (tasdiq), the negation of acceptance (qabul), and the negation of submission (idh'an). I suppose you know the difference between acceptance and submission?
For example, I accept that this matter is an obligation and I believe it is an obligation, but I do not act on it. Which one is missing?
* Students: Submission (idh'an).
* Shaykh: Submission. As for non-acceptance, one rejects it, and this is not obligatory, and we do not acknowledge it as an obligation. As for (...), it is absolute denial.
﴿Those who do not believe in the Hereafter, We have made their deeds appealing to them﴾.
* Student: What is the difference between them?
* Shaykh: Affirmation (tasdiq) and acceptance (qabul). Affirmation: one affirms that this is true but does not accept it; he says, "Yes, this man has brought the truth, but I do not accept it." Acceptance generally concerns beliefs, while submission (idh'an) concerns outward actions, such as the actions of the limbs.
﴿We have made appealing to them﴾: this clause, ﴿zayyannā﴾, is the predicate of (inna), and it indicates that the cause of the beautifying is the lack of belief in the Hereafter, and that God the Exalted only made these deeds appealing to them because of their lack of belief. ﴿So when they deviated, God caused their hearts to deviate﴾ (...).
﴿So he sees it as good. Indeed God leads astray whom He wills and guides whom He wills, so do not let your soul go to waste in grief over them﴾ [Fatir: 8] (...). From here we know that whoever has his bad deed made appealing to him, that is evidence of deficiency in his belief in the Hereafter; for if his belief in the Hereafter were complete, he would know good from evil, so he would do good and avoid evil. But because his belief in the Hereafter is weak, this ugly act is made to appear good to him and he sees it as good.
There is no need to enumerate types of this, for the examples of those whose evil deeds have been made appealing to them are very numerous, undoubtedly. Among the evil deeds made appealing is that when a man descends upon a land, he takes four stones, placing three for a cooking pot and one that he worships.
There is no doubt that among the appealing evil deeds is that a man makes dates into a shape of an idol and worships it; when he becomes hungry, he eats it. And there is no doubt that among the evil deeds made appealing is that a man brings his daughter, who is the fruit of his heart, digs a pit for her and buries her alive. This is not done even by beasts of prey, may God protect us; yet this deed was made appealing to a people of the Jahiliyyah, to the point that they would stand at the pit to throw her in, and when he intended to throw her, she would cling to him and say, "O father, O father!" seeking refuge in him, while he is the cause of her affliction. We ask God for well-being.
As for his saying (﴿So they wander blindly﴾: they are bewildered in them): this, may God protect us, is from the lack of belief, that a person is not granted guidance; you find him bewildered because he has not believed. The clearest example of this is the bewilderment that befalls the people of kalam (scholastic theology), because they did not believe in God with true belief. They denied His attributes and denied what His Book and the Sunnah of His Messenger brought, so they became bewildered. For this reason some people said: the people with the most doubt at death are the people of kalam, may God protect us, because, may God grant us well-being, they did not believe.
So every person whose belief weakens will have these two evil consequences:
First: the evil deed is beautified in his eyes, until he practises it and is not diverted from it.
Second: his doubt, bewilderment and hesitation.
From this we now know that whenever belief in the Hereafter is strong, a person recognizes the ugly and does not hesitate about it, does he not? Because this is a practical, precise consequence: when this attribute requires that attribute, its absence requires its absence. A very clear equation.
So those who do not believe in the Hereafter are afflicted with these two matters, and those who believe in the Hereafter are free of these two matters. We ask God to make us and you among the believers.
* Student: What about those Sufis who believe in the Hereafter, Shaykh?
* Shaykh: No, they do not have true belief. If they had true belief, these things would not have been made appealing to them, because this verse is the measure: whoever has his evil deed made appealing to him, know that his belief is always deficient, because if they had genuine belief, what would take them off the path of the Messenger, peace be upon him?
* Student: In the name of God, the Most Merciful, the Most Compassionate; praise be to God, Lord of the worlds, and blessings and peace upon the most noble of the prophets and messengers (...).
* Shaykh: So whenever belief in the Hereafter weakens, the beautifying of ugliness increases in a person's eyes, and whenever his belief in the Hereafter increases, he hates vices. This is now an accepted matter.
On this basis we can deduce that a man who finds vices appealing is weak in belief in the Hereafter, for if his belief in the Hereafter were strong, ugly deeds would not seem good in his soul. This verse indicates it.
The verses show that lack of belief in the Hereafter is a cause of bewilderment, as in His saying: ﴿so they wander blindly﴾.
And on this basis, belief in the Hereafter is a cause of certainty and light, and this is also something observed; a person is not afflicted with lack of certainty except because of his deeds and deficiency of belief. And as belief strengthens, a person's knowledge increases, even regarding non-religious matters; God, blessed and exalted, gives him insight by which he discerns things.

* * *

God the Exalted says: (﴿Those are the ones for whom is the worst torment﴾ [An-Naml: 5]: its severest form in this world is killing and captivity.)

﴿Those﴾: who is the referent? Those who do not believe in the Hereafter. When He mentioned their path, may God protect us, and that their evil deeds were made appealing to them, He mentioned their recompense and their end, saying: ﴿Those are the ones for whom is the worst torment﴾. The author, may God have mercy on him, restricted it to what happens in this world of captivity and killing, but it should not be restricted to that; rather, it is said that this is part of the worst torment that befalls them. They receive the worst torment in this world and in the Hereafter, and for this reason they have no share in the Hereafter; rather He said: ﴿and in the Hereafter they are the greatest losers﴾.

﴿And they, in the Hereafter, they are the greatest losers﴾: (hum) the first is a subject (mubtada'), and the second?
* Student: Emphasis.
* Shaykh: Emphasis. It could also be a pronoun of separation (damir al-fasl), but since the word (hum) has a precedent of the same form, it is better to take it as emphasis.
We derive restriction (hasr) from the definiteness of the subject and predicate, ﴿they are the greatest losers﴾. And (al-akhsar) is an elative noun (ism tafdil), derived from loss (khusran), which is deficiency. Restricting greatest loss to them is evidence that there is loss for others, but they are the greatest losers.
The loss that applies to others is that sinful believers are punished according to the measure of their sins, and this is a loss, because the full bliss was not granted to them in the Hereafter, since they were punished for the sins they committed. This is undoubtedly a deficiency and a loss, is it not?
But the greatest losers are those who will be eternally in the Fire, and for this reason the author says: (because their destination is the everlasting Fire upon them), so they are the greatest losers.
Accordingly, people in the Hereafter divide into three categories: winners, losers, and greatest losers.
The winner is the one whom God has favoured, who leaves this world not deserving punishment in the Hereafter, whether by repentance, or by calamities that expiate sins, or by very great righteous deeds that overwhelm the evil deeds, like the people of Badr, to whom God said: "Do whatever you wish, for I have forgiven you"[[Agreed upon; al-Bukhari (3007), and Muslim (2494/161), from 'Ali ibn Abi Talib.]]. Whatever sins they committed, God forgives them because of the great good deed they performed at the Battle of Badr.
It may also be that this person who did evil in this world is pardoned by God, for God says: ﴿Indeed God does not forgive that partners be associated with Him, but He forgives what is less than that for whomever He wills﴾ [An-Nisa: 48]; so his state in the Hereafter is complete.
The second is the loser who is not the greatest loser, who committed some sins and was not granted release from them, so he was punished for them.
The greatest loser is the one who has no share in the Hereafter: ﴿he has no portion in the Hereafter﴾ [Al-Baqarah: 200], and they are the disbelievers.
﴿And they, in the Hereafter, they are the greatest losers﴾. There are benefits in the verse (...).
The main point is that the verse indicates they are the greatest losers, in what?
* Student: In this world and the Hereafter.
* Shaykh: No, in the Hereafter only: ﴿And they, in the Hereafter, they are the greatest losers﴾. Must it be that they are the greatest losers in this world?
* Students: No, it is not necessary.
* Shaykh: It is not necessary.
* Student: But it is from the implication of the verse.
* Shaykh: Yes, but the verse does not imply that they are winners in this world; it implies that in this world they are passed over in silence: they may profit, and they may lose; it is silent about them.
* Student: (...).
* Shaykh: The severity of the torment may be forgiven for a person, if we explain "the worst torment" with the author's words, "worse than killing": one may be killed and taken captive while being wealthy, and thus be a winner despite being captured and killed. Does this not establish the Hereafter?
* Student: It may be.
* Shaykh: ﴿And they, in the Hereafter, they are﴾, and what is the meaning of this as well?
* Student: We say: whoever does not believe in the Hereafter is a disbeliever.
* Shaykh: From where do we take this?
* Student: From His saying: ﴿they are the greatest losers﴾.
* Shaykh: "Whoever does not believe in the Hereafter is a disbeliever"? That does not contradict it. (They) means: those who do not believe in the Hereafter are the greatest losers, meaning if we return the verse to what precedes it.
* Student: (...) they are the greatest losers.
* Shaykh: Yes, but ﴿they, in the Hereafter﴾ is a predicate, because they are losers in the Hereafter. But why? Because the verse begins: ﴿Indeed, those who do not believe in the Hereafter﴾, then mentions...
* Student: (...).
* Shaykh: Correct.

﴿And indeed you are receiving the Qur'an from the Presence of One who is All-Wise, All-Knowing﴾ [An-Naml: 6]
* Student: We could say, for example: the disbelievers' loss is in them, the severe loss in religion.
* Shaykh: Yes, indeed the greatest loser...
* Student: It is no longer attributed to a connected pronoun...
* Shaykh: Correct. In any case, there is restriction, and there is no doubt that they are the greatest losers; others, if they lose, do not have this description.
* Student: (...).
* Shaykh: What would be in it?
* Student: (...).
* Shaykh: Because if they were eternal, they would be greater losers.
* Student: (...).
* Shaykh: Yes, perhaps this can be derived from it. It is correct. He says: the verse is taken as a refutation of the Khawarij and the Mu'tazilah. Why? Because if the people of major sins were eternal in the Fire, as these people claim, they would be among the greatest losers, since the people of major sins believe in the Hereafter, and who are the greatest losers? Those who do not believe in the Hereafter. So if we say that people of major sins who believe in the Hereafter are also greatest losers, then the restriction or the loss or the superlative would not be exclusive to these people. I think it is clear to everyone.
If we said that people of major sins who believe in the Hereafter are eternal in the Fire, they would be described by this description and would be among the greatest losers, would they not? Yet God restricted the greatest loss to those who do not believe in the Hereafter.
* Student: (...).
* Shaykh: That is, he has some profit, not that he is a winner; because he may lose. We said that people are three categories: a loser; a winner with no loss in it; and a greatest loser. So the sinner among believers is in the category of losers, but he is not the greatest loser.
* Student: It makes the believers see (...).
* Shaykh: That God makes believers see by describing the states of non-believers and their recompense.
* Student: By the states of disbelievers in the Hereafter.
* Shaykh: By the states of disbelievers in the Hereafter. Why? As a warning.
* Student: This is from His saying: ﴿guidance﴾.
* Shaykh: From His saying: ﴿guidance﴾? No, this is different from what he is saying; he means: it is evidence of the eloquence of the Qur'an, for example, that it makes clear the states of disbelievers in order to warn against them (...).
What we will examine, God willing, in the next lesson; since, praise be to God, we have understood from you the grasp of the benefits, I would like the extraction of them to come from you, and in the next lesson, God willing, we will see.
* Student: His saying: ﴿And they, in the Hereafter, they are the greatest losers﴾.
* Shaykh: No, it is not derived from His saying: ﴿And they, in the Hereafter, they are the greatest losers﴾, because punishment in the Hereafter may come along with mere loss.
* * *
Then he said: (﴿And you﴾ is an address to the Prophet ﷺ), and this address is emphasized by (inna), then emphasized by another emphasis, namely His saying: ﴿are receiving﴾, because this lam is for emphasis.
In the grammar of some of you yesterday, someone said it is the displaced lam (al-lam al-muzahlaqah). What does "displaced" mean?
* Students: Delayed.
* Shaykh: That is, postponed. This is its meaning. They say the original position is at the beginning of the sentence, but since another emphasis is already at the beginning of the sentence, it is more appropriate to postpone it, so that two emphatics do not gather in one place. Or it is called for emphasis; but if we are asked where its position is, we say: at the beginning of the sentence, but it was shifted because there is another emphatic at the beginning of the sentence.
(﴿And indeed you are receiving the Qur'an﴾: i.e., it is cast upon you with intensity, ﴿from the Presence of﴾: from the side of, ﴿One who is All-Wise, All-Knowing﴾ in that...) and so on.
﴿Are receiving﴾: the meaning of talaqqi is instruction and giving; "laqqaytuka kadha" means: I taught him it, if it is a remembrance, and I gave it to him if it is a physical object. Here it is the remembrance of the Qur'an, not an object given, but a remembrance that is taught. The Prophet, peace be upon him, was taught the Qur'an, and when he heard it from Jibril at the beginning he would hasten to recite it, so God forbade him, saying: ﴿Do not move your tongue with it to hasten it. Indeed, upon Us is its collection and its recitation﴾ [Al-Qiyamah: 16–17], a guarantee from God the Exalted that He will gather it and recite it.
﴿So when We have recited it, follow its recitation. Then upon Us is its clarification﴾ [Al-Qiyamah: 18–19]: its clarification in wording, meaning, and ruling.
﴿Indeed you are receiving the Qur'an﴾; the meaning of Qur'an has been mentioned, and that it is derived from (qara'a) meaning (recited), and from (qara'a) meaning (gathered).
The author's words: "i.e., it is cast upon you with intensity": from where did he take the word "with intensity" from the wording?
* Student: From the emphasis.
* Another student: From the doubling (tashdid).
* Shaykh: "Tulaqqa," and he did not say "tulaqqa anta," so it is as if he is being taught it, as if it suggests intensity; but it is not very clear to me. Undoubtedly the Messenger, peace be upon him, finds hardship in receiving revelation. Do you have the commentary?
* Student: His words: "with intensity, i.e., because of the arduous obligations in it."
* Shaykh: But the indication of "tulaqqa" for this is ambiguous in reality.
("From the Presence of": from the side of.) That is, "ladun" means "ʿind" (near, from). It is also said "ladā," as in ﴿The word is not changed in My presence﴾ [Qaf: 29], and ﴿and We taught him knowledge from Our presence﴾ [Al-Kahf: 65]. "Ladunna" is "ladun," and "ladi" is "ladā"; so both are said, but the Qur'an, as is known, is tawqifi (revealed as is), so one cannot substitute one word for another, even if it has the same meaning.
His saying: ﴿from the Presence of One who is All-Wise, All-Knowing﴾ means God the Exalted. "Al-Hakim" has been explained to us as derived from hukm and ihkam, which means perfection, and this is wisdom (hikmah).
The ruling that belongs to God, mighty and majestic, or with which God the Exalted is described, divides into two kinds: a legislative ruling (hukm shar'i) and a decreed ruling (hukm qadari).
The legislative ruling is abundant in the Qur'an, as in His saying in Surat al-Mumtahanah: ﴿That is the judgment of God; He judges between you﴾ [Al-Mumtahanah: 10], when He mentioned the rulings concerning disbelieving and emigrant women, He said: ﴿That is the judgment of God; He judges between you﴾.

The decreeing judgment (al-hukm al-qadari) is like the words of my brother Yusuf: ﴿So I will not leave this land until my father permits me or God decides for me﴾ [Yusuf 80]. That is, it means what is predetermined. He was not waiting for a legal ruling (hukm shar'i), but for a decreed one (hukm qadari).

Is it possible to oppose a legal ruling?
* Students: Yes.
* The Shaykh: Yes, it is possible. Some people accept it and some people do not accept it. And the decreeing judgment?
* Students: No.
* The Shaykh: It cannot be opposed. So it certainly comes to pass. When God, may He be exalted, decrees something by His decree, it will certainly come to pass.

Is the legal ruling loved by God or hated by Him?
* A student: Both, it is loved and hated.
* The Shaykh: Loved and hated. So when He rules that something be done?
* The student: Then it is loved.
* The Shaykh: Then it is loved. And if He rules that it be abandoned, then it is...?
* Students: Hated.
* The Shaykh: Then it is disliked. So, does God rule that adultery is forbidden, for example, or not?
* A student: Yes.
* The Shaykh: And He dislikes it. He rules that shirk is forbidden, and He dislikes it.

And the decreeing judgment?
* A student: The same.
* The Shaykh: The same. In it there is what is loved and what is disliked by God. We cannot object to this by saying: how can the decreeing judgment take place if He dislikes it? Then it would mean that God is compelled, that He does something while He dislikes it. That only happens to a person who is compelled, or to a doer who is compelled. Is God compelled?
* A student: No.
* The Shaykh: Then how can you say that the decreeing judgment includes what God dislikes?
* A student: It is real. A person may do something he dislikes for a wisdom behind it, just as a person, for example, dislikes cauterizing his son with fire, but he wants it because of the other benefits in it, such as the healing of the patient.
* The Shaykh: So it means that it is disliked from one aspect and loved from another aspect. In its essence, it is disliked by God, may He be glorified and exalted, like acts of disobedience. God decrees them, although He dislikes them. But it is loved by Him from another aspect, and this aspect is stronger than the other, so the matter takes place.

So, O brothers, (ḥakīm, the All-Wise) is derived from ḥukm (judgment) and iḥkām (perfecting). The judgment that God, may He be exalted, is described with is divided into two types: the cosmic (kawnī) and the legislative (shar'ī), and each of them has a ruling.

First: the legislative judgment does not necessarily entail that what is judged will occur, because it may occur and it may not occur.
The cosmic judgment necessarily entails that what is judged will occur in every case.

As for their division with respect to dislike and hatred by God, we say: both are loved and disliked by God, may He be glorified and exalted.
* A student: Shaykh, shouldn't we say: the legislative is loved by God, but it is a judgment in a disliked manner? Adultery, from the aspect of the ruling, God's ruling on it, is loved by God that it be forbidden?
* The Shaykh: It is disliked by Him.
* The student: His ruling that it be forbidden is loved by God.
* The Shaykh: No, I mean now the legislative judgment, the prohibition of adultery.
* The student: The prohibition of adultery is loved by God.
* The Shaykh: This ruling, the prohibition of adultery, is loved by Him. But the thing judged, this is disliked by God.
* A student: How can the legislative judgment be loved?
* The Shaykh: Some legislative judgments are loved and some are disliked, meaning the thing judged. For example: God, may He be glorified and exalted, rules that adultery be forbidden because adultery is disliked by Him. He rules that prayer be obligatory because prayer is loved by Him.
As for the act of ruling itself, it is well known that He does not rule on something except that He wants it to be so.
* A student: He loves the abandonment of adultery.
* The Shaykh: He loves the abandonment of adultery and He loves the performance of prayer.

As for perfecting (iḥkām), it means excellence (itqān), and this is wisdom (ḥikmah), placing things in their proper positions and setting them in their proper places. There is no doubt that this is excellence, and God, may He be blessed and exalted, is described with perfect wisdom: ﴿profound wisdom﴾ [al-Qamar 5]. So wisdom is placing things in their right places.

We have mentioned in the lessons on Tawhid, and we repeat it now as a reminder, that wisdom exists in the form of a thing and in its purpose. It exists in the form of the thing and how it occurs in this way, and it also exists in the purpose of the thing.

Wisdom also exists in legislative matters and in decreed matters, because the two earlier judgments, the cosmic and the legislative, both include wisdom. So wisdom exists in the cosmic judgments and in the legislative judgments. It is wisdom in form, meaning that this particular form is wise, and it is wisdom in purpose, meaning the praiseworthy outcomes that result from it or from it.

For example, when you reflect on the Shari'ah, you find that its formulation as it is is of the utmost wisdom, because it all seeks benefits and wards off harms. This is the general principle of the Shari'ah.

So it is, in this aspect or in this form, in accord with wisdom. Then, the purpose of wisdom is the fruit of this Shari'ah and of holding fast to it: happiness in this world and in the Hereafter. This is undoubtedly a praiseworthy goal, and the legislation of matters for the sake of this goal is wisdom. Is it clear?

Likewise, we come to decreed matters. We say: the placement of decreed matters in this form is also wisdom, and then their purpose is also wisdom. But this wisdom, in the form of a thing and in the purpose of a thing, whether legislated or decreed, may be known to the servants and may be unknown. But what is our duty regarding what we do not know of the judgment on these matters? Our duty is faith and submission. We believe that there is nothing God legislates and nothing God does except that it has wisdom. We must believe this, because this is what His description as the All-Wise requires.

But we may understand this matter and we may not understand it: ﴿He gives wisdom to whom He wills﴾ [al-Baqarah 269]. It is not all people, ﴿and whoever is given wisdom has indeed been given much good﴾ [al-Baqarah 269].

But we must hold this faith. When we hold this faith, we will submit and be content with the Shari'ah, what else? And with the decree, because we know that this is for a wisdom.

When we now reflect on the state of Muslims, the weakness of their religion, and their turning away from religion, there is no doubt that this concerns us and saddens us. But when we look at it from another angle, we find that it is decreed by God, and that there must be a wisdom in it, though we may not know it.

You must make this a guiding principle in all your conditions, both private and public: that you are certain this is for a wisdom. But our certainty about the wisdom does not stop us from taking the legitimate means we have been commanded to take.

For example, the example we mentioned, the matter of the weakness of Muslims and their turning away, this requires us to be more active in calling to Islam, explaining its virtues, warning against opposing it, and the bad end for sinners and wicked people. Isn't that so? This requires us to be more active.

It is part of wisdom that the people of goodness are active in calling to God, may He be glorified and exalted, and in explaining the truth, and in explaining the praiseworthy outcome for whoever holds fast to the religion of God, so that their reward increases, and so that people enter the religion of God by conviction. I think you imagine, as I imagine, that if people were found in a certain state, would they find themselves in this particular state, or would they perceive this particular state as it really is? No, because it is a customary matter for them, and they may not understand what results from it of good or evil. But when they go deep into evil and reach its end, and then the truth is made clear to them and they return to it, this is better for them than the first state, in which they found their fathers following something and walked in their footsteps. Because now they come, in what manner?
* Students: By conviction.
* The Shaykh: They come by conviction, and out of love for this new matter that has been made clear to them.

For this reason, now, praise be to God, there is a good sign in all the Islamic lands, a sign of return to Islam by conviction, without any doubt. This is part of the wisdom by which God, may He be glorified and exalted, decrees such disliked matters in religion, so that they may be the means to what is more praiseworthy.

﴿From One who is All-Wise, All-Knowing﴾. Al-'Alim (the All-Knowing) means the one described with knowledge. Knowledge, as the scholars of usul (legal theory) defined it, is perceiving a thing as it is, with a firm and correspondent perception. There is no doubt that God, may He be glorified and exalted, has this attribute in its most complete and highest form. He, may He be glorified and exalted, is All-Knowing with absolute knowledge. It is not preceded by ignorance, nor followed by forgetfulness, nor limited by any limit. The knowledge of the created being is preceded by ignorance, followed by forgetfulness, and limited as well: ﴿and you have been given of knowledge only a little﴾ [al-Isra' 85]. This is unlike the knowledge of God.

Here, al-Hakim (the All-Wise) is placed before al-'Alim (the All-Knowing). Most often in the Qur'an, al-'Alim is placed before al-Hakim, isn't that so?
* Students: Yes.
* The Shaykh: What is the wisdom in placing al-Hakim before al-'Alim here?
* A student: Perhaps because the description with wisdom is closer to the style of the Qur'an than the description with knowledge.
* The Shaykh: How is that? (...)
* A student: Then God, may He be glorified and exalted, mentioned the people of faith and their reward, and mentioned those who do not believe in the Hereafter and their reward and their punishment for their evil deeds. The description with wisdom fits this better than knowledge.
* The Shaykh: Yes, but this last sentence is independent from the first, because the waw seems to be for a new sentence (istiʾnāf).

Let us now say: receiving the Qur'an. The Qur'an includes the Shari'ah, does it not? And the Shari'ah includes commands and prohibitions. If we do not believe that these commands and prohibitions are based on wisdom, our submission to them will weaken. For this reason, wisdom was placed first.

As for knowledge, it is understood from His words: ﴿and indeed you receive the Qur'an﴾, because by the very act of receiving the Qur'an, knowledge is attained. But is what is found in the Qur'an in accordance with wisdom? Yes, it is in accordance with wisdom in reality. For this reason wisdom was placed first, so that a person feels before anything else that what the Messenger ﷺ received of the Qur'an is wisdom. A parallel to this is in Surat al-Dhariyat, where He says: ﴿She struck her face and said, "An old barren woman!" They said, "So your Lord has said. Indeed, He is the All-Wise, the All-Knowing"﴾ [al-Dhariyat 29-30]. Why did He not say "the All-Knowing, the All-Wise"? Because the birth of an old woman is a matter outside of custom and what is familiar. How can an old woman give birth, and why? So wisdom was placed first, so that a person feels before anything else that this rare matter, which is outside custom, comes from wisdom, not from folly, nor from something occurring by chance.

So this is similar. We say: the name al-Hakim, which indicates God's description with wisdom, was placed first in this context, because what the Messenger ﷺ received of the Qur'an includes legislation, does it not? And what needs an explanation of wisdom so that a person may be convinced by it. So wisdom was placed before knowledge.

As for knowledge, it is understood from the word (tulaqqā, is received), since when the Qur'an is received, knowledge has been attained. Therefore it came in the second position.

Second question: what is the wisdom in combining wisdom and knowledge, "All-Wise, All-Knowing"? You always find in the Qur'an that al-Hakim is frequently paired with al-'Alim, and it is also paired with al-'Aziz: "Al-'Aziz, al-Hakim." So what is the wisdom in that?
* A student: Because ḥukm also comes from iḥkām and from ḥukm. Judgment needs knowledge, and wisdom also needs knowledge, so a judgment without knowledge is considered deficient.
* The Shaykh: Is that so? Do you agree with it?
* A student: The Hakim is more specific than the 'Alim, because a person may know a thing without knowing its wisdom, for example.
* The Shaykh: So it may have two answers, and a third answer will become clear afterward.
* A student: It indicates that this knowledge is based on wisdom.
* The Shaykh: Or wisdom is based on knowledge. Which of them is based on the other? Which one comes first in your mind now?
* The student: The Hakim comes first.
* The Shaykh: No, leave aside the order here. What comes first according to a person's mind?
* The student: Hakim.
* The Shaykh: Strange. It seems that knowledge comes before wisdom. How do you know that this is appropriate or not appropriate?
* The student: If you know.
* The Shaykh: If you know that it is appropriate and you place it in its right place.
* A student: That the judge (al-hakam) necessarily implies knowledge.
* The Shaykh: In any case, all these are acceptable answers. But the clear answer is that wisdom may be hidden from some people. Does its being hidden from us here mean that it is not known to God? No.

So He combined them to make clear that this wisdom is known to God even if it is hidden from us. He, may He be exalted, is All-Wise, All-Knowing, who places things in their right places, even if that is hidden from us. We do not say, for example, that if God legislates something or decrees something, this is not from knowledge. Rather it is from knowledge, even if we did not know its wisdom and its purpose.

This is the reason for the combination of knowledge and wisdom in many verses of the Noble Qur'an.

The conclusion is that we say: since wisdom may be hidden from the servants, God, may He be exalted, paired it with knowledge, so that a person may be assured that this wisdom is known to God, may He be mighty and majestic, even if it is hidden from us.

* * *

He says: ﴿When Musa said﴾ [al-Naml 7].

The mufassir said: "Mention when he said" (udhkur idh qāla). This is his method, and it is also known among the grammarians that idh is an adverb (ẓarf), and an adverb must have a governing element, which is the thing it is connected to. So in this kind of construction they always estimate "udhkur" (mention): "Mention when Musa said to his family﴾." Musa is well known as the son of Imran, the brother of Maryam.
* Students: No.
* The Shaykh: How? ﴿and Maryam daughter of Imran﴾ [al-Tahrim 12]?
* A student: There is a difference. Maryam, meaning she came first...
* Another student: Musa is older.
* The Shaykh: What is the clear answer to this, if someone says that Musa was the brother of Maryam?
* A student: A similarity in name.
* The Shaykh: Because this Musa is the son of Imran, and she is Maryam the daughter of Imran, and Musa is the brother of Harun, and ﴿O sister of Harun﴾ [Maryam 28].
* A student: They name people after their prophets.
* The Shaykh: Yes, they name people after their prophets. And history, as you know and have just said, the history between Musa and Maryam is very long. Musa, peace be upon him, is the best of the prophets of the Children of Israel, and he stands among the Ulu al-'Azm (the resolute messengers) in rank...
* Students: The second.
* The Shaykh: The third. Because the best of the resolute messengers, peace be upon them, is the Prophet ﷺ, then Ibrahim, then Musa. Between Nuh and Isa, one cannot find a ranking, because each of them has a merit the other does not have. For this reason we do not prefer one of them over the other. As for the first three, the preference among them is clear.
* A student: Is there a prohibition on preferring among them?
* The Shaykh: No, but explaining their excellence is fine. However, comparing them in a way that boasts is not permitted. For this reason there is the story of the Jew and the Muslim.
* A student: Does their order in the Qur'an not indicate preference?
* The Shaykh: Except the placement first.
* A student: ﴿And when We took from the prophets their covenant, and from you, and from Nuh and Ibrahim and Musa and Isa son of Maryam﴾ [al-Ahzab 7].
* The Shaykh: And in the second verse: ﴿He has prescribed for you of religion what He enjoined upon Nuh, and what We revealed to you, and what We enjoined upon Ibrahim and Musa and Isa﴾ [al-Shura 13].
It seems, and God knows best, that Nuh was placed first here because he was first in the messages as a message, not because he is the best. And undoubtedly he was the first messenger.
* A student: Who is Harun?
* The Shaykh: Harun was her brother, but no prophethood is mentioned for him in the Qur'an.
* A student: Was he named after Harun because Harun was a prophet?
* The Shaykh: Yes, as came in the hadith from the Prophet, peace be upon him (...).
* A student: Maryam had a brother named Harun.
* The Shaykh: Yes.
* The student: But she was not his mother, O Shaykh. She vowed what was in her womb to God, may He be glorified and exalted?
* The Shaykh: It is possible that he was her brother from her father (...).

* * *

I seek refuge with God from the accursed Satan. Yesterday we said that, given your advancement, praise be to God, in deriving benefits, we will leave that to you.

First, His words, may He be exalted: ﴿Those are the ones for whom is the worst punishment, and in the Hereafter they are the greatest losers﴾. What is derived from this verse?

First: from His words ﴿These are the verses of the Qur'an and a clear Book﴾ [al-Naml 1]. Come on, give us a benefit?

Commentary of Ibn 'Uthaymin (Tafsir al-Quran al-Karim) on surah 27, verse 1–6 (part 5 of 5):

* Student: That these verses are from the Noble Qur'an: ﴿These are the verses of the Qur'an﴾, that the Qur'an is a sign (āyah) and evidence of the truthfulness of the Messenger ﷺ.
* Shaykh: Good. That is one: the Qur'an is a sign, because of what it contains of true reports and just rulings, and so on. What is the second benefit?
* Student: That the Qur'an is written, earlier and later.
* Shaykh: Because of what statement?
* Student: ﴿And a Book that makes things clear﴾.
* Shaykh: The third?
* Student: That...
* Shaykh: That the Qur'an is written, earlier and later.
* Student: The mention of some verses encompasses the mention of guidance; he pointed to some verses.
* Shaykh: No. ﴿These are the verses of the Qur'an and a Book that makes things clear﴾, only this, and this verse does not (...) encompass.
* Student: ﴿And a Book that makes things clear﴾: "clear" means the Qur'an is clear in itself and makes other things clear.
* Shaykh: In general, or in some matters?
* Student: In some of them.
* Shaykh: Eh?
* Student: "Clear" (mubīn), the word "mubīn" in this verse, indicates that it...
* Shaykh: What do you say?
* Student: In this verse?
* Shaykh: Yes. Is it clear in all things or in some things, in general?
* Student: It did not say "clear in some of them"...
* Shaykh: Is there an explicit verse on this subject?
* Student: A verse that is explicit about that?
* Shaykh: Yes, that the Qur'an is clear concerning every thing.
* Student: ﴿And We have sent down to you the Book as an explanation of all things﴾ [al-Nahl 89].
* Shaykh: ﴿And We have sent down to you the Book as an explanation of all things﴾.
* Also derived from the verse (it may be far-fetched, but I will explain it): the Qur'an does not cease to be the Qur'an even if it is written down, because of His saying ﴿a Book that makes things clear﴾. It is the speech of Allah, whether it is recited or written, and this is understood from His saying ﴿the verses of the Qur'an﴾, and it is not a sign unless it is the speech of Allah.
﴿A guidance and good tidings for the believers﴾ [al-Naml 2]. What is derived from it?
* Student: That the Qur'an is guidance, guiding, meaning it guides to (...), but in itself it is a guide, like "hudā", that the Qur'an guides people ﴿and good tidings for the believers﴾, and likewise that in this Book there is what gives good news, informing the believers of good (...).
* Shaykh: Perhaps this is in your mind but you did not express it well. Does anyone have an answer other than this? Good. It may be said: "guidance for mankind" – the guidance meant here is the guidance of direction; all people can be guided by it if they wish, meaning that there is no deficiency in its indication. But guidance of success (tawfīq), for whom?
* Students: For the believers.
* Shaykh: For the believers, specific to the believers. Complete the verse: ﴿guidance and good tidings for the believers﴾.
* Student: (...).
* Shaykh: That it is good tidings for the believers of what thing, of Paradise only?
* Student: (...).
* Shaykh: Emphasized with "inna" and the lām.
* Also in it: the defense of Allah, blessed and exalted, of the people of His guardianship (walāya), because there is no doubt that this defense is from Allah on behalf of the Messenger, peace and blessings be upon him.
* Also in it: that the wisdom of Allah, blessed and exalted, is founded on knowledge. That is, it does not come by chance. Among us a person may do something and it is appropriate in its place, yet it may have come by chance, as people say (...). But the wisdom of Allah, blessed and exalted, proceeds from what?  From knowledge.
* Also in it: convincing people of what Allah, blessed and exalted, decrees, whether a decree of predestination (qadar) or a legislative decree (sharʿī). The reasoning: when we know that it proceeds from wisdom, we submit and are content, and we do not say "why" or "how" as long as we know this. If we know the wisdom, then it is from Allah, glorified and exalted, and this without doubt increases the servant's tranquility. And if we do not know, we are certain that it is wisdom.
* Student: The demonstration of the excellence of the Messenger, peace and blessings be upon him.
* Shaykh: From where do we take this? Do you mean the sublimity of the Sharia?
* Student: No, the excellence of the Messenger, peace and blessings be upon him.
* Shaykh: The excellence of the Messenger.
* Student: Yes, in that he was singled out with the Qur'an...
* Shaykh: Yes, in that he was singled out with the message, you mean.
* Student: Yes, the knowledge and the wisdom.
* Shaykh: Yes, we have mentioned this: the knowledge and the wisdom.
* Student: Does it not also include what indicates that the Qur'an contains knowledge, just as it contains wisdom?
* Shaykh: Indeed the Qur'an is knowledge in reality, yes, there is no doubt of it. Yes, it indicates that the Qur'an is knowledge (...).
﴿ ﴾

Commentary of Ibn 'Uthaymin (Tafsir al-Quran al-Karim) on surah 27, verse 1–6 (part 1 of 5):

In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful. ﴿Ta Sin. These are the verses of the Quran﴾ to the end of the verse [An-Naml: 1].

He says: this is Surah An-Naml (The Ant), and it was named so because the ant is mentioned in it. The naming of surahs occurs on the basis of even the slightest connection; for this reason, Surah Al-Baqarah (The Cow) was named so because the cow is mentioned in it. It is not impossible for a surah to have several names for several connections.

As for his saying that it is Meccan: the correct view regarding the Meccan and the Medinan is that the distinction between them is that what was revealed before the Hijrah is Meccan, and what was revealed after it is Medinan.

It has also been said: the Meccan is what was revealed in Makkah, and the Medinan is what was revealed in Madinah. And it has been said: the Meccan is that which contains mention of the foundations (the foundations of Islam or of faith), and the Medinan is that which contains mention of the branches (details).

According to the first view, the criterion is time; according to the second, the criterion is place; and according to the third, the criterion is subject matter.

However, what the verifiers (muhaqqiqun) hold is that what was after the Hijrah is Medinan, and what was before it is Meccan. They have mentioned for this, in the principles of tafsir (usul al-tafsir), rules to which one refers.

As for the basmalah, the discussion of it has already been presented several times, and we have explained that the best way to estimate it is that it be a verb that is delayed and suitable (to the context).

It should be a verb, because it is the original in governing (the governing word, al-'amil); and delayed, for two benefits: the first is seeking blessing by placing the name of Allah first, and the second is to convey restriction (hasr), meaning: by the name of Allah and not by the name of anyone else.

And suitable (munasib), because it is more specific than the general.

As for "verb," we said: because it is the original in governing, and it is also more indicative of occurrence (hudus).

In the basmalah, "In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful," the estimate is: "In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful, I recite." It is also permissible to estimate: "I recite in the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful," or: "My recitation is in the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful," or "In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful is my recitation."

But what we mentioned first is the more preponderant, and Shaykh al-Islam Ibn Taymiyyah pointed to its preponderance in the saying of the Messenger (ﷺ): "Whoever has not slaughtered, let him slaughter in the name of Allah" [Agreed upon; al-Bukhari (985), and Muslim (1960/1) from Jundub ibn Sufyan], where he mentioned it as a verb, and did not say "let his slaughter be," but said: "let him slaughter in the name of Allah."

When he said: Allah the Exalted said: (﴿Ta Sin﴾ Allah knows best what He means by that).

This is what the author and a group of scholars adopted: that these disjointed letters found at the beginnings of some surahs, our stance regarding them is to say: Allah knows best what He means by that.

It has been previously stated in the night tafsir lesson that the preponderant view on this is that these letters are alphabetic, and that, by the necessity of the Quran being in clear Arabic, they have no meaning. We mentioned that this has been narrated from Mujahid, that they are alphabetic letters with which Allah began, having no meaning. On this basis we affirm that they have no meaning, because they have no meaning; but they have a purpose, which is that this Quran, which rendered these eloquent and articulate people incapable, is composed of these same alphabetic letters from which their speech is made. That is, He did not come with new letters. For example, they say: "By Allah, these are letters we do not know!" He came with the very same letters they speak with.

This is supported by the fact that there is no set of disjointed letters except that mention of the Quran follows it, with the exception of two surahs or similar. Yet these two surahs, such as: ﴿Alif Lam Mim. Did the people think that they would be left﴾ [Al-'Ankabut: 1, 2], ﴿Alif Lam Mim.
