The second says: "inna" is a particle of emphasis (...) and puts the predicate in the nominative, and the "hā'" is its noun and not a pronoun of the matter, and "anā" is its predicate. They take "anā" to be the predicate. The first takes "anā Allāhu" to be the predicate, meaning that Allah said to Musa: "Innahu anā," meaning: the one speaking to you is I.

Does the statement "innahu anā" make clear who it is? It does not make it clear. For this reason, a person is forbidden, when he asks permission at the door and is asked, "Who is it?" to say, "I." So "anā" here is ambiguous, and it was clarified by His saying: "Allāhu al-'Azīzu al-Ḥakīm."

* Student: This meaning is sound.

* The Shaykh: It is sound, but the first is more upright. "Innahu" meaning the matter, "anā Allāhu al-'Azīzu al-Ḥakīm." So what the author estimated is better than what some exegetes estimated, such as al-Zamakhsharī.

* Student: I said: "Allāhu al-'Azīzu al-Ḥakīm" (...).

* The Shaykh: They become an explanation of the pronoun. "Allāhu" is the subject, "al-'Azīzu" is the predicate, and "al-Ḥakīm" is a second predicate, and they are an explanation of "anā."

"Innahu anā Allāhu al-'Azīzu al-Ḥakīm." He said: "Allāh," beginning with the divinity. And Allāh, blessed and exalted is He, is the proper name upon Allah that no other may be named by. You will always find that all the names of Allah that come afterward follow this name. Always begin the names of Allah with the word "Allāh," because it is the proper name that no other is named by; then the names come afterward following it.

And "al-'Azīz," what does it mean?

* Student: The Mighty who is not overcome.

* The Shaykh: The Mighty who is not overcome, rather He is the Overcomer. It is said that might (al-'izzah) is divided into three categories. What are they?

* Student: Might of rank, might of subjugation, and might of station..

* The Shaykh: No.

* Student: Might of subjugation and exaltedness (...).

* The Shaykh: No, might of inaccessibility (al-imtina'). They said it is derived from "al-arḍ al-'azāz," the "al-arḍ al-'azāz" meaning the hard, strong earth. We in colloquial speech call it "'azā," dropping the second zāy. So "al-'Azīz" means: He is the strong, the Overcomer, who is not overcome. If we say these three, we have brought the three meanings.

* Student: Might of subjugation..

* The Shaykh: And of rank and of inaccessibility.

As for His saying "al-Ḥakīm," we have already discussed it. Allah mentioned that to make him feel that his outcome is toward honor, and that what will be revealed to him is wisdom, because what proceeds from the Mighty is mighty, and from the All-Wise is wisdom.

* * *

"Wa-alqi 'aṣāka" [al-Naml 10]: "His staff." What is the staff that he has with him?

A staff upon which he leans and with which he herds his sheep, an ordinary staff. Its attribution to Musa, upon him be peace, is the attribution of what is owned to its owner, and it is not specifically attributed to one who has a special connection with it; that is, this staff has no special distinction, nor is it a staff of a particular substance or the like. It is an ordinary staff.

("Wa-alqi 'aṣāka," so he threw it, "falamma ra'āhā tahtazz") this too is brevity by omission, as has passed, and stories always contain brevity by omission, because what is omitted is always known from the context, so its omission is easy and facilitated.

Ibn Malik, may Allah have mercy on him, stated in the Alfiyya a rule of the most beneficial kind; he mentioned it in the chapter on the subject, and it is applicable to everything. He said:

"Wa-ḥadhfu mā yu'lamu jā'izun kamā ... taqūlu: Zaydun ba'da: man 'indakumā"

("And omitting what is known is permissible") this is a rule.

He said: ("so he threw it, 'falamma ra'āhā tahtazz,' it moves").

But explaining "ihtizāz" merely as general movement is open to question, because "ihtizāz" is more emphatic than "taḥarruk," as if "ihtizāz" contains a kind of strength and agitation.

("Ka-annahā jann," a light snake) and it is said: a great snake; and it is said: the male of snakes is the jann. Whichever it is, this staff that was in his hand became a staff he threw, and it became a snake that moves, quakes and convulses like a jann, meaning a great snake.

* Student: Light.

* The Shaykh: No, you have "light."

* Student: (...) the jann.

* The Shaykh: It applies to both, it is one of the shared names.

* Student: (...).

* The Shaykh: His saying, exalted is He, in Surat Ta-Ha: "Fa-alqāhā fa-idhā hiya ḥayyatun tas'ā" [Ta-Ha 20].

* Student: (...).

* The Shaykh: No, the story is the same thing, one story.

* Student: O Shaykh, "falamma ra'āhā tahtazz" [al-Naml 10], the sayings on brevity?

* The Shaykh: No, there is no brevity there. The brevity is in His saying "fa-alqāhā," the estimate "fa-alqāhā" is brevity.

* Student: "Wa-alqi 'aṣāka."

* The Shaykh: Except "Wa-alqi 'aṣāka," so he threw it.

* Student: Okay, the explanation of "fa-alqāhā"?

* The Shaykh: No, this is an omitted clause.

* Student: (...) the verse.

* The Shaykh: Yes, "Alqi 'aṣāka," its explanation: place your staff.

* Student: So "Alqi 'aṣāka" the verse..

* The Shaykh: Is not the explanation of this. So "Alqi 'aṣāka falamma ra'āhā tahtazz": if we took the verse by its apparent meaning, it would be that it moved while it was in his hand before he threw it. But the verse necessarily requires something omitted: so he threw it, and behold it moved.

* Student: So the brevity is not at His saying "falamma ra'āhā tahtazz."

* The Shaykh: Before it, its prior part, as the author estimated.

* Student: The brevity is that there is omitted speech, so there is brevity in it.

* The Shaykh: This "fa-alqāhā" is omitted.

* Student: It is the one that is omitted.

* The Shaykh: Yes, it is the omitted one, and it must be estimated, because when he, upon him be peace, was told, "Alqi 'aṣāka falamma ra'āhā tahtazz," if we took the Qur'an's apparent meaning, it would be that when he was commanded to throw his staff, it moved. So something must be estimated.

"Ka-annahā jann, wallā mudbiran" ("wallā" is the answer to "lammā," and "mudbiran" is a circumstantial state).

"Wallā mudbiran" means fleeing. For this reason Allah, glorified and exalted, says: "Wallā mudbiran wa-lam yu'aqqib" (did not return). Why did he flee?

* Students: Out of fear.

* The Shaykh: Out of fear of this, because it is in human nature that a person who throws his staff and it becomes a snake that moves must be afraid, especially since he, upon him be peace, did not know that he would be sent, and that he was a messenger; rather Allah had spoken to him, and until now nothing had happened.

So the conclusion is that this is human nature; he must flee. There is no deficiency in this for the Prophet ﷺ, because human matters befall the messengers and others. For this reason the Messenger, upon him be peace, would forget even in the greatest acts of worship, in prayer, and he said: "Verily I am a human being like you; I forget as you forget." [Agreed upon; al-Bukhari (401), and Muslim (572/89), from the hadith of Ibn Mas'ud.] And there is nothing in this that disparages the messengers.

("Wallā mudbiran wa-lam yu'aqqib," then Allah the Exalted said to him: "O Musa, do not fear" from it).

Then Allah the Exalted said: "O Musa." There is also brevity by omission here. To summarize: all stories, especially long stories, generally contain brevity by omission, and sometimes it is a sentence, and sometimes sentences. What is coming to us, Allah willing, in the stories in the surah that follows this one contains much of this.

* Student: (...) the author's saying (...).

* The Shaykh: This is the meaning of "jann."

He said: "Lā takhaf" and called him by his name to reassure him, because a person who calls you while knowing you, you feel more at ease with him. He did not say: "O you, do not fear," or "O master, do not fear," but said: "O Musa," because it is known that the one who knows you, you feel more at ease with. Is that not so?

Now, if, for example, you saw an enemy whom you thought was an enemy and then fled from him, and he said: "O so-and-so, O so-and-so," would you be reassured or not? You would be more reassured, because you would say: "This one I know, he will not harm me."

("O Musa, do not fear" from it.) The restriction with "from it" which the author felt compelled to include is the apparent context, because it is apparent that Musa, upon him be peace, only fled from it, so He said: "Lā takhaf."

("Innī lā yakhāfu ladayya" with me "al-mursalūn" from a snake and other things.) It is known that one who is in the presence of Allah, mighty and majestic is He, cannot fear anything, because he is under Allah's protection and in His neighborhood, so he cannot fear while he is with Allah.

His saying: "Innī lā yakhāfu ladayya al-mursalūn" also contains good tidings to Musa, upon him be peace, that he is with Allah and that he is among the messengers. It is known that when one is given glad tidings of such a thing, fear will wholly depart from him, and in place of fear will come security, and in place of terror will come joy: "Lā takhaf, innī lā yakhāfu ladayya al-mursalūn."

* Student: Is this the staff with which he struck the sea?

* The Shaykh: Yes.

* Student: It did not change?

* The Shaykh: It did not change, and it is also the one he threw before the magicians, and it swallowed their magic.

* * *

("Lā yakhāfu ladayya al-mursalūn" from a snake and other things, "illā" but "man ẓalama" [whoever] wronged his own soul, "thumma baddala ḥusnan" then did good, "ba'da sū'in" after evil, i.e., he repented, "fa-innī ghafūrun raḥīm" I accept repentance and forgive him.)

Glory be to Allah the Mighty! One may say: what is the connection of this sentence to the statement: "Illā man ẓalama thumma baddala ḥusnan ba'da sū'," but when Allah said to Musa, upon him be peace: "Innī lā yakhāfu ladayya al-mursalūn," perhaps he remembered that a sin had occurred from him. What was the sin?

* Student: That he killed..

* The Shaykh: That he killed a soul. And it seems that when he remembers this, he may think it unlikely that he is among the messengers, so Allah the Exalted said: "Illā man ẓalama," to remind him of the repentance with which Allah had favored him.

"Illā man ẓalama thumma baddala ḥusnan ba'da sū'." The author explained "baddala" by his saying "ata" (came with); because its apparent meaning in reality does not yield the sense: he exchanged good for evil, which is taken? (...) exchanged good for evil; because "badala" indicates there is a substitute and a substituted-for. If you say: "baddala ḥusnan," what did he exchange it for? For evil. Then the good is pushed away and the evil is taken, or not? ("I exchanged my garment for his garment") where is what is taken?

* Student: The last.

* The Shaykh: The last, is that so or not? So here "baddala ḥusnan," if we took its apparent meaning, would mean that he left good and took evil. For this reason the author explained His saying "baddala" with "ata."

The evidence for this: if the intended meaning of the exchange were its apparent meaning, it would not be correct to express it with His saying "ba'da sū'." If that were so, He would say: "baddala ḥusnan bi-sū'," not "ba'da." Since He said "ba'da sū'," it is known that "baddala" here means "istabdala," and "istabdala" means "akhadha" (took), like His saying: "Atastabdilūna alladhī huwa adnā bi-alladhī huwa khayr" [al-Baqarah 61], and "akhadha" like "ata" (came). The meaning of the noble verse is that whoever comes with good after evil (...) certainly.

* Student: (...)?

* The Shaykh: Yes, it is a conditional noun of condition, and not a relative pronoun in an exception, because the exception here is disconnected.

"Man ẓalama" ("ẓalama") is the verb of the condition, and the sentence "fa-innī ghafūrun raḥīm" is the answer.

* Student: The answer of the condition.

* The Shaykh: The answer of the condition. I say: if someone said: what is the connection of the answer to the condition?

* Student: We say (...) with the good (...) but by reason (...) or he said: mercy, or he deserves forgiveness and mercy.

* The Shaykh: Yes. The answer to this: when Allah the Exalted mentioned these two names, "fa-innī ghafūrun raḥīm," He wills their requirement. The requirement of forgiveness is that He forgives the one who wronged and then exchanged good for evil, and the requirement of mercy is also that He shows him mercy.

A parallel to this is His saying, exalted is He, regarding those who wage war: "Illā alladhīna tābū min qabli an taqdirū 'alayhim fa-'lamū anna Allāha ghafūrun raḥīm" [al-Ma'idah 34], meaning the penalty is dropped from them, because this is the requirement of forgiveness and mercy. So here, the requirement of forgiveness and mercy is that whoever exchanges good for evil, Allah, blessed and exalted, forgives him and shows him mercy. Does this include messengers and non-messengers?

* The students: Yes.

* The Shaykh: Yes, it includes messengers and non-messengers. Yes, it includes messengers and others. And therefore it is good that the author says, and we say with him as well: that "illā" here is the exception?

* Students: Disconnected.

* The Shaykh: Disconnected, because it includes messengers and non-messengers.

* * *

* Student: "Wa-adkhil yadaka fī jaybika takhruj bayḍā'a min ghayri sū'in fī tis'i āyātin ilā Fir'awna wa-qawmihi innahum kānū qawman fāsiqīn (12). Falammā jā'athum āyātunā mubṣiratan qālū hādhā siḥrun mubīn (13). Wa-jaḥadū bihā wa-istayqanathā anfusuhum ẓulman wa-'uluwwan fa-nẓur kayfa kāna 'āqibatu al-mufsidīn (14). Wa-laqad ātaynā Dāwūda wa-Sulaymāna 'ilman wa-qālā al-ḥamdu lillāhi alladhī faḍḍalanā 'alā kathīrin min 'ibādihi al-mu'minīn (15). Wa-waritha Sulaymānu Dāwūda wa-qāla yā ayyuhā al-nāsu 'ullimnā manṭiqa al-ṭayri wa-ūtīnā min kulli shay'in inna hādhā lahuwa al-faḍlu al-mubīn" [al-Naml 12–16].

* The Shaykh: I seek refuge in Allah from the accursed Satan. Allah, blessed and exalted, said: "Idh qāla Mūsā li-ahlihi innī ānastu nāran sa-ātīkum minhā bi-khabarin aw ātīkum bi-shihābin qabasin la'allakum taṣṭalūn" [al-Naml 7].

* First: What is derived from this verse is the good character of Musa, upon him be peace, shown by his gentleness with his family and his consulting them about what concerns everyone, meaning that he did not go off without saying this to them; which indicates that he consults with them about what concerns them.

* And in this is evidence that the wife is among the family, and this is the correct view. Accordingly, the family of the Prophet ﷺ includes his wives, because they are among the family.

**Commentary of Ibn 'Uthaymin (Tafsir al-Quran al-Karim) on Surah 27, verses 7–13 (part 3 of 7):**

Scholars have differed over whether wives are included when a person bequeaths or endows something "to his family" (ahl). Those who say they are not included refer the matter to custom ('urf), and they say: according to common custom, wives are not counted as "family"; rather, "family" means blood relatives.

If that is the case, it is said: wives are part of one's family. So if a person endows something for "the family of so-and-so" or bequeaths to them, wives are included according to linguistic usage. Then, if there is a consistent custom in this matter, we refer to that custom, because the sound view among the opinions is that the meanings of such terms are referred to the customs and practices of people. If no custom is found, we refer to the Sharia or to language, as the case requires. In this there is evidence..

* Student: (...).
* The Shaykh: Yes, indeed, because here "the people of the house" (...).

* It also shows that human conditions befall even the prophets, peace be upon them. Moses, on that night, had lost his way and had not found it, and the cold had afflicted him and his family. The prophets and messengers do not differ from others except in what?
* Students: In the message.
* The Shaykh: In the message: *"Say: I am only a human being like you, to whom it is revealed"* [al-Kahf 110]. The first is similarity in humanity; the second is the specificity of *"it is revealed to me"* with revelation.

* It also shows that a person is not blamed for taking a protection that either wards off or removes (harm), from His saying: *"that you may warm yourselves"* [an-Naml 7]. Is this protection preventive or remedial?
* Student: Preventive.
* Another student: Remedial.
* Another student: Both preventive and remedial.
* The Shaykh: Both preventive and remedial: remedial against the cold that has already come, and preventive against the cold that is coming. So a person is not blamed for taking a protection, whether preventive or remedial. Indeed, he may even be commanded to do it, either as a command of obligation or a command of recommendation, according to what the situation requires that he remove or prevent.

In the verse there is evidence for accepting the report of a trustworthy person. From where is this taken?
* Student: *"I will bring you from it a piece of news"* [an-Naml 7].
* The Shaykh: *"I will bring you from it a piece of news."* Acting on the report of a trustworthy person is permissible. As for one who is not trustworthy, Allah the Exalted has said: *"O you who believe, if a defiant one brings you a report, verify it, lest you harm a people in ignorance"* [al-Hujurat 6].

(...) In this matter there are three categories: one that is trusted, one that is not trusted, and one that is uncertain.
What is not trusted is not accepted; what is trusted is accepted; and what is unknown or uncertain must be clarified, and one waits until it is clarified.
* Student: (...).
* The Shaykh: Yes indeed. *"I will bring you"* addresses his family, and in it is evidence for addressing one person with a plural form. But this is a linguistic benefit.
* Student: The report of a trustworthy person (...), so he would be trustworthy among his family.
* The Shaykh: The discussion is about one who is trusted.
* The Student: Generally, O Shaykh.
* The Shaykh: No, generally and specifically. That is, a person may be of known condition to me, and I trust him, while to people he is unknown; they hold back regarding his matter. The discussion concerns the trust that you place in someone. If a man said that he had seen the crescent moon, and his eyesight was weak, and he reported that he had seen it, while the people with him had not seen it?
* Students: His statement is not accepted, O Shaykh.
* The Shaykh: It is not accepted, even if he mentions it.
* The Students: It is not accepted.
* The Shaykh: Because he is not a just person. Yes indeed, it is not accepted. This is why it happened before some judges that the people had seen the crescent. One of their shaykhs said: "I have seen the crescent." The people with him, who had sharper sight than him, said: "We did not see it." This shaykh (...) was known for his religion and his trustworthiness, and he insisted that he had seen the crescent. The judge said: "Come close to me." He came close, and the judge wiped his eyebrow and said: "Look." He said: "Now I have not seen it." Yes indeed, it was a white hair. This was from the judge's shrewdness, because the people with him had not seen it and he had seen it, so it was impossible for him to be trustworthy and not be a man of bad report. But he may err.

Then He says: *"So when he came to it, he was called: Blessed is whoever is in the fire and whoever is around it, and glory be to Allah, Lord of the worlds"* [an-Naml 8].

* From this verse the following is derived, first: the affirmation of the speech of Allah the Exalted, from His saying *"he was called."* If someone says: the verb here is in the passive and does not specify who called, so there is no evidence in it for the speech of Allah. What is the answer?
* Students: (...).
* The Shaykh: First, verifying it (the text) is part of that. Second, His saying to Moses, peace be upon him: *"O Moses, indeed I am Allah, the Exalted in Might, the Wise"* [an-Naml 9].

* It also shows that the speech of Allah the Exalted is with a voice, from His saying *"he was called,"* and calling is only with a voice. In this there is a refutation of two groups. Their view was mentioned to us yesterday. Who are they?
* Students: The Ash'ariyyah (an school of kalam theology)..
* The Shaykh: The Ash'ariyyah and the Kullabiyyah (followers of Ibn Kullab), who say that the speech of Allah is a meaning subsisting in Himself. This view is false, and it has been discussed with us many times.

* It also shows that one who is being addressed should be told something, the person being addressed, so that he is reassured and becomes receptive to what is conveyed to him, because the one who is addressed does not accept what is conveyed to him, meaning he is not able to accept it. Is this taken from His saying?
* Student: (...).
* The Shaykh: Someone else before him: *"he was called: Blessed is whoever is in the fire."* Because affirming blessing for whoever is in the fire and around it increases his assurance for his family. This is why the first thing Allah addressed him with in this verse was *"he was called: Blessed is whoever is in the fire and whoever is around it."*

* It also shows the glorifying of Allah the Exalted above what is not fitting for Him, from His saying *"and glory be to Allah."*

* It also shows the generality of the lordship of Allah the Exalted, from His saying *"Lord of the worlds."* And is there another lord with Him? If there were, He would not be Lord of the worlds. If there were another lord with Him, Allah would not be Lord of the worlds, but only Lord of some of the worlds. Allah the Exalted is Lord of the worlds. Allah the Exalted has mentioned that it is impossible, by reason, for there to be another god with Allah, and He said: *"Had there been in them gods besides Allah, they would have been ruined"* [al-Anbiya' 22], and they were not ruined. This shows the impossibility of multiple gods, from the impossibility of their ruin. And He the Exalted said: *"Allah has not taken any son, and there is not with Him any god; otherwise, each god would have taken away what he created, and some of them would have overcome others. Glory be to Allah above what they describe"* [al-Mu'minun 91]. This matter (...).
The matter of the oneness of Allah the Exalted in His lordship is well known. Even the polytheists in the time of the Messenger ﷺ used to affirm His oneness in lordship.

* It also shows that Allah the Blessed and Exalted praises Himself, and that this is from His perfection. For He praised Himself by His saying: *"Glory be to Allah, Lord of the worlds."* Did He praise Himself by negation and affirmation, or not? Negation?
* Student: Glory be to Allah.
* The Shaykh: Glory be to Allah. And affirmation?
* The Student: Lord of the worlds.
* The Shaykh: Lord of the worlds. From here we know that the perfection of attributes is not complete except through these two matters, namely negation and affirmation, because affirming perfections alone does not indicate the negation of deficiencies, and negating deficiencies alone does not indicate the affirmation of perfections. By their combination, absolute praise is achieved. This is why they said: there must be both clearing away (takhliyah) and adorning (tahliyah).

* It also shows, in the verse, that all creation is under the lordship of Allah the Exalted, and He disposes of them according to His lordship, from His saying *"Lord of the worlds."* For this reason, no one can oppose the rule of lordship.
* Student: (...).
* The Shaykh: Now (...).
* The Student: (...).
* The Shaykh: Then Allah the Blessed and Exalted said: *"O Moses"*..
* Student: (...).
* The Shaykh: Yes indeed, in it (...) is blessed, from His saying *"and whoever is around it."*

In His saying the Exalted: *"O Moses, indeed I am Allah, the Exalted in Might, the Wise."*
* First: in the verse there is evidence that specifying a person by calling him has a benefit. We mentioned it yesterday. What is it?
* Students: Reassurance.
* The Shaykh: Reassurance and familiarity. For when you say "O so-and-so," you are undoubtedly reassured. You say: this one knows me; no harm will reach me. This is why He said *"O Moses."*
* It also shows the affirmation of might and wisdom for Allah the Mighty and Majestic, from His saying *"I am Allah, the Exalted in Might, the Wise."*
* It also shows that whoever wishes to identify himself should state his name, from His saying *"I am Allah, the Exalted in Might, the Wise."* He did not say "I am, for example, I am speaking to you, I am, I am," or the like, but Allah the Exalted made clear who it is who speaks to him.
Does it contain the affirmation of divinity for Allah? I mean, the restriction of divinity to Allah?
* Student: Yes.
* The Shaykh: How so?
* The Student: (...).
* The Shaykh: Because describing Him with might and wisdom requires that He alone be the one worshipped. And who knows (...) the subject and the predicate? Is this a restriction of Him?
* It also contains the affirmation of absolute judgment for Allah the Exalted, and it is derived from *"the Wise,"* because we have mentioned that *al-Hakim* is the one possessing judgment and wisdom.
* Students: (...).
* The Shaykh: Yes, the affirmation of absolute judgment for Allah the Exalted is from His saying *"the Wise."*

*"And throw down your staff." And when he saw it moving as if it were a snake, he turned back in flight and did not return. "O Moses, do not fear; indeed, the messengers do not fear in My presence. Except one who has wronged"* [an-Naml 10–11].

* First: this great verse indicates the complete power of Allah the Exalted, and it is from His saying *"when he saw it moving."* Because he was commanded to throw it, and he threw it, and as soon as it reached the ground it became a living snake. This is why in Surat Taha: *"So he threw it, and suddenly it was a snake"* [Ta-Ha 20]. The particle *idha* ("suddenly") is for sudden occurrence and indicates the matter happening immediately.
So in it there is clear evidence for what? For the complete power of Allah the Exalted, and that when He says to a thing "Be," it is.
* It also shows the wisdom of Allah the Exalted in the signs of the messengers, and that they suit the age, from His saying *"moving as if it were a snake."* Because this is the most like what they knew. In that time, the field that had advanced greatly among them was sorcery. If someone took a staff in front of him and placed it on the ground, and then you saw it as a snake, what would you say? You would say: this is sorcery. For this reason Moses, peace be upon him, was given signs that overcame their sorcery.
* It also shows that among the eloquence is brevity through omission, and this does not produce deficiency or stinginess.
* Student: (...).
* The Shaykh: From where (...) on the first?
* The Student: (...).
* The Shaykh: *"When he saw it moving"* here has three aspects: (*"And throw down your staff," so he threw it, "when he saw it moving"*). Because if the speech were taken literally, it would say: "throw down your staff," and when he was commanded with this, it moved while in his hand, and the matter is not like that.
* It also shows that this staff was not merely a moving animal, but was more than that: *"as if it were a snake."* It is known that a snake in itself is frightening; a serpent in itself is frightening. If it was of the great snakes, it becomes more evil and more eloquent.
* It also shows the permissibility of fear, or that fear may befall the prophets: *"he turned back in flight,"* and that this is not considered a deficiency in them, because it is a requirement of human nature.
And what follows from the requirement of human nature, the prophets are not blamed for it (...). They sneeze, they feel cold, they fall ill, and they also die: *"Say: I am only a human being like you"* [al-Kahf 110].
* It also shows the mercy of Allah the Blessed and Exalted toward His prophet Moses, from His saying *"O Moses, do not fear."* This is from Allah's mercy toward him, because when He says to him, and He knows that He is the Lord of the worlds, if He says "do not fear," it is not possible for him to fear.
* It also shows the permissibility of directing legal rulings toward matters of jurisprudence, meaning like "do not fear." If someone says: I was (...) fear is natural, how can one be distanced from it?
* Student: (...).
* The Shaykh: No, my intention is: does the ruling apply to such natural matters?
* The Student: (...).
* The Shaykh: (...) it is possible; because a person (...) fear is a natural matter (...) comes upon a person against his will, but he can treat it (...).
This is why a man came to the Messenger, peace be upon him, and said: "Advise me." He said: *"Do not become angry."* [Recorded by al-Bukhari (6116) from the hadith of Abu Hurayrah.] Anger is part of human nature, but the meaning of *"do not become angry"* is that you try to reduce your anger, and that you be calm at all times. Then, if you become angry, do not carry out what that anger demands. Have you understood now?
So the natural human matters that are the requirement of human nature may be directed by a ruling, as a command or a prohibition. This is by way of repelling them, or by way of reducing their effects: repelling them before they occur, or reducing their effects. A person is not commanded to do what he cannot do; he cannot avoid anger, yet he must be angry. He is commanded not to fear, yet he must fear when there is reason to fear.
* Student: (...).
* The Shaykh: What did he say when he turned toward Madyan?
* The Student: (...).
* The Shaykh: (...) prophethood is above the knowledge of (...).
* It also shows that whoever is with Allah the Exalted should not fear: *"indeed, the messengers do not fear in My presence"* (*"indeed, the messengers do not fear in My presence"* means: with Me, *"the messengers"*).
This is why, whenever a person remembers his Lord, fear departs from him: *"O you who believe, when you meet a company, stand firm and remember Allah much, that you may succeed"* [al-Anfal 45]. In the remembrance of Allah the Exalted there is the removal of fear, strength, and eagerness to carry out what Allah the Exalted has commanded. This is why Allah commanded it in jihad.
* It also shows that whoever has wronged and then turns back with righteous deeds, Allah the Exalted erases the evil deed with the righteous deed, from His saying: *"except one who has wronged and then substituted good after evil; indeed, I am Forgiving and Merciful."*

We were told yesterday of the connection of this sentence: *"except one who has wronged and then substituted good after evil."* What is the connection mentioned in this place?
* Student: When Moses, peace be upon him, was told by Allah the Exalted: *"indeed, the messengers do not fear in My presence,"* he mentioned his sin (...), so Allah the Exalted said: *"except one who has wronged and then substituted good after evil,"* so that Moses, peace be upon him, would be reassured and see that Allah had forgiven him.
* The Shaykh: In it there is also the affirmation of forgiveness and mercy for Allah: *"indeed, I am Forgiving and Merciful."*
* It also contains the derivation of rulings from the requirements of Allah's names and attributes. From where do we derive the rulings from the requirements of the names and attributes? For His saying *"indeed, I am Forgiving and Merciful"* means "I forgive him," and this is a ruling. Deriving rulings from the requirements of the names and attributes is one of the finest forms of inference. It is mentioned that a man recited before a Bedouin, who did not read the Qur'an: *"And the thief, male and female, cut off their hands as a recompense for what they earned, as a punishment from Allah; and Allah is Forgiving and Merciful."* The Bedouin said: "Repeat the verse, you have made a mistake in it." He repeated it a second time and said: *"And the thief, male and female, cut off their hands as a recompense for what they earned, as a punishment from Allah; and Allah is Forgiving and Merciful."* He said: "Repeat the verse." He repeated it a third time correctly: *"as a punishment from Allah; and Allah is Mighty and Wise"* [al-Ma'idah 38]. He said: "Now, for He is Mighty and has judgment, so He cuts off. If He were Forgiving and Merciful, He would not cut off." He said: "Correct."
[Cf. al-Bahr al-Muhit (4/255), and al-Kashkul (2/112).]

Commentary of Ibn 'Uthaymin (Tafsir al-Quran al-Karim) on surah 27, verse 7–13 (part 4 of 7):

This understanding is supported by the words of Allah the Exalted concerning those who wage war: ﴿Except for those who repent before you gain power over them. So know that Allah is Forgiving and Merciful﴾ [al-Ma'idah 34]. Its meaning, then, is: if he knows that Allah is Forgiving and Merciful, He will forgive them and they will be left alone. For this reason, if a highway robber repents before he is overpowered, the prescribed punishment (hadd) falls from him. Does it then return, so that the other offenders subject to prescribed punishments are also liable, or not? I say: no.

From this it is derived that rulings are taken from what is required by the names and attributes of Allah the Exalted, because of His words: ﴿for indeed I am Forgiving and Merciful﴾ (...).
* Student: (...).
* The Shaykh: (...) Without doubt, the Prophets are not protected from what does not undermine the message (...). From what contradicts the message, honour and manliness, they are protected. But they are protected from being left to persist in it. They must be granted success in repentance, and this is the difference between them and others. I think we mentioned (...).
He says: whoever distinguishes between them and others does so in two respects, in terms of sins and disobedience.
First: it is impossible that from them there should proceed what undermines the message, such as lying and betrayal, or what undermines honour and manliness, such as fornication and the like.
Second: if something from the category of what is possible in sins does occur from them, they are not left to persist in it. There must occur in them what necessitates their abandoning this thing, because they are exemplary messengers (...) in sins, sins would have been part of their law. As for the claim of infallibility (ʿiṣmah) in an absolute sense, there is no basis for it. Nothing is absolutely infallible. Rather, the correct position is that such things do occur from them, but they are not left to persist in them.
* Student: (...).
* The Shaykh: (...).
* The Student: (...).
* The Shaykh: He acknowledged that he was a wrongdoer: ﴿He said: "My Lord, I have wronged myself"﴾ [al-Qasas 16]. He acknowledged that he was a wrongdoer, and he also excused himself on the basis of mere bravery.
* The Student: (...) that Musa killed a soul, meaning he did not wrong himself. Rather, he defended his people. He is not a wrongdoer. If he saw, for example, a virtuous man (...) a people who would oppress him (...).
* The Shaykh: That is not correct, his statement is not correct, because (...) on earth, and this particular man had a covenant (...) between him and the second man, specifically.
* Student: (...).
* The Shaykh: This is an issue (...) but it is contrary to what is preferable (awla), and for this reason Allah rebuked him for it. But ﴿May Allah pardon you! Why did you grant them permission?﴾ [al-Tawbah 43], ﴿O Prophet, why do you prohibit what Allah has made lawful for you, seeking the pleasure of your wives? Allah is Forgiving and Merciful﴾ [al-Tahrim 1]. This shows that the matter did occur from the Messenger, peace be upon him, but he was forgiven for what he was rebuked for.
* Student: (...).
* The Shaykh: Yes, indeed, that is our view. ﴿Indeed, I, the messengers do not fear in My presence﴾. The indication is that Musa, peace be upon him, was indicated by the message.
* Student: (...).
* The Shaykh: Yes indeed. The call does not necessarily entail nearness or distance. The call is by an audible voice.
* The Student: (...).
* The Shaykh: (...) he may raise his voice and nothing is understood from it (...). They say: Allah called him from afar, then brought him near as a confidant, just as He said: ﴿And We called him from the right side of the mountain and brought him near as a confidant﴾ [Maryam 52].
* The Student: (...).
* The Shaykh: That is, the ruling that (...) this fire. Allah knows best, I do not know. But perhaps there is a wisdom in the place being specifically in the blessed sacred valley. This valley is blessed and sacred, so the beginning of the revelation came from that place, because he, peace be upon him, was far from it (...).
* Student: (...).
* The Shaykh: Yes? Clearly (...).
* The Student: (...).
* The Shaykh: And what is the ruling on being distant from (...)?
* The Student: (...).
* The Shaykh: It does not contradict it. A person may endure it. For this reason, when Musa chose seventy men from his people and Allah spoke to Musa while they listened, they said: ﴿We will not believe you until we see Allah plainly﴾ [al-Baqarah 55]. Now, it only becomes clear to me, and Allah knows best, that this was in a specific place, the blessed sacred one, and perhaps after research we will arrive at it.
* Student: (...).
* The Shaykh: Except, from His words: ﴿and those around it﴾.
* The Student: (...).
* The Shaykh: ﴿those in the fire and those around it﴾.
* * *
I seek refuge in Allah from the accursed Satan. The beginning of the speech: (﴿and put your hand into your pocket﴾, the collar of the shirt). This explanation of al-jayb as the collar of the shirt is given.
As for His words ﴿and put your hand﴾: the word "yad" (hand) in its entirety is used of the palm only, and does not include the forearm except when qualified.
The evidence for this is that when Allah the Exalted said concerning tayammum (dry ablution): ﴿wipe your faces and your hands﴾ [al-Nisa' 43], it became specific to the two palms. When Allah, blessed and exalted, intended the forearm, He said in wudu' (ablution): ﴿and your hands up to the elbows﴾ [al-Ma'idah 6]. So what nullifies this text in the Arabic language is that what Musa was commanded to insert was not the hand including the forearm, but the palm (...) into his pocket, like this.
﴿and it will come out white﴾: "takhruj" (it comes out) is jussive, although it is an imperfect verb, and no jussive particle precedes it. So by what is it jussive?
* The Students: Response to the imperative (jawab al-talab).
* The Shaykh: By the response to the imperative, the response to the imperative being "adkhil" (insert). It is known that when the fa' (of consequence) is dropped and the meaning is conditional, the verb is jussive. This is the rule: when the fa' of consequence comes after an imperative, the verb is made jussive by it, or by the implied "an". If the fa' is dropped after an imperative and a conditional meaning is intended, the verb is jussive.
* The Students: Jussive.
* The Shaykh: Jussive. This is a well-known rule of grammar (nahw).
(﴿it comes out﴾ - meaning the hand - contrary to its colour which was of a dark complexion, ﴿white without blemish﴾.) From where did the author take that its colour was dark?
* The Students: From His words: ﴿it comes out white﴾.
* The Shaykh: From His words ﴿it comes out white﴾, because if it had been white before, He would not have said "it comes out white". So it must have changed from the first colour to the second.
And His words ﴿white﴾ are a circumstantial (ḥāl) qualifier of the subject of "takhruj", meaning: in the state of being white.
﴿without blemish﴾ is a restriction, due to His words ﴿white﴾, because white may be a blemish, such as vitiligo (baras), which is a blemish because it is a defect that distresses its bearer. But He said ﴿without blemish﴾. So the whiteness is not like the whiteness of vitiligo.
For this reason the author says: (﴿white without blemish﴾, vitiligo, a ray for it that dazzles the sight, a sign).
As for his saying "a ray for it" (lahā shuʿāʿ), this requires evidence. Allah, blessed and exalted, mentioned only that it was a colour, and that is sufficient as a sign: that the hand enters with one colour and comes out with another colour. As for the addition of a ray, Allah the Exalted did not mention it. We are not permitted to go beyond what the Qur'an indicates in these matters, because we mentioned earlier that informative matters (khabariyyat) have no room for opinion. In informative matters there is no room for opinion, and one restricts oneself to what is conveyed by the report. So we say: it was white, and that is sufficient as a sign.
The author said: (a sign ﴿among nine signs﴾). The "fi" is for locality, so this sign and the sign of the staff are among the nine, and not additional to the nine.
(﴿among nine signs﴾, sent ﴿to Pharaoh and his people﴾). Musa knew two of these nine. Which are they?
* The Students: The staff...
* The Shaykh: The staff and the hand. But what remains?
* Students: Seven.
* The Shaykh: Seven signs. So what are the signs (...)?
* Students: (...).
* The Shaykh: We say: among the nine signs, two are well known now. The remaining nine: ﴿So We sent upon them the flood and the locusts and the lice and the frogs and the blood﴾ [al-A'raf 133]. How many is this with the two? Seven. ﴿And We certainly afflicted the people of Pharaoh with years of drought and shortage of fruits﴾ [al-A'raf 130]. So what is the total?
* Student: Nine.
* The Shaykh: Nine signs. These are the nine signs.
﴿We sent upon them the flood﴾. What is the flood?
* Student: The overflowing.
* The Shaykh: The overflowing, the overflow of water. "The locusts" are well known. "The lice."
* Student: The ants.
* The Shaykh: No, the worm is what is in grains. This is the lice.
* Student: (...).
* The Shaykh: No. The frogs are well known. And "the blood"?
* Students: (...).
* The Shaykh: Well known. Let us now see. Some scholars say that the blood is this: the water, when they drink it, becomes blood, and when the Copt hands it to the Israelite, it is water.
However, Shaykh 'Abd al-Rahman al-Sa'di, may Allah have mercy on him, also adopted this view. The "flood" is the overflowing, which spoils crops before they come out. The "locusts" eat crops after they come out, meaning you find nothing cultivated. The water spoils this. What is spoiled in stored goods?
* Students: The lice.
* The Shaykh: The lice. Or the frogs spoil it, so (...) edible and drinkable things only. Is it clear? (...) If a person eats or drinks it, it turns into blood. He sent upon them blood also, and it is haemorrhage, nosebleed. On this basis, their food was spoiled, and what they obtained through food became impure also. This last is the sound meaning. Because it being from water and becoming blood occurs (...) by the frogs, the frogs (...) enter the body of one, and its smell becomes foul...
He sent upon them blood also, which is haemorrhage, nosebleed.
On this basis, their food was spoiled, and what they obtained through food also became impure. This is indeed the meaning of blood, because its being with water becoming blood occurs through the spoiling of water by frogs. When the frogs (...) it is not possible to find frogs (...) its smell is foul and its appearance is foul, and one cannot put one's lips to it (...).
In sum: the correct view is what the Shaykh, may Allah have mercy on him, adopted in the interpretation. These are nine signs: ﴿with years of drought and shortage of fruits﴾ [al-A'raf 130]. "Years" (al-sinin), what does it mean? Barrenness and famine, which is the absence (...).

Allah the Exalted said: ﴿Except one who wrongs, then substitutes good after evil﴾ [al-Naml 11], to remind him of the blessing of repentance that was bestowed upon him. ﴿Except one who wrongs, then substitutes good after evil﴾. The author explained "substitutes" (baddala) with his words: "brings" (atā), because its apparent meaning does not yield the intended sense. "He substitutes good for evil": which of them is taken? Because "baddala" indicates that there is a substitute and something substituted. If you say "he substituted good", what does it say?
* Student: For evil.
* The Shaykh: For evil. Then good is pushed away and evil is taken, or not? I exchanged my garment for your garment. Where is what is taken?
* Student: The latter.
* The Shaykh: The latter. Is that so or not? So here, ﴿substitutes good﴾: if we take its apparent meaning, it means that he left good and took evil. For this reason the author explained "substitutes" as "brings" (atā).
The evidence for this: if the intended meaning of substitution were its apparent meaning, it would not be correct to express it with His words ﴿after evil﴾. If that were so, He would have said "substitutes good for evil". He did not say "after", so when He said "after evil", it is known that "baddala" here means "istabdala" (to take in exchange), and "istabdala" means "akhadha" (to take), as in ﴿Do you exchange that which is lower for that which is better?﴾ [al-Baqarah 61]. And "akhadha", as He said, means "atā" (to bring).
The meaning of the noble verse: whoever brings good after evil (...).
Yes indeed, it is a conditional noun (ism sharṭ jāzim), not a relative pronoun with an exception, because the exception here is disjunctive (munqaṭiʿ).
﴿whoever wrongs﴾: "ẓalama" is the conditional verb, and the clause ﴿then indeed I am Forgiving and Merciful﴾ is the response of the condition.
I say: if someone asks, what is the connection of the response with the condition?
* Student: That wrongdoing, and substituting good for wrongdoing, is fitting for Allah's pardon, or deserves forgiveness and mercy.
* The Shaykh: Yes indeed. The answer to this is that when Allah the Exalted mentioned these two names, ﴿then indeed I am Forgiving and Merciful﴾, He intends what they require. The requirement of forgiveness is that He forgives the one who wronged and then substituted good for evil, and the requirement of mercy is also that He has mercy on him.
A parallel to this is His words concerning those who wage war: ﴿Except for those who repent before you gain power over them. So know that Allah is Forgiving and Merciful﴾ [al-Ma'idah 34], meaning: the prescribed punishment falls from him, because this is what forgiveness and mercy require. So here, what forgiveness and mercy require is that whoever substitutes good for evil, Allah, blessed and exalted, forgives him and has mercy on him.
Does this include Messengers and non-Messengers?
* Students: Yes.
* The Shaykh: Yes, it includes Messengers and non-Messengers.
For this reason it is good for the author, and we also say with him, that the "illa" here is a disjunctive exception, because it includes Messengers and non-Messengers.
* * *
* Student: ﴿And put your hand into your pocket; it will come out white, without blemish, among nine signs, to Pharaoh and his people. Indeed, they were a defiant people.﴾ (12) ﴿But when Our signs came to them, visible, they said: "This is manifest magic."﴾ (13) ﴿And they denied them while their souls were convinced of them, out of wrongdoing and arrogance. So see how was the end of the corrupters.﴾ (14) ﴿And We had certainly given knowledge to Dawud and Sulayman. And they said: "Praise be to Allah, who has favoured us over many of His believing servants."﴾ (15) ﴿And Sulayman inherited Dawud, and he said: "O people, we have been taught the speech of birds, and we have been given of all things. Indeed, this is evident bounty."﴾ [al-Naml 12–16].
* The Shaykh: I seek refuge in Allah from the accursed Satan. Allah, blessed and exalted, said: ﴿When Musa said to his family: "Indeed, I have perceived a fire. I will bring you from it news or bring you a burning brand that you may warm yourselves."﴾ [al-Naml 7].
* First: from this verse is derived the good character of Musa, peace be upon him, through his speaking with his family and consulting them on what concerns everyone. That is, he did not go off without saying this statement to them, which indicates that he consults them on what concerns them.
* In this is evidence that the wife is among the family (ahl). This is the correct view. On this basis, the family (āl) of the Prophet, peace be upon him, includes his wives, because they are among the family.
Scholars have differed regarding whether, if a person bequeaths to his family or endows for his family, the wives enter into that or not.
Those who say they do not enter refer that to custom ('urf), and they say: the custom among people is that wives are not among the family, and the family is only the relatives.
If that is so, it is said: wives are among the family. So if a person endows for the family of so-and-so, or bequeaths to them, the wives enter among them by the requirement of language.
Then, if a consistent custom is found that contradicts that, we refer to custom, because the correct view is that the meanings of words are referred to the customs and habits of people. If no custom is found, we refer to the Shari'ah or the language, as the case may be.
* Student: (...)?
* The Shaykh: Yes indeed. Meaning, here the household (ahl al-bayt) (...).
* And in it is evidence that human conditions befall even the Prophets, peace be upon them. Musa, on that night, had lost his way and had not found it, and the cold had afflicted him and his family. The Prophets and Messengers do not differ from others except in what?
* Student: In the message.
* The Shaykh: In the message. ﴿Say: "I am only a human being like you, to whom it is revealed"﴾ [al-Kahf 110]. The first is likeness in humanity, and the second is the distinction: that revelation is given to him.
* And also in it is evidence that a person is not blamed for taking precautions, whether to ward off or to remove harm; because of His words: ﴿that you may warm yourselves﴾. Is this precaution preventive or remedial?
* Students: Preventive and remedial.
* The Shaykh: Preventive and remedial: remedial for the cold already present, and preventive against the cold to come. So taking a precaution, whether preventive or remedial, is not blameworthy for a person. Rather, it may be commanded, either as an obligation or as a recommendation, according to what the situation requires in what one wants to remove or prevent.
* And in the verse is evidence for accepting the report of a trustworthy person. From where is it derived?
* Student: ﴿I will bring you﴾.

Commentary of Ibn 'Uthaymin (Tafsir al-Quran al-Karim) on surah 27, verse 7–13 (part 5 of 7):

* The Shaykh: ﴿I will bring you from it some news﴾. Acting on the report of a trustworthy person is permissible. As for one who is not trustworthy, Allah the Exalted says: ﴿O you who have believed, if there comes to you a deviator with information, investigate, lest you harm a people out of ignorance﴾ [al-Hujurat 6].
People in this matter fall into three categories: one who is trusted, one who is not trusted, and one who is in between.
Whoever is not trusted is not accepted; whoever is trusted is accepted; and the unknown or the doubtful has his matter examined and is held in abeyance until it becomes clear.
* A student: (...)?
* The Shaykh: Yes indeed. ﴿I will bring you﴾ is addressed to his family, and in it is evidence for addressing a single person with a plural form, but this is a linguistic benefit.
* A student: Shaykh, the report of a trustworthy person is mentioned when it concerns his family, meaning they do not distract people, so it is among the people of trust?
* The Shaykh: The discussion concerns the one who is trusted.
* The student: The general public or the specific?
* The Shaykh: No, both general and specific. That is, this person may be of known condition to me, one I trust, while to people he is unknown and they hold back regarding his matter. The discussion concerns the trust that you place.
If a man said that he saw the crescent moon, while his eyesight is weak and the people with him did not see it?
* A student: His statement is not accepted.
* The Shaykh: His statement is not accepted, even if he is trustworthy?
* The student: Even if he is trustworthy.
* The Shaykh: Because he has a defect in his reliability. Yes indeed, it is not accepted. For this reason, something occurred in the past before some judges: the people looked for the crescent, and an elderly man among them said: "I have seen the crescent." The people with him, who had stronger eyesight than he, said: "We did not see it." This shaykh was, in terms of his religion and his trustworthiness, reliable, and he insisted that he had seen the crescent. The judge said: "Come close to me." He came close, and the judge wiped his eyebrow and said to him: "Look." He said: "Now I have not seen it." And behold, it was a white hair. This was from the judge's shrewdness, for he said: how is it that the people did not see it while he did? This is not possible. He was trustworthy; he was not a man whose report is doubtful, but he may have been mistaken.
﴿So when he came to it, he was called: Blessed is whoever is in the fire and whoever is around it, and exalted is Allah, Lord of the worlds﴾ [an-Naml 8].
From this verse is derived: First, the affirmation of the speech of Allah the Exalted, by His saying: ﴿was called﴾.
If someone says: the verb here is in the passive and does not specify who called, so there is no evidence in it for the speech of Allah. What is the answer?
* A student: It is mentioned in another verse.
* The Shaykh: First, it is mentioned in another verse; second, also His saying at the opening of the speech: ﴿O Musa, indeed I am Allah, the Mighty, the Wise﴾ [an-Naml 9].
* And in it is evidence that the speech of Allah the Exalted is with a voice, by His saying: ﴿was called﴾, and a call is not except with a voice. In it is a refutation of two groups whose statement we passed over yesterday: who? The Ash'aris and the Kullabiyyah, who say that the speech of Allah the Exalted is a meaning subsisting in Himself. This statement is false for many reasons.
* And in it is evidence that one should put at ease the one who is frightened. A person who is frightened, you may say to him or do with him what reassures him so that he becomes calm and receptive to what is conveyed to him, because the frightened person does not accept what is laid upon him; meaning, he is not able to accept it. Is this derived from His saying? 
* Students: (...).
* The Shaykh: And others before Him: ﴿was called: that blessed is whoever is in the fire﴾. The affirmation of blessing for whoever is in the fire and around it increases tranquility without doubt; for this reason, the first thing Allah addressed him with in this verse was: ﴿was called: that blessed is whoever is in the fire and whoever is around it﴾.
* And in it is evidence of the glorification of Allah the Exalted above what is not befitting Him, by His saying: ﴿and exalted is Allah﴾.
* And in it is evidence of the comprehensive lordship of Allah the Exalted, by His saying: ﴿Lord of the worlds﴾.
Is there with Him another lord? If there were another lord with Him, Allah would not be Lord of the worlds, but Lord of some of the worlds. Allah the Exalted is the Lord of the worlds. Allah the Exalted has mentioned that it is not possible by reason that there be another god with Allah, so He said: ﴿Had there been within them gods other than Allah, they would have been ruined﴾ [al-Anbiya 22], and they were not ruined, which shows the impossibility of multiple gods. And He the Exalted said: ﴿Allah has not taken any son, nor was there with Him any god; for then each god would have taken what he created, and some of them would have overcome others. Exalted is Allah above what they describe﴾ [al-Muminun 91]. This is a matter that has never occurred.
So the affirmation of the oneness of Allah the Exalted in His lordship is well known; even the polytheists in the time of the Messenger ﷺ used to acknowledge the oneness of lordship.
* And in it is evidence of Allah the Blessed and Exalted praising Himself, and that this is from His perfection, for He praised Himself by His saying: ﴿And exalted is Allah, Lord of the worlds﴾. Did He praise Himself by negation and affirmation, or not? Negation: ﴿exalted is Allah﴾; affirmation: ﴿Lord of the worlds﴾.
From here we know that the perfection of attributes is not complete except by these two matters, namely negation and affirmation; because affirming perfections alone does not indicate the negation of deficiencies, and negating deficiencies alone does not indicate the affirmation of perfections, and by their combination absolute perfection is attained. For this reason they said: there must be both clearing away and adornment.
* And in it is evidence that all creation is under the lordship of Allah the Exalted, He disposing of them according to the requirement of His lordship, by His saying: ﴿Lord of the worlds﴾. For this reason, no one can oppose the ruling of lordship.
* A student: (...)?
* The Shaykh: Yes, no one opposes it, but now what is its aspect?
* The student: ﴿Lord of the worlds﴾: the Lord is the Owner who disposes of His property as He wills.
* Another student: (...)?
* The Shaykh: Yes indeed, in it that (...) is blessed, by His saying: ﴿and whoever is around it﴾.
And in the saying of the Exalted: ﴿O Musa, indeed I am Allah, the Mighty, the Wise﴾.
* First: in the verse is evidence that designating a person by calling him has a benefit, which we mentioned yesterday: reassurance and putting at ease; because when you say: "O so-and-so," you reassure him without doubt, since he says: this one knows me, he will not harm me. For this reason He said: ﴿O Musa﴾.
* And in it is evidence of the affirmation of might and wisdom for Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, by His saying: ﴿I am Allah, the Mighty, the Wise﴾.
* And in it also is evidence that whoever wishes to identify himself should state his name, by His saying: ﴿I am Allah, the Mighty, the Wise﴾. He did not say, for example: "I am the one speaking to you, I am I," or the like; rather, Allah the Exalted made clear who was speaking to him.
Does it contain the restriction of divinity to Allah?
* A student: Yes indeed.
* The Shaykh: How do you know it?
* The student: (...).
* The Shaykh: Meaning: its sense, describing Him with might and wisdom requires that He alone be the one worshipped?
* The student: That He be the one worshipped.
* Another student: ﴿I am Allah﴾.
* The Shaykh: And among the rules of the subject and predicate, this is a verbal restriction.
* And also in it: the affirmation of absolute judgment for Allah the Exalted, derived from ﴿the Wise﴾; because we mentioned that the Wise is the one possessing judgment and wisdom.
﴿And throw down your staff.' But when he saw it moving as if it were a snake, he turned in retreat and did not return. 'O Musa, do not fear; indeed, in My presence the messengers do not fear. (10) Except one who has wronged﴾ [an-Naml 10–11].
First: in this great verse is evidence of the perfection of the power of Allah the Exalted, and it is from His saying: ﴿So when he saw it moving﴾; because he was commanded to throw it down, and he threw it, and as soon as it reached the ground it became a serpent. For this reason, in Surah Ta-Ha: ﴿So he threw it, and suddenly it was a serpent﴾ [Ta-Ha 20]. The word "idha" (suddenly) indicates the suddenness of the matter and its occurrence immediately.
* So in it is clear evidence of what? Of the perfection of the power of Allah the Exalted, and that when He says to a thing "Be," it is.
* And in it also is evidence of the wisdom of Allah the Exalted in the signs of the messengers, and that they are suited to the age, in His saying: ﴿moving as if it were a jann﴾; because this is most like what had developed greatly among them at that time, namely magic. For if someone brought a staff before you and placed it on the ground, then you saw it become a serpent, what would you say? You would say: this is magic. Therefore Musa, peace be upon him, was given signs that overcame their deeds.
* And in it is evidence that eloquence includes brevity through omission, and this does not produce any deficiency or shortcoming.
* A student: (...).
* The Shaykh: Good, from where do you point to the first?
* The student: (...).
* The Shaykh: ﴿So when he saw it moving﴾ here, without doubt, there is an omitted element: ﴿And throw down your staff﴾, so he threw it, ﴿so when he saw it moving﴾; because if the speech were taken at its apparent sense, if it were: "throw down your staff," then he would not have been commanded to do this while it moved in his hand, and the matter is not so.
* And in it also is evidence that this staff was not merely an animal that moves, but greater than that: ﴿as if it were a jann﴾, and it is known that the jann by itself is frightening, and the serpent by itself is frightening; so if it was of the greatest of serpents, it became even more intense and eloquent.
* And in it is evidence that prophets may experience fear, ﴿he turned in retreat﴾, and that this is not considered a deficiency in them, because it is a requirement of human nature; and what is a requirement of human nature is not blamed on anyone. The prophets become hungry, thirsty, cold, ill, and also die: ﴿I am only a human being like you﴾ [al-Kahf 110].
* And in it is evidence of the mercy of Allah the Blessed and Exalted toward His prophet Musa, by His saying: ﴿O Musa, do not fear﴾; for this is from the mercy of Allah toward him, because when He says to him, while knowing that He is the Lord of the worlds: ﴿do not fear﴾, it is not possible for him to fear.
* And in it is evidence of the permissibility of directing legal rulings toward natural matters. For example: ﴿do not fear﴾. If someone says: when you say to a person "do not fear," fear is natural, how can he repel it?
* A student: (...).
* The Shaykh: No, my intent is: does a ruling apply to such natural matters? We say: yes, it is possible; because a person, even though fear is a natural matter, not within his control, as when a person is overcome against his will, nevertheless he can treat it by resisting.
For this reason, "a man came to the Messenger, peace be upon him, and said: Advise me. He said: 'Do not become angry'" [narrated by al-Bukhari (6116) from the hadith of Abu Hurayrah], and anger is from human nature; but the meaning of "Do not become angry" is: try to reduce your anger, be always calm, and if you become angry, do not carry out what that anger demands.
So the natural human matters which are the requirement of human nature may be directed by a ruling, as a command or prohibition, and that is by way of resisting them before they occur, or by way of reducing their effects.
One should not say: the human being is commanded what he cannot do; he is commanded not to be angry while he must become angry, commanded not to fear while he must fear what is frightening.
* A student: (...)?
* The Shaykh: He, when he turned toward Madyan, what did he say?
* The student: ﴿He said: Perhaps my Lord will guide me﴾ [al-Qasas 22].
* The Shaykh: (...) prophethood is above knowledge of Allah and worship.
* And in it also is evidence that whoever is with Allah the Exalted should not fear: ﴿Indeed, in My presence the messengers do not fear﴾, meaning: in My presence are ﴿the messengers﴾. For this reason, whenever a person remembers his Lord, fear departs from him: ﴿O you who have believed, when you meet a company, then stand firm and remember Allah much that you may succeed﴾ [al-Anfal 45]. In the remembrance of Allah the Exalted is the removal of fear, strength, and eagerness to carry out what Allah the Exalted has commanded; for this reason Allah commanded it in jihad.
* And in it is evidence that whoever has wronged and then does a righteous deed, Allah the Exalted erases the evil deed with the good deed; by His saying: ﴿Except one who has wronged and then substituted good after evil, indeed I am Forgiving and Merciful﴾ [an-Naml 11].
We passed yesterday the connection of this sentence: ﴿Except one who has wronged and then substituted good after evil﴾, a connection mentioned in this context. What is it?
* A student: That Musa, peace be upon him, when Allah the Exalted said: ﴿in My presence the messengers do not fear﴾, he recalled his sin of killing the Copt, so he thought he was not deserving of forgiveness, and Allah the Exalted said: ﴿Except one who has wronged and then substituted good after evil﴾, until (...) Musa, peace be upon him, sees that he has been forgiven.
* The Shaykh: * And in it also: the affirmation of forgiveness and mercy for Allah; by His saying: ﴿indeed I am Forgiving and Merciful﴾.
* And in it also: deriving rulings from what is required by the names and attributes of Allah the Exalted. From where do we derive it? For His saying: ﴿indeed I am Forgiving and Merciful﴾ means: I forgive him. This is a ruling, and deriving rulings from the requirements of the names and attributes is one of the finest forms of inference.
It is mentioned that a man recited before a Bedouin: ﴿And the thief, male and female, cut off their hands as recompense for what they earned, a punishment from Allah﴾ [al-Ma'idah 38], and then "and Allah is Forgiving and Merciful," in the presence of an Arab. The Bedouin, who did not read the Quran, said: "Repeat the verse, you made a mistake in it." He repeated it a second time and said: ﴿cut off their hands as recompense for what they earned, a punishment from Allah﴾ and "and Allah is Forgiving and Merciful." He said to him: "Repeat the verse." He repeated it the third time correctly: ﴿a punishment from Allah, and Allah is Mighty and Wise﴾. He said: "Now, for He is mighty and has judgment, so He cut off; had He forgiven and shown mercy, He would not have cut off." This is correct.
This understanding is supported by the saying of the Exalted about the highway robbers: ﴿Except those who repent before you overpower them; so know that Allah is Forgiving and Merciful﴾ [al-Ma'idah 34].
So its meaning: if it is known that Allah is Forgiving and Merciful, He forgives them and they are left alone; for this reason, if a highway robber repents before being overpowered, the prescribed punishment falls from him. Whether others among those liable to prescribed punishments are then attached to him or not is a matter of scholarly disagreement.
* So from this is derived: deriving rulings from what is required by the names and attributes of Allah the Exalted; by His saying: ﴿indeed I am Forgiving and Merciful﴾.
* A student: (...)?
* The Shaykh: No. There is no doubt that the prophets do not sin in matters that do not undermine the message; sins that do not undermine the message, dignity, and honor, they are not sinful in them. But they are sinful if they persist in them; they must be granted repentance, and this is the difference between them and others. I think we mentioned it in detail, that they are distinguished from others in two respects regarding sins and disobedience:
First: it is not possible for them to commit what undermines the message, such as lying and betrayal, nor what undermines dignity and honor, such as fornication and the like.
Second: if there occurs from them what is possible among sins, they are not left to persist in it; there must occur for them what necessitates their abandoning that thing, because they are exemplary messengers, and if they were left in sins, the sins would become part of their legislation.
As for the claim of absolute infallibility, there is no basis for it; there is no absolute infallibility, rather the correct view is that what occurs from them occurs, but they are not left to persist in it.
* A student: (...) from the major sins?
* The Shaykh: Yes, killing a soul is a major sin.
* The student: (...)?
* The Shaykh: "He said: My Lord, indeed I have wronged myself" [al-Qasas 16]. He acknowledged that he was a wrongdoer and also sought forgiveness for that in the matter of intercession, because he considers that he wronged a soul.
* The student: (...) defends his people; he is not a wrongdoer; if he sees a person (...)?
* The Shaykh: The matter is not correct; (...) and this particular man specifically (...).
* A student: (...)?
* The Shaykh: No, this is a matter (...), it is not a disobedience, but it is contrary to the better course; for this reason Allah rebuked him for it: ﴿Allah pardon you; why did you grant them permission?﴾ [at-Tawbah 43], ﴿O Prophet, why do you prohibit what Allah has made lawful for you, seeking the approval of your wives? And Allah is Forgiving and Merciful﴾ [at-Tahrim 1]. This shows that the matter occurred from the Messenger, peace be upon him, but he was forgiven for it and was not left to persist in it.
* The student: (...)?

Commentary of Ibn 'Uthaymin (Tafsir al-Quran al-Karim) on surah 27, verses 7–13 (part 6 of 7):

* The Shaykh: Yes, that is correct, and it can be derived from it. ﴿Indeed, the messengers do not fear in My presence﴾: this indicates that Musa (peace be upon him) was given the good news of his messengerhood.
* The student: (...)?
* The Shaykh: The call itself does not necessarily imply nearness or distance. A call with an unrestricted voice may come from a distance, and one may also raise one's voice to Musa even when close. So it may be that Allah called to him from afar and then brought him near in intimate conversation, as He said: ﴿And We called to him from the right side of the mount and brought him near as a confidant﴾ [Maryam 52]. The wisdom behind the appearance of this fire, Allah knows best, I do not know for certain. But perhaps part of the wisdom is that this very place, in the sacred valley, is blessed and holy, so the beginning of revelation occurred in that place. And he (peace be upon him) was at a distance during his journey.
* The student: (...)?
* The Shaykh: What is (...)?
* The student: (...).
* The Shaykh: That does not contradict it. A person may be able to bear it. For this reason, when Musa chose seventy men from his people, and Allah spoke to Musa while they listened, they said: ﴿We will not believe you until we see Allah openly﴾ [al-Baqarah 55]. So what appears to me now is that, Allah knows best, this specific place is the holy and blessed one, and perhaps by reflection (...) will be reached.
* A student: (...)?
* The Shaykh: From His saying: ﴿those in the fire and those around it﴾.

* * *

I seek refuge with Allah from the accursed Satan. ﴿And put your hand into your pocket﴾ [al-Naml 12]. "Pocket" (jayb) here is explained as the collar of the shirt.

His saying ﴿put your hand﴾: the word "yad" (hand) in its full sense refers only to the palm, and does not include the forearm unless it is qualified. The evidence for this is that when Allah mentioned tayammum (dry ablution), He said: ﴿wipe your faces and your hands﴾ [al-Ma'idah 6], and this became specific to the two palms. When Allah, blessed and exalted, intended the forearm, He said in wudu': ﴿and your hands up to the elbows﴾.

So, according to the requirements of the Arabic language, what Musa was commanded to put in is not the forearm but the palm, which he places into his pocket in this manner.

﴿into your pocket, it will come out white﴾: the verb ﴿will come out﴾ is in the jussive mood (jazm, the grammatical mood that shortens or drops the final vowel), even though it is an imperfect verb and no jussive particle precedes it. So by what is it jussive?

* The students: By the response to the imperative.
* The Shaykh: By the response to the imperative, which is ﴿put in﴾.

It is well known that when the fa' (the conjunctive "then") is dropped and a conditional meaning is intended, the verb takes the jussive. This is the rule: when the fa' of causation (fa' al-sababiyyah) comes after an imperative, the verb is put in the subjunctive by it or by an implied "an". If the fa' is dropped after an imperative and a conditional meaning is intended, the verb is put in the jussive. This is a known rule in grammar (nahw).

﴿It will come out﴾ means: the hand (differing in color from its former skin tone), ﴿white without harm﴾. From where did the author derive that its color was the skin tone?

* A student: ﴿It will come out white﴾.
* The Shaykh: From His saying ﴿it will come out white﴾, because if it had been white before, He would not have said ﴿it will come out white﴾. So it must have changed from the first color to the second.

His saying ﴿white﴾ is a circumstantial accusative (hal) referring to the subject of ﴿will come out﴾; that is, while it is white.

﴿without harm﴾ is a restriction on His saying ﴿white﴾, because whiteness may be a defect, like vitiligo (baras), which is a defect because it displeases its bearer. But He said ﴿without harm﴾. So this whiteness is not like the whiteness of vitiligo. For this reason the author says: (﴿white without harm﴾: vitiligo, it has a radiance that dazzles the sight, a sign).

As for his saying (it has a radiance), this requires evidence. Allah, blessed and exalted, mentioned only that it was white, and that is enough as a sign: that a hand enters with one color and comes out with another. As for adding a radiance, Allah did not mention it, and we have no right to go beyond what the Qur'an indicates in these matters. We mentioned earlier that factual matters (al-masa'il al-khabariyyah) have no room for personal opinion. What should one restrict oneself to in them? One restricts oneself to what the report (khabar) has brought. So we say: it was white, and that is a sufficient sign.

The author said: (a sign among ﴿nine signs﴾). The "in" here indicates location (zarfiyyah), so this sign is among the nine, and likewise the sign of the staff is among the nine, not in addition to them.

(﴿among nine signs﴾, sent with him ﴿to Pharaoh and his people﴾.) Musa knew two of these nine signs, which are the staff and the hand. But seven remain. What are the signs?

We say: ﴿among nine signs﴾: two are well known. The rest of the nine: ﴿So We sent upon them the flood, the locusts, the lice, the frogs, and the blood﴾ [al-A'raf 133]. These are five. With the two, that makes seven. ﴿And We certainly seized the people of Pharaoh with years of drought and shortage of fruits﴾ [al-A'raf 130]. So all together they were nine signs. These are the nine signs.

﴿We sent upon them the flood﴾ [al-A'raf 133]: and what is the flood? The inundation, a flood of water.

The locusts are well known. The lice (qummal) are the worms that appear in grains; this is the qummal. The frogs are well known.

Blood is also well known. Some scholars say that the water, when they drank it, became blood, and when the Copt handed it to the Israelite, it returned to being water. But Shaykh 'Abd al-Rahman al-Sa'di, may Allah have mercy on him, took a different view. He said: the flood is the inundation, which spoils crops before they emerge; the locusts eat crops after they emerge; because some crops are still growing and the water spoils them, while what has come out is eaten by the locusts, and what is stored is spoiled by the lice. The water is spoiled by the frogs. Is that right?

So now: the food and drink were spoiled. This food and drink, when a person eats or drinks it, turns into blood, and blood was also sent upon them, namely nosebleeds (ru'af).

On this view, their food was spoiled, and what came from the food was also impure. This, in reality, is the sound meaning. Because when the water becomes blood, the water is spoiled by the frogs. When frogs are in the water, it becomes (...), its smell becomes foul and its appearance becomes repulsive, and one cannot put one's lips to it except (...).

In summary: the correct view is what the Shaykh, may Allah have mercy on him, adopted in his tafsir. These are the nine signs: the years and the shortage of fruits. The "years" (al-sinin): what does it mean? Drought and famine, which is the absence of (...). For everyone who ruled Egypt while a disbeliever, like Kisra, a generic name for everyone who ruled Persia while a disbeliever, and likewise Qaysar for everyone who ruled Rome while a disbeliever. Yes.

His saying "the people" (al-qawm) means the companions (al-as-hab), and companions are called "qawm" because a person's stability (qiwam) depends on them; a person takes pride in his people and stands by them.

His saying ﴿Indeed, they were a defiantly disobedient people﴾ is the reason for sending him to them. That is: We sent you with nine signs to these people because they were a defiantly disobedient people, meaning people who had left obedience. We have already learned in the lesson on tawhid (monotheism) that fisq (defiant disobedience) is divided into two kinds: the greater fisq, which is leaving obedience altogether, and the lesser fisq, which is leaving complete obedience. Is that right, everyone? Let us see whether someone can explain the difference between the two expressions.

* A student: (...).
* The Shaykh: "Complete obedience" (al-ta'ah al-mutlaqah). What is the difference between complete obedience and "obedience in general" (mutlaq al-ta'ah)?
* The student: Complete obedience (...).
* The Shaykh: That is, it includes every instance of obedience; complete obedience.
* The student: (...).
* The Shaykh: That is, he obeys in every command. Yes.
* The student: (...).
* The Shaykh: In practice, when one says, "This man has obeyed Allah," meaning complete obedience, it means in everything he was commanded. So if he commits fisq, he has gone out of complete obedience, because the difference between "the absolute of a thing" (mutlaq al-shay') and "the thing in its absolute form" (al-shay' al-mutlaq) is this: the absolute of a thing means the existence of any part of it, while the thing in its absolute form means the complete thing. Therefore, according to the people of the Sunnah and the community (ahl al-sunnah wa al-jama'ah), does the defiant sinner have complete faith or the basic level of faith?

* The students: He has the basic level of faith.
* The Shaykh: He has the basic level of faith. "Complete obedience," when one says "this man is a fasiq," means he has gone out of complete obedience. So his fisq is...?
* A student: Lesser.
* The Shaykh: No, greater. That is, it cannot be said of him that he has even the least obedience; he never obeyed at all. This is a disbeliever.

And when one says "this defiant person has left complete obedience," it means he still has some obedience, but he does not have complete obedience.

For this reason, they also say in fiqh (jurisprudence): this is "absolute water" (ma' mutlaq), and this is "water in general" (mutlaq ma'). They said: water that has been changed by pure substances is not purifying, because it is not absolute water; it is only water in general.

So the difference between these expressions is known to the jurists, the scholars of usul (legal theory), and the theologians. The difference between "the absolute of a thing" and "the thing in its absolute form" is: the thing in its absolute form means its perfection, and the absolute of a thing means its basic form.

Here, ﴿Indeed, they were a defiantly disobedient people﴾: which of the two kinds of fisq?

* A student: The greater fisq.
* The Shaykh: The greater fisq, because they have left obedience in general; they had no obedience at all.

Allah, may He be exalted, said: ﴿But when Our signs came to them, visible﴾ [al-Naml 13]. The pronoun in ﴿came to them﴾ refers to Pharaoh and his people.

His saying ﴿Our signs﴾ means the indications that confirm the truthfulness of Musa (ﷺ) in his messengerhood and the correctness of what he called to. The signs with which Allah sent Musa indicate two things: the truthfulness of Musa, which is a confirmation of him, and the soundness of what he brought. So these signs include both.
