The first ground: explaining affirmation by negation, which is a deficiency.
The second: it loses a meaning, namely denial when asked; it is takdhib when presented, and jahd when sought.
* Student: The words of Allah the Exalted: ﴿And they denied them, though their souls were convinced of them﴾ (...)?
* Shaykh: Yes, it is known that they denied and concealed, but they were certain.
* Student: (...)?
* Shaykh: Yes, they did not openly acknowledge; the point is only that his explanation of it in this way is wrong.

He said: (﴿And﴾ indeed ﴿their souls were convinced of them﴾, i.e., they were certain).
Pay attention, brothers. The author said: (﴿And﴾ indeed ﴿they were convinced of them﴾). What required him to supply (qad)?
We say: because the clause is a circumstantial clause (ḥāl), and a circumstantial clause that is a past verb has qad supplied before it for emphasis (taḥqīq).

Second, he said: ﴿their souls were convinced of them﴾; he said: (i.e., they were certain that it was from Allah). He explained (istayqana) as (tayaqqana), indicating that the sīn and tā' are extra. But it is better that the sīn and tā' remain in their proper function and not be judged as extra, because istiyqān is more intensive than tayaqqun. It is well known among them that they say: an increase in form indicates an increase in meaning. So istiyqān is more emphatic: they were certain of them with complete certainty, having no doubt in them, and yet they denied them. This denial alongside certainty is more severe; for this reason He said: ﴿in injustice and haughtiness﴾, and so on.

His saying, ﴿And they denied them, though their souls were convinced of them﴾, and He did not say "and they were convinced of them." The attribution of the certainty to the souls is more emphatic: that is, it is a certainty that reached their souls so that it took firm hold of them, yet, may Allah protect us, they denied and rejected them.

His saying: ﴿in injustice and haughtiness﴾. The author says: (haughtiness against believing in what Moses brought), explaining the two words with one word, which is pride. But if we look at the noble verse, we find that it is more eloquent than how he explained it.

As for ﴿injustice﴾: zulm in origin means deficiency. From it is His saying: ﴿Each of the two gardens brought forth its produce and did not fall short of it in anything﴾ [al-Kahf 33]. What is the meaning of ﴿did not fall short of it﴾? That is, did not diminish.

So its origin is the meaning of diminishing, and whoever diminishes the right of another is a wrongdoer; if a person diminishes his own right, he is a wrongdoer to himself, and if he diminishes the right of another, he is a wrongdoer to that other.

Here, these people diminished the right of Moses, peace be upon him, so they are wrongdoers; and they diminished the right of their own souls, in that they did not lead them to what is good for them, so they too are wrongdoers.

Then, what drove this injustice and diminishing? He said: ﴿haughtiness﴾, and this is a meaning other than injustice; that is, arrogance toward what Moses, peace be upon him, brought. They saw that Moses: who is Moses, who comes to Pharaoh, who says to his people, "I am your Lord, the Most High," and then says, "I am a messenger to you, you must follow me!" By the nature of the wicked human, he becomes arrogant and says: never! So they denied, ﴿in injustice﴾ toward whom? Toward Moses and themselves. ﴿Haughtiness﴾: arrogance toward Moses and toward what he brought as well. So they, may Allah protect us, were characterized by both qualities.

His saying: ﴿in injustice and haughtiness﴾. The author says: (it refers back to the denial).
Correct, not to the certainty; for certainty is not injustice. If they were certain that Moses was truthful, that is not injustice; that is the truth, and their certainty would be justice and humility. But they did not submit to that certainty; that is, they did not yield to it.

So it refers back to the denial: they denied them in injustice and haughtiness.

But the benefit of introducing the circumstantial clause ﴿and their souls were convinced of them﴾, placed between the verb and its complements, is: hastening to censure them, because their denying while certain is more grave and severe. One who denies while in doubt may be excused, but with certainty there is no excuse.

So the benefit of the interjected circumstantial clause ﴿and their souls were convinced of them﴾ between the verb and its object is: what is its benefit? Hastening to censure them, and showing that they reached the extreme of this description, which is injustice and haughtiness.

What is the grammatical status of ﴿injustice and haughtiness﴾: is it an object of purpose (maf'ūl li-ajlih), that is, for the sake of injustice and haughtiness, or is it a verbal noun in the sense of a circumstantial state, that is, "being unjust and haughty"?
* Students: The latter is better.
* Shaykh: The latter is better, because if we make injustice and haughtiness an object of purpose, they precede the denial, since they were unjust and haughty and then denied.

So on this basis we say that "injustice and haughtiness" is a verbal noun in the sense of an active participle; that is, they denied them while being in what state?
* Student: Unjust and haughty.
* Shaykh: Unjust and haughty.

Allah, Blessed and Exalted, said: (﴿So look﴾, O Muhammad) and so on. ﴿So look﴾: is it a look of reflection or a look of sight?
* Students: A look of reflection.
* Shaykh: A look of reflection, because a look of sight is impossible here, why? Because its time has passed. But it is a look of reflection.

According to the author's words, the address returns to the Messenger of Allah ﷺ: (﴿So look﴾, O Muhammad).

It has been mentioned to us several times that the singular address in the Qur'an is not restricted to the Messenger, peace be upon him, except where evidence indicates it. Where evidence indicates it, it is as the evidence shows; otherwise it is general, and the sense becomes: "So look, O addressee," not "O Muhammad, so look," because the Qur'an is in the hands of everyone.

As for what evidence shows is specific to the Messenger, peace be upon him, it is specific to him, such as the words of Allah the Exalted: ﴿O Messenger, convey what has been sent down to you from your Lord﴾ [al-Ma'idah 67], and His words: ﴿Did We not expand for you your breast?﴾ [al-Sharh 1].

What shows that the singular address is general: first, the reason we mentioned, that the Qur'an is in the hands of all people. Second, Allah the Exalted said: ﴿O Prophet, when you divorce women, divorce them﴾ [al-Talaq 1]; He addressed with the singular and the plural: ﴿O Prophet, when you divorce...﴾, and this shows that the address directed to the Messenger, peace be upon him, is directed to the community unless evidence indicates that it is specific to him, as with the two examples we gave. Likewise from this: ﴿O Prophet, why do you forbid what Allah has made lawful for you?﴾ [al-Tahrim 1]; this is specific to the Messenger, peace be upon him, since he is the one who forbade, yet the ruling is general.

So ﴿So look﴾: what do we say? We say: O addressee.

﴿So look how was the end of the corrupters﴾. In this verse, first: kāna raises the subject and puts the predicate in the accusative, is that not so? This is known to you: kāna raises the subject and puts the predicate in the accusative, ﴿And Allah was ever Forgiving﴾ [al-Nisa' 96].

Second: if the subject is feminine, the verb is feminine. Here we do not see a predicate for kāna in ﴿how was the end of the corrupters﴾.
* Student: (...).
* Shaykh: Good. And the second?
* Student: The second: that ʿāqibah is a metaphorically feminine noun (...).
* Shaykh: Good, the second answer is correct; that is, ʿāqibah is metaphorically feminine, not truly feminine. The difference between metaphorical and true feminine: whatever has a female sex is truly feminine, and whatever has no sex and whose femininity is merely grammatical is metaphorically feminine.

As for the first, namely his saying that it is incomplete or complete, that is not correct.
* Student: Kāna is complete, and the predicate is fronted, which is (kayfa).
* Shaykh: Yes, this is correct: the predicate is fronted, which is (kayfa). Is it fronted obligatorily or optionally?
* Student: Obligatorily.
* Shaykh: Why? Because it is an interrogative, and interrogatives have precedence; an interrogative cannot occur in the middle of speech, it must come first. We have understood the grammar.

So ʿāqibah: what is the meaning of ʿāqibah? Originally, ʿāqibah means lateness, and from it ʿaqb of the foot, the heel, the back part. What is the meaning of ʿāqibah? A matter that comes later; that is, look at what their affair came to in the end.

His saying: ﴿the corrupters﴾: those whose condition became corruption. Corruption here does not mean the corruption of civilization, for civilization in Pharaoh's time may have reached its peak; rather, the intended corruption is moral corruption: the corruption of morals and beliefs.

It may be followed by corruption of civilization, as Allah the Exalted said: ﴿Corruption has appeared on land and sea by what the hands of people have earned﴾ [al-Rum 41], and ﴿Allah presents an example: a town that was secure and at peace, its provision coming to it abundantly from every place, but it denied the favors of Allah﴾ [al-Nahl 112]. By this estimation, namely that the basic corruption mentioned in the Qur'an is corruption of morals and beliefs, which is followed by corruption of deeds, we come to know that what people now boast about regarding luxury, tranquillity, security and the like, and when they come to mention religion they say: "the tolerant creed," and do not mention action. Then the word "tolerant" itself indicates weakness in this creed: "tolerant" means that everything is permitted. It is true that it is the tolerant Hanafiyyah beyond doubt, but it has deeds and it has firmness. For this reason, concentrating on physical comfort and bodily pleasure while mentioning belief alone is, in my view, dangerous, because each one begins to chant what? These two matters. He says: I have a sound creed, a tolerant creed, gentle, easy, accepting of everything; and he says: I also seek bodily comfort and security and the like. But the uprightness of religion and striving to establish it among people through enjoining good, forbidding evil, and jihad in the way of Allah: this is a matter that is hardly mentioned.

In reality, if luxury is only for the body, it is corruption, and it does not last at all. Moreover, absolute physical luxury must be accompanied by anxiety in the heart, because Allah the Exalted only guaranteed a good life to whom? ﴿Whoever does righteousness, whether male or female, while being a believer﴾ [al-Nahl 97]. Note belief and action, and He began with action as well: ﴿Whoever does righteousness, whether male or female, while being a believer, We will surely cause him to live a good life, and We will surely give them their reward according to the best of what they used to do﴾: a good life in this world and a good reward in the Hereafter.

This is what must be emphasized. As for absolute luxury, it is a great harm to a person; it causes heedlessness of Allah, the Exalted, and the preoccupation of a person with seeking fleeting bodily comfort.

One of the salaf said: If the kings and the sons of kings knew what we are in, they would fight us for it with swords (...), of the bliss and joy and expansion of the breast that you are in, and the like.

* * *

I seek refuge in Allah from Satan the accursed. Allah the Exalted said: ﴿And for Solomon were gathered his soldiers of the jinn and mankind and birds, and they were marshaled in ranks﴾ [al-Naml 17]. And before we speak...
* Student: (...).
* Shaykh: Yes, no, we took that (...), and we told you: the emphasis in ﴿Indeed, this is the clear favor﴾ is not emphasized with speech.
* From this verse is derived: ﴿And they denied them, though their souls were convinced of them, in injustice and haughtiness. So look how was the end of the corrupters﴾ [al-Naml 14].
* Several benefits are derived from it. First: despite the strength of the signs that Moses brought, these people did not benefit from them. This is taken from His saying: ﴿and they denied them﴾, and when signs are strong, there is no room left for denial; but, may Allah protect us, Allah blinded their insight, so they denied them.
* And it is derived from this: the denial of these addressed people was out of obstinacy, not out of doubt, from His saying: ﴿and their souls were convinced of them﴾. Did this happen to the Quraysh with the Prophet, peace be upon him?
* Students: It happened (...).
* Shaykh: Yes, it happened, by His saying: ﴿We know indeed that what they say grieves you, but it is not you they deny; rather, the wrongdoers deny the signs of Allah﴾ [al-An'am 33]. There is no doubt that this occurred among the leaders and chiefs; but the common people may not have had this matter, rather they are either followers. As for the leaders and the great, there is no doubt about this. In this is evidence of the evil condition of the family of Pharaoh, from His saying: ﴿in injustice and haughtiness﴾: ﴿injustice﴾ toward whom? Toward themselves and toward Moses; ﴿haughtiness﴾: arrogance toward the truth.
* And in it is evidence that the attribution of these two qualities makes a person one of the Pharaonic nation, namely injustice and haughtiness. There is no quality by which a servant leaves the even path except that he has in it a leader from the people of disbelief. For this reason the Prophet, peace be upon him, informed that people would follow the ways of those before them[[Agreed upon; related by al-Bukhari (3456), Muslim (2669/6), and al-Hakim in al-Mustadrak (8610) from Ibn 'Abbas, and the wording is his.]].
* Rejection of the truth has a leader for the one who does it, like Pharaoh and Qarun; envy has a leader for the human being, like the Jews; showing off has a leader for the human being, like the hypocrites; and so on. Indeed, it also belongs to the hypocrites. There is no trait by which a servant leaves the even path except that it has a leader from the people of disbelief.
* And in this is evidence of the blameworthiness of arrogance toward the truth, from His saying: ﴿and haughtiness﴾. There is no difference whether that is out of good intention or not? This way is blameworthy even if out of good intention. Our saying "out of good intention" is to include some imitators who, when the evidence from the Book and the Sunnah is presented to them, say: "We follow so-and-so, because he is more knowledgeable than us." This is out of apparent good intention. And what is the aspect of good intention? Because they see that this imam they followed is more knowledgeable than you, and say: "We are ignorant and have nothing but to imitate, and this man is more knowledgeable than us." And what do you say?
* Student: (...) this is the word of Allah and His Messenger, he said: but this statement is the statement of so-and-so, which (...) out of good intention, not out of partisanship for opinion. So this statement contains blame, because he followed him when the saying of the Messenger was presented to him, and he did not accept it.
* Shaykh: Yes.
* And it is derived from this verse: if this attribute is blameworthy and Pharaonic, then its opposite is praiseworthy. What is the opposite?
* Students: Humility.

Commentary of Ibn 'Uthaymin (Tafsir al-Quran al-Karim) on surah 27, verse 14–16 (part 2 of 3):

* The Shaykh: Humility before the truth and accepting it is undoubtedly praiseworthy, because when Allah the Exalted dispraises a quality, its opposite is praised with good.

* The verse also indicates that a person should, or must, reflect and contemplate the outcomes of those who came before, based on His saying: ﴿So look how was the end of the corrupters﴾. Does a person look at the outcome of the corrupters, or at the outcome of the corrupters and the reformers?

* A student: Both.

* The Shaykh: Good. So what is the benefit of (...) ﴿So look how﴾? Because the context is one of threat. When the context is one of encouragement, we say to a person: Look how was the end of the reformers.
﴿So look how﴾, because the context is one of warning; and when the context is one of encouragement, we say to a person: Look how was the end of the righteous. Yes, it is clear. ﴿Why were there not among the generations before you those of remaining virtue who forbade corruption on earth, except a few of those We saved from among them?﴾ [Hud 116].
So the matter differs: in the context of intimidation, we refer the person to the outcome of the corrupters, in the context of intimidation. And in the context of encouragement, we refer him to the outcome of the reformers, so that he may beware of those and be eager for these.

It also contains evidence for the virtue of reflecting and contemplating the reports of those who passed away, and that the study of history is among the things the Sharia has brought, for we cannot look at how their end was except by studying and tracing their reports. Yes, so the knowledge of history is among the intended matters, but is it intended in itself or incidentally?

Incidentally, except for the biography of the Prophet ﷺ and his rightly guided Caliphs, for it is part of the religion, because it is all rulings. This is unlike looking into history merely for the sake of taking lessons. So every context has its own speech, because looking into history merely for lessons may let a person learn from others and thus be content without it, but looking into the biography of the Prophet ﷺ is jurisprudential rulings; this is intended in itself, and a person cannot do without it by means of anything else. ﴿So look how was the end of the corrupters﴾.

* A student: (...).

* The Shaykh: Yes indeed. If a person reflects on their civilization and their strength, and yet Allah destroyed them, there is no harm in that. But if he wants to reflect on their strength in order to praise them and extol them, this is not permissible. For this reason Allah the Exalted did not command us to look at their strength except after He commanded us to look at their end.

On this basis, those who go to the dwellings of Thamud for sightseeing and recreation are sinners. The Messenger ﷺ said: «Do not enter upon these punished people except while weeping». So it is not permissible for a person to go on a trip, for example, to that place unless he enters while weeping. «And if you are not weeping, then do not enter upon them» [[Agreed upon; al-Bukhari (433) and Muslim (2890 / 38) from the hadith of Ibn 'Umar.]].

Praise be to Allah, a person has no need of this; it is not necessary to go there for recreation. But unfortunately, now they have become monuments, meaning that they are visited to show the strength of these people, their creativity and their firm management of their affairs, while they do not pay attention to what punishment Allah brought upon them, and we seek refuge in Allah.

* A student: The Messenger ﷺ commanded hastening, how for example..

* The Shaykh: Yes, that is it.

Allah the Exalted says: ﴿And We had certainly given knowledge to Dawud and Sulayman. And they said, "Praise be to Allah, who has favored us over many of His believing servants."﴾ [An-Naml 15].

From this verse is derived: the explanation of what Allah the Exalted bestowed upon Dawud and Sulayman, based on His saying: ﴿And We had certainly given knowledge to Dawud and Sulayman﴾.

And it also contains evidence for Allah the Exalted's praise of Himself, because His praising Himself by giving Dawud and Sulayman knowledge is a form of praise. Is it praiseworthy for creation that a person praise himself for his own virtue or not? It is not praiseworthy unless there is a benefit to others in it, not to you. As for Allah the Exalted, He praises Himself to be praised. But you do not do this. However, if there is a benefit to others in it, such as a person who narrates something about himself so that he may be followed in goodness, there is no harm in that, or so that people may benefit from what he has.

Ibn Mas'ud, may Allah be pleased with him, said: «If I knew that someone whom camels could reach knows the Book of Allah better than I do, I would seek him out» or as he said [[Agreed upon; al-Bukhari (5002) and Muslim (2463 / 115) from the hadith of Ibn Mas'ud, with the wording: "If I knew someone more knowledgeable of the Book of Allah than me whom camels could reach, I would ride to him."]].

And the scholars have continued to praise their books. Ibn Malik says:
It brings the far near with concise wording, and extends generosity with a fulfilled promise,
and it draws contentment without anger: the Alfiyya of Ibn Mu'tit, surpassing all others.

* A student: If he had not said: "surpassing" (...).

* The Shaykh: The point in any case is that such (praise) is not for the benefit of the person himself; it is for the benefit of others, so that they may benefit from this composition, for example.

* A student: Sometimes he exaggerates, O Shaykh, or overdoes it.

* The Shaykh: In any case.. there is no extravagance; (...) although in reality a person may be accused, whatever his intention, he may be accused. But a person need not concern himself with people's opinion if he has put right what is between him and his Lord.

The main point in this verse is evidence for Allah the Exalted praising Himself for what He has graciously bestowed upon His servants, by His saying: ﴿And We had certainly given knowledge to Dawud and Sulayman﴾.

The third: the virtue of Dawud and Sulayman, and that they were worthy of this blessing, because Allah the Blessed and Exalted says: ﴿Allah knows best where to place His message﴾ [Al-An'am 124]. So there is no bounty Allah gives to a servant except that it is in its proper place, because Allah is All-Wise.

* A student: (...).

* The Shaykh: Yes indeed. And it contains evidence for the virtue of knowledge, based on His saying: ﴿And We had certainly given knowledge to Dawud and Sulayman﴾.

There is no doubt about this, the virtue of knowledge. Allah the Exalted says: ﴿Say, "Are those who know equal to those who do not know?"﴾ [Az-Zumar 9]. But the question remains: what is the praiseworthy knowledge? This is what people are now disputing: what is the praiseworthy knowledge?

* A student: (...).

* The Shaykh: What is meant is the knowledge of the Sharia, what is meant is the knowledge of the Sharia. That is the praiseworthy knowledge. As for whatever is other than the knowledge of the Sharia, it is not praised except insofar as it leads to something praiseworthy. Knowledge other than the knowledge of the Sharia is not praised except where it leads to a praiseworthy matter.

The opposite of what the people of today are upon: many ignorant people praise knowledge other than Sharia. Some people, and we seek refuge in Allah, see that the knowledge of the Sharia is backwardness and that the knowledge of nature is progress. For this reason such people praise these scholars (...) and the layers of the earth and other things, and you find him, for example, praising: "This is the origin of knowledge," or "This is knowledge," and similar things. Or if he sees some strange crafts (...), "Knowledge, knowledge!" There is no doubt that such a person prefers this age over the age of the Companions. This is not the intended meaning. Whatever Allah has praised of knowledge, this is not what is intended; rather what is intended is the knowledge of the Sharia, because the knowledge of the Sharia is what benefits creation. Even the knowledge of the Sharia is what guides them to these sciences they boast of, because Allah commands us to strive upon the earth: ﴿He it is who made the earth submissive to you, so walk in its tracts and eat of His provision﴾ [Al-Mulk 15], and ﴿Have they not looked into the dominion of the heavens and the earth?﴾ [Al-A'raf 185], and similar.

So the summary, O brothers, is that the knowledge with which Allah favored Dawud and Sulayman and praised them for is the knowledge of the Sharia. Likewise, all that the texts say in praise of knowledge refers to the knowledge of the Sharia, because it is what is praised for its own sake. And whatever else, when is it praised?

* Students: When it leads to something praiseworthy.

* The Shaykh: When it leads to something praiseworthy. Otherwise, if it leads to something blameworthy, it is blameworthy, and if it leads to something neither praised nor blamed, it is neither praised nor blamed.

* A student: (...).

* The Shaykh: (...).

* A student: (...) they bring a doubt (...), this doubt deceives some ignorant people (...) he says: it increases lifespan (...) perhaps, I mean, it did not agree (...) the Messenger ﷺ nor the knowledge of the Companions, and despite this (...) we reached the depths of the seas (...). I have read a lot about these people.

* The Shaykh: This is from ignorance. For this reason, their knowledge now is not praiseworthy unless it leads to something praiseworthy; otherwise it is not praiseworthy. Would that they had reached the depths of the seas and the horizons of space! These are the ones who made what destroys creation, such as bombs and weapons. Is this praiseworthy?

* A student: No.

* The Shaykh: Then we say: do these sciences contradict Sharia knowledge? We wish that the Muslims also would reach these matters so that they benefit themselves and benefit creation.

* A student: O Shaykh, the texts in the Book and the Sunnah that praise knowledge, do you mean Sharia knowledge?

* The Shaykh: Not at all, Sharia knowledge.

* A student: The saying of the Exalted (...) together with His saying (...), how is this?

* The Shaykh: There is nothing in it. There is no contradiction between them.

* A student: (...) mercy, just mercy.

* The Shaykh: But this mercy is in its proper place. This mercy is in its proper place.

* There is also evidence here for the virtue of Dawud and Sulayman from the aspect of their acknowledging Allah's blessing and thanking Him for it, based on His saying: ﴿And they said﴾.

* A student: (...).

* The Shaykh: No, we mentioned it from one aspect, and this is from another aspect, namely their performing the thanks for Allah's blessing: ﴿And they said, "Praise be to Allah, who has favored us..."﴾. They did not say: "We were given this on account of knowledge from ourselves," or "because we are clever," or similar things. They said: ﴿Praise be to Allah, who has favored us over many of His believing servants﴾.

* In this is also evidence that thanks is given by speech as it is by action, by speech and by action, and also by belief, by conviction. Thanks has three locations: the heart, the tongue, and the limbs.

The poet said:
Blessings from me have benefited you in three: my hand, my tongue, and the hidden inner self.

The evidence that thanks occurs in three places: here in the tongue. The Prophet ﷺ, when it was said to him, "Why do you do this, when you were – he would stand until his feet swelled – and Allah has forgiven you what preceded of your sin?" He said: «Should I not love to be a grateful servant?» [[Agreed upon; al-Bukhari (1130) and Muslim (2819 / 79) from the hadith of al-Mughira.]] So he made the action thanks to Allah the Exalted. And Allah the Exalted says: ﴿Work, O family of Dawud, in gratitude﴾ [Saba' 13].

As for acknowledging blessings in the heart, it is part of thanks. What is the evidence? His saying: ﴿And whatever blessing you have is from Allah; then when adversity touches you, to Him you cry for help﴾ [An-Nahl 53].

Allah wants us to believe this news. For this reason Allah the Blessed and Exalted dispraised those who attributed His blessing to themselves, did they not? And what did He say about Qarun? ﴿He said, "I was only given it on account of knowledge I have."﴾ [Al-Qasas 78]. Then Allah the Exalted said: ﴿Did he not know that Allah had destroyed before him generations who were greater than him in strength and greater in accumulation?﴾ [Al-Qasas 78].

And regarding this matter, all three locations of thanks: few people fulfill them. Some people, for example, rely on the means by which a blessing reaches them and forget the Causer. Understood? When a person gives you something, a need of your needs, you find that gratitude for this giver arises in his heart more than gratitude to Allah; you find him praising this person more than he praises Allah; you find him serving this person more than he serves Allah.

Yet the one through whose hand the blessing reached you is only a means to bring it to you. Otherwise, who placed in his heart that he should convey this blessing to you? Allah the Exalted, and it is He who facilitated this.

So the summary is that most people now, or the majority, fall short in the station of thanks, whether in the heart, the tongue, or the limbs.

* And in this is evidence that when Allah bestows a blessing upon a person, it is prescribed for him to praise Him for it. Texts have come concerning this: when you finish eating and drinking you say: "Praise be to Allah"; when you wake up you praise Allah; when you put on a garment you praise Allah. And so on. This is among the lawful matters: praising Allah the Exalted for blessings.

* The verse also contains evidence for the humility of Dawud and Sulayman and their knowledge of the reality, in His saying: ﴿who favored us over many of His believing servants﴾. He did not mention absolute favor over all the believers: ﴿over many of His believing servants﴾. Does this imply describing the prophets with faith?

* A student: (...).

* The Shaykh: No, meaning: does His saying ﴿over many of His believing servants﴾ suggest that they are among the believers?

* A student: Yes.

* The Shaykh: Apparently it does suggest this, meaning that we share with them the description of faith, and Allah favored us over many of them.

* The verse also contains evidence that when a person sees that he is better than others by Allah's blessing upon him, this does not contradict humility. That is: when you feel that Allah has blessed you with wealth and favored you over this person, does that mean you have elevated yourself and become arrogant? No. Rather, you cannot recognize Allah's blessing upon you until you know its opposite in others, right? You cannot know this unless you know its opposite.

If you see, for example, a person afflicted in his body while Allah has granted you health, you recognize the virtue of Allah's blessing, so say: "Praise be to Allah who has granted me health from what He has afflicted him with, and favored me over him."

When you see an ignorant person while Allah has blessed you with knowledge, you likewise recognize the virtue of Allah's blessing upon you in this, and this is not counted as elevation or looking down on others. For this reason He said: ﴿Praise be to Allah who has favored us over many of His believing servants﴾. Someone may appear to think that if he sees his own superiority over others by what Allah has bestowed on him, this is a blameworthy matter and includes elevation (...) and looking down on others. But the matter is not so.

* A student: (...).

* The Shaykh: Yes indeed. In it there is also this benefit: that speaking of it is a form of thanks. From it is derived this benefit: the legitimacy of speaking of Allah's blessing, but not in the manner of boasting or exalting oneself over others. For this reason it has come in the hadith from the Messenger ﷺ that he said: «I am the master of the children of Adam, and I say so without boasting» [[Narrated by al-Tirmidhi (3148) from the hadith of Abu Sa'id.]].

So if a person speaks of Allah's blessing without boasting of it, there is no harm in that, no harm at all. Indeed, this may even be prescribed, because it is praise of Allah the Blessed and Exalted for what He has bestowed upon him.

* A student: (...).

* The Shaykh: (...).

* The student: (...).

* The Shaykh: How so?

* The student: (...) Allah said: ﴿over many of His believing servants﴾, that they both had acted (...).

* The Shaykh: (...) there is, I mean, there is a difficulty in it; because we now have no knowledge that the prophets knew that Muhammad would be sent. In the Qur'an: ﴿And when Allah took the covenant of the prophets: "Whatever I have given you of Scripture and wisdom, and then there comes to you a messenger confirming what is with you, you must believe in him and you must support him."﴾ [Aal 'Imran 81]. The word "messenger" (rasul) is indefinite or definite?

* A student: Indefinite.

* The Shaykh: Indefinite. It does not indicate that Allah specified Muhammad ﷺ to them. Although Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with him, said: «Allah took the covenant from the prophets: if Muhammad is sent...»[[Tafsir Ibn Kathir (8 / 110).]]. This is his interpretation; as for the verse, it does not indicate this.

Student: (...).

Shaykh: Yes, it does not contradict... (...) it is correct and indicates it.

Student: (...).

Shaykh: Certainly, David had access to the Torah, since he came after Moses. Yes, this is (...).

Student: (...).

Shaykh: (...).

Student: (...) proof of Allah's knowledge (...).

Shaykh: What do you think of this benefit? Proof of Allah's knowledge, because He gave knowledge, and one who lacks a thing cannot give it.

Student: (...).

Shaykh: (...) This is testimony that it is very strong. Yes, then (...) proof of Allah's knowledge. Its explanation: Allah, glorified and exalted, gave these two knowledge, and He does not give knowledge except to one who has knowledge, because He teaches them. Teaches them what? What He Himself knows.

Student: (...).

Shaykh: Yes.

Student: (...).

Shaykh: Neither this nor that; it depends on the intention of the person. Even the first, a person's feeling of superiority over others by what Allah has favoured him with, may be arrogance. And this is similar: it may be disdain. And a person may look at Allah's blessing upon others with the perspective of wisdom, saying: Allah is Wise, and had this person not been worthy, He would not have given him. Then he strives to perfect virtues (...). The point is that this matter returns to intention in this and that.

Student: O Shaykh (...).

Shaykh: I have no knowledge; I do not know.

Student: O Shaykh (...) the benefit (...) does not conflict with saying (...) because I know (...) David and Solomon; nevertheless he was preferred (...).

Shaykh: By what do you weigh?

Student: I weigh it by this.

Shaykh: By knowledge.

Student: (...) the speech of the birds (...).

Shaykh: In any case, the benefit is attained. It is correct, meaning that it does not necessarily follow that a person's superiority in one attribute makes him superior to others absolutely. Yes, but, taking from this, can it be derived from this verse that one who excels another in an attribute is not necessarily more excellent than him absolutely? Is it derived from...?

Students: It is derived from the verse that follows.

Shaykh: The one that follows (...).

Student: The clarification of the wisdom of David and Solomon, in that they joined praise with its cause (...).

Shaykh: Here, if they did not mention that, for what would they praise Allah? They want to praise Him for this matter.

* * *

The next verse: ﴿And Solomon inherited from David, and he said: O people, we have been taught the speech of the birds, and we have been given of everything. Indeed, this is evidently the great bounty.﴾ [An-Naml 16].

* In this is evidence that Solomon came after David, because of His saying: ﴿And Solomon inherited from David﴾. Inheritance, as we have said, is that a person succeeds another in something, whether knowledge or wealth.

* And in it is evidence for the legitimacy of a person speaking of Allah's blessing, because of His saying: ﴿O people, we have been taught the speech of the birds﴾.

* And in it also is evidence that this speaking is not objectionable to be public, meaning my intention is that it is comprehensive, because His saying: ﴿O people﴾ is a call addressed to one at a distance, so it is as if he (that is, Solomon) announced that to all people.

* And in this is evidence that the birds speak, because of His saying: ﴿the speech of the birds﴾.

* And in it, that their speech is understood and known. But is it known among themselves, and known to others?

* Students: (...).

* Shaykh: It is unknown except to one whom Allah has taught. Therefore Allah, exalted, said: ﴿And there is not a thing but that it glorifies [Allah] by His praise, but you do not understand their glorification﴾ [Al-Isra 44].

* And also in this verse is evidence that Allah, glorified and exalted, gave Solomon of everything by which kingship is completed, because of His saying: ﴿and we have been given of everything﴾. This is similar to His saying about the queen of Sheba: ﴿and she has been given of everything﴾ [An-Naml 23], meaning, of what completes kingship. If we restrict it so that "everything" means everything by which kingship is completed, then "min" (of) is explanatory of the kind. If we say that ﴿of everything﴾ is general for every thing, then "min" is partitive, because they were not given everything, but rather some of everything.

* And in it is evidence that what Allah, exalted, gives the servant of knowledge and understanding is from His bounty, because of His saying: ﴿Indeed, this is evidently the great bounty﴾, and Allah, exalted, said: ﴿Say: By the bounty of Allah and by His mercy, so in that let them rejoice; it is better than what they accumulate﴾ [Yunus 58].

Now, is it derived from this that one who knows the language of others has an advantage over others? Yes, an advantage over others, because he was praised by His saying: ﴿we have been taught the speech of the birds﴾.

So learning a language other than Arabic is in reality one of Allah's blessings upon the servant, but how does he use it? If he uses it in place of the Arabic language, he is mistaken, and Umar used to beat people for that. If he uses it for a religious benefit, then he has a reward for that. So if he uses it to call to Allah and to make the creatures who do not understand Arabic understand, by this means, then it is a means.

The point is that there is no doubt that the person who learns the language of others has an advantage over others in this, but whether he is praiseworthy or not returns to what he reaches through this language.

* Student: (...).

* Shaykh: How? This is correct, but his being praised for having been taught this speech, is it because it is a sign, or because it is a matter hidden from others? The correct view is that it is a sign and is hidden from others.

In any case, this matter (...) into the matter of the divisions of this verse: that a person is praised if he knows the language of others, but there is no doubt that he has knowledge, and that if it is used to reach a desired matter, then it is praiseworthy, and if it is used to reach a blameworthy matter, then it is blameworthy.

For example, if a person learns a non-Arabic language, and he puts it in place of Arabic and begins to address others in this language, then there is no doubt that he is blameworthy and is forbidden from it, because it opposes the Sharia on one side, and opposes reason on the other side.

Nations now strive by every means to preserve their languages, and indeed they strive to revive their dead languages, just as the Jews do now. They try by all means to get their people to return to the Hebrew language. So how is it that we lose the Arabic language, which is the language of the world? The language of the world, by law or by decree?

* Students: By law.

* Shaykh: Therefore it is obligatory upon all the world to learn the Arabic language, because the Qur'an is in Arabic, and it cannot be understood except through Arabic. But we now, regrettably, see that non-Arabic is the international language. Yes, just as we now see that the non-Arabic months are the international ones, because in reality we have not known our own worth. Whereas the Muslims are the world in their religion, in their book, and in their history.

Allah, glorified and exalted, says: ﴿They ask you about the crescent moons. Say: They are measures of time﴾ [Al-Baqarah 189]. For whom?

* Student: For the people.

* Shaykh: Or for the Arabs? And the Arabs are losing (...) there are no measures of time for people.

﴿Indeed, the number of months with Allah is twelve months in the register of Allah﴾ when? ﴿the day He created the heavens and the earth﴾ [At-Tawbah 36]. The Messenger (ﷺ) explained it as these Arabic months. Yes, but:

*"You would have made [them] hear, had you called out to a living one, / but there is no life for one you call to."*

* Student: (...).

* Shaykh: (...) clarifies (...). So the conclusion is that I say: it is, regrettably and greatly, that some people now learn the language of those people and make it the language of communication among themselves, and this is without doubt a deficiency in the Sharia and in reason.

* Student: Impressed without reason, impressed by others without reason.

* Shaykh: Yes, correct, without discernment.

* Student: (...).

* Shaykh: How?

* Student: (...).

* Shaykh: If this happened, it would be good. That is, if people were moved from the colloquial language to the Arabic language, this would be good, among the best there could be, because it is evidence of understanding the Qur'an and the Sunnah.

But if that is not possible, then this is merely a change of dialect. If you reflect on what people now speak in colloquial language, you will find that all their words have origins in the Arabic language originally, but with differing dialects. So our wish, in truth, is to return to classical Arabic, but we must abandon this colloquial language of ours (...) return to the classical.

But I am impressed by a Muslim Sri Lankan who, at one of our institutions, once came to speak with me, speaking in classical Arabic without making any grammatical errors. This is remarkable: the remarkable thing is that he does not make errors. He is Sri Lankan originally, but he learned Arabic in the classical language, because the dictionaries are in classical Arabic, and he speaks to me entirely in classical Arabic without any error. This is good.

Commentary of Ibn 'Uthaymin (Tafsir al-Quran al-Karim) on surah 27, verse 14–16 (part 1 of 3):

Then He said: ﴿And they denied them, though their souls were convinced of them﴾. ﴿They denied﴾: the pronoun refers to ﴿Pharaoh and his people﴾. Al-jahd (denial, rejection) means refusal. Jahada is transitive in itself, but it may be given the meaning of takdhib (denying as false), in which case it takes the preposition bi, so that ﴿wa jahadu bihā﴾ means "denying them."

Here jahd is given the meaning of takdhib, and for this reason it takes bi. That is because jahd may be takdhib, and it may be concealment out of regard for some interest; its causes are many, since someone may say to you, "What did you do?" and you deny it to gain an interest you want, not as a matter of takdhib.

But here it is takdhib; their denial is takdhib. And what is the evidence?
* Student: (...).
* Shaykh: No, the evidence is that it takes bi, and what takes bi is takdhib.
﴿And they denied them﴾, i.e., they denied them in rejection. They denied, and yet they did not show it. For this reason the author says: (i.e., they did not acknowledge them). The meaning is takdhib, and the author gave "they did not acknowledge" for two reasons. The first: so that the construction with bi is sound, since (aqarra) takes what? With bi.

The second: according to his view, so that this does not include concealing them from one who asks for them. So it is as if the author made jahd the negation of acknowledgment. But we do not agree with him on this specification. First: he explained the affirmed with the negated, is that not so? Jahd is affirmative; lam yuqirr is negative.

Second: by this explanation he loses a meaning that the verse indicates, namely their concealment of these signs if they were asked about them, because a person not acknowledging something is not the same as one who denies it and conceals it from others. So the verse is left as it is. It is said that jahd takes bi, why? Because it includes the meaning of takdhib, and it indicates two things: concealing them when they are sought, and denying them when they are presented. So the verse, without doubt...

There is no need to say that the verse is more eloquent than what the author mentioned, but we say that the author's explanation of it is open to objection on two grounds:
The first ground: explaining affirmation by negation, which is a deficiency.
The second: it loses a meaning, namely denial when asked; it is takdhib when presented, and jahd when sought.
* Student: The words of Allah the Exalted: ﴿And they denied them, though their souls were convinced of them﴾ (...)?
* Shaykh: Yes, it is known that they denied and concealed, but they were certain.
* Student: (...)?
* Shaykh: Yes, they did not openly acknowledge; the point is only that his explanation of it in this way is wrong.

He said: (﴿And﴾ indeed ﴿their souls were convinced of them﴾, i.e., they were certain).
Pay attention, brothers. The author said: (﴿And﴾ indeed ﴿they were convinced of them﴾). What required him to supply (qad)?
We say: because the clause is a circumstantial clause (ḥāl), and a circumstantial clause that is a past verb has qad supplied before it for emphasis (taḥqīq).

Second, he said: ﴿their souls were convinced of them﴾; he said: (i.e., they were certain that it was from Allah). He explained (istayqana) as (tayaqqana), indicating that the sīn and tā' are extra. But it is better that the sīn and tā' remain in their proper function and not be judged as extra, because istiyqān is more intensive than tayaqqun. It is well known among them that they say: an increase in form indicates an increase in meaning. So istiyqān is more emphatic: they were certain of them with complete certainty, having no doubt in them, and yet they denied them. This denial alongside certainty is more severe; for this reason He said: ﴿in injustice and haughtiness﴾, and so on.

His saying, ﴿And they denied them, though their souls were convinced of them﴾, and He did not say "and they were convinced of them." The attribution of the certainty to the souls is more emphatic: that is, it is a certainty that reached their souls so that it took firm hold of them, yet, may Allah protect us, they denied and rejected them.

His saying: ﴿in injustice and haughtiness﴾. The author says: (haughtiness against believing in what Moses brought), explaining the two words with one word, which is pride. But if we look at the noble verse, we find that it is more eloquent than how he explained it.

As for ﴿injustice﴾: zulm in origin means deficiency. From it is His saying: ﴿Each of the two gardens brought forth its produce and did not fall short of it in anything﴾ [al-Kahf 33]. What is the meaning of ﴿did not fall short of it﴾? That is, did not diminish.

So its origin is the meaning of diminishing, and whoever diminishes the right of another is a wrongdoer; if a person diminishes his own right, he is a wrongdoer to himself, and if he diminishes the right of another, he is a wrongdoer to that other.

Here, these people diminished the right of Moses, peace be upon him, so they are wrongdoers; and they diminished the right of their own souls, in that they did not lead them to what is good for them, so they too are wrongdoers.

Then, what drove this injustice and diminishing? He said: ﴿haughtiness﴾, and this is a meaning other than injustice; that is, arrogance toward what Moses, peace be upon him, brought. They saw that Moses: who is Moses, who comes to Pharaoh, who says to his people, "I am your Lord, the Most High," and then says, "I am a messenger to you, you must follow me!" By the nature of the wicked human, he becomes arrogant and says: never! So they denied, ﴿in injustice﴾ toward whom? Toward Moses and themselves. ﴿Haughtiness﴾: arrogance toward Moses and toward what he brought as well. So they, may Allah protect us, were characterized by both qualities.

His saying: ﴿in injustice and haughtiness﴾. The author says: (it refers back to the denial).
Correct, not to the certainty; for certainty is not injustice. If they were certain that Moses was truthful, that is not injustice; that is the truth, and their certainty would be justice and humility. But they did not submit to that certainty; that is, they did not yield to it.

So it refers back to the denial: they denied them in injustice and haughtiness.

But the benefit of introducing the circumstantial clause ﴿and their souls were convinced of them﴾, placed between the verb and its complements, is: hastening to censure them, because their denying while certain is more grave and severe. One who denies while in doubt may be excused, but with certainty there is no excuse.

So the benefit of the interjected circumstantial clause ﴿and their souls were convinced of them﴾ between the verb and its object is: what is its benefit? Hastening to censure them, and showing that they reached the extreme of this description, which is injustice and haughtiness.

What is the grammatical status of ﴿injustice and haughtiness﴾: is it an object of purpose (maf'ūl li-ajlih), that is, for the sake of injustice and haughtiness, or is it a verbal noun in the sense of a circumstantial state, that is, "being unjust and haughty"?
* Students: The latter is better.
* Shaykh: The latter is better, because if we make injustice and haughtiness an object of purpose, they precede the denial, since they were unjust and haughty and then denied.

So on this basis we say that "injustice and haughtiness" is a verbal noun in the sense of an active participle; that is, they denied them while being in what state?
* Student: Unjust and haughty.
* Shaykh: Unjust and haughty.

Allah, Blessed and Exalted, said: (﴿So look﴾, O Muhammad) and so on. ﴿So look﴾: is it a look of reflection or a look of sight?
* Students: A look of reflection.
* Shaykh: A look of reflection, because a look of sight is impossible here, why? Because its time has passed. But it is a look of reflection.

According to the author's words, the address returns to the Messenger of Allah ﷺ: (﴿So look﴾, O Muhammad).

It has been mentioned to us several times that the singular address in the Qur'an is not restricted to the Messenger, peace be upon him, except where evidence indicates it. Where evidence indicates it, it is as the evidence shows; otherwise it is general, and the sense becomes: "So look, O addressee," not "O Muhammad, so look," because the Qur'an is in the hands of everyone.

As for what evidence shows is specific to the Messenger, peace be upon him, it is specific to him, such as the words of Allah the Exalted: ﴿O Messenger, convey what has been sent down to you from your Lord﴾ [al-Ma'idah 67], and His words: ﴿Did We not expand for you your breast?﴾ [al-Sharh 1].

What shows that the singular address is general: first, the reason we mentioned, that the Qur'an is in the hands of all people. Second, Allah the Exalted said: ﴿O Prophet, when you divorce women, divorce them﴾ [al-Talaq 1]; He addressed with the singular and the plural: ﴿O Prophet, when you divorce...﴾, and this shows that the address directed to the Messenger, peace be upon him, is directed to the community unless evidence indicates that it is specific to him, as with the two examples we gave. Likewise from this: ﴿O Prophet, why do you forbid what Allah has made lawful for you?﴾ [al-Tahrim 1]; this is specific to the Messenger, peace be upon him, since he is the one who forbade, yet the ruling is general.

So ﴿So look﴾: what do we say? We say: O addressee.

﴿So look how was the end of the corrupters﴾. In this verse, first: kāna raises the subject and puts the predicate in the accusative, is that not so? This is known to you: kāna raises the subject and puts the predicate in the accusative, ﴿And Allah was ever Forgiving﴾ [al-Nisa' 96].

Second: if the subject is feminine, the verb is feminine. Here we do not see a predicate for kāna in ﴿how was the end of the corrupters﴾.
* Student: (...).
* Shaykh: Good. And the second?
* Student: The second: that ʿāqibah is a metaphorically feminine noun (...).
* Shaykh: Good, the second answer is correct; that is, ʿāqibah is metaphorically feminine, not truly feminine. The difference between metaphorical and true feminine: whatever has a female sex is truly feminine, and whatever has no sex and whose femininity is merely grammatical is metaphorically feminine.

As for the first, namely his saying that it is incomplete or complete, that is not correct.
* Student: Kāna is complete, and the predicate is fronted, which is (kayfa).
* Shaykh: Yes, this is correct: the predicate is fronted, which is (kayfa). Is it fronted obligatorily or optionally?
* Student: Obligatorily.
* Shaykh: Why? Because it is an interrogative, and interrogatives have precedence; an interrogative cannot occur in the middle of speech, it must come first. We have understood the grammar.

So ʿāqibah: what is the meaning of ʿāqibah? Originally, ʿāqibah means lateness, and from it ʿaqb of the foot, the heel, the back part. What is the meaning of ʿāqibah? A matter that comes later; that is, look at what their affair came to in the end.

His saying: ﴿the corrupters﴾: those whose condition became corruption. Corruption here does not mean the corruption of civilization, for civilization in Pharaoh's time may have reached its peak; rather, the intended corruption is moral corruption: the corruption of morals and beliefs.

It may be followed by corruption of civilization, as Allah the Exalted said: ﴿Corruption has appeared on land and sea by what the hands of people have earned﴾ [al-Rum 41], and ﴿Allah presents an example: a town that was secure and at peace, its provision coming to it abundantly from every place, but it denied the favors of Allah﴾ [al-Nahl 112]. By this estimation, namely that the basic corruption mentioned in the Qur'an is corruption of morals and beliefs, which is followed by corruption of deeds, we come to know that what people now boast about regarding luxury, tranquillity, security and the like, and when they come to mention religion they say: "the tolerant creed," and do not mention action. Then the word "tolerant" itself indicates weakness in this creed: "tolerant" means that everything is permitted. It is true that it is the tolerant Hanafiyyah beyond doubt, but it has deeds and it has firmness. For this reason, concentrating on physical comfort and bodily pleasure while mentioning belief alone is, in my view, dangerous, because each one begins to chant what? These two matters. He says: I have a sound creed, a tolerant creed, gentle, easy, accepting of everything; and he says: I also seek bodily comfort and security and the like. But the uprightness of religion and striving to establish it among people through enjoining good, forbidding evil, and jihad in the way of Allah: this is a matter that is hardly mentioned.

In reality, if luxury is only for the body, it is corruption, and it does not last at all. Moreover, absolute physical luxury must be accompanied by anxiety in the heart, because Allah the Exalted only guaranteed a good life to whom? ﴿Whoever does righteousness, whether male or female, while being a believer﴾ [al-Nahl 97]. Note belief and action, and He began with action as well: ﴿Whoever does righteousness, whether male or female, while being a believer, We will surely cause him to live a good life, and We will surely give them their reward according to the best of what they used to do﴾: a good life in this world and a good reward in the Hereafter.

This is what must be emphasized. As for absolute luxury, it is a great harm to a person; it causes heedlessness of Allah, the Exalted, and the preoccupation of a person with seeking fleeting bodily comfort.

One of the salaf said: If the kings and the sons of kings knew what we are in, they would fight us for it with swords (...), of the bliss and joy and expansion of the breast that you are in, and the like.

* * *

I seek refuge in Allah from Satan the accursed. Allah the Exalted said: ﴿And for Solomon were gathered his soldiers of the jinn and mankind and birds, and they were marshaled in ranks﴾ [al-Naml 17]. And before we speak...
* Student: (...).
* Shaykh: Yes, no, we took that (...), and we told you: the emphasis in ﴿Indeed, this is the clear favor﴾ is not emphasized with speech.
* From this verse is derived: ﴿And they denied them, though their souls were convinced of them, in injustice and haughtiness. So look how was the end of the corrupters﴾ [al-Naml 14].
* Several benefits are derived from it. First: despite the strength of the signs that Moses brought, these people did not benefit from them. This is taken from His saying: ﴿and they denied them﴾, and when signs are strong, there is no room left for denial; but, may Allah protect us, Allah blinded their insight, so they denied them.
* And it is derived from this: the denial of these addressed people was out of obstinacy, not out of doubt, from His saying: ﴿and their souls were convinced of them﴾. Did this happen to the Quraysh with the Prophet, peace be upon him?
* Students: It happened (...).
* Shaykh: Yes, it happened, by His saying: ﴿We know indeed that what they say grieves you, but it is not you they deny; rather, the wrongdoers deny the signs of Allah﴾ [al-An'am 33]. There is no doubt that this occurred among the leaders and chiefs; but the common people may not have had this matter, rather they are either followers. As for the leaders and the great, there is no doubt about this. In this is evidence of the evil condition of the family of Pharaoh, from His saying: ﴿in injustice and haughtiness﴾: ﴿injustice﴾ toward whom? Toward themselves and toward Moses; ﴿haughtiness﴾: arrogance toward the truth.
* And in it is evidence that the attribution of these two qualities makes a person one of the Pharaonic nation, namely injustice and haughtiness. There is no quality by which a servant leaves the even path except that he has in it a leader from the people of disbelief. For this reason the Prophet, peace be upon him, informed that people would follow the ways of those before them[[Agreed upon; related by al-Bukhari (3456), Muslim (2669/6), and al-Hakim in al-Mustadrak (8610) from Ibn 'Abbas, and the wording is his.]].
* Rejection of the truth has a leader for the one who does it, like Pharaoh and Qarun; envy has a leader for the human being, like the Jews; showing off has a leader for the human being, like the hypocrites; and so on. Indeed, it also belongs to the hypocrites. There is no trait by which a servant leaves the even path except that it has a leader from the people of disbelief.
* And in this is evidence of the blameworthiness of arrogance toward the truth, from His saying: ﴿and haughtiness﴾. There is no difference whether that is out of good intention or not? This way is blameworthy even if out of good intention. Our saying "out of good intention" is to include some imitators who, when the evidence from the Book and the Sunnah is presented to them, say: "We follow so-and-so, because he is more knowledgeable than us." This is out of apparent good intention. And what is the aspect of good intention? Because they see that this imam they followed is more knowledgeable than you, and say: "We are ignorant and have nothing but to imitate, and this man is more knowledgeable than us." And what do you say?
* Student: (...) this is the word of Allah and His Messenger, he said: but this statement is the statement of so-and-so, which (...) out of good intention, not out of partisanship for opinion. So this statement contains blame, because he followed him when the saying of the Messenger was presented to him, and he did not accept it.
* Shaykh: Yes.
* And it is derived from this verse: if this attribute is blameworthy and Pharaonic, then its opposite is praiseworthy. What is the opposite?
* Students: Humility.

Commentary of Ibn 'Uthaymin (Tafsir al-Quran al-Karim) on surah 27, verse 14–16 (part 2 of 3):

* The Shaykh: Humility before the truth and accepting it is undoubtedly praiseworthy, because when Allah the Exalted dispraises a quality, its opposite is praised with good.

* The verse also indicates that a person should, or must, reflect and contemplate the outcomes of those who came before, based on His saying: ﴿So look how was the end of the corrupters﴾. Does a person look at the outcome of the corrupters, or at the outcome of the corrupters and the reformers?

* A student: Both.

* The Shaykh: Good. So what is the benefit of (...) ﴿So look how﴾? Because the context is one of threat. When the context is one of encouragement, we say to a person: Look how was the end of the reformers.
﴿So look how﴾, because the context is one of warning; and when the context is one of encouragement, we say to a person: Look how was the end of the righteous. Yes, it is clear. ﴿Why were there not among the generations before you those of remaining virtue who forbade corruption on earth, except a few of those We saved from among them?﴾ [Hud 116].
So the matter differs: in the context of intimidation, we refer the person to the outcome of the corrupters, in the context of intimidation. And in the context of encouragement, we refer him to the outcome of the reformers, so that he may beware of those and be eager for these.

It also contains evidence for the virtue of reflecting and contemplating the reports of those who passed away, and that the study of history is among the things the Sharia has brought, for we cannot look at how their end was except by studying and tracing their reports. Yes, so the knowledge of history is among the intended matters, but is it intended in itself or incidentally?

Incidentally, except for the biography of the Prophet ﷺ and his rightly guided Caliphs, for it is part of the religion, because it is all rulings. This is unlike looking into history merely for the sake of taking lessons. So every context has its own speech, because looking into history merely for lessons may let a person learn from others and thus be content without it, but looking into the biography of the Prophet ﷺ is jurisprudential rulings; this is intended in itself, and a person cannot do without it by means of anything else. ﴿So look how was the end of the corrupters﴾.

* A student: (...).

* The Shaykh: Yes indeed. If a person reflects on their civilization and their strength, and yet Allah destroyed them, there is no harm in that. But if he wants to reflect on their strength in order to praise them and extol them, this is not permissible. For this reason Allah the Exalted did not command us to look at their strength except after He commanded us to look at their end.

On this basis, those who go to the dwellings of Thamud for sightseeing and recreation are sinners. The Messenger ﷺ said: «Do not enter upon these punished people except while weeping». So it is not permissible for a person to go on a trip, for example, to that place unless he enters while weeping. «And if you are not weeping, then do not enter upon them» [[Agreed upon; al-Bukhari (433) and Muslim (2890 / 38) from the hadith of Ibn 'Umar.]].

Praise be to Allah, a person has no need of this; it is not necessary to go there for recreation. But unfortunately, now they have become monuments, meaning that they are visited to show the strength of these people, their creativity and their firm management of their affairs, while they do not pay attention to what punishment Allah brought upon them, and we seek refuge in Allah.

* A student: The Messenger ﷺ commanded hastening, how for example..

* The Shaykh: Yes, that is it.

Allah the Exalted says: ﴿And We had certainly given knowledge to Dawud and Sulayman. And they said, "Praise be to Allah, who has favored us over many of His believing servants."﴾ [An-Naml 15].

From this verse is derived: the explanation of what Allah the Exalted bestowed upon Dawud and Sulayman, based on His saying: ﴿And We had certainly given knowledge to Dawud and Sulayman﴾.

And it also contains evidence for Allah the Exalted's praise of Himself, because His praising Himself by giving Dawud and Sulayman knowledge is a form of praise. Is it praiseworthy for creation that a person praise himself for his own virtue or not? It is not praiseworthy unless there is a benefit to others in it, not to you. As for Allah the Exalted, He praises Himself to be praised. But you do not do this. However, if there is a benefit to others in it, such as a person who narrates something about himself so that he may be followed in goodness, there is no harm in that, or so that people may benefit from what he has.

Ibn Mas'ud, may Allah be pleased with him, said: «If I knew that someone whom camels could reach knows the Book of Allah better than I do, I would seek him out» or as he said [[Agreed upon; al-Bukhari (5002) and Muslim (2463 / 115) from the hadith of Ibn Mas'ud, with the wording: "If I knew someone more knowledgeable of the Book of Allah than me whom camels could reach, I would ride to him."]].

And the scholars have continued to praise their books. Ibn Malik says:
It brings the far near with concise wording, and extends generosity with a fulfilled promise,
and it draws contentment without anger: the Alfiyya of Ibn Mu'tit, surpassing all others.

* A student: If he had not said: "surpassing" (...).

* The Shaykh: The point in any case is that such (praise) is not for the benefit of the person himself; it is for the benefit of others, so that they may benefit from this composition, for example.

* A student: Sometimes he exaggerates, O Shaykh, or overdoes it.

* The Shaykh: In any case.. there is no extravagance; (...) although in reality a person may be accused, whatever his intention, he may be accused. But a person need not concern himself with people's opinion if he has put right what is between him and his Lord.

The main point in this verse is evidence for Allah the Exalted praising Himself for what He has graciously bestowed upon His servants, by His saying: ﴿And We had certainly given knowledge to Dawud and Sulayman﴾.

The third: the virtue of Dawud and Sulayman, and that they were worthy of this blessing, because Allah the Blessed and Exalted says: ﴿Allah knows best where to place His message﴾ [Al-An'am 124]. So there is no bounty Allah gives to a servant except that it is in its proper place, because Allah is All-Wise.

* A student: (...).

* The Shaykh: Yes indeed. And it contains evidence for the virtue of knowledge, based on His saying: ﴿And We had certainly given knowledge to Dawud and Sulayman﴾.

There is no doubt about this, the virtue of knowledge. Allah the Exalted says: ﴿Say, "Are those who know equal to those who do not know?"﴾ [Az-Zumar 9]. But the question remains: what is the praiseworthy knowledge? This is what people are now disputing: what is the praiseworthy knowledge?

* A student: (...).

* The Shaykh: What is meant is the knowledge of the Sharia, what is meant is the knowledge of the Sharia. That is the praiseworthy knowledge. As for whatever is other than the knowledge of the Sharia, it is not praised except insofar as it leads to something praiseworthy. Knowledge other than the knowledge of the Sharia is not praised except where it leads to a praiseworthy matter.

The opposite of what the people of today are upon: many ignorant people praise knowledge other than Sharia. Some people, and we seek refuge in Allah, see that the knowledge of the Sharia is backwardness and that the knowledge of nature is progress. For this reason such people praise these scholars (...) and the layers of the earth and other things, and you find him, for example, praising: "This is the origin of knowledge," or "This is knowledge," and similar things. Or if he sees some strange crafts (...), "Knowledge, knowledge!" There is no doubt that such a person prefers this age over the age of the Companions. This is not the intended meaning. Whatever Allah has praised of knowledge, this is not what is intended; rather what is intended is the knowledge of the Sharia, because the knowledge of the Sharia is what benefits creation. Even the knowledge of the Sharia is what guides them to these sciences they boast of, because Allah commands us to strive upon the earth: ﴿He it is who made the earth submissive to you, so walk in its tracts and eat of His provision﴾ [Al-Mulk 15], and ﴿Have they not looked into the dominion of the heavens and the earth?﴾ [Al-A'raf 185], and similar.

So the summary, O brothers, is that the knowledge with which Allah favored Dawud and Sulayman and praised them for is the knowledge of the Sharia. Likewise, all that the texts say in praise of knowledge refers to the knowledge of the Sharia, because it is what is praised for its own sake. And whatever else, when is it praised?

* Students: When it leads to something praiseworthy.

* The Shaykh: When it leads to something praiseworthy. Otherwise, if it leads to something blameworthy, it is blameworthy, and if it leads to something neither praised nor blamed, it is neither praised nor blamed.

* A student: (...).

* The Shaykh: (...).

* A student: (...) they bring a doubt (...), this doubt deceives some ignorant people (...) he says: it increases lifespan (...) perhaps, I mean, it did not agree (...) the Messenger ﷺ nor the knowledge of the Companions, and despite this (...) we reached the depths of the seas (...). I have read a lot about these people.

* The Shaykh: This is from ignorance. For this reason, their knowledge now is not praiseworthy unless it leads to something praiseworthy; otherwise it is not praiseworthy. Would that they had reached the depths of the seas and the horizons of space! These are the ones who made what destroys creation, such as bombs and weapons. Is this praiseworthy?

* A student: No.

* The Shaykh: Then we say: do these sciences contradict Sharia knowledge? We wish that the Muslims also would reach these matters so that they benefit themselves and benefit creation.

* A student: O Shaykh, the texts in the Book and the Sunnah that praise knowledge, do you mean Sharia knowledge?

* The Shaykh: Not at all, Sharia knowledge.

* A student: The saying of the Exalted (...) together with His saying (...), how is this?

* The Shaykh: There is nothing in it. There is no contradiction between them.

* A student: (...) mercy, just mercy.

* The Shaykh: But this mercy is in its proper place. This mercy is in its proper place.

* There is also evidence here for the virtue of Dawud and Sulayman from the aspect of their acknowledging Allah's blessing and thanking Him for it, based on His saying: ﴿And they said﴾.

* A student: (...).

* The Shaykh: No, we mentioned it from one aspect, and this is from another aspect, namely their performing the thanks for Allah's blessing: ﴿And they said, "Praise be to Allah, who has favored us..."﴾. They did not say: "We were given this on account of knowledge from ourselves," or "because we are clever," or similar things. They said: ﴿Praise be to Allah, who has favored us over many of His believing servants﴾.

* In this is also evidence that thanks is given by speech as it is by action, by speech and by action, and also by belief, by conviction. Thanks has three locations: the heart, the tongue, and the limbs.

The poet said:
Blessings from me have benefited you in three: my hand, my tongue, and the hidden inner self.

The evidence that thanks occurs in three places: here in the tongue. The Prophet ﷺ, when it was said to him, "Why do you do this, when you were – he would stand until his feet swelled – and Allah has forgiven you what preceded of your sin?" He said: «Should I not love to be a grateful servant?» [[Agreed upon; al-Bukhari (1130) and Muslim (2819 / 79) from the hadith of al-Mughira.]] So he made the action thanks to Allah the Exalted. And Allah the Exalted says: ﴿Work, O family of Dawud, in gratitude﴾ [Saba' 13].

As for acknowledging blessings in the heart, it is part of thanks. What is the evidence? His saying: ﴿And whatever blessing you have is from Allah; then when adversity touches you, to Him you cry for help﴾ [An-Nahl 53].

Allah wants us to believe this news. For this reason Allah the Blessed and Exalted dispraised those who attributed His blessing to themselves, did they not? And what did He say about Qarun? ﴿He said, "I was only given it on account of knowledge I have."﴾ [Al-Qasas 78]. Then Allah the Exalted said: ﴿Did he not know that Allah had destroyed before him generations who were greater than him in strength and greater in accumulation?﴾ [Al-Qasas 78].

And regarding this matter, all three locations of thanks: few people fulfill them. Some people, for example, rely on the means by which a blessing reaches them and forget the Causer. Understood? When a person gives you something, a need of your needs, you find that gratitude for this giver arises in his heart more than gratitude to Allah; you find him praising this person more than he praises Allah; you find him serving this person more than he serves Allah.

Yet the one through whose hand the blessing reached you is only a means to bring it to you. Otherwise, who placed in his heart that he should convey this blessing to you? Allah the Exalted, and it is He who facilitated this.

So the summary is that most people now, or the majority, fall short in the station of thanks, whether in the heart, the tongue, or the limbs.

* And in this is evidence that when Allah bestows a blessing upon a person, it is prescribed for him to praise Him for it. Texts have come concerning this: when you finish eating and drinking you say: "Praise be to Allah"; when you wake up you praise Allah; when you put on a garment you praise Allah. And so on. This is among the lawful matters: praising Allah the Exalted for blessings.

* The verse also contains evidence for the humility of Dawud and Sulayman and their knowledge of the reality, in His saying: ﴿who favored us over many of His believing servants﴾. He did not mention absolute favor over all the believers: ﴿over many of His believing servants﴾. Does this imply describing the prophets with faith?

* A student: (...).

* The Shaykh: No, meaning: does His saying ﴿over many of His believing servants﴾ suggest that they are among the believers?

* A student: Yes.

* The Shaykh: Apparently it does suggest this, meaning that we share with them the description of faith, and Allah favored us over many of them.

* The verse also contains evidence that when a person sees that he is better than others by Allah's blessing upon him, this does not contradict humility. That is: when you feel that Allah has blessed you with wealth and favored you over this person, does that mean you have elevated yourself and become arrogant? No. Rather, you cannot recognize Allah's blessing upon you until you know its opposite in others, right? You cannot know this unless you know its opposite.

If you see, for example, a person afflicted in his body while Allah has granted you health, you recognize the virtue of Allah's blessing, so say: "Praise be to Allah who has granted me health from what He has afflicted him with, and favored me over him."

When you see an ignorant person while Allah has blessed you with knowledge, you likewise recognize the virtue of Allah's blessing upon you in this, and this is not counted as elevation or looking down on others. For this reason He said: ﴿Praise be to Allah who has favored us over many of His believing servants﴾. Someone may appear to think that if he sees his own superiority over others by what Allah has bestowed on him, this is a blameworthy matter and includes elevation (...) and looking down on others. But the matter is not so.

* A student: (...).

* The Shaykh: Yes indeed. In it there is also this benefit: that speaking of it is a form of thanks. From it is derived this benefit: the legitimacy of speaking of Allah's blessing, but not in the manner of boasting or exalting oneself over others. For this reason it has come in the hadith from the Messenger ﷺ that he said: «I am the master of the children of Adam, and I say so without boasting» [[Narrated by al-Tirmidhi (3148) from the hadith of Abu Sa'id.]].

So if a person speaks of Allah's blessing without boasting of it, there is no harm in that, no harm at all. Indeed, this may even be prescribed, because it is praise of Allah the Blessed and Exalted for what He has bestowed upon him.

* A student: (...).

* The Shaykh: (...).

* The student: (...).

* The Shaykh: How so?

* The student: (...) Allah said: ﴿over many of His believing servants﴾, that they both had acted (...).

* The Shaykh: (...) there is, I mean, there is a difficulty in it; because we now have no knowledge that the prophets knew that Muhammad would be sent. In the Qur'an: ﴿And when Allah took the covenant of the prophets: "Whatever I have given you of Scripture and wisdom, and then there comes to you a messenger confirming what is with you, you must believe in him and you must support him."﴾ [Aal 'Imran 81]. The word "messenger" (rasul) is indefinite or definite?

* A student: Indefinite.

* The Shaykh: Indefinite. It does not indicate that Allah specified Muhammad ﷺ to them. Although Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with him, said: «Allah took the covenant from the prophets: if Muhammad is sent...»[[Tafsir Ibn Kathir (8 / 110).]]. This is his interpretation; as for the verse, it does not indicate this.

Student: (...).

Shaykh: Yes, it does not contradict... (...) it is correct and indicates it.

Student: (...).

Shaykh: Certainly, David had access to the Torah, since he came after Moses. Yes, this is (...).

Student: (...).

Shaykh: (...).

Student: (...) proof of Allah's knowledge (...).

Shaykh: What do you think of this benefit? Proof of Allah's knowledge, because He gave knowledge, and one who lacks a thing cannot give it.

Student: (...).

Shaykh: (...) This is testimony that it is very strong. Yes, then (...) proof of Allah's knowledge. Its explanation: Allah, glorified and exalted, gave these two knowledge, and He does not give knowledge except to one who has knowledge, because He teaches them. Teaches them what? What He Himself knows.

Student: (...).

Shaykh: Yes.

Student: (...).

Shaykh: Neither this nor that; it depends on the intention of the person. Even the first, a person's feeling of superiority over others by what Allah has favoured him with, may be arrogance. And this is similar: it may be disdain. And a person may look at Allah's blessing upon others with the perspective of wisdom, saying: Allah is Wise, and had this person not been worthy, He would not have given him. Then he strives to perfect virtues (...). The point is that this matter returns to intention in this and that.

Student: O Shaykh (...).

Shaykh: I have no knowledge; I do not know.

Student: O Shaykh (...) the benefit (...) does not conflict with saying (...) because I know (...) David and Solomon; nevertheless he was preferred (...).

Shaykh: By what do you weigh?

Student: I weigh it by this.

Shaykh: By knowledge.

Student: (...) the speech of the birds (...).

Shaykh: In any case, the benefit is attained. It is correct, meaning that it does not necessarily follow that a person's superiority in one attribute makes him superior to others absolutely. Yes, but, taking from this, can it be derived from this verse that one who excels another in an attribute is not necessarily more excellent than him absolutely? Is it derived from...?
