Furthermore, it is a cause for laughter not only from the words themselves but from the import of this speech; and for this reason he counted it among God's favor and said: ﴿My Lord, inspire me to be grateful for Your favor﴾. The import of this speech, perhaps, is that Solomon, peace be upon him, saw that even insects acknowledge his greatness and the greatness of his hosts. Yes, this is undoubtedly one of God's favors upon him. So this smile at the speech is from its content and significance, and likewise from its import and what it contains of God, blessed and exalted be He, favor upon Solomon.

﴿So he smiled, laughing at her speech﴾ (and he heard it from three miles away; the wind carried it to him, so he halted his hosts when he came upon their valley until they [the ants] had entered their dwellings; and his hosts were riders and walkers on this journey).

He says: (and he heard it from three miles away). From where did he get this?
* Student: Israelite reports.
* Shaykh: Israelite reports. Indeed, the Qur'an says ﴿until, when they came upon the valley of the ants﴾; what does this indicate? That they reached it. The most that can be said is that as soon as the ants were warned, they entered their dwellings. That is, between them and trampling those ants there was only the ants' entering their dwellings, and this does not require that there were three miles between him and them; there is no evidence for that. It is only said that he heard it from nearby. Did any of his other hosts hear it?
* Student: He does not know.
* Shaykh: It appears that they neither knew nor heard it; for His saying ﴿We have been taught the speech of birds﴾ indicates that this teaching, the speech of animals, was specific to Solomon, peace be upon him, and not as some common people claim. Some common people say that he understood everything that speaks, and they recount stories based on this. This is not correct; there is no known speech except among nations among themselves. As for humans, for example, knowing the speech of jinn, or knowing the speech of insects, this is not so without evidence. If evidence from the infallible one is found, it is correct, just as "the Prophet, peace be upon him, informed of the wolf that speaks, and he also informed of the cow that its owner rode, and it said to him: we were not created for this." [Agreed upon; al-Bukhari (3471) and Muslim (2388/13), from the hadith of Abu Hurayrah.]
The point is that what evidence establishes we must accept; otherwise the principle is that each thing speaks in its own language, and that each kind does not understand the language of another...
* Student: He says, exalted is He: ﴿And mention Our servant Dawud, possessor of strength; indeed, he was one who often turned back [to Allah]. Indeed, We subjected the mountains to exalt [Allah] with him in the evening and at sunrise, and the birds assembled; all were to him returning [in repentance]﴾ [Sad 17–19]. If the birds, the returning ones, were subservient to him...
* Shaykh: ﴿all were to him﴾: to whom?
* Student: To Dawud.
* Shaykh: Or to God.
* Student: Or to the nearer of Dawud?
* Shaykh: No, the matter requires reciting it; even the recitation is not fixed by what you have recited.
* Student: ﴿Be patient over what they say, and remember Our servant Dawud, possessor of strength; indeed, he was one who often turned back. Indeed, We subjected the mountains to exalt [Allah] with him in the evening and at sunrise, and the birds assembled; all were to him returning.﴾
* Shaykh: I do not know; I did not vocalize the verse...

* * *

He says: ﴿So he smiled, laughing at her speech, and said, "My Lord, inspire me [to be grateful]"﴾ (inspire me) ﴿to be grateful for Your favor which You have bestowed upon me﴾.

﴿He said: My Lord﴾: this is a vocative, from which the particle of calling has been dropped, and its original form is "O my Lord" (ya rabbi). The ya of the first person pronoun is also dropped for lightness; otherwise its original form is "rabbi" with the ya. Supplication always comes with the particle of calling dropped. Why?
* Student: The ya.
* Shaykh: Why does supplication always come with the particle of calling dropped?
* Student: Beginning with the mention of God, for blessing.
* Shaykh: Beginning with the name of God and care for the intended object, which is God, glory be to Him. "Lord" is begun before anything else, and it is as if a person, out of his intense longing for his Lord during supplication, utters nothing but the name of God, glory be to Him.

He says: ﴿My Lord, inspire me﴾: "inspire me" (awzi'ni) in terms of grammatical analysis is called an imperative verb, but the grammarians, may God have mercy on them, out of courtesy toward God, do not say "imperative verb," because you do not command God. They call it: a verb of supplication. When we parse ﴿My Lord, inspire me﴾, we say: awzi' is a verb of supplication, and we do not say it is an imperative verb intended for supplication. It is in fact an imperative verb and the intended meaning is supplication, but out of courtesy toward God we say "verb of supplication."

(﴿Inspire me﴾: direct me) ﴿to be grateful for Your favor which You have bestowed﴾ upon me ﴿and upon my parents, and to do righteousness that You will accept﴾.

﴿He said: My Lord, inspire me to be grateful for Your favor﴾: what moved Solomon, peace be upon him, to say this was acknowledgment of God's favor, glory be to Him, and fear of self-conceit. For if the ant speaks like this out of fear of him and his hosts, and apologizes to them, and its speech is understood, this may lead a person to conceit, thinking that this thing is by his own essence or from himself, just as Qarun said: ﴿I was only given it because of knowledge I have﴾ [al-Qasas 78]. So at this juncture, where a person may be led to conceit, and a human is a human, he asked God to inspire him to thank Him for His favor which He bestowed upon him and his parents, and to do righteousness that He is pleased with.

Thus a person, when he receives a blessing, should ask God, blessed and exalted be He, to inspire him to thank for it, so that conceit does not overtake him regarding the blessing God has bestowed upon him, whether the blessing is material or physical, moral or sensible.

﴿My Lord, inspire me that I may be grateful﴾: the "an" here is verbal (masdariyya); what is its place in grammar?
* Student: (...).
* Shaykh: It is the second object of "awzi'ni," since the first object is the ya, and the second object is ﴿an ashkura﴾. That is: inspire me to thank You for the favor You have bestowed upon me and upon my parents.

As for His saying ﴿an ashkura ni'matak﴾: what is the meaning of "ni'mah" (favor)? It is the kindness that the benefactor bestows upon the one benefited. And favor, as you know, is of two kinds: either obtaining what is desired, or deliverance from what is feared.

God, blessed and exalted be He, always bestows His favors upon His servant, and the servant moves between these two kinds of favor: he always obtains what he desires and is delivered from what he fears. As for the commentator's words: (﴿bestowed﴾ upon me, by it). Why did he estimate "by it"?
* Student: He thinks that "bestowed" (...).
* Shaykh: No; because it is well known that a relative clause must have a resumptive pronoun referring back to the relative pronoun; there must be a returning pronoun referring to the relative.
Here, ﴿which You have bestowed upon me﴾: the clause "bestowed" needs a pronoun referring back to "which," and the author estimated it by his saying "by it." Does anyone among you dispute this estimate? That is, the estimation of the pronoun so that it refers back to the relative pronoun is clear and accepted; this is the grammatical rule. ﴿He eats of what you eat and drinks of what you drink﴾ [al-Mu'minun 33], meaning: of it. This is clear. This is common in Arabic speech: in the Qur'an, the Sunnah, and people's speech, there must be a returning pronoun referring to the relative pronoun to link the clause to its relative. But do you have any objection with the author regarding the estimation of the returning pronoun in this way?
* Student: (...) after the detached pronoun (...).

**Commentary of Ibn 'Uthaymin (Tafsir al-Quran al-Karim) on Surah 27, verses 17–19 (part 3 of 4)**

* Shaykh: Because the separate pronoun is *iyyahu*, *iyyaya*, *iyyaka*. This is a separate pronoun, so the pronoun here is undoubtedly attached (*muttasil*).
* Student: (...) but (...) the *ba'* (preposition "with") is there.
* Shaykh: Yes, even if it is attached, even if (...) it is attached, even with the *ba'* present. He would say, "*anamtuha 'alayya*" (I bestowed it upon myself). That is correct, but it is not the cause. The estimate you made is correct, but the cause is not the cause ('illah).

They say: the returning pronoun (*al-'a'id*) is not deleted when it is in the genitive case unless the relative pronoun is governed by a preposition similar to the deleted one in form, meaning and implied sense. Do you understand? This came up for us; we used to read in grammar in *al-Qatr* (a grammar primer), and that when it is in the genitive, it must be governed by the same preposition that governs the relative pronoun, and that it must agree with it in form, and its complement must be the same, agreeing in form, estimate and meaning.

The author now estimated (*bi-ha*) ("with it"), although it is not present in the Qur'an: (*"ni'matakal-lati an'amta*" [the blessing You bestowed] *bi-ha*). Accordingly, the sound estimate is to say: *an'amtaha 'alayya wa-'ala walidayya* (You bestowed it upon me and upon my parents), because the returning pronoun in the genitive cannot be deleted unless the relative pronoun is governed by the same preposition that governs that returning pronoun.

As for His saying ﴿upon me and upon my parents﴾: regarding "upon me," it is clear that God's blessing upon you requires gratitude from you. But God's blessing upon your parents, what is the reason it requires gratitude from you?

Because God's blessing upon the parents is a blessing upon the child, especially this blessing which occurred, namely that he inherited prophethood from David and succeeded him in it. So this blessing, God's blessing upon his parents, is in reality a blessing upon him. For this reason He said: ﴿upon me and upon my parents﴾.

And His saying: ﴿*walidayya*﴾ (my parents). Is this plural or dual?

* Students: Dual.
* Shaykh: *Walidayya* is a dual in the construct state (*mudaf*), and for this reason the *nun* was deleted from it. Its original form is *walidan li* (two parents for me), but the *nun* was deleted because of the construct.

Now, *walidayya*: what is meant by "father" (*walid*)?

* Student: The word *walid* means the father, in the plural form.
* Shaykh: That is, is it the father who is your biological parent, or even the grandfather and whoever is above him?

We say: in reality, the word *walid* sometimes includes the grandfather and those above him, and sometimes it is specified to the father. What determines this are the indications (*qara'in*), either verbal indications or circumstantial indications. For example: it is not permitted for a giver to take back what he gave, except a parent (*walid*) regarding what he gives his child. What is meant by "parent" here?

* Student: The father.

The direct father. The nearer parent; the grandfather is not included. "Parent" in the prohibition of marriage? It includes the nearer and the farther.

"Parent" in inheritance?

* Student: According to the correct view, it includes both.
* Shaykh: It includes the nearer and the farther, if the father is absent. What is meant is males and females. That is: do not suppose, according to the correct view, that we mean the grandfather, the male parent. Even the female, for example the mother, in inheritance, *walid* includes the farther ancestor if the nearer one is absent. Or not?

So in reality the word "parent" (*walid*) is sometimes meant as the nearer one, and sometimes meant as the nearer and farther together, or separately, and sometimes meant as the nearer and farther... no, what? What is it?

* Student: Not together.
* Shaykh: Not together. And what determines this are the indications: verbal indications or circumstantial ones.

* Student: (...) includes (...)?
* Shaykh: No, the word *walid*.
* Student: There is no difference between *walidayya* and *walidayya* (the other form).
* Shaykh: Yes, there is no difference between them. If we say *walidayya*, it means the father and the mother. If it is said *walidiyya*, that is not the expression used with *walidiyya*.
* Student: (...) my parent.
* Shaykh: There is no expression *walidiyya*. If a person expresses it that way, we say this expression is not correct. But *walidina* (our parents), when we are a group, is clear, because if you say *walidayna* and we are two, how many parents will there be? Four. If we are three, there will be six. And so on.

For this reason, some brothers who recite in Ramadan say: "O God, forgive us and our *walidayna*." This is not correct, except as a figurative usage (*tajawwuz*), because *walidayna*: we are not the children of one man. Yes, if we were children of one man and one mother, we would say *walidayna*, because our father is one and our mother is one. But if there were a thousand people in the mosque, is the parent of each one of us a parent of the other? We are not brothers.

* Student: Abbreviation of the wording.
* Shaykh: For this reason, *walidayna* is used only as a figurative usage, meaning: the *walidayya* of each one of us. For this reason, the correct expression in such a case is to say: "O God, forgive us and our *walidayna* (parents)."

* Student: (...) wrong.
* Shaykh: No. This is the correct form.
* Student: (...).
* Student: But everyone says it, except rarely.
* Shaykh: In any case, we cannot say that all of them do this or that. But we are now analyzing it from the standpoint of the Arabic language. The correct form in this is, when we are a group, *walidayna*, because *walidayna* is used only as a figurative usage.

All right, ﴿and upon my parents﴾.

* Student: His father and mother?
* Shaykh: Yes, his father and mother.

He says: ﴿and that I should do righteous deeds﴾. ﴿That I should do﴾ is coordinated with His saying ﴿that I should be grateful﴾, meaning: and inspire me to do righteous deeds that You approve.

And here His saying ﴿that I should do righteous deeds﴾ means: that I do a righteous deed. A righteous deed is not righteous unless it includes two essential conditions. What are they? Sometimes we ask, and there is no harm in asking.

* Student: Sincerity (*ikhlas*) and following the Prophet's way (*muttaba'ah*).
* Shaykh: Sincerity and following. Because of His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And they were commanded only to worship God, sincere to Him in religion, upright﴾ [al-Bayyinah 5]. All of it. Sincerity is clear for the prophets and others. Following is clear for you regarding those other than the prophets. Regarding the prophets it is not clear to you, but it is clear, because the prophet follows a law revealed to him. Is that not so?

* Student: Yes.
* Shaykh: He may not follow this law? He may not follow it. But as we have already mentioned, the prophets, peace be upon them, are protected from what? From being upheld in sins absolutely. So following exists in the prophets too, because following is from the law that was revealed to them.

So this righteous deed: it combines two matters, sincerity and following. If sincerity is lacking, there is *shirk* (associating partners with God). If following is lacking, there is *ibtida'* (innovation).

A deed that contains *shirk* is rejected. God said in the hadith qudsi (a saying of the Prophet in which God speaks in the first person): "I am the most self-sufficient of partners in regard to partnership. Whoever does a deed in which he associates others with Me, I abandon him and his association" [recorded by Muslim (2985/46) from the hadith of Abu Hurayrah].

Even showing off (*riya'*) is a kind of *shirk*. If a person performs an act of worship while showing off in it, then along with the sin, his deed is rejected.

Likewise in innovation. The Prophet ﷺ said: "Whoever does a deed that is not in accordance with our command, it is rejected" [recorded by Muslim (1718/18) from the hadith of 'A'ishah], and this is more general than the second wording: "Whoever introduces into this matter of ours something which is not part of it, it is rejected" [agreed upon; al-Bukhari (2697) and Muslim (1718/17) from the hadith of 'A'ishah].

Unless we say: whoever introduces into his essence and attributes. But if we say: whoever introduces into our affair what is not part of it, whether in the deed itself or in the description of the deed, then it agrees with the other wording. In any case, a deed that is not sincere is not accepted, and a deed that is not correct, meaning in accordance with the Sunnah, is not accepted either, and it is not righteous either. Rather it is corrupt.

His saying: ﴿You approve﴾. ﴿That I should do righteous deeds You approve﴾. Approval means acceptance. Does the word ﴿You approve﴾ after ﴿righteous﴾ have a meaning? Because every righteous deed is approved. So would the clause then be a *descriptive* qualifier that clarifies, or a *restrictive* qualifier? That is, clarifying or restricting?

* Student: Clarifying.
* Shaykh: It appears that it is clarifying, meaning that a righteous deed is approved. Someone may say: a deed may be righteous in its outward appearance, but not approved in its outcome or in what accompanies it. A person may do a deed sincerely for God and following the Messenger of God ﷺ, but self-admiration arises in his deed. This self-admiration prevents God's approval of it. ﴿They consider it a favor to you that they have embraced Islam. Say: Do not consider your Islam a favor to me. Rather, God confers a favor upon you that He has guided you to faith﴾ [al-Hujurat 17]. A deed may be righteous at its beginning and at its end, yet God does not approve it. ﴿O you who believe, do not nullify your charities with reminders and injury﴾ [al-Baqarah 264]. A man gives charity sincerely for God, Exalted is He, following the Messenger of God ﷺ in it, but he follows it with reminders and injury, and then the charity is nullified. Yes, according to this interpretation, His saying ﴿You approve﴾ is a restrictive qualifier, a restrictive qualifier.

Which of the two is better for us to adopt in this and similar cases, when a qualifier comes: is it better to make the qualifier clarifying, meaning merely explanatory, or to make it restrictive?

* Student: Restrictive.
* Shaykh: It is better that it be restrictive, because restriction adds meaning, while explanation adds nothing beyond what was already stated. So every qualifier that comes in speech, in this or other cases, the default is that it should be what?

* Student: Restrictive.
* Shaykh: That it be restrictive. We may not resort to making it explanatory merely to state the matter, except when? Except in necessity, when it is impossible for it to be restrictive: ﴿O mankind, worship your Lord, who created you and those before you﴾ [al-Baqarah 21].

﴿Who created you and those before you﴾, this one?

* Student: Clarifying.
* Shaykh: Clarifying and explanatory, and not restrictive. Because if we made it restrictive ﴿your Lord who created you﴾...

Shaykh: What?

* Student: To restrict.
* Shaykh: That it be restrictive. We may not resort to making it explanatory merely to state the matter, except when? Except in necessity, when it is impossible for it to be restrictive.

﴿O mankind, worship your Lord who created you and those before you﴾ [al-Baqarah 21]. ﴿Who created you and those who were before you﴾: this is clarifying and explanatory and not restrictive, because if we made it restrictive?

* Student: What is it?
* Shaykh: ﴿your Lord who created you﴾ (...).

Yes, everything speaks. Because some say: the body speaks, and it appears that in the case of the thief it is possible in the *jassah* (a storage place for dates), and it speaks. The *jassah* is the store for dates.

There is in this a refutation of the author's statement, when he says that the ant is the queen of the ants, because of His saying ﴿an ant﴾, which is indefinite. And it is not strange that an ant, one of the ants, is the one who said this.

* In this verse there is evidence of the eloquence of this ant, her sincere advice, and her intelligence, because the words she spoke include all of this. From her eloquence, she used in every place what fits it. ﴿O ants﴾ [al-Naml 18]: she used the vocative particle for the distant, because the ants are not all near her; some are far and some are near.

And from the perfection of her advice: her guidance to shelters and refuges, in her saying ﴿Enter your dwellings﴾.

And from the perfection of her intelligence: she used alarming, disturbing expressions, in her saying ﴿Lest Solomon and his hosts crush you﴾.

And in it, also, from her justice: she said ﴿while they do not perceive﴾. So this speech includes many kinds of eloquence, sincere advice, warning, admonition, and other things that have passed in the explanation.

Now the benefits I have are finished. Do you have benefits?

* Student: The greatness of Solomon's kingdom, if (...).
* Shaykh: Yes, indeed. In this also: the greatness of Solomon's kingdom and his hosts, because the ant knew that and warned against it.
* Student: Does it include that a person guards against the trampling of feet (...)?
* Shaykh: Yes, it is known that he guards against it. And the ant, in reality, her homes are now deep in the earth. Also, it is a habit of the ant that she builds her homes only in elevated places, and generally the soldiers (...) that as long as they find the plain they do not go to them.
* Student: It may be hard, Shaykh; sometimes it is hard, meaning one digs through the tiles and (...).
* Shaykh: No, she does not dig through tiles.
* Student: This.
* Shaykh: Yes, on top it is fine, but digging she cannot do.

He says: ﴿So he smiled, laughing at her words, and said: My Lord, inspire me to be grateful for Your blessing which You have bestowed upon me and upon my parents, and to do righteous deeds that You approve, and admit me by Your mercy among Your righteous servants﴾ [al-Naml 19].

In this is the permissibility of smiling when its cause is present, and the permissibility of laughing as well, from His saying ﴿so he smiled, laughing﴾. This is the action of a prophet, and the actions of the prophets are a proof, even if they were other than our Prophet ﷺ, except what our law has explicitly confirmed; this does not count.

The evidence that the actions of the prophets are a proof is His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Those are the ones whom God guided, so follow their guidance﴾ [al-An'am 90], and His saying: ﴿There was certainly in their stories a lesson for people of understanding﴾ [Yusuf 111].

* And in it is evidence of the humility of Solomon, peace be upon him, before God, Exalted is He, for the great kingdom did not make him arrogant, so that he said: ﴿My Lord, inspire me to be grateful for Your blessing﴾.

* And in it is evidence of acknowledging the blessing, God's blessing, and that this is not boasting, because Solomon mentioned God's blessing upon him, but he did not intend by that boasting or exalting himself over others. God Exalted said to the Messenger ﷺ: ﴿As for the blessing of your Lord, proclaim it﴾ [al-Duha 11], but not as boasting and exalting, because in that case it would turn into a curse.

* And in it is evidence that God's blessing upon the parents is a blessing upon the child, by His saying ﴿You bestowed upon me and upon my parents﴾, and especially the blessing of Islam, for it is among the greatest blessings upon the child. If a child died and his parents were both disbelievers, this child would be, in this world, in the ruling of the disbelievers; and in the Hereafter, God knows his condition. And if a child died between two Muslim parents, this child would be?

* Student: In Paradise.
* Shaykh: Muslim in this world and the Hereafter. Accordingly, God's blessing upon the parents, especially in religion, is a blessing upon the child, and this is the meaning of His saying: ﴿that I should be grateful for Your blessing which You bestowed upon me﴾.

* And in this is evidence that it is from reason, justice and the law to attribute the favor to the one who grants it, by His saying ﴿that I should be grateful for Your blessing﴾. This is an acknowledgment, and it is more eloquent than if a person said: "Inspire me to be grateful for the blessing," and that is all, because His saying ﴿Your blessing﴾ is very clear in the submission of this person to this great blessing which God bestowed upon him. So this is evidence that it is from reason, justice and the law to attribute the favor to the one who grants it, even if he is unwilling.

*"Only those who are worthy of it recognize favor among people..." ∗∗∗ .............................*

Among the well-known verses of poetry among them: what does *dhawuhu* mean? The people of merit. Only the people of merit recognize merit, while those who are not people of merit deny merit. Indeed, if you were to show them favor, they would consider it a duty owed to them by you (...). The greatest of this is one who claims favor upon God, Exalted is He, for what God has bestowed upon him, as in the story of the Bedouins: ﴿They consider it a favor to you that they have embraced Islam. Say: Do not consider your Islam a favor to me. Rather, God confers a favor upon you that He has guided you to faith﴾ [al-Hujurat 17].

* And in it is evidence that the prophets, peace be upon them, like others, depend upon God's enabling, and that without God's enabling, they would not walk a path that pleases God, by His saying: ﴿and that I should do righteous deeds that You approve﴾.

* It indicates that deeds other than righteous ones have no benefit. Rather, they fall between two matters: either sin, or mere safety. If it is done knowingly, it is sin. If it is done out of ignorance, the person is safe, but there is no benefit in it. For example, if a person prays a prayer while in a state of ritual impurity (hadath), the prayer is invalid. If he does so deliberately, he is sinful. If he is ignorant, it does not clear his obligation, and he must repeat it. As for reward, he may be rewarded for it because of his intention and the effort he exerted. But the point concerns benefit: whether he gains from it in clearing his obligation. It does not discharge him from the obligation.

* It indicates that the goal toward which the prophets and those who followed them strive is the pleasure of Allah, based on His words: ﴿and that I may do righteous deeds which You approve﴾. The purpose of a person's deeds is to attain the pleasure of Allah, the Exalted. Indeed, the pleasure of Allah is a goal above everything. Allah, the Exalted, said about the attributes of the believers: ﴿And the believing men and believing women are allies of one another. They enjoin what is right and forbid what is wrong, establish prayer, give zakah, and obey Allah and His Messenger. Those—Allah will have mercy on them. Indeed, Allah is Almighty and Wise.﴾ [At-Tawbah 71] ﴿Allah has promised the believing men and believing women gardens beneath which rivers flow, abiding therein eternally, and pleasant dwellings in gardens of perpetual residence. And approval from Allah is greater.﴾ [At-Tawbah 72]. That is, greater than everything. When the pleasure of Allah settles upon a person, this is the ultimate of what he wants.

* In the verse there is also evidence that the prophets, peace be upon them, seek nearness (tawassul) to Allah; that is, they ask Allah, the Exalted, through the means (wasilah), based on His words: ﴿And admit me by Your mercy among Your righteous servants.﴾ Allah, the Exalted, said: ﴿Those whom they call upon﴾ [Al-Isra 57]. That is, those whom these polytheists call upon, those ﴿seek means of access to their Lord, whichever of them is nearest, and they hope for His mercy﴾. So all people, all creation, ask Allah, the Exalted, and seek nearness to Him by what is permissible.

* It indicates the permissibility of seeking nearness to Allah by His attributes.

* Student: (...).

* The Shaykh: The same verse? "By His mercy."

* And there is also evidence, indeed a difficulty: ﴿among Your righteous servants﴾. If someone says: the rank of prophethood is higher than the rank of righteousness. ﴿Those are with the ones upon whom Allah has bestowed favor from among the prophets, the truthful, the martyrs, and the righteous﴾ [An-Nisa 69]. So how did he (Moses) ask Allah to admit him among His righteous servants, when he is a prophet, of a rank higher than the rank of righteousness?

* Student: (...) included in it (...) the prophets and the martyrs, if it is (...).

* The Shaykh: And in detail the ranks come.

* Student: Yes.

* The Shaykh: So? This is the closest view. The closer view is that what is meant here by righteousness is absolute righteousness, and absolute righteousness is the highest rank. Yusuf, peace be upon him, said: ﴿Cause me to die as a Muslim and join me with the righteous﴾ [Yusuf 101]. And Allah, the Exalted, said about Ibrahim: ﴿And We gave him his reward in this world, and indeed he is in the Hereafter among the righteous﴾ [Al-Ankabut 27]. So what is meant here is absolute righteousness, not the righteousness that is mentioned alongside the ranks. For the rank of righteousness alongside the ranks is below the rank of prophethood. ﴿And admit me by Your mercy among Your righteous servants.﴾

* It also indicates that worship is a noble, great rank, which even the prophets ask for, based on His words: ﴿among Your servants﴾. For this reason, Allah, the Exalted, describes His Prophet Muhammad ﷺ by the attribute of servanthood at the highest of his stations, when the Qur'an was revealed, and when defending it, and similar situations. And a poet, addressing someone, said:

*Do not call me except "O slave of her,"*
*for it is the noblest of my names.*

This—I seek refuge in Allah—is a lovesick man! Let us suppose his name is, for example, Bakr (young camel). He says: Do not call me "O Bakr," say: "O slave of Layla," for it is the noblest of my names. So servanthood to Allah, the Exalted, there is no doubt that it is the noblest of human attributes, that a person be a servant of Allah. A person must be a servant, and must take a god. Even the communists and atheists must be servants and have gods. Is that not so? Correct. Do you agree with this?

* Student: It must be..

* The Shaykh: Yes indeed, it must be, even if their only gods are their desires. ﴿Have you seen the one who takes his own desire as his god, and Allah has sent him astray knowingly and sealed over his hearing﴾ [Al-Jathiyah 23]. And the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "Woe to the slave of the dinar, woe to the slave of the dirham" [Narrated by al-Bukhari (6435) and at-Tabarani in al-Awsat (2595) from Abu Hurayrah; the wording is that of at-Tabarani.], and these without doubt worship the dinar and the dirham. Indeed, they strive for nothing but that. These atheists strive for nothing but that.

So every person must be a servant. If he is a servant of Allah, then he has truly been freed from servitude, for the servant of Allah is free. He sees nothing in this world or among creatures as a master over him, but he sees his Creator as his master and his god, and that he is a servant of this Creator. ﴿And admit me by Your mercy among Your righteous servants.﴾ That is what I have. Is there anything from you, or is that sufficient?

* Student: (...).

* The Shaykh: It may be derived from it. And there is no doubt that gratitude for blessings is itself a blessing. The poet said:

*If my gratitude is a blessing from Allah, a blessing upon me for which, for the like of it, gratitude is due,*
*then how can gratitude be attained except by His grace, even if the days are long and life continues?*

And this is true. If Allah enables you to be grateful, that is a blessing. It is obligatory upon you to thank Allah for this blessing. When you thank Him, it becomes a second blessing that requires thanks, because Allah says: ﴿And few of My servants are grateful﴾ [Saba 13]. So when you see (...).

* Student: The refutation of the Qadariyyah (Qadariyya, those who deny divine decree of human acts).

* The Shaykh: In what?

* Student: His saying, Mighty and Majestic: ﴿Indeed, Allah is Knowing and Acquainted﴾.

* The Shaykh: Good, well done. Correct. There is a refutation of the Qadariyyah, because the Qadariyyah hold that a person is independent in his deeds, needing no help from Allah at all. There is no doubt that this is a false view, but this verse refutes them.

Also there is a refutation of the Jabriyyah (Jabriyya, those who deny human choice in acts), because He attributed the deed to the person, saying: ﴿that I may do righteous deeds which You approve﴾. And His words ﴿that I may do righteous deeds﴾ mean: it is possible that I do other than righteous deeds, so he is choosing. So in it is a refutation of both groups: the Qadariyyah and the Jabriyyah. What is the difference between them?

* Student: The Qadariyyah say that the person (...), and the Jabriyyah say that the person is compelled in his deeds.

* The Shaykh: He has no choice or anything.

* Student: (...).

* The Shaykh: How is that?

* Student: (...).

* The Shaykh: We said: using it as evidence for this is not strong, because Allah has a blessing upon the disbeliever, does He not? Allah has a blessing upon the disbeliever, but absolute blessing is only through Islam. From this aspect, do we say?

* Student: (...).

* The Shaykh: In any case, he is close to being a Muslim, but if something more correct than this were obtained, it would be good.

Then Allah, the Exalted, said: ﴿And he inspected the birds﴾ [An-Naml 20]..

* Student: (...).

* The Shaykh: No, we cannot say that. (...) we say what he says, for the Prophet, peace be upon him, said: "Every prophet used to be sent to his own people specifically" [Agreed upon; al-Bukhari (335) and Muslim (521/3) from Jabir ibn Abdullah; the wording is al-Bukhari's.].

* Student: Shaykh, (...).

* The Shaykh: That a person does not reach his goal except by the mercy of Allah?

* Student: (...) the goal (...).

* The Shaykh: Yes, no. Here He said: ﴿among His righteous servants﴾; that is, he does not reach his aim unless Allah has mercy on him. Everything, the Garden and other than the Garden; that is, if Allah does not have mercy on you, (...) never.

* Student: Shaykh, the line of poetry (...).

* The Shaykh:
*If my gratitude is a blessing from Allah, a blessing upon me for which, for the like of it, gratitude is due,*
*then how can gratitude be attained except by His grace, even if the days are long and life continues?*

* Student: The second line.

* The Shaykh:
*Then how can gratitude be attained except by His grace, even if the days are long and life continues?*

* Student: (...).

* The Shaykh: (...) so you have done well.

* Student: (...).

* The Shaykh: Correct. He is born upon the fitrah in the sight of Allah, but the outward matter is different from the matter of the inward. For this reason, the children of disbelievers are not buried in the cemeteries of the Muslims.

* Student: (...).

* The Shaykh: Yes, outwardly. Disbelief is treated under the rulings of this world.

Commentary of Ibn 'Uthaymin (Tafsir al-Quran al-Karim) on surah 27, verse 17–19 (part 1 of 4):

Allah the Exalted said: ﴿And there were gathered for Solomon his hosts of the jinn and mankind and the birds﴾ [An-Naml 17].

Solomon, peace be upon him, was given by Allah, blessed and exalted is He, a kingdom that is not fitting for anyone after him. "Even the Messenger, peace and blessings of Allah be upon him, when he intended to seize the devil, said: 'I remembered the word of my brother Solomon: ﴿Grant me a kingdom that is not fitting for anyone after me﴾'"[[Agreed upon; al-Bukhari (461) and Muslim (541 / 39) from the hadith of Abu Hurayrah.]]. Among the features of this kingdom is its great organisation. Ḥushira (was gathered): was assembled. And who does the gathering?
* A student: Allah, glorified and exalted.
* The Shaykh: No. Allah is over all things capable, but the one who gathers is the naqibs (chiefs) and the 'urafa' (overseers) whom he appointed to gather these hosts. He organised his kingdom to the utmost degree of organisation, and he appointed for every group leaders and overseers who gather them.
﴿There were gathered for Solomon his hosts of the jinn and mankind and the birds﴾. And others besides them? The jinn is clear, and mankind are the responsible ones, and the birds are not responsible but they fly. We are left with the other animals, the grazing and the crawling ones. Do they enter this by way of greater priority, so that we say: if the birds, which cannot be controlled in their flight, are gathered, then others are more so?
* A student: By greater priority.
* The Shaykh: By greater priority. Or we say: Solomon, peace be upon him, used only birds, because he employed them for his interests.
* A student: (...).
* The Shaykh: No. From everything, it is possible in this generality. That is: if we take "min" (from) as partitive and not general, and if we take "from everything" as that by which the kingdom is established and strengthened, it is not necessarily like this thing. So it is a matter of difficulty for us. Now we say: he was silent about the rest of the animals; are they included in his hosts or not?
You may say: they are included by way of greater priority, and you may say: they are not included. What is the basis of our saying "by way of greater priority"? That we say: if the bird, which cannot be controlled in its flight, is gathered and assembled, then others are more so. Or not?
And you may say: it is not necessary, because it is possible that Solomon, peace be upon him, used only birds from among the animals, and if he used no others, there is no need for him to gather the rest.
﴿So they were marshalled﴾. Look at this too: ﴿So they were marshalled﴾. The author says: (they are gathered and then driven). This too is part of the organisation. ﴿So they were marshalled﴾ means: they are driven. That is: organised in their gathering and their march; they are gathered first, and after being gathered they are marshalled, so they are driven in an orderly manner.
There is no doubt that this is from the organisation that preserves for people their time and work, because most of what wastes a person's time and work is the lack of organisation.
For this reason I say: it is incumbent upon us to have an organisation for our daily affairs to the extent possible, but this does not mean that we insist on these affairs even if something better is found. No, rather the person should simply be orderly and organised, not letting his time become chaos, when he reads in a book (...) with the second (...), no, or does this regulated work and then abandons it.
But you should have an organisation, and it is commendable that whenever a matter is more important he begins with it first, begins with it first. Some people used to say: among their organisation is making the reading of newspapers and journals after lunch, for example, and not making the reading of important books that require effort after lunch, because reading newspapers is superficial reading, like ordinary conversation, with no strain in it.
But books and deep study require effort, and this does not suit the state of having eaten one's fill.
* * *
* A student: ﴿I found a woman ruling over them, and she has been given of everything, and she has a mighty throne (23). I found her and her people prostrating to the sun besides Allah, and the devil has made their deeds fair-seeming to them and barred them from the way, so they are not guided (24). [They do so] so that they do not prostrate to Allah, who brings forth what is hidden in the heavens and the earth, and knows what you conceal and what you declare (25). Allah — there is no deity except Him, Lord of the Mighty Throne﴾ [An-Naml 23–26].
* The Shaykh: I seek refuge in Allah from the accursed devil.
First, from the words of the Exalted: ﴿And there were gathered for Solomon his hosts of the jinn and mankind and the birds, so they were marshalled﴾.
* From this noble verse it is derived that Solomon, peace be upon him, organised and arranged his hosts, such that they are gathered at the time of gathering and dispersed at the time of dispersal; by His saying: ﴿There were gathered for Solomon his hosts﴾.
* And in the verse is evidence that the hosts that Solomon took with him were three categories: the jinn, mankind and the birds.
As for mankind, his taking them is evident, since he was one of them. As for the jinn, it is for their use in what mankind cannot do. As for the birds, some scholars said: they accompany him to shade him, being a canopy of shade from the sun above his head, and this may be intended; and it may also be that among the purposes of taking the birds is that they bring distant news, as in the story of the hoopoe.
* And also in His saying: ﴿so they were marshalled﴾ is evidence of perfect organisation as well, because what does "wazaʿa" mean? Gathering and driving. ﴿And on the Day when the enemies of Allah are gathered to the Fire, they will be marshalled﴾ [Fussilat 19]: they are gathered toward it and driven toward it. This too is evidence of perfect organisation.
* And in it is evidence for the use of a rearguard (sāqah); in armies and hosts there should be a driver just as there is a leader and guide, so they also have a driver. It was of the guidance of the Messenger, peace and blessings of Allah be upon him, that he would be in the rearguard at the back of the people, even though he was their leader and chief, but he would lag behind in order to assist whoever fell short and help whoever was in need, and for the great benefits that are achieved by this.
Then: ﴿until, when they came upon the valley of the ants, an ant said: "O ants, enter your dwellings, lest Solomon and his hosts crush you while they do not perceive"﴾.
* In it is evidence that among eloquence is brevity through omission; because His saying: ﴿until when they came﴾ comes after a omitted thing. What is the estimate? "So they journeyed until, when they came..." ﴿until when they came upon the valley of the ants﴾: (until) denotes a limit, so there must be something before it that is limited.
* And in it is evidence for attributing a place to its inhabitant; by His saying: ﴿the valley of the ants﴾, as is said now of neighbourhoods in towns: "this is the quarter of so-and-so", as is well known from ancient times, that neighbourhoods are attributed to their residents. Do we say: is there in this evidence that if the ants settle a land they own it, such that it is not permissible to revive it or benefit from it, or not?
* A student: The apparent meaning is that there is evidence.
* The Shaykh: There is evidence.
* The student: The apparent meaning.
* The Shaykh: Let us leave it, we do not know. Alright, now two have disagreed, one says: no, and the second says: yes. Which do you prefer?
* A student: (...).
* The Shaykh: No. Alright, ﴿the valley of the ants﴾ is the house of so-and-so; do you have a right to come to the house of so-and-so and live in it? (...).
* Students: (...).
* The Shaykh: Yes, indeed. We say: correct. If we looked at the bare wording, the valley of the ants would belong to them, to the ants. But Allah the Exalted says: ﴿He it is who created for you all that is on the earth﴾ [Al-Baqarah 29]. If the ant were edible we would eat it, so how would we not eat its dwellings? The children of Adam have more right to the earth than others. So if, for example, a person needs to cultivate this land and there are ants in it, there is no harm in his cultivating it, and if it entails that the ants die, if it entails that the ants die, because this death is not intended, and what is not intended but comes about necessarily from taking up something permissible, it does no harm. This principle is well known in the Shariah: that a thing which arises necessarily from doing something permissible, and which is not intended, is not harmful. So consider, for example, the killing of women and children in war: is it permitted or not?
* A student: It is not permitted.
* The Shaykh: It is not permitted. But if we cannot reach the fighters except by shelling with the catapult and general artillery, is it permitted or not?
* A student: It is permitted.
* The Shaykh: Even if it entails the killing of women and children, even if it entails; because this is not intended. Likewise, the cutting of palm trees: the palm trees of the enemy, is it permitted or not?
* Students: It is not permitted.
* The Shaykh: But if we cannot reach them except by cutting their palms, it is permitted; as the Prophet, peace be upon him, did with Banu al-Nadir.
The summary is that we say: if killing the ant is necessary for reviving the land, there is no harm in it, because it was not intended, but arose out of necessity in taking up a matter that is permissible for us.
* A student: (...).
* The Shaykh: Yes indeed, its killing is permitted; every harmful creature. Even a human being, if he harms you and attacks you and it cannot be repelled except by killing, you kill him, and he is the most sacred of living beings.
* And in this verse is evidence that insects have speech; by His saying: ﴿an ant said﴾.
* And in it is evidence that her speech was also heard, heard by those of her kind; because if they did not hear it there would be no benefit in it. They hear her speech, and Allah, blessed and exalted, may make whomever He wills hear it.
* And in it is evidence that the common people used this to argue that everything speaks by nature. This is not correct, but Allah the Exalted may make creatures hear the speech of some animals, either as a sign, or as a miracle, or the like.
* A student: Everything speaks by nature (...).
* The Shaykh: Yes, everything speaks; some of them said: the gypsum speaks. And it is apparent that there is a message possible for the gypsum, and it speaks, and the gypsum is a store for dates.
* * *
Allah, blessed and exalted, said: ﴿until, when they came upon the valley of the ants, an ant said: "O ants, enter your dwellings, lest Solomon and his hosts crush you while they do not perceive"﴾ [An-Naml 18].
His saying ﴿until when they came﴾ is a limit to what preceded it, namely His saying: ﴿and there were gathered﴾; ﴿until when﴾. Accordingly, there is an omission in the speech, its estimate being: "and they journeyed, until when they came." After the hosts were gathered and marshalled, their first was returned to their last, and they were ordered, and they set out.
﴿until when they came upon the valley of the ants﴾: they came, that is, Solomon and his hosts, that is, they passed by.
His saying: ﴿upon the valley of the ants﴾: the apparent meaning of the speech is that this valley was known by this title, that it is called the valley of the ants. It is possible, though this is contrary to the apparent meaning, that this valley was a valley in which there were ants, that is, "until when they came upon a valley in which there were ants", and it was not known by this title of "the valley of the ants"; but the better course is to adopt the apparent wording, namely that this valley was known for the abundance of its ants, and was given this title because of its abundance.
The ant is well known, and it is among the creatures whose killing has been forbidden, as in the Sunan: "that the Prophet ﷺ forbade the killing of four of the animals, and he mentioned among them the ant"[[Narrated by Abu Dawud (5267) and Ibn Majah (3224) from the hadith of Ibn 'Abbas.]].
And in the Sahih also: "concerning one of the prophets, peace be upon them, that an ant bit him, so he ordered the whole ant-colony to be burned; Allah rebuked him for that and said: 'Why not one ant?'"[[Narrated by al-Bukhari (3319) and Muslim (2241 / 148) from the hadith of Abu Hurayrah.]].
This ant is among the creatures that know their Lord and know what benefits them and what harms them, according to the guidance placed within them. Moses, peace be upon him, said to Pharaoh when he said: ﴿Who is your Lord, O Moses?﴾ [49] ﴿He said: "Our Lord is He who gave everything its creation, then guided it"﴾ [Ta-Ha 49–50]. ﴿Gave everything its creation﴾: the creation fitting for it. Every thing, of animals and others, has a creation fitting to it, which Allah gave, and then guided it; He guided this creation also to what its interests depend upon.
So this ant is among the creatures to which Allah, blessed and exalted, gave their creation and guided them.
(﴿They came upon the valley of the ants﴾ and it was in al-Ta'if or in Syria), there is difference of opinion, and there is no evidence either for al-Ta'if or for Syria, and the closer view is that it was in Syria; yet we do not affirm this definitively, because the seat of Solomon, peace be upon him, was in Syria, and even so we do not affirm it. Is specifying the place one of the matters that are indispensable in the story?
* Students: No.
* The Shaykh: No; because the purpose is taking a lesson from what happened in whatever place on earth it occurred.
And he said: (its ants were small or large) as well. What concern is it of ours? Some say: its ants are large, the ant being the size of a wolf. That is, the ants become donkeys. This is not correct; rather the ant is the one known in the language of the Arabs, and whoever interprets any part of the Qur'an contrary to what the Arabic language requires, must have proof, otherwise it is rejected, because we have a fundamental principle in the interpretation of the Qur'an, which is His saying, the Exalted: ﴿in a clear Arabic tongue﴾ [Ash-Shu'ara 195]. Whoever claims that any part of the Qur'an is contrary to this clear Arabic tongue, the burden of proof is on him.
On this basis we say: the ant is the well-known ant, and as for the claim that it is large, the size of a wolf, there is no evidence for it.
* A student: (...).
* The Shaykh: No, this well-known ant.
﴿The ant said﴾: this is the answer of ﴿when﴾: "until when they came, an ant said" (the queen of the ants, who had seen the hosts of Solomon) ﴿O ants, enter your dwellings﴾ to the end.
He said: ﴿an ant said﴾; he says: (the queen of the ants, who had seen the hosts of Solomon). As for his saying: (who had seen the hosts of Solomon), this is clear. Allah knows whether she saw them or perceived them; it may be perception without looking, or it may be looking; in any case she perceived his nearness and the arrival of Solomon with his hosts upon them.
And the Exalted's saying: ﴿an ant said﴾: "an ant" is indefinite, whereas the apparent meaning of the exegete's words is that it is definite, since he said: "the queen of the ants." This would require the expression to be: "the ant said," meaning the known ant, which is the queen. And since the expression was not "the ant said," this shows that the speaker is not necessarily the queen of the ants, but rather one ant from among the ants. This is not strange: just as if a host of soldiers approached a group of people, and one of them saw them and cried out to them, and it is not necessary that this crier be the commander or the king.
Therefore the correct view is to leave the Qur'an on its apparent meaning, that she was an ant from among these ants, and it is not necessary that she be the queen; because in such situations any one of the group who feels fear cries out to them and warns: "I am the naked warner."
﴿an ant said﴾: so the correct statement is that we say: an ant from among the ants said, and we do not specify her as the queen.
Alright, "(who had seen the hosts of Solomon)": is it also necessary that it be by sight, or is perception permissible (...)?
* A student: (...) if she saw (...).
* The Shaykh: Yes, but must the perception be by sight? Or is perception by feeling and hearing also permissible? It is possible. Then we ask: do ants have eyes?
* Students: Yes, they have antennae.
* The Shaykh: This requires study in biology. Indeed, I have seen a statement that says: when the ant walks, by God's permission, it secretes something, and the other ants walk following its scent. This is something I witnessed with my own eyes: there was a carpet like this carpet, only large; the point is that it was of this kind, and this ant would walk and come to a corner and then return, that is, it walks in a rectangle, comes to the corner and returns; all the ants do this, that is, they do not go straight and cut across. I was amazed (...) it knows the way. But if it were on dirt, the ones on the dirt would show the trace of the ant and walk one after another; but this was not on dirt. However, after I read this about it, I understood that when it walks it has a scent, and the rest of the ants walk upon it. Yes, and this is among the signs of Allah, the Glorified and Exalted. This is the meaning of His saying: ﴿gave everything its creation, then guided﴾ [Ta-Ha 50].
In any case, what we are obliged to take from this noble verse is that the ant perceived that, by sight or otherwise.

Commentary of Ibn 'Uthaymin (Tafsir al-Quran al-Karim) on surah 27, verse 17–19 (part 2 of 4):

He says: ﴿Until, when they came upon the valley of the ants, an ant said, "O ants, enter your dwellings, lest Solomon and his hosts crush you while they do not perceive."﴾ Note that this sentence contains a call (nida'), a command, guidance, a warning, and other things that we may grasp, God willing, after a detailed discussion.

﴿O you ants﴾: This is a call (nida'). We have mentioned many times that opening a sentence with a call serves the purpose of alerting the listener. That is, if you say "Do such-and-such" or "O so-and-so, do such-and-such," the latter is greater and more emphatic, because it is to alert him.

Then her saying ﴿O you ants﴾ is a distant call, introduced with an alerting expression, ﴿O you ants﴾. For if she had said "O ants" (ya namlu), it might have been missed. As you see, when a person speaks to you and begins with something to alert you before entering the intended subject, nothing of the intended meaning is lost to the one addressed; but if the beginning is missed, something of the intended meaning may be lost. She said "O you ants" and did not say "O ants."

Furthermore, the call to a distant party also indicates that she raised her voice so that everyone heard ﴿O you ants﴾.

In her saying ﴿enter﴾, this is a command, and what is meant by it is guidance. In specifying "dwellings," which are shelters, this is like the air-raid sirens among people: when the siren sounds, where do they go? To the rooftops? No, to the shelters. She too guided them to their shelters: ﴿enter your dwellings﴾.

Furthermore, there is also an indication that these dwellings, just as they are coverings in which a person is sheltered, are also fortresses by which a person protects himself: ﴿Did We not make the earth a receptacle, for the living and the dead?﴾ [al-Mursalat 25–26].

In her saying ﴿your dwellings﴾, is the idafa (genitive construction) here by way of the lam (for) or not? Or by way of (min)?
* Student: No, the lam: dwellings for you.
* Shaykh: Yes, by way of the lam; not (min) nor (fi). The idafa is by way of (min) when the mudaf is of the same kind as the mudaf ilayh, like "a ring of iron" or "a door of wood." It is by way of (fi) when the mudaf ilayh is a container for the mudaf, as in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Rather, it is the plotting of the night and the day﴾ [Saba' 33], meaning: plotting in the night. And it is by way of the lam, which is the most common and frequent, and here it is by way of the lam. And is the lam implied in the idafa here the lam of specification (ikhtisas) or the lam of ownership (milk)?
For us, it is the lam of specification; but for them, the ants among themselves, it appears to be the lam of ownership, in that each one of them knows her own dwelling and that no one enters upon her.
* Student: (...).
* Shaykh: She owns it. If it is known to be a sale contract, and it is not possible (...), you also register it.

﴿your dwellings, lest Solomon and his hosts crush you﴾: This is the warning, and the evidence is the warning.
(﴿lest they crush you﴾: break you.) This sentence is like a reason for the command in her saying ﴿enter your dwellings﴾. That is, as if someone were to say: why? "Lest Solomon crush you." So the sentence is a reason and a warning, a reason and a warning. This is also part of its eloquence: she did not merely say "enter your dwellings," but specified the thing to be feared, which is ﴿lest Solomon crush you﴾.

Then she brought this sentence of severe impact. She did not say "lest they trample you"; she said "lest they crush you." Which is more forceful?
* Students: The latter is more forceful.
* Shaykh: The latter is more forceful, because trampling may or may not entail breaking and destruction, whereas the word "crushing" (tahtim) is more severe than trampling. Is that clear?
Does the situation require such a harsh expression? Yes, because the situation is one of warning and urgency: if they do not do this quickly, they will be crushed. He said ﴿lest they crush you﴾, and here she said ﴿lest they crush you﴾ and she said ﴿enter﴾.

The use of ﴿enter﴾ and ﴿lest they crush you﴾ with the mim (plural masculine ending) is used only for rational beings, because non-rational beings are feminine: "enter your dwellings" (idkhulna masakinakunna) and "lest they crush you" (la yahtimanakunna). But she said ﴿enter﴾ and ﴿lest they crush you﴾, treating them as if they were rational. Or it may be said: with respect to one another, they are rational, just as we said that the dwellings are possession with respect to them and specification with respect to us.

﴿lest Solomon and his hosts crush you﴾: It is as if this expression indicates that the greatness of Solomon is firmly established in their minds, and so it is.

As for her saying ﴿Solomon and his hosts﴾, she did not say "and his host," because what we understand from the Qur'an is that with him are three kinds of hosts: who? Humans, jinn, and birds, as already mentioned.

As for her saying ﴿and his hosts while they do not perceive﴾: this is an excuse for whom? For Solomon and his hosts: that they did not intend to crush you, but did so without their awareness. For you know that a host and a vast, great army, and these are small ants: indeed, it is possible for them to crush them without being aware. Moreover, it is generally the case that such a large host cannot restrain some of its members from others when they come upon an ant hole, for example. This is the meaning of her saying ﴿while they do not perceive﴾.

That is, if someone says: how, when they do not perceive? Do they walk without guidance?
We say: no, they walk with guidance, but it is well known that when we compare this vast, great host with the smallness of these ants, it is generally the case that they do not perceive them.

So these eloquent, great sentences, from this creature that is nothing in the eyes of people and is among the smallest of creatures, what do they show us?
They show the greatness of the Creator, glory be to Him, and that what is greater than these creatures, the ants, is greater than them also in such matters; for He who gave the small this gift and guided it with this guidance, the great is even more in need of guidance than that, and has whatever knowledge it has. He says: ﴿while they do not perceive. So he smiled, laughing at her speech﴾ [al-Naml 19]. The ants were treated as rational beings in the address, by addressing them as such. Where is the address to them as rational?
* Student: In her saying: ﴿An ant said, "O you ants, enter﴾.
* Shaykh: ﴿enter﴾, and ﴿your dwellings﴾, and ﴿lest they crush you﴾; because the mim here is for a group of rational beings, and the waw as well is for a group of rational beings, so they were addressed with the address of rational beings, just as we said: either because some of them are rational with respect to others, or because since this address is understood and acted upon, it is as if she were addressing rational beings.
* Student: She expressed ﴿lest they crush you﴾, meaning: broken. And ants are soft animals or soft insects.
* Shaykh: No, the meaning of breaking is not that it breaks only one limb. The meaning of breaking is destruction by way of crushing. For example, if you tread on an ant, it is cut and torn; this is broken. It does not mean that its leg is broken and it remains hanging by it, for example. No.
* Student: ﴿lest they crush you﴾: lest they destroy you?
* Shaykh: No, crushing (hatm) is more intense and stronger in warning: ﴿And what will make you know what the crushing is?﴾ [al-Humazah 5]. This crushing is more emphatic.

He said: (﴿So he smiled﴾, Solomon at first, ﴿laughing﴾ at the end, ﴿at her speech﴾.)
They say that laughter has three kinds: initial, intermediate, and final. The initial is smiling (tabassum). The intermediate is laughter (dahk). The final is guffawing (qahqaha).

Guffawing does not befit a sensible, dignified person, and smiling is the most common laughter of the prophets, peace be upon them; laughter occurs from the prophets at times. So here he smiled, laughing.

The author, may God have mercy on him, holds that Solomon, peace be upon him, had two stages in this laughter: the first smiling, and the second laughing. He began with smiling and ended with laughing. It is also possible that "smiled, laughing" means he laughed while smiling, that is, laughed in a smiling manner, meaning that no sound appeared from him, but he smiled a smile. And God knows best.

On this interpretation, "laughing" is a circumstantial clause confirming and specifying the kind, meaning that his laughter was a smile.

In any case, this matter does no harm: whether his laughter began with a smile and ended with laughter. The difference: smiling is when the mouth opens without sound; laughter involves sound but without guffawing. Guffawing is when the sound is repeated, "karkara," as the common people say.
* Student: (...).
* Shaykh: Yes indeed. He says: ﴿laughing at her speech﴾: the min is explicative (bayaniyya), and the explicative min indicates cause: that is, because of her speech he smiled. What was the source of this smile? He smiled at her speech: at her warning, her excuse, her guidance. From where? From her eloquence.
* Student: From all of these.
* Shaykh: From everything this speech contains; for in reality it is a matter of wonder that she speaks with such eloquent speech, and with such speed... Yes, she did not go (...) and bring the elements and explain. Yes, this is undoubtedly a cause for laughter. Furthermore, it is a cause for laughter not only from the words themselves but from the import of this speech; and for this reason he counted it among God's favor and said: ﴿My Lord, inspire me to be grateful for Your favor﴾. The import of this speech, perhaps, is that Solomon, peace be upon him, saw that even insects acknowledge his greatness and the greatness of his hosts. Yes, this is undoubtedly one of God's favors upon him. So this smile at the speech is from its content and significance, and likewise from its import and what it contains of God, blessed and exalted be He, favor upon Solomon.

﴿So he smiled, laughing at her speech﴾ (and he heard it from three miles away; the wind carried it to him, so he halted his hosts when he came upon their valley until they [the ants] had entered their dwellings; and his hosts were riders and walkers on this journey).

He says: (and he heard it from three miles away). From where did he get this?
* Student: Israelite reports.
* Shaykh: Israelite reports. Indeed, the Qur'an says ﴿until, when they came upon the valley of the ants﴾; what does this indicate? That they reached it. The most that can be said is that as soon as the ants were warned, they entered their dwellings. That is, between them and trampling those ants there was only the ants' entering their dwellings, and this does not require that there were three miles between him and them; there is no evidence for that. It is only said that he heard it from nearby. Did any of his other hosts hear it?
* Student: He does not know.
* Shaykh: It appears that they neither knew nor heard it; for His saying ﴿We have been taught the speech of birds﴾ indicates that this teaching, the speech of animals, was specific to Solomon, peace be upon him, and not as some common people claim. Some common people say that he understood everything that speaks, and they recount stories based on this. This is not correct; there is no known speech except among nations among themselves. As for humans, for example, knowing the speech of jinn, or knowing the speech of insects, this is not so without evidence. If evidence from the infallible one is found, it is correct, just as "the Prophet, peace be upon him, informed of the wolf that speaks, and he also informed of the cow that its owner rode, and it said to him: we were not created for this." [Agreed upon; al-Bukhari (3471) and Muslim (2388/13), from the hadith of Abu Hurayrah.]
The point is that what evidence establishes we must accept; otherwise the principle is that each thing speaks in its own language, and that each kind does not understand the language of another...
* Student: He says, exalted is He: ﴿And mention Our servant Dawud, possessor of strength; indeed, he was one who often turned back [to Allah]. Indeed, We subjected the mountains to exalt [Allah] with him in the evening and at sunrise, and the birds assembled; all were to him returning [in repentance]﴾ [Sad 17–19]. If the birds, the returning ones, were subservient to him...
* Shaykh: ﴿all were to him﴾: to whom?
* Student: To Dawud.
* Shaykh: Or to God.
* Student: Or to the nearer of Dawud?
* Shaykh: No, the matter requires reciting it; even the recitation is not fixed by what you have recited.
* Student: ﴿Be patient over what they say, and remember Our servant Dawud, possessor of strength; indeed, he was one who often turned back. Indeed, We subjected the mountains to exalt [Allah] with him in the evening and at sunrise, and the birds assembled; all were to him returning.﴾
* Shaykh: I do not know; I did not vocalize the verse...

* * *

He says: ﴿So he smiled, laughing at her speech, and said, "My Lord, inspire me [to be grateful]"﴾ (inspire me) ﴿to be grateful for Your favor which You have bestowed upon me﴾.

﴿He said: My Lord﴾: this is a vocative, from which the particle of calling has been dropped, and its original form is "O my Lord" (ya rabbi). The ya of the first person pronoun is also dropped for lightness; otherwise its original form is "rabbi" with the ya. Supplication always comes with the particle of calling dropped. Why?
* Student: The ya.
* Shaykh: Why does supplication always come with the particle of calling dropped?
* Student: Beginning with the mention of God, for blessing.
* Shaykh: Beginning with the name of God and care for the intended object, which is God, glory be to Him. "Lord" is begun before anything else, and it is as if a person, out of his intense longing for his Lord during supplication, utters nothing but the name of God, glory be to Him.

He says: ﴿My Lord, inspire me﴾: "inspire me" (awzi'ni) in terms of grammatical analysis is called an imperative verb, but the grammarians, may God have mercy on them, out of courtesy toward God, do not say "imperative verb," because you do not command God. They call it: a verb of supplication. When we parse ﴿My Lord, inspire me﴾, we say: awzi' is a verb of supplication, and we do not say it is an imperative verb intended for supplication. It is in fact an imperative verb and the intended meaning is supplication, but out of courtesy toward God we say "verb of supplication."

(﴿Inspire me﴾: direct me) ﴿to be grateful for Your favor which You have bestowed﴾ upon me ﴿and upon my parents, and to do righteousness that You will accept﴾.

﴿He said: My Lord, inspire me to be grateful for Your favor﴾: what moved Solomon, peace be upon him, to say this was acknowledgment of God's favor, glory be to Him, and fear of self-conceit. For if the ant speaks like this out of fear of him and his hosts, and apologizes to them, and its speech is understood, this may lead a person to conceit, thinking that this thing is by his own essence or from himself, just as Qarun said: ﴿I was only given it because of knowledge I have﴾ [al-Qasas 78]. So at this juncture, where a person may be led to conceit, and a human is a human, he asked God to inspire him to thank Him for His favor which He bestowed upon him and his parents, and to do righteousness that He is pleased with.

Thus a person, when he receives a blessing, should ask God, blessed and exalted be He, to inspire him to thank for it, so that conceit does not overtake him regarding the blessing God has bestowed upon him, whether the blessing is material or physical, moral or sensible.

﴿My Lord, inspire me that I may be grateful﴾: the "an" here is verbal (masdariyya); what is its place in grammar?
* Student: (...).
* Shaykh: It is the second object of "awzi'ni," since the first object is the ya, and the second object is ﴿an ashkura﴾. That is: inspire me to thank You for the favor You have bestowed upon me and upon my parents.

As for His saying ﴿an ashkura ni'matak﴾: what is the meaning of "ni'mah" (favor)? It is the kindness that the benefactor bestows upon the one benefited. And favor, as you know, is of two kinds: either obtaining what is desired, or deliverance from what is feared.

God, blessed and exalted be He, always bestows His favors upon His servant, and the servant moves between these two kinds of favor: he always obtains what he desires and is delivered from what he fears. As for the commentator's words: (﴿bestowed﴾ upon me, by it). Why did he estimate "by it"?
* Student: He thinks that "bestowed" (...).
* Shaykh: No; because it is well known that a relative clause must have a resumptive pronoun referring back to the relative pronoun; there must be a returning pronoun referring to the relative.
Here, ﴿which You have bestowed upon me﴾: the clause "bestowed" needs a pronoun referring back to "which," and the author estimated it by his saying "by it." Does anyone among you dispute this estimate? That is, the estimation of the pronoun so that it refers back to the relative pronoun is clear and accepted; this is the grammatical rule. ﴿He eats of what you eat and drinks of what you drink﴾ [al-Mu'minun 33], meaning: of it. This is clear. This is common in Arabic speech: in the Qur'an, the Sunnah, and people's speech, there must be a returning pronoun referring to the relative pronoun to link the clause to its relative. But do you have any objection with the author regarding the estimation of the returning pronoun in this way?
* Student: (...) after the detached pronoun (...).

**Commentary of Ibn 'Uthaymin (Tafsir al-Quran al-Karim) on Surah 27, verses 17–19 (part 3 of 4)**

* Shaykh: Because the separate pronoun is *iyyahu*, *iyyaya*, *iyyaka*. This is a separate pronoun, so the pronoun here is undoubtedly attached (*muttasil*).
* Student: (...) but (...) the *ba'* (preposition "with") is there.
* Shaykh: Yes, even if it is attached, even if (...) it is attached, even with the *ba'* present. He would say, "*anamtuha 'alayya*" (I bestowed it upon myself). That is correct, but it is not the cause. The estimate you made is correct, but the cause is not the cause ('illah).

They say: the returning pronoun (*al-'a'id*) is not deleted when it is in the genitive case unless the relative pronoun is governed by a preposition similar to the deleted one in form, meaning and implied sense. Do you understand? This came up for us; we used to read in grammar in *al-Qatr* (a grammar primer), and that when it is in the genitive, it must be governed by the same preposition that governs the relative pronoun, and that it must agree with it in form, and its complement must be the same, agreeing in form, estimate and meaning.

The author now estimated (*bi-ha*) ("with it"), although it is not present in the Qur'an: (*"ni'matakal-lati an'amta*" [the blessing You bestowed] *bi-ha*). Accordingly, the sound estimate is to say: *an'amtaha 'alayya wa-'ala walidayya* (You bestowed it upon me and upon my parents), because the returning pronoun in the genitive cannot be deleted unless the relative pronoun is governed by the same preposition that governs that returning pronoun.

As for His saying ﴿upon me and upon my parents﴾: regarding "upon me," it is clear that God's blessing upon you requires gratitude from you. But God's blessing upon your parents, what is the reason it requires gratitude from you?

Because God's blessing upon the parents is a blessing upon the child, especially this blessing which occurred, namely that he inherited prophethood from David and succeeded him in it. So this blessing, God's blessing upon his parents, is in reality a blessing upon him. For this reason He said: ﴿upon me and upon my parents﴾.

And His saying: ﴿*walidayya*﴾ (my parents). Is this plural or dual?

* Students: Dual.
* Shaykh: *Walidayya* is a dual in the construct state (*mudaf*), and for this reason the *nun* was deleted from it. Its original form is *walidan li* (two parents for me), but the *nun* was deleted because of the construct.

Now, *walidayya*: what is meant by "father" (*walid*)?

* Student: The word *walid* means the father, in the plural form.
* Shaykh: That is, is it the father who is your biological parent, or even the grandfather and whoever is above him?

We say: in reality, the word *walid* sometimes includes the grandfather and those above him, and sometimes it is specified to the father. What determines this are the indications (*qara'in*), either verbal indications or circumstantial indications. For example: it is not permitted for a giver to take back what he gave, except a parent (*walid*) regarding what he gives his child. What is meant by "parent" here?

* Student: The father.

The direct father. The nearer parent; the grandfather is not included. "Parent" in the prohibition of marriage? It includes the nearer and the farther.

"Parent" in inheritance?

* Student: According to the correct view, it includes both.
* Shaykh: It includes the nearer and the farther, if the father is absent. What is meant is males and females. That is: do not suppose, according to the correct view, that we mean the grandfather, the male parent. Even the female, for example the mother, in inheritance, *walid* includes the farther ancestor if the nearer one is absent. Or not?

So in reality the word "parent" (*walid*) is sometimes meant as the nearer one, and sometimes meant as the nearer and farther together, or separately, and sometimes meant as the nearer and farther... no, what? What is it?

* Student: Not together.
* Shaykh: Not together. And what determines this are the indications: verbal indications or circumstantial ones.

* Student: (...) includes (...)?
* Shaykh: No, the word *walid*.
* Student: There is no difference between *walidayya* and *walidayya* (the other form).
* Shaykh: Yes, there is no difference between them. If we say *walidayya*, it means the father and the mother. If it is said *walidiyya*, that is not the expression used with *walidiyya*.
* Student: (...) my parent.
* Shaykh: There is no expression *walidiyya*. If a person expresses it that way, we say this expression is not correct. But *walidina* (our parents), when we are a group, is clear, because if you say *walidayna* and we are two, how many parents will there be? Four. If we are three, there will be six. And so on.

For this reason, some brothers who recite in Ramadan say: "O God, forgive us and our *walidayna*." This is not correct, except as a figurative usage (*tajawwuz*), because *walidayna*: we are not the children of one man. Yes, if we were children of one man and one mother, we would say *walidayna*, because our father is one and our mother is one. But if there were a thousand people in the mosque, is the parent of each one of us a parent of the other? We are not brothers.

* Student: Abbreviation of the wording.
* Shaykh: For this reason, *walidayna* is used only as a figurative usage, meaning: the *walidayya* of each one of us. For this reason, the correct expression in such a case is to say: "O God, forgive us and our *walidayna* (parents)."

* Student: (...) wrong.
* Shaykh: No. This is the correct form.
* Student: (...).
* Student: But everyone says it, except rarely.
* Shaykh: In any case, we cannot say that all of them do this or that. But we are now analyzing it from the standpoint of the Arabic language. The correct form in this is, when we are a group, *walidayna*, because *walidayna* is used only as a figurative usage.

All right, ﴿and upon my parents﴾.

* Student: His father and mother?
* Shaykh: Yes, his father and mother.

He says: ﴿and that I should do righteous deeds﴾. ﴿That I should do﴾ is coordinated with His saying ﴿that I should be grateful﴾, meaning: and inspire me to do righteous deeds that You approve.

And here His saying ﴿that I should do righteous deeds﴾ means: that I do a righteous deed. A righteous deed is not righteous unless it includes two essential conditions. What are they? Sometimes we ask, and there is no harm in asking.

* Student: Sincerity (*ikhlas*) and following the Prophet's way (*muttaba'ah*).
* Shaykh: Sincerity and following. Because of His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And they were commanded only to worship God, sincere to Him in religion, upright﴾ [al-Bayyinah 5]. All of it. Sincerity is clear for the prophets and others. Following is clear for you regarding those other than the prophets. Regarding the prophets it is not clear to you, but it is clear, because the prophet follows a law revealed to him. Is that not so?

* Student: Yes.
* Shaykh: He may not follow this law? He may not follow it. But as we have already mentioned, the prophets, peace be upon them, are protected from what? From being upheld in sins absolutely. So following exists in the prophets too, because following is from the law that was revealed to them.

So this righteous deed: it combines two matters, sincerity and following. If sincerity is lacking, there is *shirk* (associating partners with God). If following is lacking, there is *ibtida'* (innovation).

A deed that contains *shirk* is rejected. God said in the hadith qudsi (a saying of the Prophet in which God speaks in the first person): "I am the most self-sufficient of partners in regard to partnership. Whoever does a deed in which he associates others with Me, I abandon him and his association" [recorded by Muslim (2985/46) from the hadith of Abu Hurayrah].

Even showing off (*riya'*) is a kind of *shirk*. If a person performs an act of worship while showing off in it, then along with the sin, his deed is rejected.

Likewise in innovation. The Prophet ﷺ said: "Whoever does a deed that is not in accordance with our command, it is rejected" [recorded by Muslim (1718/18) from the hadith of 'A'ishah], and this is more general than the second wording: "Whoever introduces into this matter of ours something which is not part of it, it is rejected" [agreed upon; al-Bukhari (2697) and Muslim (1718/17) from the hadith of 'A'ishah].

Unless we say: whoever introduces into his essence and attributes.
