This specification has no proof. So we say: it is undoubtedly a large gift, and that it was carried by a group shows its greatness. As for specifying it with this list, we do not affirm it. If it was reported from the Children of Israel, then it is among the reports that are neither confirmed nor denied.

(Then the hoopoe hastened to Sulayman to inform him of the news.) Because Sulayman had said to him: ﴿Deliver it to them, then withdraw from them and see what they return﴾, or not? The apparent meaning is that the hoopoe remained until their affair settled on something, and it settled on sending the gift.
The author says: (The hoopoe hastened to Sulayman to inform him of the news, so he (Sulayman) ordered that gold and silver bricks be struck, and that a field be spread from his place to a distance of nine farsakhs, and that a high wall of gold and silver be built around it, and that the best beasts of land and sea be brought, together with the sons of the jinn, on the right and left of the field.)

* Student: This is more severe than the first.

* Shaykh: Yes indeed. All of this has no proof. All of these things the author mentions have no proof. They are among the strange reports, meaning that they must be brought to the author and he should produce them.

* Student: Difficult.

* Shaykh: Although it is brief, and although the verse contains no proof whatsoever for this matter, that they make gold and silver spread from his place to nine farsakhs. How large is a nine-farsakh distance in miles? Three times nine?

* Students: Twenty-seven.

* Shaykh: Twenty-seven miles.

* Student: And a mile is about a kilometer and a half.

* Shaykh: And a mile is about a kilometer and a half.

* * *

(﴿When he came﴾, the envoy came with the gift and with his followers, ﴿to Sulayman﴾.) The word (jāʾa, came) is in the accusative, and (jāʾa) means (atā, came).

﴿So when he came to Sulayman, he said: Would you supply me with wealth?﴾

The author said: (and with him his followers), and the woman says: ﴿with what the envoys return﴾, and Sulayman says: ﴿Would you supply me with wealth?﴾ (ʾAtumiddūna) is plural, so he is addressing a group, while the one who came is singular. The woman says she sent a group. How do we reconcile these things? The woman's speech shows that she sent a group.
And Allah's saying: ﴿So when he came to Sulayman﴾ shows that the one who came was singular. Sulayman's saying: ﴿Would you supply me with wealth?﴾ shows that the addressees are a group. The reconciliation of these is very simple: this group had an opinion, and the one who approached Sulayman with the gift was their leader together with his group. So the one who came forward to Sulayman with the gift was one person with his group. For this reason the author says: (and with him his followers).

* Student: O Shaykh, what if the one sent to him came?

* Shaykh: No, because the subject is not mentioned.

* Student: The subject not being mentioned is evidence.

* Shaykh: If the subject is not mentioned, it is implicit, and it is known that (jāʾa, came) is singular. If the intended meaning were the group, he would say: "When they came to Sulayman" (fa-lammā jāʾū Sulaymāna).

* Student: The subject is understood from what precedes it.

* Shaykh: That is not correct. (Jāʾa) is for a single person. (Jāʾa) for one person presents no problem.

* Student: If it were the messenger, as when one says: "If Khalid came, the messenger came," is that permissible (...)?

* Shaykh: No, the original form is that it is singular.

﴿He said: Would you supply me with wealth?﴾ The ya' here was dropped for what reason? It was dropped for lightness, just as it was also dropped for lightness in His saying earlier: ﴿until you witness﴾.
The interrogative in His saying: ﴿Would you supply me﴾ is for denial and astonishment; that is, how would you supply me with wealth, when I have wealth that you do not have.

For this reason he said: (﴿What Allah has given me﴾ of prophethood and kingship ﴿is better than what He has given you﴾ of worldly things). And likewise in wealth, because Sulayman has wealth that this woman does not have, since Allah, Glorified and Exalted, gave him a kingdom that none after him may have.

So the interrogative in His saying: ﴿Would you supply me﴾ is for rebuke and astonishment; that is, how would you supply me with wealth! That is, these gifts.
﴿What Allah has given me﴾ of wealth, kingship, prophethood and other things, of everything Allah has given, ﴿is better than what He has given you﴾.

﴿Rather, you rejoice in your gift﴾; that is, I do not rejoice in the gift, and the gift does not concern me, but you are the ones who rejoice in it and take pride in it.
Does the meaning "you rejoice" refer to when it is given to you, or to when you give it and see yourselves as having superiority over the recipient?

* Student: Both are possible.

* Shaykh: Yes, both are possible. But the apparent meaning, and Allah knows best, is that he means the first: that you are the ones who rejoice in the gift, and it has an effect on you, it increases your resolve, and it obliges you to deviate from what you are upon. As for me, the gift does not concern me.

* Student: He did not say "our gift," but: ﴿your gift﴾.

* Shaykh: That is, when it comes to you, because (hadiyyah, gift) is a verbal noun that may be annexed to the agent, and may be annexed to the object. ﴿Rather, you rejoice in your gift﴾. The second possibility is that it means your giving it to us.
﴿You rejoice﴾, you take pride; that is, you take pride in it. But the first meaning is more fitting to the context.

(﴿Return to them﴾ with what you brought of the gift.) The address is now to the envoy, and this is an expressive style with a benefit, because those who carried the gift were the whole group, so it was appropriate to address them all as those who carried this gift. Here, when he wanted to assign them the delivery of the message, the assignment of delivering a message to a group causes responsibility to be lost. He assigned the delivery to whom? Only to their leader, because if you charge a group with something, for example, to a person, responsibility is lost, and each one relies on the others, so the message is not delivered. But if you assign it to one person, then he bears it and delivers it. For this reason he assigned it to the leader, saying: ﴿Return to them﴾; that is, to your group who sent you, with what you brought of the gift.

(﴿Then We will surely come to them with hosts they cannot withstand﴾, ﴿they cannot withstand﴾ means no power against them, ﴿and We will surely expel them from it﴾, from their land, Saba, which was named after the father of their tribe, ﴿humbled, and they will be debased﴾; that is, if they do not come to me in submission.)

This is the kind of force: because he does not want wealth, and does not want worldly things; otherwise he would have yielded and been content with this great gift that was sent with a group. But he does not want that, so he addressed them with these strong words: ﴿Then We will surely come to them﴾. And the lam?

* Student: It is for the oath.

* Shaykh: It is a preface to the oath, and the nun in ﴿We will surely come﴾ is for emphasis. So this sentence is emphasized by three emphases: the oath, the lam, and the nun, and in it there is also glorification.
﴿Then We will surely come to them﴾, and he did not say (fa-ʾātīhim, then I will come to them), because this is more emphatic in terms of awe, whether he intended to glorify himself or intended by it: I will come to them with hosts.

His saying: ﴿they cannot withstand﴾ contains a belittling of this group who were sent with this gift. He belittled them in the financial aspect, in His saying: ﴿What Allah has given me is better than what He has given you﴾.
And in the military aspect, in His saying: ﴿they cannot withstand﴾, meaning they have no power against it, because he has soldiers from the jinn and mankind, and even birds. They have no power against this thing. Also: ﴿and We will surely expel them from it humbled﴾, we will occupy their lands and expel them from them, humbled.

﴿and they will be debased﴾. The difference between "humbled" (adhillah) and "debased" (ṣāghirūn): humiliation (dhull) is in the soul, and debasement (ṣaghār) is in the body; that is, one is submissive outwardly and inwardly: submissive outwardly through debasement, and submissive inwardly through humiliation.
Allah, Exalted, says: ﴿And you will see them presented before it, humbled by abasement, glancing with a furtive glance﴾ [al-Shura 45]. Khushūʿ (humbling) here means debasement, and dhull is the humiliation of the soul, and we seek refuge in Allah.

This is evidence that Sulayman, peace be upon him, had such firmness of resolve and strength of authority that he could express himself in this manner to those who presented him with this gift.

If someone says: how is it fitting for Sulayman, peace be upon him, to confront a group who sent him a gift with this harsh style?
The answer is evident in this, because he...?

* Student: (...).

* Shaykh: Who?

* Student: (...).

* Shaykh: Yes, it does not contradict it. He did not accept the gift. But why did he not respond in a gentle manner, not a harsh one?

* Student: If they fight him, he does not want fighting. He wants only their entry into Islam. If he responds to them harshly, they will fear and enter the religion of Allah, Blessed and Exalted.

* Shaykh: Yes indeed. We say: the answer to this is that he, peace be upon him, wanted to show them his strength, and that he did not concern himself with their affair. Furthermore, their testing him, although he had said: ﴿Do not exalt yourselves over me, and come to me in submission﴾, their testing him indicates doubt about his call. He called them to Islam, and they doubted it by sending the gift and thought he wanted worldly things. So they were the ones who began the harm against him, by sending him a gift to test him with. Therefore his response was appropriate.

(When the envoy returned to her with the gift, she placed her throne inside seven gates, inside her palace, and her palace inside seven palaces?)

* Student: There is no evidence for it.

* Shaykh: Yes, excellent. (And she closed the gates and placed guards over them, and prepared herself to go to Sulayman to see what he would order her to do. She set out with twelve thousand elephants, with each elephant thousands upon thousands, until she came near him at a distance of one farsakh. He perceived her and said: ﴿O chiefs, which of you will bring me her throne?﴾)

Strange. I do not know from where the author brings this!?

* Student: We have here, Shaykh: (twelve thousand qeel, with each qeel).

* Shaykh: No, twelve thousand elephants.

* Student: That means qeel (...).

Commentary of Ibn 'Uthaymin (Tafsir al-Quran al-Karim) on surah 27, verses 20–37 (part 6 of 7):

* The Shaykh: Even among us, I have heard it said, but it is not authentic, that (twelve thousand elephants). Elephants may well have been numerous in Yemen. That is why the owner of the elephant, who wanted to demolish the Ka'bah, came with an elephant.
He says: (with every elephant many thousands of people), that is, twelve thousand men with each elephant, and "many thousands" with every elephant means a whole world.
(Until, when she had come within a farsakh of him, he perceived it, and said: ﴿O chiefs, which of you will bring me her throne?﴾), and so on to the end.
Restricting oneself to the narratives that are in the Qur'an is what befits the Mushaf (the written copy of the Qur'an), except for what is authentically reported from the Prophet ﷺ. This is because God says: ﴿Has there not come to you the report of those before you: the people of Noah, 'Ad and Thamud, and those after them, whom none knows but God?﴾ [Ibrahim 9]. So the knowledge of these nations is referred to God, glorified and exalted is He, and it befits us not to go beyond what the Qur'an has brought.
Yet generosity (karam) is according to the nature of each thing. Generosity with wealth means giving it out lavishly, and "generosity" with wealth is also applied to its best part, as the Prophet ﷺ said: «Beware of the choicest of their property» or «Avoid the choicest of their property» [Agreed upon; al-Bukhari (1496) and Muslim (19/31) from the hadith of Ibn 'Abbas]. Likewise, something that contains an important matter is described as noble (karim), because of what this description implies, as in the letter of Sulayman, peace be upon him.
* In this there is evidence that the better practice for the writer is to begin with his own name, saying: "From so-and-so," before beginning with the name of the recipient or addressee. Is this a matter of ta'abbud (acts of worship that are fixed by revelation) or of 'adah (custom)?
* A student: It is a matter of custom.
* The Shaykh: Apparently it is a matter of custom. Nevertheless, the custom followed by the early generations (al-salaf) is better than the custom people have adopted today. Today people have become accustomed to beginning with the addressee: "To so-and-so, son of so-and-so." But the earlier custom is better, because when a person reads a letter, he reads it from the beginning. When he reads "From so-and-so," he knows now what this is and what the letter's importance is, before he has read all of it.
Furthermore, the natural order requires this, because the letter comes from someone to someone, does it not? So it requires that one begin with the one it comes from before the one it goes to.
So we say: it is better for a person to begin with his own name when he sends a letter to someone, because this is the established Sunnah.
Can one derive from this letter that there is no need to mention the addressee, since it says: ﴿Indeed it is from Sulayman﴾ [al-Naml 30], and does not say "to the Queen of Sheba"?
* A student: It may have been mentioned.
* The Shaykh: But what is before us now?
* A student: (...).
* The Shaykh: That is possible. Or we may say: if the evidence indicates the addressee, there is no need to mention him. For example, if you send this letter to a person, especially in a story like that of Sulayman, where this bird brought it to its owner, then the possibility that the letter reaches someone other than the addressee is weak.
The purpose of stating the addressee is that he be identified and that the letter reach him. Here, if the letter comes in this manner, the greatest identification is achieved. So we say there is no need to mention him if the matter is achieved without it. Nevertheless, mentioning him is better, especially if something will follow from it in the future. If we suppose that the person to whom it was sent is known and has received it, we still do not know, in the future, to whom this message was addressed. So mentioning him is without doubt better.
* And in this there is evidence for the recommendation of beginning letters with "In the name of God, the Most Merciful, the Especially Merciful," because of His words: ﴿And indeed it is: In the name of God, the Most Merciful, the Especially Merciful﴾.
* And in this there is evidence for the use of brevity when it does not involve shortcoming, because this letter which Sulayman wrote is as concise as possible: only two sentences: ﴿Do not exalt yourselves against me, and come to me in submission﴾ [al-Naml 31]. But this is on condition that the brevity does not undermine the purpose. If it undermines the purpose, it becomes a shortcoming.
* And in this there is evidence that Sulayman, peace be upon him, called them to God, glorified and exalted is He, and did not want domination and control. He wanted by this that they enter Islam, because when the hoopoe (al-hudhud) informed him that she and her people were prostrating to the sun instead of God, this is kufr (disbelief), so they must come out of it into Islam. This is shown by His words: ﴿and come to me in submission﴾.
* And in this also there is evidence of the strength of Sulayman, peace be upon him, because he did not say "and submit," but said "come to me in submission." He asked them to come to him while they were already in a state of Islam.
Does this mean that they should all come? No. What is meant is their notables and nobles, because the notables and nobles stand in place of the common people.
* And in this there is evidence for the recommendation of consultation (mushawarah) in public affairs, because of her words: ﴿O chiefs, advise me in my affair﴾ [al-Naml 32]. Although she is a queen with complete authority, she still did not dispense with consultation: ﴿She said: O chiefs, advise me in my affair﴾.
* And in this there is evidence of this woman's firmness and that she wanted her governance to be based on the responsibility shared by all. This is shown by her words: ﴿I would not decide an affair until you bear witness to me﴾. Then, if the result turned out contrary to what was intended, she would not be blamed, since she had called these people to witness and had explained the matter to them.
* And in this also there is evidence that it is permissible for the one seeking counsel to differ from the one he consults if he does not think the adviser is right in his advice. When they mentioned what indicated that they wanted to fight him, and she did not see that, she disagreed with them, did she not? She said: ﴿Indeed, when kings enter a town they corrupt it﴾ [al-Naml 34], and so on to the end.
* And in this there is evidence of this woman's standing among her people, because after she consulted them and they gave their opinions, they showed her respect and said: ﴿The command is yours, so see what you will command﴾ [al-Naml 33]. Can one also derive from this that if an adviser offers his counsel to someone greater than him in rank, or understanding, or knowledge, he may say such a thing? Yes. He says it out of good manners, and the one being advised has the choice: if he wills, he takes the advice, and if he wills, he does not.
* And in this there is evidence of this woman's firmness also in that she considered the consequences: ﴿Indeed, when kings enter a town they corrupt it﴾. Thus a sensible person should not judge affairs by their first appearances and outward signs, but should judge affairs by their outcomes. For a thing may have first appearances and outward signs that seem beneficial to a person, but upon reflection the matter turns out to be the opposite. But is it better to act quickly or to be deliberate?
In principle, deliberation is better, because when a person is deliberate he does not regret what he has done. But if he hastens, he is the one exposed to regret. How many a word a person has said, wishing "I had not said it," and how many an action he has done, wishing "I had not done it."
Nevertheless, firmness (hazm) must be used in affairs. One should not be so deliberate that it prolongs the purpose, nor so hasty that it brings regret. I think I recited to you two verses on this meaning. Do you remember them?
* A student: On firmness?
* The Shaykh: No, on the point that sometimes haste is better and sometimes deliberation is better.
* A student: (...)
* The Shaykh:
Sometimes the one who is deliberate attains some of his need, / and sometimes error accompanies the one who hastens.
And often a people lose the greater part of their affair, / through deliberation, when the right course would have been to hasten.
Yes, and this is true and real. The first verse:
Sometimes the one who is deliberate attains some of his need, / and sometimes error accompanies the one who hastens.
The point is that we say: if the matter stands between hastening and deliberation, and hastening is not preferable to it, then deliberation is better, because the matter is in a person's hands as long as he has not done anything. But if he does something, the matter escapes him and he cannot free himself from it.
* A student: Is this derived from the verse?
* The Shaykh: Yes, indeed.
* A student: How?
* The Shaykh: It is derived from the verse, because she said: ﴿Indeed, when kings enter a town they corrupt it and make the most honoured of its people abased﴾ [al-Naml 34]. So she considered the consequences, and considering consequences requires either haste or deliberation. For example, a person may see that if he does not hasten, the purpose will be lost, so he hastens. Or, if he hastens, a disorder will occur, so he is deliberate. This is derived from her words: ﴿Indeed, when kings enter a town they corrupt it and make the most honoured of its people abased﴾ [al-Naml 34].
* And also in it: ﴿And indeed, I am sending them a gift, and I will wait to see with what the messengers return﴾ [al-Naml 35].
* From this verse the following is derived. First: the intelligence and shrewdness of this woman.
* Second, from this is derived: the permissibility of testing and examining, and that this is not considered deception. If a person wants to test another with something, this is not considered deception, because he wants to ascertain his condition by it, and there is no objection to this.
* And in the verse there is also the third benefit, which is: acting on indicators (qara'in), because she wanted to send this gift to test Sulayman's intention. Does he want only wealth? Would this gift satisfy him? Or does he want them to submit, so that this gift would not help him and he would not refrain from his first demand, which is: ﴿Do not exalt yourselves against me, and come to me in submission﴾ [al-Naml 31].
So there are three benefits in it. Has the like of this been reported? Yes. In the story of Sulayman with the two women who brought a dispute to him about the son of one of them: two women went out of the town, each with a son. The wolf ate the son of the elder, and they brought their dispute to Dawud, peace be upon him. He judged the living son to belong to whom? To the elder, on the basis that the younger could bear more children later. But when they brought their dispute to Sulayman, peace be upon him, he said: "That is not the ruling. The ruling is that we bring a knife and split the child in two, so that the elder gets half and the younger gets half." The elder agreed that it should be split in two, why? Because it was not her son, and she was saying: "Just as my son perished, let her son perish." As for the younger, she said: "No, O Prophet of God, the child..." So it became known that the child belonged to the younger, and he judged it to her [Agreed upon; al-Bukhari (3427) and Muslim (1720/20) from the hadith of Abu Hurayrah]. This is from the category of establishing the truth by means of indicators, and there is no objection to it. The judges used to do this.
So this matter, sending the gift to Sulayman, peace be upon him, is of this kind: to establish his condition by it, and so one acts on the indicator.
* A student: (...) It is derived from her action.
* The Shaykh: Yes, because there is no objection to it.
* A student: Even if she was a disbeliever?
* The Shaykh: Even if she was a disbeliever. For when God, glorified and exalted is He, relates something, He has said: ﴿Certainly there is in their stories a lesson for people of understanding﴾ [Yusuf 111]. So when God, exalted is He, relates something from a disbeliever and does not intend to nullify it, it remains on its original permissibility.
* The fourth benefit of the verse: the gift was large. From where is this derived?
* A student: ﴿And I will wait to see with what the messengers return﴾ [al-Naml 35].
* The Shaykh: A group is not sent with a gift unless it is large. Moreover, perhaps we may also say, along with its largeness, that it was valuable, so that these messengers could defend it if anyone tried to attack them. So the greatness of this gift is established in both quantity and quality, and for this reason it needed to be sent with a group.
And in His words: ﴿So when [the messenger] came to Sulayman, he said: Do you provide me with wealth? What God has given me is better than what He has given you. Rather, it is you who rejoice in your gift. (36) Return to them, for we will surely come to them with soldiers they cannot resist, and we will surely expel them from it in humiliation, and they will be debased﴾ [al-Naml 36–37].
* From His words: ﴿So when [the messenger] came to Sulayman﴾ it is derived that it is commendable for the leader, the head of the delegation or of the people, to go forward with speech or action when the task is to be performed by action. The essential thing is that the one who goes forward is the leader, because for everyone to advance at once is not fitting, since responsibility is lost. So someone must go forward, one person, and the more the matter is limited, the closer it is to understanding and to achieving the purpose.
* And in it also there is evidence for addressing the group, even if the one who goes forward is their leader. This is shown by His words: ﴿Do you provide me with wealth?﴾ [al-Naml 36].
* And in it there is evidence for the permissibility of harshness in speech when there is a benefit in it, because this manner of Sulayman, peace be upon him, is a strong manner. As we have said, the interrogative in His words: ﴿Do you provide me with wealth?﴾ is for reproach and astonishment, meaning that he reproaches them for their action and is astonished at it: how could they provide him with wealth when he is a king, known and famous?!
* And in it there is evidence for the permissibility of speaking of God's blessing.
* The fourth benefit: it is permissible for a person to speak of God's blessing, because of the words of the Prophet ﷺ: ﴿What God has given me is better than what He has given you﴾. But should one speak of this blessing in a manner of boasting, or in a manner of humble need and belittling oneself? It depends on the situation. We see that it depends on the situation.
So in the presence of the enemy it is permissible to speak of it in boasting. That is why pride (khuyala') is permitted in war, although pride is forbidden, is it not? It is forbidden, one of the major sins. But in war, for the purpose of attacking the enemy, there is no harm in it. So Sulayman, peace be upon him, here spoke of God's blessing in boasting, as it appears to me, boasting over these people. This is not objectionable when it is in front of the enemy. But when it is to display the blessing, it is not permissible except in the manner of belittling oneself and need of God, glorified and exalted is He, not in the manner of boasting and exalting oneself over creation.
* The fifth benefit: it is permissible for a person to describe another by what appears of his condition. This is shown by His words: ﴿Rather, it is you who rejoice in your gift﴾, since joy, as you know, is an inward matter, whose signs appear on the outward body, though in origin it is inward. For the one who rejoices does not make a sound for his joy, nor is any movement seen in him, but its signs appear.
So there is no harm in a person judging another by indicators from what appears of his condition. This matter has come before you many times. The man who had intercourse with his wife during the day in Ramadan said: «By God, between its two lava plains there is no household poorer than mine» [Agreed upon; al-Bukhari (1936) and Muslim (1111/81) from the hadith of Abu Hurayrah].
Yet this man did not go around the houses of the people of Madinah searching them to know that there was no one poorer than himself.
* And in it also there is evidence, the sixth benefit: evidence for displaying strength to enemies, because of His words: ﴿Return to them, for we will surely come to them with soldiers they cannot resist﴾ [al-Naml 37]. This falls under His words, exalted is He: ﴿And prepare against them whatever you are able of power﴾ [al-Anfal 60]. For "power" (quwwah) here is indefinite and includes every kind of strength that is possible, whether it is power of speech, material power, or moral power. The essential thing is that a person should employ all kinds of strength in dealing with enemies. Indeed, it has come in a hadith: «War is deception» [Agreed upon; al-Bukhari (3029) and Muslim (1740/18) from the hadith of Abu Hurayrah].
But is treachery (khiyanah) permissible or not?
* A student: It is not permissible.
* The Shaykh: Treachery against the enemy is not permissible. It is not permissible for a person to betray his enemy. This is why God, exalted is He, said: ﴿And if you fear treachery from a people, then throw back to them [their treaty] on equal terms﴾ [al-Anfal 58], and do not betray them. Likewise, if they betray, they have broken the covenant. We have already gone over this matter, that it has three cases concerning those with whom we have a treaty:
Either they remain upright toward us: ﴿So as long as they are upright with you, be upright with them﴾ [al-Tawbah 7].
Or they break the covenant, and then there is no covenant: ﴿And if they break their oaths after their covenant and attack your religion, then fight the leaders of disbelief﴾ [al-Tawbah 12].

And if they do not break the covenant, and their outward conduct is upright, but we fear treachery from them, then we announce the termination of the covenant to them and inform them that we have annulled it. Even if they say, "We will remain bound by the covenant," we say, "No. Each of us is now free."

Here there is strength in the speech: ﴿Return to them, for we will surely come to them with hosts that they cannot repel﴾. This threat and warning is undoubtedly a display of strength, and so it falls under the words of God Most High: ﴿And prepare against them whatever you are able of power﴾ [Al-Anfal 60].

* Student: How do we reconcile the permissibility of deceiving the enemy with the impermissibility of treachery?

* Shaykh: Yes. Treachery means that you deceive him in a position of trust, whereas deception (khada'ah) means that you deceive him in a context other than trust. War is ongoing, so you set an ambush for them, for example, or something similar. You show, for instance, that you have a large number, so that people hesitate, as al-Qa'qa' ibn 'Amr did in his battles with the Persians and in other matters. You have not betrayed them, because there is no covenant between you and them.

* Student: Some of the Companions (...) tells him that so-and-so grants him safe conduct, and then kills him.

* Shaykh: That is not considered treachery, because that person is a combatant with whom there is no covenant. For this reason the Messenger said regarding the story of Ka'b ibn al-Ashraf: "Who will deal with Ka'b ibn al-Ashraf for me? He has harmed God and His Messenger" [[Agreed upon (muttafaqun 'alayh); al-Bukhari (2510) and Muslim (1801/119), from the hadith of Jabir ibn 'Abdullah.]].

* Student: Shaykh, the Prophet ﷺ explained "power" by saying: "Indeed, power is archery. Indeed, power is archery" [[Narrated by Muslim (1917/167), from the hadith of 'Uqbah ibn 'Amir.]]. So here, is power specifically archery?

* Shaykh: Yes. The Messenger, peace and blessings be upon him, and likewise what is reported from the Companions in explaining some verses, sometimes mention a thing by way of example. At that time, power was archery, and it still is. Archery now is among the strongest forms of power; that is, it is the highest kind of power.

Whether people's shooting was with the bow in the past, or with the rifle or with missiles, the important point is that archery at every time is the pinnacle of power.

* Student: (...).

* Shaykh: This is not meant as an exclusive limitation, but the Messenger wished to clarify the ultimate degree of power, so this power is the ultimate at every time.

* Also in His words, peace and blessings be upon him: ﴿Then we will surely come to them with hosts that they cannot repel﴾, there is evidence for the great number of Solomon's hosts. This queen, who possesses great intellect and has a people who obey her and are humbled before her commands, says: ﴿Then we will surely come to them with hosts that they cannot repel﴾. She did not specify these hosts. But it was mentioned at the beginning of the story that Solomon's hosts consisted of three categories: the jinn, mankind, and the birds. All of these he could set against them. If he sends the jinn, they have no way to resist them; and if he sends the birds to gouge out their eyes, they likewise have no way to resist them.

So the outcome is that the hosts that belong to Solomon cannot be opposed by these people, neither in number nor in quality. Is there anything more?

* Student: Shaykh (...) sending a letter ought to (...) the sender. Now how was it (...) the officials used to send to the Commander of the Faithful from an official (...).

* Shaykh: This falls under the category of wonder and exaggeration. Otherwise, without doubt, the first way is preferable. But as you have just said, they began to say: "From so-and-so to so-and-so," and then they began to say: "To so-and-so," placing the name at the end. This falls under the category of wonder and honouring others.

* Student: (...)?

* Shaykh: I do not know whether it is (...) or whether people recite it as an act of worship. But this is among ordinary matters, as we have said, not an act of worship.

* Student: Before the basmalah or after it, with this, with Solomon, before the basmalah?

* Shaykh: No. She reported: ﴿Indeed, it is from Solomon, and indeed it says: In the name of God, the Most Merciful, the Especially Merciful﴾ [Al-Naml 30]. Did Solomon write: "In the name of God, the Most Merciful, the Especially Merciful, from Solomon: Do not exalt yourselves against me, but come to me in submission"? Because this is a report from her. She is not reading out the writing to them now, so it is not like a narrator of a book, such that we would say: "From Solomon, in the name of God, the Most Merciful, the Especially Merciful." For this reason she said: ﴿Indeed, it is from Solomon, and indeed it says: In the name of God, the Most Merciful, the Especially Merciful. Do not exalt yourselves against me﴾ [Al-Naml 30–31]. Even in the course of the exegesis (...) that she understood it to be from Solomon in a manner other than this, even though he did not write it.

* Student: (...)?

* Shaykh: Correct. The disbeliever has no right to God's earth or to God's wealth; even wealth, he has no right to it.

* Student: (...)

* Shaykh: Yes. The reasoning for that is that if it were not so, then his threatening them with this would be impermissible, since it would not be lawful for him to do this. If they had a right, he would not have been permitted to act and expel them from their land.

* Student: Shaykh, (...) he said: the humiliation (al-sighar) (...) there is a difference between dhillah and sighar.

* Shaykh: No, it is not so. (...) dhillah is in the soul, and sighar is in the body.

* Student: ﴿Then we will surely come to them﴾ (...) on the doctrine of compulsion (al-jabriyyah).

* Shaykh: (...) it can be cited as evidence that a person acts by his own choice, because of His words: ﴿Then we will surely come to them with hosts﴾ [Al-Naml 37].

Commentary of Ibn 'Uthaymin (Tafsir al-Quran al-Karim) on surah 27, verses 20–37 (part 1 of 7):

He said: ﴿And he inspected the birds﴾ [al-Naml 20]. Is the definite article in ﴿al-tayr﴾ (the birds) for a specific reference (al-'ahd) or for the whole category ( 'umum al-jins)?

I say: It is for a specific reference, because it refers back to the birds mentioned earlier: ﴿And for Solomon were gathered his hosts of jinn and men and birds﴾ [al-Naml 17]. On this basis, his inspection of the birds took place during this same march.

﴿He inspected the birds and said, "Why do I not see the hoopoe?"﴾ He says: (He inspected the birds in order to see the hoopoe, which sees water beneath the earth, and indicates it by pecking there, so that the devils would extract it, since Solomon needed it for prayer, but he did not see it). This is from the author's own imagination.

He says: ﴿He inspected the birds﴾ in order to look for the hoopoe, the hoopoe (...)? It sees water beneath the earth; if it saw rivers flowing under the earth, it would peck with its beak, meaning it would say: "Dig here," and then he would order the devils and they would dig.

* Student: What is the evidence?
* Shaykh: The evidence is that (...). Who says this? Rather, his inspection of the birds was because, as has passed, he, peace be upon him, was organizing his troops, and so he inspected them to see where they had gone. That is why he did not say "the hoopoe" or "the hoopoes," but said "the birds" entirely, because you know that birds fly through the air, and something among them may be missing. So he, peace and blessings be upon him, inspected them in order to complete the organization.

Then, their claim that the hoopoe sees what is under the earth is not correct. Bury some grain and let the hoopoes come here: do you see them or not? Certainly you do not see them. If it cannot see nearby grain, how can it see distant water? The point is that the hoopoe, like others, has its eyesight blocked by density and sees nothing.

Then, Solomon, peace be upon him, had no need of this. Rather, in this respect Solomon was like any other human: if he found water he benefited from it, and if he did not, Allah the Exalted would make water available to him by some means.

He says: ﴿He inspected the birds and said, "Why do I not see the hoopoe?"﴾ ﴿Mā﴾ (what/why) is an interrogative. Is the purpose of it seeking information (istikhbar) or disapproval (istinkar)?

* Student: Seeking information.
* Shaykh: It has been said that the purpose is seeking information, that he is asking a real question: "Where is the hoopoe?" It has also been said that it is disapproval. The apparent view is that this has no basis, because the original function of the interrogative is seeking information.

Some of them said: There is an inversion (qalb) in the verse, and the intended order is: "What is the matter with the hoopoe that I do not see it?" But this is not correct. Rather, the verse is in its proper order. He asks, saying: "Why is it that I do not see the hoopoe? Is there something that prevented me from seeing it, or was it simply not present?" For this reason he turned away from the first question and said: ﴿Or is he among the absent?﴾ The ﴿am﴾ here is disjunctive (munqati'a), and disjunctive ﴿am﴾, as we have passed several times, means "rather" (bal), with the hamza, meaning: "Rather, was he among the absent?" At that point he set aside the first statement, and he realized that there was no defect in his sight, and that the only cause was the absence of this hoopoe.

Then he, peace be upon him, said: ﴿Or is he among the absent?﴾ I did not see it because of its absence. When he confirmed this, he said: ﴿I will surely punish him with a severe punishment﴾ [al-Naml 21], a severe punishment.

﴿La-u'adhdhibannahu﴾ (I will surely punish him): this sentence is emphasized with three emphatics. These are: the lam of the oath-preparation (al-lam al-muwatta'a lil-qasam), and the oath before it is implied (muqaddar). These are two. The third is the nun: ﴿la-u'adhdhibannahu﴾.

He says: ﴿'adhāban﴾. The author said: (a severe punishment), indicating that ʿadhāban is a verbal noun in form (ism al-masdar), because the verbal noun of ʿadhdhaba is (ta'dhīban), and the form derived from it as a noun is (ʿadhāban). Similarly, the verbal noun of kallama is (takliman), and the noun form is (kalāman). And the verbal noun of sallama is (taslīman), and the noun form is (salāman).

"I will punish him with a severe punishment": what is the severe punishment according to the author's opinion? By plucking his feathers and tail and throwing him into the sun so that he is not protected from vermin. This is a strange thing. On what evidence is this punishment defined in this way? For this reason some have said that this severe punishment the author mentioned, plucking, and leaving him in the sun, the poor thing with no feathers or anything else.

Some say: ﴿I will punish him with a severe punishment﴾ means: I will confine him with something not of his kind. Put the hoopoe with sparrows. They say: among the greatest torments for an animal is to be gathered with those not of its kind. If a human is placed with jinn, he suffers, or if jinn are placed with humans, they suffer. But this is also not correct, because we now observe that things are kept with their own kinds and do not suffer. Someone has cattle, sheep, and camels, and the sheep are of two kinds, sheep and goats. Who does this in one pen, and they do not suffer?

The correct view, then, is that this punishment which Solomon mentioned is not known to us. It is simply a severe punishment, and Allah, blessed and exalted, did not specify it. But it is enough for us to know that it is severe. That is one point.

﴿Or I will surely slaughter him﴾: this ﴿la-adhbahannahu﴾ (I will surely slaughter him) is for variety (li-l-tanwī'), meaning either this or that.

His saying: ﴿Or I will surely slaughter him﴾: he says, by cutting its throat. This is correct. That is, (...) for slaughter, either by cutting the windpipe and gullet, meaning from the neck.

The third: ﴿Or he must bring me clear authority﴾. ﴿La-ya'tiyannī﴾ with a doubled, kasra-vowelled nun, or with a fatha vowel followed by a kasra nun. ﴿La-ya'tiyannī﴾ is one form. ﴿Or la-ya'tiyannī﴾: look, with a doubled kasra nun: (ya'tiyannī), or with a fatha, what is the fatha form?

* Student: With the nun, "an ya'tiya."
* Shaykh: With a nun. No, a doubled kasra nun, or a fatha followed by a kasra nun.
* Student: And the ya.
* Shaykh: Yes, (ya'tiyannanī). That is the second reading: ﴿la-ya'tiyannī﴾ and ﴿la-ya'tiyannanī﴾. What is the difference between them?
* Student: Completeness.
* Shaykh: Yes, there is a protective nun (nūn al-wiqāya), which is either deleted or present. Otherwise the emphatic nun (nūn al-tawkīd) is present. The emphatic nun is doubled, but if it is deleted for protection, the emphatic nun is given a kasra (ya'tiyannī), and if it is not deleted, (ya'tiyannanī), in which case it remains with a fatha.

This is a third matter. So Solomon threatened him with one of two things unless he brought something: ﴿clear authority﴾, a clear proof manifest in support of his excuse.

The word ﴿sultān﴾ (authority) occurs often in the Qur'an, and its general meaning is: the power by which a person is able to reach his goal. That is its general meaning: the power by which a person is able to reach his goal. Sometimes what is meant by it is proof: ﴿Or do you have clear authority?﴾ [al-Saffat 156]. Sometimes what is meant is power: ﴿You will not pass except by authority﴾ [al-Rahman 33]. And sometimes what is meant is evidence, as in this verse.

His saying: ﴿la-ya'tiyannī bi-sultānin mubīn﴾ means: with evidence for his excuse. And what did we say the general meaning of ﴿sultān﴾ is? The power by which a person, or its possessor, is able to reach his goal, whether that is in defending himself or in establishing a matter.

His saying: ﴿mubīn﴾ (clear): the author explained it as "clear" (bayyin), and it cannot mean "making manifest" (muzhir) in the sense of being transitive. That is, it is not used transitively. The author has now explained it as intransitive. It could also be transitive, meaning: with an authority that makes manifest his excuse. If we explain it this way, we have taken the explanation the author gave and added to it.

﴿Famakatha﴾ (he stayed): with a damma or a fatha on the kaf, makatha and makutha. And who is the subject? The hoopoe. It is possible that the subject is Solomon, meaning: he remained not far, that is, for a short time, and came before Solomon.

His saying: (and came before Solomon). What is the evidence for this?

* Student: Its presence before him.
* Shaykh: Because he had said earlier that the hoopoe was absent: ﴿Or is he among the absent?﴾ And the absent is not addressed unless he is present. But the author's statement, "humbly, lowering his head, and drooping his tail and wings," is among the matters we do not know about.

* Student: Apparently the author was there with him!
* Shaykh: Yes, as if he were there, meaning the hoopoe came and stood, lifted its head, and lowered its tail and wings.
* Student: No, this is an inference from observed birds.
* Another student: There is an implied meaning here, sir.
* Shaykh: But we cannot say this at all. We cannot describe how it came. It is enough for us to say what Allah the Exalted said in the Qur'an. We mentioned before a principle: all that is past, we have no way to know except through revelation: ﴿Has there not come to you the news of those before you, the people of Noah and 'Ad and Thamud, and those after them, none knows them but Allah?﴾ [Ibrahim 9]. There is no way except revelation, either in the Qur'an or in authentic Sunnah.

﴿So he stayed not long and said, "I have encompassed [knowledge of] what you have not encompassed."﴾ [al-Naml 22]. ﴿Aḥaṭtu﴾ (I have encompassed) means: he speaks about himself. ﴿I have encompassed what you have not encompassed﴾: whom is he addressing?

* Student: Solomon.
* Shaykh: Solomon. In reality this hoopoe was very bold, as they say. How does he address Solomon, who has this great kingdom, and say: ﴿I have encompassed what you have not encompassed﴾? He did not say "what you have not encompassed" in the plural honorific. We ourselves, as humans, sometimes address the manager or someone above him, and we say, for example: "You" (antum), "your excellency" (sayyidukum), "your honor" (sa'adatukum), "your presence" (hadratukum)... (...) excessive, beyond what is necessary, as if he were not a human. In reality all these are formalities that indicate nothing and are not even fitting. The Companions addressed the Messenger, peace and blessings be upon him, with this kind of address, though he was more honored in their eyes than any human, and likewise the rightly guided caliphs were not addressed with such titles.

Among the wonders of this community is that some of those who are addressed with such titles, their hearts seethe toward those who address them, so that this address becomes like mockery of them. If people addressed one another in ordinary terms: what is this hoopoe's rank with Solomon? It is one of his weakest soldiers, yet it says with such candor: ﴿I have encompassed what you have not encompassed﴾, and this was the first thing it said to him, straight away. But in reality there is a kind of courtesy in it. It did not say, for example: "You are ignorant and do not know, while I have learned and searched and found something you do not know about." Rather it said: ﴿I have encompassed what you have not encompassed﴾, meaning so that Solomon would know its worth, and that he does not encompass everything. So this hoopoe became more encompassing than him, and the human being is weak in everything. Has anyone taught us how to bury our dead, except...?

* Student: The crow.
* Shaykh: Except the crow, which shows that in reality we are nothing.

﴿I have encompassed what you have not encompassed﴾ resembles Abraham's saying to his father: ﴿O my father, indeed there has come to me of knowledge that which has not come to you﴾ [Maryam 43]. He did not say: "O my father, you are ignorant." This is the delicacy of the style. Here it said: ﴿I have encompassed what you have not encompassed﴾, and the expression is strong, meaning: I have come to know what you have not come to know.

﴿And I have come to you from Saba' with certain news. Indeed, I found a woman ruling them﴾ [al-Naml 22–23], until he said: ﴿He said, "We will see whether you have told the truth or were among the liars."﴾ [al-Naml 27]. Solomon responded to him after (...), and confirmed the report: ﴿I have come to you from Saba' with certain news﴾, and yet he said to him: ﴿We will see whether you have told the truth or were among the liars.﴾

This is a shock to the hoopoe, because the hoopoe was certain, and yet it was told: ﴿We will see whether you have told the truth or were among the liars.﴾ Why did Solomon say this, when the hoopoe had said to him: "with certain news"?

Because the reality is that the hoopoe's speech was in the position of defending itself, a defender, since it had been threatened with severe punishment, or slaughter, or with a clear authority. So when it was in the position of defense, it needed to establish its claim with proof. Something similar happened to 'Umar ibn al-Khattab, may Allah be pleased with him. Abu Musa asked permission to enter upon him three times and then left. When (...) about this, he said: "Thus the Messenger of Allah, peace and blessings be upon him, commanded us." He said: "Bring proof for what you say," even though Abu Musa was a trustworthy Companion, and it was impossible for him to fabricate against the Messenger, peace and blessings be upon him. But the situation required it. What did it require? Greater verification, because a person may understand from the text something that is not intended. So 'Umar asked Abu Musa to bring a witness.

Here, with this hoopoe, Solomon, peace be upon him, even though the report was certain to him, said: ﴿We will see whether you have told the truth or were among the liars.﴾ Then he gave it a sign and an indicator: ﴿Take this letter of mine and deliver it to them, then turn away from them﴾ [al-Naml 28]. The story is in reality very great, with many benefits.

﴿I have encompassed what you have not encompassed, and I have come to you from Saba'.﴾ He says: ﴿min Saba'﴾ with the diptote (ṣarf) and without the diptote (ṣarf): ﴿min Saba'in﴾ and its absence: (min Saba'a), like this?

* Student: No, the opposite.
* Shaykh: The opposite?!
* Student: (min Saba'a) is prohibited from declension (mamnū' min al-ṣarf).
* Shaykh: Yes, this is non-declension, correct. And ﴿min Saba'in﴾ is with declension. (min Saba'a) is in the genitive with a fatha because it is a non-declinable noun (ism lā yanṣarif), and ﴿min Saba'in﴾ is in the genitive with a kasra because it is a declinable noun (ism yanṣarif). On which basis do we consider it either declined or not declined?

He said: It is a tribe in Yemen, named after a forefather of theirs. Considered as a man, it is declined (...).

* * *

Its meaning: (so that the People of the Book may know), and the lam was added for emphasis. The author holds that this verse is like the verse he cited as a witness for it, where ﴿lā﴾ (not) is added. Other exegetes hold a view different from the author's, and they say that ﴿So they are not guided﴾ is a complete sentence, and that his saying ﴿that they do not prostrate to Allah﴾ [al-Naml 25] means: "why do they not prostrate," and that it is for exhortation. But this interpretation also has a problem, namely the deletion of the nun from the five verbs without a governing or jussive particle, because ﴿allā﴾ neither governs nor jusses.

If we say that in ﴿yasjudū﴾ the ﴿allā﴾ is hortatory (li-l-taḥḍīḍ), and it neither governs nor jusses, and we look at ﴿yasjudū﴾, we find that the nun is deleted, whether in the subjunctive or jussive, and here there is no governing or jussive particle. So this is a point of difficulty. But the answer to this may be easy, because deleting the nun of the five verbs without a governing or jussive particle is permissible and attested in the Arabic language. Among its examples is the saying of the Prophet, peace be upon him: "By Allah, you will not enter Paradise until you believe."[[Recorded by Muslim (54/93), and Ahmad in al-Musnad (10650), from Abu Hurayra, the wording being Ahmad's.]]

"Lā tadkhulū" (you will not enter): ﴿lā﴾ is a negation that neither governs nor jusses, and yet the nun was deleted, and he did not say "lā tadkhulūna" (you will not enter).

So the answer to this is that the nun of the five verbs may be deleted without a governing or jussive particle, especially in an expression like ﴿allā yasjudū﴾, which indicates exhortation, because the presence of this particle preceding the verb makes deleting the nun easier here.

In any case, if it is according to the author's interpretation, then this sentence in relation to what precedes it is like an emphasis. When it said: ﴿Satan made their deeds appealing to them and averted them from the way﴾ [al-Naml 24], this implies that they would not be guided to the truth, nor to prostrating to Allah, the Exalted.

As for the second view: ﴿that they do not prostrate to Allah﴾, that ﴿allā﴾ is hortatory, meaning "hallā" (why not), then it indicates that the hoopoe criticized them for this act, and showed that the better, indeed the obligatory, course is that prostration be to Allah, the Exalted, and the sentence is then separate from what precedes it.

His saying: ﴿Who brings forth what is hidden (al-khabʾ) in the heavens and the earth﴾: al-khabʾ is a verbal noun in the sense of what is hidden, such as rain and plants.

﴿...in the heavens and the earth, and knows what you conceal and what you declare.﴾

﴿al-khabʾ﴾ means "al-makhbūʾ" (what is hidden), as the author said. It is a verbal noun used in the sense of the passive participle (ism al-maf'ūl), and the verbal noun used in the sense of the passive participle is very common in the Arabic language. Among its examples is the Exalted saying: ﴿And if they are pregnant﴾ [al-Talaq 6], meaning "mahmūl" (carried), because pregnancy (al-ḥaml) is the woman's act, while what is carried (al-mahmūl) is the fetus. Likewise His saying: ﴿And for those with pregnancy, their term is that they deliver their burden﴾ [al-Talaq 4]. And among its examples is the saying of the Prophet, peace be upon him: "Whoever does an action that is not in accordance with our affair, it is rejected,"[[Agreed upon; al-Bukhari (2697), and Muslim (1718/18), from 'A'isha, the wording being Muslim's.]] meaning "mardūd" (rejected).

Also from the same commentary: Allah the Exalted says, ﴿This is the creation of Allah, so show me what those besides Him have created﴾ [Luqman 11].

﴿This is the creation of Allah﴾, meaning His creation, not His action. So *al-khabʾ* here means the thing that is brought out, in the sense of the passive participle. He said: "from the rain." This is considering what is hidden in the sky. And the plants?

Student: What is hidden in the earth.

Shaykh: What is hidden in the earth. Allah, blessed and exalted is He, is the One who brings forth what is in this and what is in that, in the heavens and the earth, and He knows what they conceal in their hearts and what they declare with their tongues. The author did not refer to the second reading, which is one of the seven canonical readings, in His saying ﴿yukhfūna wa-yuʿlinūn﴾. The one in the Mushaf is the reading of ʿAsim. What is it?

Student: ﴿And He knows what you conceal and what you declare﴾.

Shaykh: ﴿And He knows what you conceal and what you declare﴾, addressed to Solomon.

As for the author's words, "what you conceal in your hearts and what you declare with your tongues," there is something to examine in restricting it to the tongues. If he had said "with your tongues and your limbs," that would be better, because what is done by the limbs is also declared, just as what is spoken by the tongue is declared.

﴿And He knows what you conceal and what you declare.﴾ These two attributes, bringing forth what is hidden and knowing what the servant conceals and what he declares, belong to no created being, neither to the sun nor to anything other than the sun. They belong exclusively to Allah, blessed and exalted is He. For this reason the hoopoe mentioned them as one of the grounds that necessitate that worship be for Allah alone, since He is the One who knows them. An attribute that necessitates worship can only be cited if it is specific to Allah, because it is cited as evidence for the invalidity of worshipping anything else. If it were something that could also belong to others besides Allah, it would not be evidence that Allah is characterized by being worshipped, since the worshipper of something might say: "This attribute also exists in my object of worship, so I worship it."

The important point is that the proof cannot be established except with evidence that is specific to the thing being argued for. That is, the argument that worship is for Allah alone cannot be established except with an attribute that is what?

Student: Specific.

Shaykh: Specific to Allah. If you argued with an attribute that belongs to Allah and to others, the worshipper of someone other than Allah would say: "This attribute is also possible for my object of worship." So it would not show that it is an attribute specific to Allah, glorified and exalted is He.

He said: ﴿Allah, there is no deity except Him, the Lord of the Mighty Throne﴾ [al-Naml 26]. This is a resumptive sentence of praise, containing the Throne of the Merciful in contrast with the throne of Bilqis, and between them is a great difference.

The hoopoe says: ﴿Allah, there is no deity except Him﴾. This is the statement of tawhid (affirmation of God's oneness). The author says: "It is a resumptive sentence praising Allah, blessed and exalted is He, with what does not belong to anyone else." So the first part, ﴿He brings forth what is hidden in the heavens﴾ and ﴿knows﴾, relates to tawhid al-rububiyyah (oneness of Lordship, affirming that Allah alone is the Creator, Sustainer and Lord). The second, ﴿Allah, there is no deity except Him﴾, relates to tawhid al-uluhiyyah (oneness of divinity and worship); that is, there is no deity worshipped besides Him. But there are deities worshipped besides Allah, glorified is He, though without right. So He is praised with the attribute of lordship and the attribute of divinity. We might also say: with the attributes of the names and attributes (tawhid al-asma' wa-l-sifat), because tawhid al-rububiyyah necessarily entails the names and attributes, since disposing of creation, governing and knowing are all attributes.

He said: ﴿the Lord of the Mighty Throne﴾. ﴿Lord﴾ means "owner." ﴿The Lord of the Mighty Throne﴾, that is, its owner, just as you say "the lord of the animal," meaning its owner.

As for His words ﴿al-ʿarsh﴾ (the Throne), the *alif-lam* here is *al-ʿahd al-dhihni* (the mental or known reference), meaning the Throne that is familiar in the minds of creation, the Mighty Throne, unlike the throne of Bilqis. For this reason she said ﴿and she has a mighty throne﴾, and here He said ﴿the Mighty Throne﴾ with *alif-lam*. The expression clearly shows the difference between them, because ʿarsh (indefinite) is indefinite, while al-ʿarsh is definite. This indicates that this throne is a known, mighty throne that is understood in the minds, unlike the first.

The author says: "He said it in contrast with the throne of Bilqis." Yes, this is correct. It is clear that He said it in order to show that the Lord of the Mighty Throne is the one who deserves to be the true possessor, whereas this queen has a throne but is not the Throne.

Then ﴿[Solomon] said: "We shall see whether you have told the truth or whether you were among the liars"﴾. Solomon says it. The *sīn*, as we have already noted, indicates what?

Student: (...).

Shaykh: No, it indicates certainty with delay, but it does indicate certainty. ﴿sananẓuru﴾ (we shall see) means that this looking of ours is certain, but it will have preliminaries, so it indicates emphasis.

﴿He said, "We shall see whether you have told the truth."﴾ He did not accept his statement from the outset. Why? He feared that he had come with that in order to defend himself. A parallel to this is what ʿUmar ibn al-Khattab, may Allah be pleased with him, did with Abu Musa al-Ashʿari, when he sought permission three times and then left. Afterwards he informed him that the Prophet ﷺ had commanded this, so ʿUmar asked them to bear witness for him.

Here, the accusations or the lack of trust in the statement have causes. Among them: that the informant, in this state, has a report that includes a defence of himself. So however much trust there may be, you find yourself hesitating to accept this report.

Student: My question, Shaykh, concerns His saying ﴿I found her and her people prostrating to the sun instead of Allah﴾ together with His saying ﴿that they should not prostrate to Allah﴾. What does that imply, from what was mentioned earlier (...), that they were not (...)?

Shaykh: No, because the meaning of His saying ﴿that they should not prostrate to Allah﴾ is that Allah, exalted is He, must be singled out for prostration (...). So the basis of the sin is that they assign prostration specifically to the sun. Likewise, if they associated it with Allah, (...) for this and for that, because the sin can only be removed if prostration is dedicated to Allah alone.

Student: Shaykh, a reading: ﴿Alā yā isjudū lillāh﴾ (...).

Shaykh: That reading may have *alā* as an introductory particle, because *yā* is a vocative particle and the addressee is omitted. That is: "Alā, O people, prostrate to Allah." Or *yā* is for alerting, like His saying ﴿O would that my people knew﴾ [Yā-Sīn 26] and ﴿O would that I had been with them﴾ [al-Nisāʾ 73]. This *yā* is either for alerting, since it does not precede verbs or particles, or it is a vocative particle with the addressee omitted.

Student: Is it a canonical reading?

Shaykh: I do not know; is it an anomalous reading (shādhdh)? He said ﴿and she has a mighty throne﴾.

﴿[Solomon] said: "We shall see whether you have told the truth" in what you have informed us, ﴿or whether you were among the liars﴾; that is, of this kind. So it is more emphatic than "whether you lied" in that matter.

﴿whether you have told the truth or whether you were among the liars﴾ is clear. The first is a verb. Here He said ﴿or whether you were among the liars﴾, meaning of this kind. So it is more forceful than "whether you lied," because "whether you lied" is a verb, and a verb may happen once, whereas ﴿you were among the liars﴾ is a description indicating continuous lying. This is what the author affirmed. In my view, however, there is delicacy in Solomon's address to the hoopoe, because the direct confrontation "whether you lied" is harsher in impact than His saying ﴿you were among the liars﴾. Regarding the wording, "you were among the liars" is more severe in describing him as one who has the attribute, but regarding the manner of address it is gentler than "whether you lied." This is the point of difference between ﴿whether you have told the truth or whether you were among the liars﴾.

He says: Then the hoopoe guided them to water, and it was extracted, and they drank and performed ablution and prayed. Then Solomon wrote a letter whose form was: "From the servant of Allah, Solomon son of David, to Bilqis, queen of Sheba. In the name of Allah, the Most Merciful, the Most Compassionate. Peace upon whoever follows the guidance. To proceed: do not exalt yourselves over me, and come to me in submission." Then he sealed it with musk and stamped it with his signet ring. Then he said to the hoopoe: ﴿Take this letter of mine﴾.

All of this (...) for which there is no evidence in the Qur'an: that he guided them to water and they extracted it, drank, performed ablution and prayed as well. Is there anything in it...

Student: Going back to the beginning.

Shaykh: Where?

Student: Because (...) he decided at the start that they had asked (...).

Shaykh: Yes, he checked for that. No, rather because he knew where the water was. But we say: there is no evidence for this, and it is not permissible for us to believe it or to deny it. This applies even if it is authentically transmitted from the Children of Israel, because there is a problem in it, (...) between us and the Children of Israel. Who narrated it from the Children of Israel? If it is authentically transmitted from the Children of Israel and is among what they related to this community, we say about it: it is neither to be affirmed nor denied, because nothing in it contradicts our book, and nothing in our book supports it. If our book supported it, we would accept it, and if our book contradicted it, we would reject it.

Student: Shaykh, regarding His saying ﴿or whether you were among the liars﴾, is it right for Solomon to describe him by this act alone as an absolute description?

Shaykh: No. He is among the liars who habitually lie. He did not describe him by it. That he is among the liars may mean that lying is his habit, or that he is among their number, though he may have lied only once. And he did not describe him that way either. He did not describe him, because His saying ﴿whether you have told the truth﴾ is set against His saying ﴿or whether you were among the liars.﴾ So it is not known whether he is characterized by "you have told the truth" or by "you were among the liars." He did not describe him; he is hesitant and waiting to see.

Student: No, if it were established, would it be right to describe him?

Shaykh: No, it is not right to describe him as among the liars who are constantly characterized by lying. But, as we said, this is a matter of gentleness in address.

Student: So this would be the stronger view?

Shaykh: It is stronger, and each has its own aspect. There is no actual contradiction between them that would require us to weigh one over the other. There is no contradiction. So, his being among the liars is more severe if lying is his attribute, and his not being addressed directly with "whether you lied" is gentler. It is like the words of Abraham, peace be upon him, to the guests: ﴿Peace. A people unknown﴾ [al-Dhariyat 25]. He did not say "I do not know you"; rather he said ﴿A people unknown﴾. This is a matter of gentleness in expression.

He said: Then he said to the hoopoe: ﴿Take this letter of mine and throw it to them, then withdraw from them and see what they return﴾ [al-Naml 28].

If someone asks: His saying ﴿Take this letter of mine﴾ implies that he believed him. Is this correct, or is it a test?

Because His saying ﴿Take this letter of mine and throw it to them﴾ indicates what? That he believed him in that, and so he wrote to them. Or is it said that this is part of the test?

That is, if he were lying, he would say: "There is no one there," or "I did not find anyone," so this would be part of the means of testing that follows from His saying ﴿We shall see whether you have told the truth.﴾

It may also be said that His saying ﴿We shall see whether you have told the truth﴾ implies a supposition in the verse: he looked and verified his truthfulness, so he gave him the letter. Allah knows best what happened. So either this letter is part of his testing, like what would happen if a person told you a piece of news and you said, for example: "Go and buy for me something of it now," if he said, for example, "This commodity is sold now in the market," and you said: "O Allah! Here it is (...). Take for me, for example, some of it..."

Student: I verify.

Shaykh: You test whether it is true or not? And if it is apparent, I, by giving him money to buy it, the apparent action of mine is...?

Student: I believed him.

Shaykh: I believed him. But this may be one of the means of testing.

So the conclusion is: if Solomon, peace be upon him, verified this matter and then sent the letter, the matter is apparent. But there is nothing in the Qur'an indicating that. So we say that giving him the letter is among the means that show his truthfulness.

His saying ﴿Take this letter of mine﴾ points to it for identification, because Solomon wrote to them and to others, but he specified the letter he had written to them. ﴿Then throw it to them﴾, that is, to Bilqis and her people. ﴿Then withdraw﴾, that is, turn away from them and stand near. ﴿And see what they return﴾, that is, what answer they send back. So he took it, came to her, and her soldiers surrounded her, and he threw it into her lap. When she saw it, she trembled and submitted out of fear. Then she read what was in it, and then she said to the nobles of her people: "O chiefs."

The hoopoe went with it and threw it to them, that is, he placed it before them, and withdrew from them as Solomon had instructed. But this withdrawal was not far, as shown by His saying ﴿and see what they return﴾, because His saying ﴿and see what they return﴾ indicates that this withdrawal was near her. There are benefits in it that will come, God willing.

Then ﴿and see what they return﴾: she took the letter and read it, then said to the nobles of her people: ﴿O chiefs﴾ [al-Naml 29]. The *malaʾ* (chiefs), as the author explained, are the nobles. Here she addressed them: "O chiefs," as an indication of the high rank they held in her state, because ﴿yā ayyuhā﴾ (O you) is used only for someone distant. She did not say "O chiefs" alone, but said: ﴿O chiefs, indeed I have had thrown to me a noble letter﴾, with the two hamzas pronounced clearly: *al-malaʾ inni*, and the second hamza softened by changing it into a waw: *al-malaʾ winni*, changing it into a kasra-marked waw, because when a hamza comes after a damma, it may be changed into a waw. This is a rule of the Arabic language. From it comes the common saying of many muezzins: "Allah wa-kabar," because it is permissible to say *Allahu akbar*, and it is also permissible to say *Allah wa-kabar*. So when a hamza comes after a damma, it may be softened into a waw, and depending on the context, it takes a kasra if the context calls for a kasra, or a damma if it calls for a damma, or a fatha.

He said: (with the two hamzas pronounced clearly and the second softened by changing it into a kasra-marked waw, ﴿Indeed I have had thrown to me a noble letter﴾ [al-Naml 29], sealed).

That is, he explained "noble" as "sealed." That is, its sealing is evidence of its importance, since sealed letters and documents are taken care of, and even now, if something is important, you find it sealed with wax or the like so that it cannot be forged. But explaining *karīm* as "sealed" is not correct, because the seal is evidence of its nobility, not the meaning of its nobility. The *karīm* means what contains great and influential meanings.

In her words ﴿Indeed I have had thrown to me﴾, she did not say "the hoopoe threw it," because it appears that it was thrown and she omitted the agent. It does not mean that he came, stood before her, and handed her the letter. This may be more striking in awe, that it was delivered while he was passing by, unlike if it had fallen before her, where there would be no awe. Moreover, if it had fallen in front of her, the nature of a hoopoe would require that she hold it, but it was thrown rather than placed.

﴿Indeed it﴾, that is, the letter, ﴿is from Solomon﴾. She did not attribute it to his father, because it was well known and understood among them that he, peace be upon him, was a messenger to whom Allah had given a kingdom that He had not given anyone else.

﴿And indeed it﴾, that is, its content: ﴿In the name of Allah, the Most Merciful, the Most Compassionate﴾ (30). ﴿Do not exalt yourselves over me, and come to me in submission﴾ [al-Naml 30–31]. And there is no "peace upon whoever follows the guidance," nor "to proceed," as the author said.

Student: What (...)?

Shaykh: Perhaps it is from the reports of the Children of Israel, or it follows the customary form of letters. Solomon wrote with the least that could be understood and the purpose of it. ﴿In the name of Allah, the Most Merciful, the Most Compassionate﴾ (30). ﴿Do not exalt yourselves over me, and come to me in submission.﴾ But regarding His saying ﴿Indeed it is from Solomon, and indeed it is "In the name of Allah, the Most Merciful, the Most Compassionate"﴾: did Solomon say, "From Solomon to Bilqis," or not?

Student: He (...).

Shaykh: No, he did not say that. But she may have understood it either from a signature, or from writing on the envelope, if there was an envelope. Otherwise the body of the letter read: "In the name of Allah, the Most Merciful, the Most Compassionate. Do not exalt yourselves over me, and come to me in submission." This is the body, and this is the apparent meaning, because Solomon, peace be upon him, could not begin with "From Solomon, in the name of Allah, the Most Merciful, the Most Compassionate." Rather, he would begin with what?

Student: With the basmala.

Shaykh: With the basmala first. So since he mentioned nothing but the basmala, this shows that he did not write "Indeed it is from Solomon." But there must have been something in the letter that pointed to that, otherwise she would not have understood it.

Commentary of Ibn 'Uthaymin (Tafsir al-Quran al-Karim) on surah 27, verses 20–37 (part 3 of 7):

And His saying: ﴿Do not exalt yourselves against me, and come to me in submission﴾. The intended meaning is submission to me. That is, the meaning is: humble yourselves before me, because they were not exalting themselves over him, so that he would say, "Do not exalt yourselves over me." Rather, he intended that they come to him humbled and submitting. Is it "submitting to Allah" or "submitting to him"? The intended meaning is "submitting to Allah," or "submitting to him," meaning "surrendering"?

* Student: "Submitting to him."

* Shaykh: It is possible that it means they submit to Allah, or that they surrender to me. But does it follow that if they come to him surrendering, they must be submitting to Allah?

* Student: It does not follow.

* Shaykh: It does not follow. But it does follow that if they are submitting to Allah, they will surrender to Him, and come obediently, not opposing. Then she said: ﴿O chiefs, advise me in my affair﴾ and so on to the end [An-Naml 27:32].

(...) Allah, blessed and exalted, says: ﴿So he stayed not long, and said: "I have comprehended [something] which you have not comprehended, and I have come to you from Sheba with certain news."﴾

* From this noble verse the following benefits are derived. First: the swiftness of the hoopoe's return to Solomon, which indicates that Solomon's soldiers attend to their duties and do not delay in their tasks, as shown by His saying: ﴿So he stayed not long﴾.

* Also derived from it: even though Solomon was given a great kingdom that no one else was given, he does not encompass everything. Despite the vastness of his kingdom and his power, he does not encompass everything, so others are even more so.

* From it is derived the third benefit: the weakness of a person's perception, however great his kingdom and power. This is shown by Allah's saying: ﴿And man was created weak﴾ [An-Nisa' 4:28]. This makes clear that man is weak in everything: in intellectual faculties, in physical strength, and in everything that can be described as strong or weak, the state of man is one of weakness.

* Among the benefits of the verse: it is permissible to address a leader with this kind of speech, for example saying, "You knew what you did not know," or "You did what you did not do." Similar to this is the saying of Abraham, peace be upon him, to his father: ﴿Indeed, there has come to me of knowledge that which has not come to you﴾ [Maryam 19:43].

* Also among its benefits: the speaker should emphasize his report to the listener when there is a need for it, as shown by His saying: ﴿with certain news﴾.

If someone says: what is the benefit of his emphasizing it when he is the source of the report? For emphasis is only beneficial when it comes from another party who serves as a witness for the one reporting. As for the reporter himself, how can it be said that there is a benefit in his emphasizing his report?

The answer: the purpose of this is to increase the reassurance of the listener. It also shows that it has a benefit: when a reporter gives you a report, you may say to him, "Are you certain?" and he says, "Yes," or "No." So the reporter's emphasis on his report should not be said to be of no benefit, since he is the source of the report. Rather, we say there is a benefit in it, which is removing the listener's doubt about the report, so this removes that doubt and reassures the one being addressed. That is why it was said: ﴿and I have come to you from Sheba with certain news﴾.

* Also in it, among the benefits of the verse: using the plural pronoun for an honored addressee is not required, and it is also not the practice of the prophets and the early generations (salaf) to say, when a person is honored, "I came to you" or "I have come to you" and the like, as is customary among us now. Among us, when the addressee is honored, people say, "As you wish," for instance, "your excellency," "your eminence," "your grace," "your virtue," or similar things. No, this was not customary in the past. Rather, a person is addressed according to what the situation requires. Indeed, the Prophet, peace be upon him, when someone greeted him, would reply, "Upon you be peace" [reported by al-Bukhari (6251) from the hadith of Abu Hurayrah]; if a group greeted him, he would say, "Upon you (plural) be peace."

* The last benefit: it is the custom of the early generations that they address or speak to the listener according to what the situation requires.

﴿Indeed, I found a woman ruling over them, and she has been given of everything, and she has a great throne﴾. "A woman ruling over them": the pronoun is plural. Does the pronoun it refers back to refer to a plural or a singular?

* Student: No, singular.

* Shaykh: Where?

* Student: (...).

* Shaykh: ﴿a woman ruling them﴾: the "them" is a plural pronoun. Does the pronoun it refers back to, is it singular or plural?

* Student: Plural.

* Shaykh: Where?

* Student: (...).

* Shaykh: Yes, plural. But the antecedent of the pronoun is singular or plural?

* Student: Singular.

* Shaykh: Where?

* Student: (...).

* Shaykh: Yes. But since what is meant is the tribe, it is correct for the pronoun to refer back to it in the plural. We have already explained this earlier, and we said about it: "Saba'" (Sheba) and "Saba'" (as a tribe and an ancestor).

* From this verse, ﴿I found a woman ruling them﴾, it is derived that a woman is not fit for rulership, because he did not say "queen" but said ﴿ruling them﴾. The explanatory commentator (al-mufassir) previously said: "that is, she is a queen over them," and the purpose of explaining ﴿ruling them﴾ as "queen" is to avoid the understanding that she rules them with enslaving rule and not with rule of management. Is it valid for a woman to be a queen?

No. In our Shari'ah it is not permitted for a woman to be placed over men. So she cannot be a queen, nor can she be an emir, nor a minister, nor a judge. All of this is impermissible, because the Prophet, peace be upon him, said: "A people will never prosper who entrust their affairs to a woman" [reported by al-Bukhari (4425) from the hadith of Abu Bakrah].

* Student: (...)?

* Shaykh: This is only a name. It is a name, not "princess." It means that she is from the princes, from a family of princes, only that.

* Student: And "sayyida" (lady)?

* Shaykh: "Sayyida," like now, "al-sayyida Raqiqa," everyone in the neighborhood calls her "sayyida," all people call her "sayyida." We have already warned about this earlier and said that this is borrowed from the West, who venerate women, and that this is not appropriate. For this reason, you will even find some writers saying "al-Sayyida 'Aishah," "al-Sayyida Khadijah." This is not appropriate. Rather, it should be said "the woman" or "the female." As for "sayyida," this usage is not valid, especially since it is borrowed from non-(...).

* In this is evidence of the vastness of this woman's kingdom, indeed the greatness of her kingdom, as shown by His saying: ﴿and she has been given of everything﴾. What is meant by ﴿of everything﴾ is the constituents of kingship, as the author, the explanatory commentator, said.
