Here, when he wanted to assign them the delivery of the message, the assignment of delivering a message to a group causes responsibility to be lost. He assigned the delivery to whom? Only to their leader, because if you charge a group with something, for example, to a person, responsibility is lost, and each one relies on the others, so the message is not delivered. But if you assign it to one person, then he bears it and delivers it. For this reason he assigned it to the leader, saying: ﴿Return to them﴾; that is, to your group who sent you, with what you brought of the gift.

(﴿Then We will surely come to them with hosts they cannot withstand﴾, ﴿they cannot withstand﴾ means no power against them, ﴿and We will surely expel them from it﴾, from their land, Saba, which was named after the father of their tribe, ﴿humbled, and they will be debased﴾; that is, if they do not come to me in submission.)

This is the kind of force: because he does not want wealth, and does not want worldly things; otherwise he would have yielded and been content with this great gift that was sent with a group. But he does not want that, so he addressed them with these strong words: ﴿Then We will surely come to them﴾. And the lam?

* Student: It is for the oath.

* Shaykh: It is a preface to the oath, and the nun in ﴿We will surely come﴾ is for emphasis. So this sentence is emphasized by three emphases: the oath, the lam, and the nun, and in it there is also glorification.
﴿Then We will surely come to them﴾, and he did not say (fa-ʾātīhim, then I will come to them), because this is more emphatic in terms of awe, whether he intended to glorify himself or intended by it: I will come to them with hosts.

His saying: ﴿they cannot withstand﴾ contains a belittling of this group who were sent with this gift. He belittled them in the financial aspect, in His saying: ﴿What Allah has given me is better than what He has given you﴾.
And in the military aspect, in His saying: ﴿they cannot withstand﴾, meaning they have no power against it, because he has soldiers from the jinn and mankind, and even birds. They have no power against this thing. Also: ﴿and We will surely expel them from it humbled﴾, we will occupy their lands and expel them from them, humbled.

﴿and they will be debased﴾. The difference between "humbled" (adhillah) and "debased" (ṣāghirūn): humiliation (dhull) is in the soul, and debasement (ṣaghār) is in the body; that is, one is submissive outwardly and inwardly: submissive outwardly through debasement, and submissive inwardly through humiliation.
Allah, Exalted, says: ﴿And you will see them presented before it, humbled by abasement, glancing with a furtive glance﴾ [al-Shura 45]. Khushūʿ (humbling) here means debasement, and dhull is the humiliation of the soul, and we seek refuge in Allah.

This is evidence that Sulayman, peace be upon him, had such firmness of resolve and strength of authority that he could express himself in this manner to those who presented him with this gift.

If someone says: how is it fitting for Sulayman, peace be upon him, to confront a group who sent him a gift with this harsh style?
The answer is evident in this, because he...?

* Student: (...).

* Shaykh: Who?

* Student: (...).

* Shaykh: Yes, it does not contradict it. He did not accept the gift. But why did he not respond in a gentle manner, not a harsh one?

* Student: If they fight him, he does not want fighting. He wants only their entry into Islam. If he responds to them harshly, they will fear and enter the religion of Allah, Blessed and Exalted.

* Shaykh: Yes indeed. We say: the answer to this is that he, peace be upon him, wanted to show them his strength, and that he did not concern himself with their affair. Furthermore, their testing him, although he had said: ﴿Do not exalt yourselves over me, and come to me in submission﴾, their testing him indicates doubt about his call. He called them to Islam, and they doubted it by sending the gift and thought he wanted worldly things. So they were the ones who began the harm against him, by sending him a gift to test him with. Therefore his response was appropriate.

(When the envoy returned to her with the gift, she placed her throne inside seven gates, inside her palace, and her palace inside seven palaces?)

* Student: There is no evidence for it.

* Shaykh: Yes, excellent. (And she closed the gates and placed guards over them, and prepared herself to go to Sulayman to see what he would order her to do. She set out with twelve thousand elephants, with each elephant thousands upon thousands, until she came near him at a distance of one farsakh. He perceived her and said: ﴿O chiefs, which of you will bring me her throne?﴾)

Strange. I do not know from where the author brings this!?

* Student: We have here, Shaykh: (twelve thousand qeel, with each qeel).

* Shaykh: No, twelve thousand elephants.

* Student: That means qeel (...).

Commentary of Ibn 'Uthaymin (Tafsir al-Quran al-Karim) on surah 27, verses 20–37 (part 6 of 7):

* The Shaykh: Even among us, I have heard it said, but it is not authentic, that (twelve thousand elephants). Elephants may well have been numerous in Yemen. That is why the owner of the elephant, who wanted to demolish the Ka'bah, came with an elephant.
He says: (with every elephant many thousands of people), that is, twelve thousand men with each elephant, and "many thousands" with every elephant means a whole world.
(Until, when she had come within a farsakh of him, he perceived it, and said: ﴿O chiefs, which of you will bring me her throne?﴾), and so on to the end.
Restricting oneself to the narratives that are in the Qur'an is what befits the Mushaf (the written copy of the Qur'an), except for what is authentically reported from the Prophet ﷺ. This is because God says: ﴿Has there not come to you the report of those before you: the people of Noah, 'Ad and Thamud, and those after them, whom none knows but God?﴾ [Ibrahim 9]. So the knowledge of these nations is referred to God, glorified and exalted is He, and it befits us not to go beyond what the Qur'an has brought.
Yet generosity (karam) is according to the nature of each thing. Generosity with wealth means giving it out lavishly, and "generosity" with wealth is also applied to its best part, as the Prophet ﷺ said: «Beware of the choicest of their property» or «Avoid the choicest of their property» [Agreed upon; al-Bukhari (1496) and Muslim (19/31) from the hadith of Ibn 'Abbas]. Likewise, something that contains an important matter is described as noble (karim), because of what this description implies, as in the letter of Sulayman, peace be upon him.
* In this there is evidence that the better practice for the writer is to begin with his own name, saying: "From so-and-so," before beginning with the name of the recipient or addressee. Is this a matter of ta'abbud (acts of worship that are fixed by revelation) or of 'adah (custom)?
* A student: It is a matter of custom.
* The Shaykh: Apparently it is a matter of custom. Nevertheless, the custom followed by the early generations (al-salaf) is better than the custom people have adopted today. Today people have become accustomed to beginning with the addressee: "To so-and-so, son of so-and-so." But the earlier custom is better, because when a person reads a letter, he reads it from the beginning. When he reads "From so-and-so," he knows now what this is and what the letter's importance is, before he has read all of it.
Furthermore, the natural order requires this, because the letter comes from someone to someone, does it not? So it requires that one begin with the one it comes from before the one it goes to.
So we say: it is better for a person to begin with his own name when he sends a letter to someone, because this is the established Sunnah.
Can one derive from this letter that there is no need to mention the addressee, since it says: ﴿Indeed it is from Sulayman﴾ [al-Naml 30], and does not say "to the Queen of Sheba"?
* A student: It may have been mentioned.
* The Shaykh: But what is before us now?
* A student: (...).
* The Shaykh: That is possible. Or we may say: if the evidence indicates the addressee, there is no need to mention him. For example, if you send this letter to a person, especially in a story like that of Sulayman, where this bird brought it to its owner, then the possibility that the letter reaches someone other than the addressee is weak.
The purpose of stating the addressee is that he be identified and that the letter reach him. Here, if the letter comes in this manner, the greatest identification is achieved. So we say there is no need to mention him if the matter is achieved without it. Nevertheless, mentioning him is better, especially if something will follow from it in the future. If we suppose that the person to whom it was sent is known and has received it, we still do not know, in the future, to whom this message was addressed. So mentioning him is without doubt better.
* And in this there is evidence for the recommendation of beginning letters with "In the name of God, the Most Merciful, the Especially Merciful," because of His words: ﴿And indeed it is: In the name of God, the Most Merciful, the Especially Merciful﴾.
* And in this there is evidence for the use of brevity when it does not involve shortcoming, because this letter which Sulayman wrote is as concise as possible: only two sentences: ﴿Do not exalt yourselves against me, and come to me in submission﴾ [al-Naml 31]. But this is on condition that the brevity does not undermine the purpose. If it undermines the purpose, it becomes a shortcoming.
* And in this there is evidence that Sulayman, peace be upon him, called them to God, glorified and exalted is He, and did not want domination and control. He wanted by this that they enter Islam, because when the hoopoe (al-hudhud) informed him that she and her people were prostrating to the sun instead of God, this is kufr (disbelief), so they must come out of it into Islam. This is shown by His words: ﴿and come to me in submission﴾.
* And in this also there is evidence of the strength of Sulayman, peace be upon him, because he did not say "and submit," but said "come to me in submission." He asked them to come to him while they were already in a state of Islam.
Does this mean that they should all come? No. What is meant is their notables and nobles, because the notables and nobles stand in place of the common people.
* And in this there is evidence for the recommendation of consultation (mushawarah) in public affairs, because of her words: ﴿O chiefs, advise me in my affair﴾ [al-Naml 32]. Although she is a queen with complete authority, she still did not dispense with consultation: ﴿She said: O chiefs, advise me in my affair﴾.
* And in this there is evidence of this woman's firmness and that she wanted her governance to be based on the responsibility shared by all. This is shown by her words: ﴿I would not decide an affair until you bear witness to me﴾. Then, if the result turned out contrary to what was intended, she would not be blamed, since she had called these people to witness and had explained the matter to them.
* And in this also there is evidence that it is permissible for the one seeking counsel to differ from the one he consults if he does not think the adviser is right in his advice. When they mentioned what indicated that they wanted to fight him, and she did not see that, she disagreed with them, did she not? She said: ﴿Indeed, when kings enter a town they corrupt it﴾ [al-Naml 34], and so on to the end.
* And in this there is evidence of this woman's standing among her people, because after she consulted them and they gave their opinions, they showed her respect and said: ﴿The command is yours, so see what you will command﴾ [al-Naml 33]. Can one also derive from this that if an adviser offers his counsel to someone greater than him in rank, or understanding, or knowledge, he may say such a thing? Yes. He says it out of good manners, and the one being advised has the choice: if he wills, he takes the advice, and if he wills, he does not.
* And in this there is evidence of this woman's firmness also in that she considered the consequences: ﴿Indeed, when kings enter a town they corrupt it﴾. Thus a sensible person should not judge affairs by their first appearances and outward signs, but should judge affairs by their outcomes. For a thing may have first appearances and outward signs that seem beneficial to a person, but upon reflection the matter turns out to be the opposite. But is it better to act quickly or to be deliberate?
In principle, deliberation is better, because when a person is deliberate he does not regret what he has done. But if he hastens, he is the one exposed to regret. How many a word a person has said, wishing "I had not said it," and how many an action he has done, wishing "I had not done it."
Nevertheless, firmness (hazm) must be used in affairs. One should not be so deliberate that it prolongs the purpose, nor so hasty that it brings regret. I think I recited to you two verses on this meaning. Do you remember them?
* A student: On firmness?
* The Shaykh: No, on the point that sometimes haste is better and sometimes deliberation is better.
* A student: (...)
* The Shaykh:
Sometimes the one who is deliberate attains some of his need, / and sometimes error accompanies the one who hastens.
And often a people lose the greater part of their affair, / through deliberation, when the right course would have been to hasten.
Yes, and this is true and real. The first verse:
Sometimes the one who is deliberate attains some of his need, / and sometimes error accompanies the one who hastens.
The point is that we say: if the matter stands between hastening and deliberation, and hastening is not preferable to it, then deliberation is better, because the matter is in a person's hands as long as he has not done anything. But if he does something, the matter escapes him and he cannot free himself from it.
* A student: Is this derived from the verse?
* The Shaykh: Yes, indeed.
* A student: How?
* The Shaykh: It is derived from the verse, because she said: ﴿Indeed, when kings enter a town they corrupt it and make the most honoured of its people abased﴾ [al-Naml 34]. So she considered the consequences, and considering consequences requires either haste or deliberation. For example, a person may see that if he does not hasten, the purpose will be lost, so he hastens. Or, if he hastens, a disorder will occur, so he is deliberate. This is derived from her words: ﴿Indeed, when kings enter a town they corrupt it and make the most honoured of its people abased﴾ [al-Naml 34].
* And also in it: ﴿And indeed, I am sending them a gift, and I will wait to see with what the messengers return﴾ [al-Naml 35].
* From this verse the following is derived. First: the intelligence and shrewdness of this woman.
* Second, from this is derived: the permissibility of testing and examining, and that this is not considered deception. If a person wants to test another with something, this is not considered deception, because he wants to ascertain his condition by it, and there is no objection to this.
* And in the verse there is also the third benefit, which is: acting on indicators (qara'in), because she wanted to send this gift to test Sulayman's intention. Does he want only wealth? Would this gift satisfy him? Or does he want them to submit, so that this gift would not help him and he would not refrain from his first demand, which is: ﴿Do not exalt yourselves against me, and come to me in submission﴾ [al-Naml 31].
So there are three benefits in it. Has the like of this been reported? Yes. In the story of Sulayman with the two women who brought a dispute to him about the son of one of them: two women went out of the town, each with a son. The wolf ate the son of the elder, and they brought their dispute to Dawud, peace be upon him. He judged the living son to belong to whom? To the elder, on the basis that the younger could bear more children later. But when they brought their dispute to Sulayman, peace be upon him, he said: "That is not the ruling. The ruling is that we bring a knife and split the child in two, so that the elder gets half and the younger gets half." The elder agreed that it should be split in two, why? Because it was not her son, and she was saying: "Just as my son perished, let her son perish." As for the younger, she said: "No, O Prophet of God, the child..." So it became known that the child belonged to the younger, and he judged it to her [Agreed upon; al-Bukhari (3427) and Muslim (1720/20) from the hadith of Abu Hurayrah]. This is from the category of establishing the truth by means of indicators, and there is no objection to it. The judges used to do this.
So this matter, sending the gift to Sulayman, peace be upon him, is of this kind: to establish his condition by it, and so one acts on the indicator.
* A student: (...) It is derived from her action.
* The Shaykh: Yes, because there is no objection to it.
* A student: Even if she was a disbeliever?
* The Shaykh: Even if she was a disbeliever. For when God, glorified and exalted is He, relates something, He has said: ﴿Certainly there is in their stories a lesson for people of understanding﴾ [Yusuf 111]. So when God, exalted is He, relates something from a disbeliever and does not intend to nullify it, it remains on its original permissibility.
* The fourth benefit of the verse: the gift was large. From where is this derived?
* A student: ﴿And I will wait to see with what the messengers return﴾ [al-Naml 35].
* The Shaykh: A group is not sent with a gift unless it is large. Moreover, perhaps we may also say, along with its largeness, that it was valuable, so that these messengers could defend it if anyone tried to attack them. So the greatness of this gift is established in both quantity and quality, and for this reason it needed to be sent with a group.
And in His words: ﴿So when [the messenger] came to Sulayman, he said: Do you provide me with wealth? What God has given me is better than what He has given you. Rather, it is you who rejoice in your gift. (36) Return to them, for we will surely come to them with soldiers they cannot resist, and we will surely expel them from it in humiliation, and they will be debased﴾ [al-Naml 36–37].
* From His words: ﴿So when [the messenger] came to Sulayman﴾ it is derived that it is commendable for the leader, the head of the delegation or of the people, to go forward with speech or action when the task is to be performed by action. The essential thing is that the one who goes forward is the leader, because for everyone to advance at once is not fitting, since responsibility is lost. So someone must go forward, one person, and the more the matter is limited, the closer it is to understanding and to achieving the purpose.
* And in it also there is evidence for addressing the group, even if the one who goes forward is their leader. This is shown by His words: ﴿Do you provide me with wealth?﴾ [al-Naml 36].
* And in it there is evidence for the permissibility of harshness in speech when there is a benefit in it, because this manner of Sulayman, peace be upon him, is a strong manner. As we have said, the interrogative in His words: ﴿Do you provide me with wealth?﴾ is for reproach and astonishment, meaning that he reproaches them for their action and is astonished at it: how could they provide him with wealth when he is a king, known and famous?!
* And in it there is evidence for the permissibility of speaking of God's blessing.
* The fourth benefit: it is permissible for a person to speak of God's blessing, because of the words of the Prophet ﷺ: ﴿What God has given me is better than what He has given you﴾. But should one speak of this blessing in a manner of boasting, or in a manner of humble need and belittling oneself? It depends on the situation. We see that it depends on the situation.
So in the presence of the enemy it is permissible to speak of it in boasting. That is why pride (khuyala') is permitted in war, although pride is forbidden, is it not? It is forbidden, one of the major sins. But in war, for the purpose of attacking the enemy, there is no harm in it. So Sulayman, peace be upon him, here spoke of God's blessing in boasting, as it appears to me, boasting over these people. This is not objectionable when it is in front of the enemy. But when it is to display the blessing, it is not permissible except in the manner of belittling oneself and need of God, glorified and exalted is He, not in the manner of boasting and exalting oneself over creation.
* The fifth benefit: it is permissible for a person to describe another by what appears of his condition. This is shown by His words: ﴿Rather, it is you who rejoice in your gift﴾, since joy, as you know, is an inward matter, whose signs appear on the outward body, though in origin it is inward. For the one who rejoices does not make a sound for his joy, nor is any movement seen in him, but its signs appear.
So there is no harm in a person judging another by indicators from what appears of his condition. This matter has come before you many times. The man who had intercourse with his wife during the day in Ramadan said: «By God, between its two lava plains there is no household poorer than mine» [Agreed upon; al-Bukhari (1936) and Muslim (1111/81) from the hadith of Abu Hurayrah].
Yet this man did not go around the houses of the people of Madinah searching them to know that there was no one poorer than himself.
* And in it also there is evidence, the sixth benefit: evidence for displaying strength to enemies, because of His words: ﴿Return to them, for we will surely come to them with soldiers they cannot resist﴾ [al-Naml 37]. This falls under His words, exalted is He: ﴿And prepare against them whatever you are able of power﴾ [al-Anfal 60]. For "power" (quwwah) here is indefinite and includes every kind of strength that is possible, whether it is power of speech, material power, or moral power. The essential thing is that a person should employ all kinds of strength in dealing with enemies. Indeed, it has come in a hadith: «War is deception» [Agreed upon; al-Bukhari (3029) and Muslim (1740/18) from the hadith of Abu Hurayrah].
But is treachery (khiyanah) permissible or not?
* A student: It is not permissible.
* The Shaykh: Treachery against the enemy is not permissible. It is not permissible for a person to betray his enemy. This is why God, exalted is He, said: ﴿And if you fear treachery from a people, then throw back to them [their treaty] on equal terms﴾ [al-Anfal 58], and do not betray them. Likewise, if they betray, they have broken the covenant. We have already gone over this matter, that it has three cases concerning those with whom we have a treaty:
Either they remain upright toward us: ﴿So as long as they are upright with you, be upright with them﴾ [al-Tawbah 7].
Or they break the covenant, and then there is no covenant: ﴿And if they break their oaths after their covenant and attack your religion, then fight the leaders of disbelief﴾ [al-Tawbah 12].

And if they do not break the covenant, and their outward conduct is upright, but we fear treachery from them, then we announce the termination of the covenant to them and inform them that we have annulled it. Even if they say, "We will remain bound by the covenant," we say, "No. Each of us is now free."

Here there is strength in the speech: ﴿Return to them, for we will surely come to them with hosts that they cannot repel﴾. This threat and warning is undoubtedly a display of strength, and so it falls under the words of God Most High: ﴿And prepare against them whatever you are able of power﴾ [Al-Anfal 60].

* Student: How do we reconcile the permissibility of deceiving the enemy with the impermissibility of treachery?

* Shaykh: Yes. Treachery means that you deceive him in a position of trust, whereas deception (khada'ah) means that you deceive him in a context other than trust. War is ongoing, so you set an ambush for them, for example, or something similar. You show, for instance, that you have a large number, so that people hesitate, as al-Qa'qa' ibn 'Amr did in his battles with the Persians and in other matters. You have not betrayed them, because there is no covenant between you and them.

* Student: Some of the Companions (...) tells him that so-and-so grants him safe conduct, and then kills him.

* Shaykh: That is not considered treachery, because that person is a combatant with whom there is no covenant. For this reason the Messenger said regarding the story of Ka'b ibn al-Ashraf: "Who will deal with Ka'b ibn al-Ashraf for me? He has harmed God and His Messenger" [[Agreed upon (muttafaqun 'alayh); al-Bukhari (2510) and Muslim (1801/119), from the hadith of Jabir ibn 'Abdullah.]].

* Student: Shaykh, the Prophet ﷺ explained "power" by saying: "Indeed, power is archery. Indeed, power is archery" [[Narrated by Muslim (1917/167), from the hadith of 'Uqbah ibn 'Amir.]]. So here, is power specifically archery?

* Shaykh: Yes. The Messenger, peace and blessings be upon him, and likewise what is reported from the Companions in explaining some verses, sometimes mention a thing by way of example. At that time, power was archery, and it still is. Archery now is among the strongest forms of power; that is, it is the highest kind of power.

Whether people's shooting was with the bow in the past, or with the rifle or with missiles, the important point is that archery at every time is the pinnacle of power.

* Student: (...).

* Shaykh: This is not meant as an exclusive limitation, but the Messenger wished to clarify the ultimate degree of power, so this power is the ultimate at every time.

* Also in His words, peace and blessings be upon him: ﴿Then we will surely come to them with hosts that they cannot repel﴾, there is evidence for the great number of Solomon's hosts. This queen, who possesses great intellect and has a people who obey her and are humbled before her commands, says: ﴿Then we will surely come to them with hosts that they cannot repel﴾. She did not specify these hosts. But it was mentioned at the beginning of the story that Solomon's hosts consisted of three categories: the jinn, mankind, and the birds. All of these he could set against them. If he sends the jinn, they have no way to resist them; and if he sends the birds to gouge out their eyes, they likewise have no way to resist them.

So the outcome is that the hosts that belong to Solomon cannot be opposed by these people, neither in number nor in quality. Is there anything more?

* Student: Shaykh (...) sending a letter ought to (...) the sender. Now how was it (...) the officials used to send to the Commander of the Faithful from an official (...).

* Shaykh: This falls under the category of wonder and exaggeration. Otherwise, without doubt, the first way is preferable. But as you have just said, they began to say: "From so-and-so to so-and-so," and then they began to say: "To so-and-so," placing the name at the end. This falls under the category of wonder and honouring others.

* Student: (...)?

* Shaykh: I do not know whether it is (...) or whether people recite it as an act of worship. But this is among ordinary matters, as we have said, not an act of worship.

* Student: Before the basmalah or after it, with this, with Solomon, before the basmalah?

* Shaykh: No. She reported: ﴿Indeed, it is from Solomon, and indeed it says: In the name of God, the Most Merciful, the Especially Merciful﴾ [Al-Naml 30]. Did Solomon write: "In the name of God, the Most Merciful, the Especially Merciful, from Solomon: Do not exalt yourselves against me, but come to me in submission"? Because this is a report from her. She is not reading out the writing to them now, so it is not like a narrator of a book, such that we would say: "From Solomon, in the name of God, the Most Merciful, the Especially Merciful." For this reason she said: ﴿Indeed, it is from Solomon, and indeed it says: In the name of God, the Most Merciful, the Especially Merciful. Do not exalt yourselves against me﴾ [Al-Naml 30–31]. Even in the course of the exegesis (...) that she understood it to be from Solomon in a manner other than this, even though he did not write it.

* Student: (...)?

* Shaykh: Correct. The disbeliever has no right to God's earth or to God's wealth; even wealth, he has no right to it.

* Student: (...)

* Shaykh: Yes. The reasoning for that is that if it were not so, then his threatening them with this would be impermissible, since it would not be lawful for him to do this. If they had a right, he would not have been permitted to act and expel them from their land.

* Student: Shaykh, (...) he said: the humiliation (al-sighar) (...) there is a difference between dhillah and sighar.

* Shaykh: No, it is not so. (...) dhillah is in the soul, and sighar is in the body.

* Student: ﴿Then we will surely come to them﴾ (...) on the doctrine of compulsion (al-jabriyyah).

* Shaykh: (...) it can be cited as evidence that a person acts by his own choice, because of His words: ﴿Then we will surely come to them with hosts﴾ [Al-Naml 37].

Commentary of Ibn 'Uthaymin (Tafsir al-Quran al-Karim) on surah 27, verse 38–40 (part 1 of 4):

Then Allah the Exalted said: (﴿He said, "O chiefs, which of you will bring me her throne before they come to me in submission?"﴾ Regarding the two hamzahs, what was mentioned earlier applies.) ﴿al-mala'u, ayyukum﴾. And what is the earlier point? Verifying them, verifying the two hamzahs: ﴿Yā ayyuhā al-mala'u ayyukum﴾ [An-Naml 38]. And easing the second by converting it into a waw: ﴿Yā ayyuhā al-mala'u wayyukum﴾.

(﴿Which of you will bring me her throne before they come to me in submission?﴾ "Submitting, obedient." So taking it before that, not after it.) He said: ﴿before they come to me in submission﴾. From where did he know that they would come to him in submission?

He knew that from the fact that when they heard what the messenger said to them, who was told: "Return to them, for they will surely submit and yield," so this is also a judgment based on indications. It is also possible that Allah the Exalted revealed this to him, since he is a prophet. So the matter is between his having judged that they would come in submission on the basis of an indication, and the possibility that this was by revelation from Allah the Exalted.

But his saying: ﴿before they come to me in submission﴾ alerted the commentator that if the throne was taken before they came to him in submission, it is permissible, and if it was after that, it is not permissible.

In this there is room for consideration, because her, once she leaves [her kingdom] as a Muslim, has secured her property, does she not? And she has protected it, so her property is inviolable even before she reaches Sulayman, merely by her Islam. And when she departs she will undoubtedly come in submission. For he had said to them earlier: ﴿Do not exalt yourselves against me, and come to me in submission﴾ [An-Naml 31], and his aim, Allah knows best, was not that if it was before their Islam it was permissible for him to take it, and if it was after it was not permissible.

Moreover, it is apparent that Sulayman did not intend to possess this throne, but rather to display his strength before her, and that he was able to bring her throne before they reached him. He did not intend to possess it, until what the author said is refuted.

When he said: ﴿Which of you will bring me her throne before they come to me in submission?﴾ (﴿An 'Ifrit of the jinn said, "I will bring it to you before you rise from your place. Indeed, I am strong and trustworthy for it."﴾ The 'ifrit is the strong, the mighty.)

The 'ifrit: the strong, the mighty. This meaning still exists to this day; when we say, "So-and-so is an 'ifrit," meaning strong and mighty, or we say something more emphatic than this.

﴿An 'Ifrit of the jinn said: I will bring it to you before you rise from your place, and indeed I am strong and trustworthy for it.﴾ Is "ātī" a noun of agency or a verb?
* Student: A verb.
* Shaykh: What do you all say?
* Student: Yes, a verb.
* Shaykh: Alright, that does not contradict. What is the active participle of (atā)?
* Student: Āt.
* Shaykh: Āt, (every ātin is near), and here?
* Student: Its origin is aʾtī (...).
* Shaykh: So it is not proper for me to say: "anā ātin ilayka bihi," that the estimate is: "anā ātin ilayka bihi qabla an taqūma min maqāmika"?
* Student: It is correct.
* Shaykh: It is correct, but the apparent reading is that it is a verb, because this action is among the verbs.
* Student: (...).
* Shaykh: No, even this: "anā ātin bihi."
﴿Anā ātīka bihi﴾, but the closer view is that it is a verb, which is supported by the fact that the basic form of action is verbs, and the kaf is the object, a pronoun in the accusative. So this is the basic form: ﴿Anā ātīka bihi﴾.
* Student: (...).
* Shaykh: No, we have a lengthened hamzah here.
* Student: (...).
* Shaykh: (...) No, it is not clear, it seems to be a mistake. Do you have al-Sawi's gloss? What is it? Other than al-Jalalayn?
* Student: Yes, other than al-Jalalayn.

He said: (﴿I will bring it to you before you rise from your place﴾ in which you sit to judge, which is from morning until midday.)

There is no evidence for this; this is among matters for which there is no proof. But his saying: ﴿before you rise from your place﴾ means: I will bring it to you quickly. This is a well-known idiom; to this day this idiom still exists: "I will answer you before you stand up," so the meaning is: I will bring it to you quickly.

﴿And indeed I am strong for it﴾, that is: for carrying it (﴿strong﴾, that is: upon its carrying; ﴿trustworthy﴾, that is: regarding what is in it of jewels and other things).

When he said: "I will bring it to you," this is a statement, but it needs confirmation of this matter, that he bring it before he rises from his place. So he said: ﴿And indeed I am strong for it﴾, I am not weak, rather I will bring it with this speed.

Also ﴿trustworthy﴾, that is: I will not betray anything in it, neither in the throne itself nor in what is in it of jewels and other things.

These two qualities are needed by every worker, as Allah the Blessed and Exalted said about the daughter of the man of Madyan: ﴿Indeed, the best one you can hire is the strong, the trustworthy﴾ [Al-Qasas 26]. These two qualities are required in every task, because if strength is lacking the work does not get done due to incapacity, and if strength is present but trustworthiness is lacking, the work is also hindered by betrayal.

(Sulayman said: "I want it faster than that.") Who said this?
* Student: Sulayman.
* Shaykh: There is no evidence for it. But (﴿The one who had knowledge from the Scripture said﴾, that is, the revealed Book, and he is Asaf ibn Barkhiya, who was a truthful one who knew the Greatest Name of Allah, which, when He is called upon by it, responds) — in my copy: "(da'ā bihi)" but the known wording is "(idhā du'iya bihi)." It is the known "the Greatest Name of Allah which, when called upon by it, responds." But it is possible that when this man who had knowledge from the Scripture called upon Him by it, meaning that this man had tested and known that when he called upon Allah the Exalted by this Name He responded. So here it is more fitting to say: "(idhā da'ā bihi ajāb)," because this man who had knowledge from the Scripture knows, or has tested, that when he calls by this Name He responds.

It is also not necessary that this person who had knowledge of the Scripture wanted to call upon Allah the Blessed and Exalted by His Greatest Name. Rather we say: this man was given by Allah the Exalted knowledge of the revealed Book. And there is no doubt that a knowledgeable person knows the means and formulas that are closest to being answered, whether by the Greatest Name of Allah or by other than it.

He says: (﴿I will bring it to you before your glance returns to you﴾, when you look at something.) Allahu akbar! Which of the two is faster?
* Students: The second.
* Shaykh: The second. This is like the blink of an eye.

﴿I will bring it to you before your glance returns to you﴾, that is: returns ﴿to you﴾, that is: your gaze.

So for example, if you look ahead of you like this, look like this very quickly, and reflect, glory be to Allah, the Mighty, on what comes from Yemen to Syria with such great speed, because it comes by the command of Allah the Exalted, and Allah the Exalted says: ﴿His command, when He intends a thing, is only that He says to it, "Be," and it is﴾ [Ya-Sin 82], and ﴿Our command is but one, like a blink of the eye﴾ [Al-Qamar 50].

So when Allah the Blessed and Exalted answers the one who calls upon Him, He needs no duration or delay. Yet Allah the Blessed and Exalted still decrees affairs through their causes. A person may supplicate for a sick man that Allah cure him, but is he cured in a blink of an eye? No; there are causes that are decreed. Yet the causes take effect immediately when Allah the Blessed and Exalted wills to answer, although Allah is able to heal this patient in an instant, just as the Messenger, peace and blessings be upon him, was sometimes brought a sick person and he supplicated for him, and he was cured in an instant. 'Ali ibn Abi Talib was brought to him at Khaybar while complaining of his eye; he spat into it and supplicated, and it was healed immediately as if there had never been any pain in it.

And Allah the Blessed and Exalted is over all things capable. But the delay of a thing does not indicate that Allah the Exalted is not capable of healing it immediately; rather it indicates that Allah is Wise, decreeing affairs through their causes, just as He created the heavens and the earth in six days. We mentioned previously that this was for two benefits:

First: what is well known among the scholars, that Allah the Exalted made it in six days so that the servants would learn deliberation in affairs, and that what matters is perfecting the matter, not hastening it.

Another thing: the creation of these things requires causes and components that interact and reach perfection, and therefore it took six days.

Here he said: (﴿before your glance returns to you﴾. He said to him: look at the sky, so he looked at it, then returned his gaze and found it placed before him. In his looking at the sky, Asaf called upon the Greatest Name that Allah bring it, so it happened: it moved beneath the earth until it emerged beneath the seat of Sulayman.) Allahu akbar! What wonderful stories! First: was it this one who had knowledge of the Scripture who said to Sulayman: "Look at the sky"?

Student: No evidence.

Shaykh: There is no evidence, and there is no need to say "look at the sky," ﴿before your glance returns to you﴾ [An-Naml 40], in whatever direction you turn your gaze.

Second: if we say that it came from the earth and emerged from beneath the seat! It is possible that it came from the earth, it is possible that it came from above the earth, or came from a very high place and descended; none of this should be asserted with certainty. Rather it is said: Allah is capable of all things. The point is that the throne arrived in an instant before your glance returned to you.

And in his saying: (﴿So when he saw it set in place beside him﴾, that is: at rest) this has posed a difficulty for the grammarians, because they say among their rules: if the adverbial phrase or the prepositional phrase whose complement is general, it must be elided. For example, you say: "Zayd is in the house," and you may not say: "Zayd is present in the house," rather "present" must be elided because it is general. But if it is specific, like: "Zayd is imprisoned in the house," it must be mentioned, because if "imprisoned" were omitted there would be no indication of it. Unlike "Zayd is in the house," which by merely being uttered makes its meaning clear, meaning it becomes clear to the listener that the meaning is "present in it" or "existing in it."

So they say: if the prepositional phrase or the adverbial phrase has a general complement, it must be elided. And here, is "mustaqirran" general or specific?
* Students: General; this one says: a specific verb.
* Shaykh: Let us see the word "mustaqirr" in general. If you say "Zayd is in the house," meaning "present in the house," that is, "existing in it." Ibn Malik says:
"They reported with an adverb or a prepositional phrase, intending the meaning of 'existing' or 'settled'."
But they said: the settling here is not the general settling, which would require its elision, rather it is a specific settling, not mere existence. Since it is a specific settling, not mere existence, it is like a specific meaning, and therefore ﴿mustaqirran﴾ was mentioned. Notice that if he had said "so when he saw it with him," that would not show the meaning in the word "mustaqirr." True, when he saw it with him as something existing with him, but it does not show that this being was in settledness and stability.

Also, perhaps what is understood from his saying ﴿mustaqirran﴾ is what the 'ifrit indicated at the beginning, namely strength and trustworthiness, because it is by strength and trustworthiness that the throne arrives in its state, without breaking. A weak person, for example, might drop it from his hand when carrying it while weak, or something similar, and it breaks. Or if he is not trustworthy, he does not care that a mountain or a tree or the like might strike it, or he himself might misuse it. The summary is that this settling has a specific meaning distinct from general settling, and therefore it was mentioned.

﴿So when he saw it set in place beside him, he said: "This is from the favor of my Lord"﴾, and so on to the end.

* * *

* Student: I seek refuge in Allah from Satan the accursed: ﴿And what she used to worship besides Allah hindered her; indeed, she was from a disbelieving people. (43) It was said to her, "Enter the palace." But when she saw it, she thought it was a body of water and uncovered her shins. [Sulayman] said, "Indeed, it is a palace paved smooth with glass." She said, "My Lord, indeed I have wronged myself, and I submit with Sulayman to Allah, Lord of the worlds." (44)﴾ [An-Naml 43, 44].
* Shaykh: I seek refuge in Allah from Satan the accursed. Allah the Blessed and Exalted said: ﴿He said, "O chiefs, which of you will bring me her throne before they come to me in submission?"﴾ [An-Naml 38].

In this is evidence for the permissibility of addressing an indefinite person, if he becomes specified afterward by his saying: ﴿which of you will bring me her throne﴾. Yes, he did not say: "Come to me, so-and-so." This type of address has many benefits, both in rulings and in information:

Among them, for example: it is permissible to say, "I marry you one of these two daughters of mine," and then he chooses one of them, just as the man of Madyan did with Musa.

Among them: it is permissible to say, "I sell you one of these two goods for such-and-such," and then he chooses one of them.

Among them: "I sell you this for ten in cash or twenty on credit," and he chooses one of the two prices.

This last matter is not one of "two sales in one sale," contrary to those who claim so, for this is one sale, since they did not separate except upon one of the two sales.

Also, the matter of "two sales in one sale" was previously mentioned, in which there is a sound and explicit text in Sunan Abi Dawud. What does it imply? That "two sales in one sale" is the issue of 'inah, due to the Prophet's saying, ﷺ: "Whoever sells two sales in one sale, the lesser of them is his, or it is usury."[[Narrated by Abu Dawud (3461) from Abu Hurayrah.]]

And this is explicit that this is the issue of 'inah.

* Shaykh: The issue of 'inah is that a person sells an item on credit for a price, then buys it back from the same seller for less in cash. This is the issue of 'inah.
* Student: The same seller buys it?
* Shaykh: Yes, the same seller buys it for less.

So now it is permissible to address an indefinite person in ruling and information, but on the condition that he becomes specified before the ruling is completed.

Now here: ﴿O chiefs, which of you will bring me?﴾ And in this is evidence that it is permissible for a person, before his enemy, to display greatness, because Sulayman intended by bringing this throne, what did he intend?
* Students: To display his greatness.
* Shaykh: To display his greatness and power, and that he was able to bring her throne, which was undoubtedly protected, because as is customary, the palaces of kings must be fortified and guarded, especially something like the throne.

As for the author's claim that he brought it only to possess it, there is no evidence in the verse for that; there is no evidence in the verse for that.

* Student: Does not the condition of specification with respect to the person bring any objection to this?
* Shaykh: In fact, a contract is valid only with specification. How could it be valid if one says, "I accept the marriage of so-and-so," where specification occurs, but one may not say, "I accept one of them"?

Likewise in sale: "I sell you for ten in cash or twenty on credit," and the acceptance says: "I accept for twenty on credit, I accept for ten in cash." This is necessary, because whoever gives the acceptance specifies; the point is the offer.

And in it is evidence: ﴿Which of you will bring me her throne before they come to me in submission?﴾ And in it is evidence that Sulayman, peace be upon him, either perceived insight, or it was revealed to him, that these people would come to him. That is, when the messenger returned with the gift and [Sulayman] said: ﴿We will surely come to them with soldiers they cannot resist, and we will surely expel them from there in humiliation, and they will be debased﴾ [An-Naml 37], no reply came, so he asked that her throne be brought, which indicates that he knew she and her people would come. But from where did he know that?

Either from revelation, or from insight; because phrases like these that are sent, ﴿We will surely come to them with soldiers they cannot resist, and we will surely expel them from there in humiliation, and they will be debased﴾, with such strength, imply that the enemy will be humbled and submit.

If it was by insight, it is evidence for the permissibility of judging by insight. We have mentioned several times that it is permissible to judge a matter according to the predominance of opinion, and even to swear an oath concerning it according to the predominance of opinion. Insight leads to predominant opinion, but mere suspicion does not permit judging by opinion; insight must have indications, either prior indications or accompanying indications.

As for judging something for which there is no indication, this is judgment by mere conjecture.

﴿An 'Ifrit of the jinn said: I will bring it to you before you rise from your place, and indeed I am strong and trustworthy for it.﴾

First: in this verse is evidence for the subjugation of the jinn to Sulayman, by his saying: ﴿An 'Ifrit of the jinn said: I will bring it to you﴾; he was the first to speak.

Second: It is evidence of the strength of the jinn, because he will bring this great throne, carrying it from Sheba, from Yemen to the Levant (al-Sham).

Third: It is evidence of their speed, and speed is one of the attributes of strength. This is shown by His saying: ﴿Before you rise from your place﴾. This is an extraordinary speed, a tremendous speed. It is known that they have great speed, as evidenced by their eavesdropping on the heavens, and no one can reach the heavens except one who possesses an enormous speed.

It also shows that a person may describe himself with the perfect qualities he possesses, either to encourage or to warn. From where is this derived? ﴿And indeed I am strong and trustworthy for it﴾ is for encouragement, and ﴿We will surely come to them with hosts they cannot withstand﴾ is for warning. So both are permissible. But the condition is that he must truly possess that quality. As for a mere claim, no. This is like what came in the hadith: "Whoever pretends to have what he has not been given is like one who wears two garments of falsehood" (Agreed upon: al-Bukhari (5219) and Muslim (2130/127), from the hadith of Asma' bint Abi Bakr). So the person who praises himself with what he does not have, there is no doubt that he is a forger in his report and a forger in his attribute. He has reported about himself what is not in him, so the report is false, and the attribution of that quality to himself is likewise false. Therefore he said: "like one who wears two garments of falsehood."

* Student: (...)?
* Shaykh: Yes, similar to that. For example, scholars also speak in this manner. The saying of Ibn Mas'ud: "If I knew that anyone whom camels could reach had more knowledge of the Book of Allah than I, I would ride to him" (Agreed upon: al-Bukhari (5002) and Muslim (2463/115), from the hadith of Abdullah ibn Mas'ud), or as he said.

It also shows that the basis of work rests on these two qualities, strength and trustworthiness, as shown by His saying: ﴿Strong and trustworthy﴾. Because one who is not strong does not perform the work perfectly, why? Because of his weakness. And one who is not trustworthy also does not perform the work perfectly, why? Because of his treachery.

A person may be strong and able to do this work with complete ease, but he is not trustworthy, so people do not trust him. Moreover, even if he performs the work perfectly, the person keeps feeling that he might be able to do even better, but he did not, because he is treacherous.

Likewise, if a person is trustworthy but incapable, he will not perform the work perfectly because of his incapacity. Which of them is more blameworthy?

* Student: The treacherous one is more (blameworthy), because...
* Shaykh: The treacherous one is more blameworthy. But this one also has a kind of treachery, because his entering into a work he is not capable of, or not strong enough for, is without doubt an error and a betrayal. For this reason the Prophet (ﷺ) said to Abu Dhar: "You are a weak man, so do not take charge over two people, nor be in charge of the property of an orphan" (Narrated by Muslim (1826/17) from Abu Dhar).

So a weak person may not interfere in a matter which he knows he cannot perfect, especially when there are people who do it well. This is considered a betrayal of himself and of others: a betrayal of himself because in reality he has subjected himself to a difficult task, wanting to display his weakness before people; and a betrayal of others because he accepts their work while he does not do it well. ﴿Indeed, the best one you can hire is the strong and trustworthy﴾ [al-Qasas 26].

If someone says: If there gather before us four persons: one is strong and trustworthy, the second is strong but not trustworthy, the third is trustworthy but not strong, and the fourth is weak and treacherous.

The strong and trustworthy one is given precedence, and there is no difficulty in that. The weak and treacherous one is placed last without doubt. These are the two known extremes. What remains is: strong and treacherous, and weak but trustworthy.

* Student: The weak but trustworthy one has greater claim to be given precedence.
* Another student: The weak but trustworthy one is given precedence depending on the profession. If the job requires strength above all, then the strong one is given precedence. If the matters require safekeeping and custody, then the trustworthy one is given precedence over the treacherous one.
* Shaykh: This is the correct view. That is, we must look at which of the two is more important to consider. If in a task strength is more apparent, then the strong one is given precedence, because even if the strong one has some treachery, his strength may compel him to perform the work perfectly in order to become known for this strength, for example, when no one else is found but him. But if the matter does not require strength and work but requires trustworthiness, then the trustworthy one is given precedence.

Good. This is clear if there are two jobs, one of which shows the intent of trustworthiness and the other shows the intent of strength, such as a ruler (amir). What characterizes the ruler?

* Students: The intent of strength.
* Shaykh: The intent of strength. That is, the strength of a ruler, even if he is not trustworthy, is more beneficial to society than a weak but trustworthy ruler. But the judge is the reverse: for the judge, trustworthiness is more apparent, because if he is trustworthy, even if weak, the one who executes the ruling is someone else. In our time, execution belongs to the governmental authority. The judge rules, so if he is trustworthy, then the intent of trustworthiness in judging is more apparent than the intent of strength. Based on this, measure other cases.

However, if the work involves a conflict between strength and trustworthiness, this is a matter for consideration and we cannot issue a general judgment on it. Rather, we examine the specific case and see. That is, if two people compete for a work that requires both strength and trustworthiness, and neither one's superiority over the other is evident, then I cannot pass a general ruling here. Rather, each matter is considered on its own, and we look at the indicators, and we also look at the persons, and at whose strength is more evident than the other's trustworthiness, or whose trustworthiness is more evident than the other's strength.

In any case, we do not rule on this matter with a general judgment; rather, we rule on it with what? With the specific case. We say: this one is given precedence over that one when the specific case arises.

So the conclusion is that people, with regard to performing work, fall into four categories: strong and trustworthy, strong and treacherous, weak and trustworthy, and weak and treacherous. These are four categories.

It is known that the first is given precedence in every case, and the second is deferred in every case. The third and fourth are in competition with each other. So we look at what requires strength more, and in that case the strong one is given precedence; and what requires trustworthiness more, and in that case the trustworthy one is given precedence; and what admits both, we look at the specific case until we can give precedence to this one over that one, and so on.

It also shows, as we said, that a person may describe himself with what he has, but on the condition that it is a reality. And His saying...

* Student: (...).
* Shaykh: We say it is permissible (mubah), and you know that the permissible may take on the five categories of ruling (al-ahkam al-khamsah). Sometimes it may be obligatory and sometimes forbidden. It is only by way of permissibility, and we cannot say it is always required, because the purpose may be bad, nor that it is always prohibited, because the purpose may be good. So it is on the basis of permissibility...
* Student: One also cannot find what would correct himself except when circumstances require it.
* Shaykh: We say, by Allah, it is permissible. This is the basic principle. But if circumstances require clarification, then it becomes required, either obligatory or recommended.
* Student: Would it not be a form of commending oneself (tazkiyah)?
* Shaykh: There is no difference. People differ. My intention is not self-commendation. If my intention in self-commendation is among what is forbidden, then it may be so. But if it is for speaking of the blessing of Allah, then it is required, and if it is so that someone unqualified is prevented from undertaking this work, then it may be obligatory for him to clarify himself.

Perhaps we can derive a benefit from His saying: ﴿Before you rise from your place﴾. The benefit is that Solomon, peace be upon him, had arranged the affairs of his life, and that he had a particular, known, specified sitting place. Because His saying ﴿before you rise from your place﴾ is undoubtedly limited to a known period; otherwise it would have no benefit. For if his rising from his place were not known, who would know whether he might remain in his place for a full day or only one minute? So had he, peace be upon him, not arranged his times so that they became known to the people, he would not have said such words. As for the commentator's specification (from the forenoon until midday), we do not know; Allah knows best.

In any case, it is derived from this that Solomon, peace be upon him, had arranged his times so that they became known. This is especially important for a person who is sought after, whom people want. It is one of the most important matters that he arranges his affairs, so that a person who needs him knows that at this hour he will find him, and at other hours he will not find him, and so he may rest.

For example, he may set for himself a sitting, for instance, in his home or in a suitable place, in general terms, either between the two prayers of Maghrib and Isha, or after 'Asr, or in the forenoon. The important thing is that people know it. He arranges for himself, for example, a specific task known to people, so that whoever wants him for this task comes to him. The point is that a person should benefit from this: that Solomon arranged his work in its time. And second: a person should, especially one who is sought after, such as a ruler, judge, scholar, notable, or others, set specific times for himself, so that his times are fixed, so that people feel that this man is an organized man, and they feel that a disorganized person, who sits when he wishes and stands when he wishes, is not organized, and so they do not regard him as anything.

﴿He said, "The one who had knowledge from the Book said: I will bring it to you before your glance returns to you"﴾ [an-Naml 40].

In this there is evidence that the soldiers of Allah, the Exalted, who are the angels, are stronger than the jinn, or not? Because the first said: ﴿before you rise from your place﴾, and this one said: ﴿before your glance returns to you﴾. Which is faster? The latter, without doubt and without equality.

* Student: (...).
* Shaykh: Because the one who had knowledge of the Book was a worshipper, and he had no connection except through supplication.
* Student: It is not said (...) that he should make clear to people the knowledge he possesses.
* Shaykh: No, that is not apparent, because his saying ﴿He said, "The one who had knowledge from the Book..."﴾ is separated from His saying ﴿An 'ifrit from the jinn said﴾, and the basic assumption is that the speech is with humans, so it is apparent that he is a man, not one of the jinn.
* Student: Is it said that it was Gabriel who said this?
* Shaykh: No, that is not correct, because every speaker who is not of mankind must be specified, since the basic assumption is that humans are the ones who address one another and understand one another. So if it is from other than them, it is specified.
* Student: Just as the jinn were specified.
* Shaykh: Just as the jinn were specified.

Good. In this there is evidence of the perfect power of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, because for this great throne to come from Yemen to the Levant in a moment is undoubtedly one of the perfections of the power of Allah, which a person cannot imagine how it could be.

Can we now imagine how this came from Yemen to the Levant before your glance returned to you?

Even if it flew with a flight faster than smoke, we would not imagine it could come with this speed, nor can we imagine that the earth was folded up so that this met that.

So the power of Allah, the Exalted, cannot be grasped by a human; it exceeds imagination, and so are all the attributes of Allah: ﴿It will be but one shout, and at once they will be on the surface of the earth﴾ [an-Nazi'at 13-14]. Be.

So all creatures together on the surface of the earth: who can imagine this? Can you imagine this? You cannot imagine it. That is: if it were from the earth, it would split and open (...).

The point is that this is an example of the attributes of Allah, the Exalted, in the incapacity of the intellect, however far it reaches, to comprehend the reality of Allah's power. And likewise His other attributes. You, human, your knowledge is limited and your capacity is limited, and you cannot go beyond what you witness or what Allah has made you aware of.

In this there is evidence of the favor of Allah, the Exalted, upon Solomon, in that He subjected to him people of knowledge and the jinn: the jinn first, and the one with knowledge second.

Is His saying ﴿before your glance returns to you﴾ an exaggeration or a reality? It is a reality. Otherwise we would say that exaggeration in matters is permissible. But in any case, exaggeration in matters has occurred in other texts as well, that a person exaggerates even though it is not intended literally. This has come in the Qur'an and also in the Sunnah: exaggeration in matters.

And in this (﴿So when he saw it settled before him﴾ meaning: stationary, ﴿before him, he said, "This is﴾ meaning: its being brought to me ﴿by the bounty of my Lord"﴾). ﴿So when he saw it﴾ meaning: Solomon saw the throne ﴿settled﴾.

The settling here is something beyond mere existence. If the meaning of settling here were mere existence, its mention would not be eloquent. That is why the author explained settling here as stillness, meaning that it had been in this place for some time. Whoever leaves something, for example, anything you leave, and put it in a place, you come to watch it, adjust it and beautify it. This is especially so for a throne, which normally has legs, and it is fixed, as if it had been there for years. This too is from the perfection of power.

﴿He said, "This is from the bounty of﴾ (min) here: is it for specifying the kind, or for partitive?

* Students: Partitive...
* Shaykh: Both are permissible, because if by bounty we mean the kind, then it is for specifying the kind, and if by bounty we mean this specific thing, then it is partitive in any case. It is suitable for both.

As for His saying ﴿bounty of my Lord﴾: bounty is extra giving. The bounty of Allah, blessed and exalted, upon the servant cannot be counted or enumerated: ﴿And if you tried to count the favors of Allah, you could not enumerate them﴾ [Ibrahim 34]. And among His bounty upon His servant is that He does good to him, and then counts the servant's good as good. From the bounty of Allah upon the servant is that He does good to him, then counts the servant's good deed as good. Do you understand this? ﴿Is the recompense for good anything but good?﴾ [ar-Rahman 60].

You say: the reward of the good-doers who do good in their deeds is only that good is done to them, and their good deed is good from Allah. But this is part of the completeness of His bounty upon His servants, that He counts their good deed as good, though it is from them, as if they are not independent in it. ﴿Is the recompense for good anything but good?﴾ O Allah, to You belongs praise.

His saying ﴿my Lord﴾: lordship here is specific, and for this reason He attributed it to Himself, saying ﴿my Lord﴾.

It has already passed for us that lordship is general and specific, and that servanthood is likewise general and specific, and that the specific includes what is more specific.

His saying: (﴿so that He may test me﴾ meaning: test me). The lam here is for causation. ﴿They said, "We believe in the Lord of the worlds, the Lord of Musa and Harun"﴾ [al-A'raf 121-122]. For the lordship of Musa and Harun is other than the lordship of the other righteous servants of Allah.

(﴿so that He may test me﴾ meaning: test me). The lam is for causation. (﴿Shall I be grateful﴾ with the two hamzahs made clear and the second changed to an alif, and softened, and with an alif inserted between the softened one and the other, or left out.) (...).

(With the two hamzahs made clear): ﴿a'shkuru﴾. (The second changed to an alif): ﴿ashkuru﴾, this is its change to an alif. (Softened): ﴿a-shkur﴾, leave it as a hamzah softened between the alif and the hamzah. (Inserting an alif between the softened and the other, or leaving it out): meaning that when you recite with softening, it has two forms: inserting an alif, so the hamzah after the alif is softened, or without an alif, meaning that softening allows lengthening before the softening and not lengthening.

(﴿Or am I ungrateful?﴾) for the blessing. How then is gratitude? Gratitude is by praising Allah, blessed and exalted, for this blessing in itself, and likewise by acknowledging in the heart that it is pure bounty from Allah, and that you have no claim of favor upon your Lord because of it.

The third: performing what this blessing requires as a duty. This is specific gratitude, not general gratitude. Gratitude may be general, so that a person is described as among the grateful in an absolute sense, and it may be specific, so that he is described as among the grateful for this blessing only.

For example: a man whom Allah gave wealth. Specific gratitude for this wealth is that he speaks of this wealth as a bounty and blessing from Allah, and that he acknowledges in his heart that it is a bounty from Allah, and does not say: ﴿I was given it only because of knowledge I have﴾ [al-Qasas 78].

The third: that he fulfills the duty of this wealth by paying its zakah and what is incumbent upon him in expenses because of it. But a person may, for example, in another respect disobey Allah, neglect the prayer, or neglect fasting. To him we say: Can we describe him as grateful in an absolute sense?

**Commentary of Ibn 'Uthaymin (Tafsir al-Quran al-Karim) on surah 27, verses 38–40 (part 3 of 4):**

* Student: No.
* Shaykh: But he is standing in gratitude for that specific blessing. Have you understood?

So gratitude is of two kinds: general gratitude and specific gratitude. Specific gratitude is that a person thanks God for a particular blessing in the way that blessing requires. General gratitude is that a person is always obedient to the Bestower in all circumstances. If you reflect on this, you will find it present in most praiseworthy and blameworthy attributes too. A person may be described as repentant in a specific, restricted sense, for a particular sin, and he may also be described as one of the repentant in an unrestricted sense.

Solomon, peace be upon him, said: ﴿Shall I be grateful or shall I be ungrateful?﴾ In what sense should we understand this?

* Student: He pointed to it here. Apparently it is specific.
* Shaykh: If we say it is general, it means we have accused Solomon of not being thankful to God for anything other than this. If we say it is specific, meaning for this particular blessing, then that is better. This is why he said: ﴿This is of the bounty of my Lord, to test me, whether I will be grateful or ungrateful﴾, that is, to test me with it: will I thank God for it or will I be ungrateful?

So the apparent meaning here is specific, meaning for this blessing. As for the other blessings, we believe that Solomon gave thanks for them, because, as we have already read in the story of the ant, he, peace be upon him, said something similar: ﴿So he smiled, laughing at her words, and said, "My Lord, enable me to be grateful for Your favor which You have bestowed upon me and upon my parents and to do righteousness of which You approve"﴾ [An-Naml 19].

* Student: We could say that this may indeed be (...) in its effect on what God sent down to him of other blessings...
* Shaykh: No, that is not what we say, because what we believe, and it is closer to Solomon's state, is that he gave thanks to God for the other blessings.
* Student: Could it be about an increase?
* Shaykh: Do not try. Never. It is about this blessing. ﴿Shall I be grateful﴾: he did not say "Shall I complete the gratitude"; if he had said "complete the gratitude," it would be different. "Shall I be grateful" is an unrestricted verb.

The conclusion is that what appears to us is that it refers to this blessing: whether I should be grateful for it or ungrateful for it. Every blessing requires specific gratitude, and general gratitude is well known: a person says "I thank God," and believes in his heart that he is thankful to God for all blessings. But when it comes to a specific blessing, it also requires specific gratitude. The gratitude for wealth is not like the gratitude for a child.

For example: a person has strength and ability in archery and in jihad. What is the gratitude for this blessing? That he uses it in jihad and fights. A person has the ability to explain the truth through the knowledge and understanding God has given him. His gratitude for this blessing is to explain this matter. So you find that gratitude differs when we consider what? Each blessing according to its nature. We say: the gratitude for this is not the gratitude for that. But general gratitude is that we believe all virtues and favors come from God, the Exalted, and all people share in this.

﴿To test me, whether I will be grateful or ungrateful.﴾ If someone says: how can Solomon say "or ungrateful"? Ungratefulness (kufr) is a harsh word that repels the soul. Why did he not say "Shall I be grateful or not be grateful"? Although the meaning is the same, this is gentler.

We say: it is to restrain his own soul from disobedience and from failing to give thanks, so that he makes clear to himself that if he does not give thanks, that means ungratefulness. Every situation has its own speech. You may address a person whom you see has not thanked God for His blessing upon him. You fear that if you say, "You are ungrateful for the blessing," he will recoil from you and become even more averse, even toward the blessing. If you say, "You have not thanked Him fully, or with due thanks, or something similar," you find that this is gentler, and expressions have an effect.

It is said that a king saw a dream that frightened him. He said: "Bring me the interpreters," or "the passers-by" (al-'Abirin). They brought him the 'Abirin, and he said to them: "I saw that my teeth had fallen out. What do you think?" The eldest of them stood up and said: "I see that your family will die." The king was alarmed and said: "Beat him severely." They beat him severely, and he said: "Take him away. These people have no good in them."

Then he summoned other interpreters and said to them: "I saw that my teeth had fallen out." The eldest of them stood up and said: "The king is the longest-lived of his family." The king was pleased and said: "Come on, pamper these ones!" Although the meaning is the same, because if they had died, the one who outlived them would be the longest-lived.

The conclusion is that the manner of expression has an effect on accepting the truth and on turning away from it. We have already read the story of Abraham, peace be upon him, when he said to his father: ﴿Indeed, there has come to me of knowledge that which has not come to you﴾ [Maryam 43]. He did not say: "You are ignorant, you do not understand, you do not know." He said: ﴿There has come to me of knowledge that which has not come to you, so follow me; I will guide you to a straight path﴾ [Maryam 43]. This is the bounty of God, which He gives to whom He wills. Some people God grants the ability to express themselves so well that words are in their hands like dough. Speech bends for them in whatever they want. You find that even if they want to utter a word they do not intend, they immediately find a replacement. Some people cannot do this. God, the Exalted, grants His bounty to whom He wills.

So: ﴿Whoever is ungrateful﴾. We say: he expressed it in this way in order to restrain his own soul from disobedience and from not performing gratitude.

(﴿Then indeed, my Lord is Free of need﴾ from his gratitude, ﴿Generous﴾ in bestowing on the one who is ungrateful.)

That is: whoever is ungrateful, indeed my Lord is free of need of his gratitude, or free of need absolutely. Among the things He is free of need of is this person's gratitude for God's blessing. God, the Exalted, did not bestow blessings upon His servants because He needs them to thank Him, but out of His bounty toward them and to manifest the effects of His attributes. The manifestation of the effects of His great attributes occurs only through His actions, among which are blessings, or also punishments, so that the attributes of vengeance and anger may be manifest.

His saying ﴿Generous﴾ means that He, the Exalted, may leave a blessing with one who is ungrateful for it, out of generosity at times, and at other times as istidraj (gradual enticement). God, Blessed and Exalted, is Wise and grants His bounty to whom He wills. Does God leave a blessing with an unbeliever as istidraj? Yes, based on His saying: ﴿And let not those who disbelieve think that Our giving them respite is good for them. Indeed, We give them respite only that they may increase in sin﴾ [Al 'Imran 178], and ﴿And those who deny Our signs, We will progressively draw them in from where they do not know. And I will give them respite. Indeed, My plan is firm﴾ [Al-A'raf 182–183].

God may also leave blessings with disbelief as a form of training, such that a person is granted by God the ability to reflect and becomes ashamed before God, the Mighty and Majestic, that he should hasten to commit sins while God, Blessed and Exalted, pours blessings upon him, and so he refrains.

This is the apparent meaning of His saying ﴿Generous﴾, because generosity in contrast to ungratefulness occurs only when that generosity is for whose benefit? For the benefit of the one who is ungrateful. Otherwise, the effects would be those of wisdom, not generosity. If He had said "Wise," it would include those whom God leads gradually until He destroys them. But "Generous" means generosity toward the one who is ungrateful for a blessing is complete only when leaving the blessing with him is beneficial to him, so that he may return.

Then Solomon said: ﴿Disguise for her her throne﴾ [An-Naml 41]: change it (i.e., alter it so that she will not recognize it when she sees it).

Disguising occurs by changing even the least attribute of it. Is that not so? Even the least attribute by which disguising is achieved. For example, if its legs are long, you can shorten the legs, and that is disguising. If the color of one of its panels is red, you may make it green. Whether this disguising is by parts, or by color, or by coverings, or by removing coverings, it apparently falls within disguising.

﴿Disguise for her her throne; we will see whether she will be guided or will be among those who are not guided﴾. ﴿We will see﴾: what brought this in? (...)?

* Student: ﴿He said, "Disguise for her her throne"﴾ [An-Naml 41]. "Disguise" is a command.
* Shaykh: "Disguise" is an imperative verb, and "We will see" is apocopated as the answer to the command. Yes, that is correct.

"Disguise, we will see." Notice the grandeur in the word "disguise": he did not address a specific person, which shows that all his soldiers are obedient, right? For if he feared that some soldier might rebel, he would have addressed a specific person in order to embarrass him so that he could not say "no." Similarly, the grandeur of a ruler is shown in this way. When a ruler or prince says, for example, "Coffee, boy!" all those present rush, "Coffee, coffee!" and it comes quickly.

﴿Disguise for her her throne﴾: we say this too is an address of grandeur. That is why he said: ﴿We will see whether she is guided﴾. Either he refers to himself, which is an expression of exalting himself, or he speaks with his soldiers and courtiers, all of them looking on: ﴿whether she will be guided or will be among those who are not guided﴾ [An-Naml 41].

All of this is also among the methods of testing by which Solomon tested this woman, as he also tested her in what follows concerning the palace (sarh). As for the author's statement and that of others that her leg was a donkey's leg, this is among the false Isra'iliyyat (narrations from Israelite sources), so disregard it as one disregards others.

* Student: He feared she had leprosy, so he wanted to marry her.
* Shaykh: None of this is correct, and we will come to it, God willing.
* Student: Did he marry her, Shaykh?
* Shaykh: In any case, she deserved to be married, because she embraced Islam and was intelligent.
* Student: Is there no evidence for a person acting with the property of another, so that he acts with reason?
* Shaykh: If you mean from the previous verses, we accept this benefit from you. If you mean from the following verses, the lesson of today, we do not accept it.
* Student: (...).
* Shaykh: (...).
* Student: In His saying: (...). It does not indicate that the station of prophethood is far greater than kingship (...) what ordinary people give (...) knowledge.
* Shaykh: No. Even an ordinary person says such a thing, because (...) this, it became specific to a station like Solomon's, and that is not so. Even a person (...) himself says: God gave me this only to test me: will I be grateful or ungrateful?
* Student: And what is ungratefulness for a blessing in reality? It is not absolute ungratefulness, but ungratefulness for a blessing?
* Shaykh: We said a little earlier: gratitude, repentance, disbelief, and faith, all of these have parts and are completed. Absolute and specific.
* Student: I do not mean this, that is...
* Shaykh: No. Here what is meant is ungratefulness for blessings.
* Student: Ungratefulness for one blessing, meaning that it is not removed from one [thing].
* Shaykh: They are two parts, but it is not suitable...
* Student: (...) knowledge.
* Shaykh: No, that is unnecessary. Even an ordinary person says such a thing, because if you say this, it becomes specific to a station like Solomon's, and that is not so. Even a person (...) himself says: God only gave me this to test me: will I be grateful or ungrateful?
* Student: Ungratefulness for God's blessing, not absolute ungratefulness, but...?
* Shaykh: We said it a little earlier: gratitude, repentance, disbelief, and faith, all of these have parts and are completed. Absolute and specific.
* Student: I do not mean that. Is it...?
* Shaykh: No, here what is meant is ungratefulness for blessings.
* Student: Ungratefulness for blessings is one. There is no division.
* Shaykh: It is known; there are two divisions (...).
* Student: Shaykh, the bounty of God, may He be exalted, upon His servants is only for the sake of their (...). Now, what about some rhymed saying: "He is the Creator even if the created thing did not exist"?
* Shaykh: God was Creator; meaning this attribute was His before the created thing existed.
* Student: "Even if the created thing did not exist."
* Shaykh: They mean before He created, just as He, glorified be He, is described as speaking while He speaks by His will. He is described as creating while He creates by His will (...).

﴿This is to test me, whether I will be grateful or ungrateful. And whoever is grateful, his gratitude is only for himself; and whoever is ungrateful, indeed my Lord is free of need and Generous﴾ [An-Naml 40].

* Firstly, among the benefits of this verse: mentioning God's blessing by attributing it to Him, as in His saying: ﴿This is of the bounty of my Lord﴾. This is what is obligatory by the Law and required by reason, for blessings are attributed to the one who bestows and grants them. In this is evidence for affirming causation (ta'lil) in God's cosmic decrees, just as it is established for His legal rulings. From where is this derived?
* Student: ﴿To test me﴾.
