It is also said: "Time is like a sword; if you do not cut it, it will cut you." This is correct. In the authentic hadith, the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "Each of you is a earner (ḥārith), and each of you is an aspirant (hammām)." [[The author of Tamyiz al-Tayyib min al-Khabith, p. 117, said: it is not a hadith, and close to it is: "The truest of names are Ḥārith and Hammām."]] So a person must have aspiration and must act, but either toward good or toward something else.
﴿And what she used to worship besides Allah had averted her﴾.
* It also indicates that the environment has influence, based on His saying ﴿indeed, she was from a disbelieving people﴾. These people influenced her, so she became a disbeliever who worshipped other than Allah.
* It also contains a warning against associating with evil people, based on His saying ﴿indeed, she was from a disbelieving people﴾. Even if they are your relatives, you should not befriend them. If they have a right over you by kinship, give them their due right, but do not be intimate or companionable with them. The Prophet (ﷺ) said, as is transmitted: "A person is upon the religion of his close friend," and it is a good (ḥasan) hadith: "Let each of you look at whom he befriends." [[Narrated by Abu Dawud (4833), al-Tirmidhi (2378), and Ahmad (8028), and the wording is his, from the hadith of Abu Hurayrah.]] "A person is upon the religion of his close friend; so let each of you look at whom he befriends." This is something that occurs, and history and the previous hadith attest to it.
* Student: Is the environment an excuse for a person?
* Shaykh: It is not an excuse. The obligation upon a person is to leave this environment. This is why emigration (hijrah) was made obligatory upon whoever was able to emigrate. But when the Messenger says: "Then his parents make him a Jew, or a Christian, or a Magian," he is informing, and information does not imply permissibility. The Prophet (peace be upon him) said: "You will surely follow the ways of those before you." [[Agreed upon; al-Bukhari (7320) and Muslim (2669) from Abu Sa'id.]] This is a report. Does its meaning mean that it is permissible for us to do it? He also informed: "By Allah, Allah will surely complete this matter until a woman traveler (ẓa'īnah) goes from Sana'a to Hadramawt." [[Narrated by al-Bukhari (3595) from 'Adi ibn Hatim, similarly.]] Does that mean it is permissible for a woman to travel without a mahram? No. So what the Prophet (peace be upon him) informed of, that which occurs, does not imply permissibility.

﴿It was said to her, "Enter the palace." And when she saw it, she thought it was a body of water and uncovered her shins﴾, to the end.
* It indicates the greatness of Solomon's kingdom and Allah's subjugation of things to him. At that time, as far as we know, there were no furnaces that melt glass in which a person does as he wishes. But there is no doubt that glass existed. It may have been extracted from the sea by the devils, or there may have been smelting works and furnaces suited to their condition. This is why Allah said of the devils that they ﴿make for him whatever he wills of sanctuaries, statues, bowls like water-troughs, and fixed cooking pots﴾ [Saba 13]. ﴿Jifan﴾ is the plural of jafnah, which is a large bowl.
﴿Like al-jawab﴾. What is al-jawab?
* Student: The jabiyah.
* Shaykh: It is the plural of jabiyah, which is a cistern (birkah), meaning a large one.
﴿And fixed cooking pots﴾ means: they are not moved because of their size and greatness.
So the summary is that this indicates the greatness of Solomon's kingdom, since jinn and humans were subjugated to him to make for him whatever he willed.
* It also indicates the permissibility of testing a person, as already mentioned.
This story contains several tests, based on His saying ﴿Enter the palace﴾, to see whether she would be fearful and not enter, or would take a risk and enter without caution, or what she would do. The woman, because of her intelligence, entered but with caution and wariness. She uncovered her shins, meaning she lifted her garment until the shins became visible.
* It also indicates that from ancient times, a woman's adornment is concealment. His saying ﴿and she uncovered her shins﴾ indicates that the default is that she was covered, and that is so, unlike the man. The Prophet (ﷺ) said: "The lower garment of the believer is above half his shin," or he said: "to half his shin." [[Narrated by al-Nasa'i in al-Kubra (9626) from Abu Hurayrah, similarly.]] I have forgotten the wording. Now the matter has become reversed among many Muslims, unfortunately. Men's garments have become trailing, and women's garments have become short. This goes against the natural disposition (fitrah) upon which Allah created people.
* It also indicates that sight can deceive, and that what is perceived by the senses is not exactly the reality one hundred percent. Based on His saying ﴿she thought it﴾ [i.e., "thought it a body of water"], since in reality it is a palace paved with smooth glass, and you look at it with the eye, yet you think it is a body of water. This shows that what is perceived by the senses can be mistaken. Is that not so? A person may see a moving thing as still, a still thing as moving, white as black, and a man as a woman. Indeed, something may appear in his sight that has no reality. The same applies to hearing. From this we know that testimonies, reports of news, and other things can all contain error and are not infallible one hundred percent. However, there is no doubt that whenever reports converge and multiply, it indicates the matter is confirmed. But the possibility of error cannot be ruled out, however strong the observer or hearer is and however trustworthy, because error is a risk in what one sees or what one hears. Even in touch: you may touch a thing and think it soft or smooth, and vice versa. A farmer touches a rough thing and thinks it smooth, and a delicate person touches something very simply rough and finds it like thorns.
So the summary is that even in sensory matters error can occur. So what about intellectual matters? They are more so and greater. From this we know human weakness and that he is in dire need of knowledge of the Shari'ah and revelation, however far he reaches. He is still in need of this.
* Student: (...) Are the senses among the certainties?
* Shaykh: Yes.
* Student: (...) Can it become an error?
* Shaykh: No, it is not that. That is doubt. It is among the certainties, but when considered through thought and reason it is sound in such matters. It is only illusion (wahm) that can enter into them.
* It also indicates, in His saying ﴿Indeed, it is a palace paved with glass﴾, that speech should be emphasized in its proper place. He did not say "this is a palace." He said "indeed it is a palace," and "indeed" (inna) is for emphasis. The emphasis here is appropriate, because although she was not denying it, her state was like that of one who denies, since she thought it was a body of water and uncovered her shins.
* It also indicates, in His saying ﴿She said, "My Lord, I have wronged myself"﴾, that Allah, Blessed and Exalted, may grant a person what necessitates his submission, and may even facilitate for him the causes that necessitate his Islam with great ease. According to the story, we did not find that this woman was invited, pressed, or shown her error, except in His saying at the beginning of the story: ﴿Do not be arrogant toward me, and come to me in submission﴾. But when she witnessed what she witnessed of Solomon's greatness and power, she knew that she had to submit. So likewise, when Allah facilitates for a servant what guides him, the matter becomes easy for him. And when it is not facilitated for him, every obstacle prevents him from being guided, even if it is not a strong obstacle.
* It also indicates that the woman believed in Solomon. She did not submit absolutely, because she said ﴿And I have submitted with Solomon﴾, and this indicates she believed in him, since "with" (ma'a) denotes accompaniment. So she was among his believing companions.
* Student: (...)?
* Shaykh: This last one? (...) She did not believe absolutely. That is, she did not say "I have submitted to Allah only," but she explicitly declared that she was a follower of Solomon.
* Student: (...)?
* Shaykh: I say this because of her saying ﴿with Solomon﴾. That is, for example, she did not believe in another prophet or another law. She believed in Solomon's law, so she was among his people, even though she was in Sheba in Yemen and Solomon was in al-Sham.

And in this there is an indication in His saying ﴿I have wronged myself﴾. It indicates that sins are a wrong to the self, and the reason for this has already been mentioned. A person is entrusted with his self in terms of conduct and course, entrusted with his self in terms of his disposal of his wealth, and entrusted with his self in terms of his disposal of his body. This is why he was forbidden to squander wealth, and forbidden to kill the self: ﴿And do not kill yourselves﴾ [al-Nisa' 29], ﴿And do not throw yourselves into destruction with your own hands﴾ [al-Baqarah 195]. He was commanded to seek treatment: "Seek treatment, but do not seek treatment with what is unlawful" [[Narrated by Abu Dawud (3874) from Abu al-Darda'.]]. He was commanded to eat, drink, dress, and protect himself from heat and from cold. All of this is for the preservation of the self, which is a trust with him. So a person is not free to dispose of his body as he wishes, or of his conduct as he wishes, or of his wealth as he wishes. No, he is restricted.
* Student: (...) is it the commanding self (al-ammārah)?
* Shaykh: Yes.
* Student: And here the agent is attributed.
* Shaykh: Yes, indeed. This is because a human has two selves. It has been said there are three selves: the commanding (ammārah), the tranquil (muṭma'innah), and the self-reproaching (lawwāmah). The correct view is that the self-reproaching is an attribute of the two. But there is the commanding self, which orders evil and forbids good, and there is the tranquil self, which orders good. When I wronged my self, the tranquil self says it.
* In this verse there is also an affirmation of the general lordship of Allah, based on His saying ﴿Lord of the worlds﴾. No one has the general, all-encompassing lordship except Allah, the Mighty and Majestic. A person may be a lord of his household, a lord of his animal, or a lord of his slave, as in the authentic hadith: "That a slave-girl gives birth to her master, and that you see the barefoot, naked ones..." [[Agreed upon; al-Bukhari (50) and Muslim (9) from Abu Hurayrah.]]
It has already been explained to us in the tafsir that what the author mentioned of these Israelite narratives is not obligatory to believe. Rather, whatever of them contradicts the Qur'an or is unbefitting the station of a prophet must be rejected. Whatever of them neither contradicts nor conflicts with what is befitting a prophet is neither affirmed nor denied.
* Student: And it is not written down?
* Shaykh: Yes? And it is not written down. It should not be written in the tafsir, because if it is included in the tafsir, its meaning is that it has been affirmed, since it has been made an interpretation of Allah's speech.

﴿And We had certainly sent to Thamud their brother Ṣāliḥ﴾ [al-Naml 45].
* Student: Regarding Balqis, how did she submit so quickly when she saw his wealth?

Shaykh: She saw the greatness of Sulayman and his soldiers, and she recalled his letter in which he said: ﴿Do not exalt yourselves against me, and come to me in submission﴾. She realized that this man would inevitably either bring you to submission or pass judgment against you.

Student: (...)?

Shaykh: But she did submit.

Student: (...)?

Shaykh: We see this as well-known, but we do not adopt it. The apparent meaning is that it is among the matters that are neither to be affirmed as true nor denied as false. However, there is no harm in it, since it is widely circulated, so there is no objection to it.

**Commentary of Ibn ʿUthaymin (Tafsir al-Quran al-Karim) on Surah 27, verses 41–44 (part 1 of 3):**

﴿When she came, it was said﴾ to her, ﴿"Is your throne like this?"﴾ That is, "Is your throne like this?" ﴿She said, "It is as if it were it."﴾ That is, she recognised it.

﴿When she came﴾ means: to Sulayman. When she looked at the throne, it was said to her, ﴿"Is your throne like this?"﴾ The speaker is either Sulayman or one of his soldiers, and this is not specified, because the intended meaning is the content of the statement, not who said it.

As for his words, ﴿"Is your throne like this?"﴾, the interrogative here is genuine, and it is meant as a request for information. The *hāʾ* (هاء) is for alerting (*al-tanbīh*), and the *kāf* (كاف) is a prepositional particle that intervenes between the *hāʾ* of alerting and the demonstrative noun. The *hāʾ* of alerting normally attaches to the demonstrative noun, but the *kāf* comes between them because a preposition is directly attached to what it governs. This is specific to the *kāf*. If you use any other preposition, you cannot separate it from the demonstrative. For example, if you say, "Ālihādhā ḥaḍarta?" (ألهذا حضرت؟, "Did you come for this?"), you cannot say "Ahlādhā ḥaḍarta" (أهلذا حضرت). It is not correct. In other words, the *hāʾ* of alerting can be separated from the demonstrative only by the *kāf*, and by no other preposition.

So we say: in ﴿أَهَكَذَا عَرْشُكِ﴾, the prepositional phrase (*al-jār wa-l-majrūr*) is a fronted predicate (*khabar muqaddam*), and ﴿عَرْشُكِ﴾ is a postponed subject (*mubtadaʾ muʾakhkhar*). Is fronting the predicate here optional or obligatory? It is obligatory, because of the interrogative, which requires that it come first.

Note that they did not say, "Is this your throne?" Rather they said, "Is your throne like this?" That is, "Is your throne like this?" She answered in the same form as the question she was asked, saying: ﴿"It is as if it were it."﴾ *Kaʾanna* (كأن) is for comparison. She did not say "It is it," nor did she negate it. The reason is that it resembled her throne in its essence but differed from it in its attributes, because it had been altered. This was part of her intelligence: since it occurred to her that it was her throne, but its attributes had changed, she said, "It is as if it were it." Her answer matched the question.

The author took an unusual approach here. He said: (*"That is, she recognised it, and she confused them just as they had confused her, since it was not said, 'Is this your throne?' If it had been, she would have said, 'Yes.'"*)

We do not know whether she would have said "Yes" or "It is as if it were it." Her answer matches the question and also matches the situation. It matches the question because she was asked, "Is it like this?", meaning, "Is it like this?", so the answer was "It is as if it were it." It matches the situation because the woman saw that the throne had been altered, so she did not affirm it or deny it outright. If one looks at the basic form of the throne, it is it. If one looks at its attributes, it is not it. Therefore her answer was extremely good, and it contains no comparison, contrary to what the author said. There is no comparison here.

If they had said, "Is this your throne?", we would not know whether she would say "Yes" or "It is as if it were it." The author's assertion that she would say "Yes" is not correct, because this woman was very intelligent. When a person is in such a situation, does he affirm that what he sees is what he knew before? He does not affirm it outright. Rather, the requirement of caution and prudence is to say, what would he say?

*Student:* "*Kaʾannahu*" ("it is as if it were").

*Shaykh:* ﴿"It is as if it were it."﴾ This is what caution requires, especially with the indications that make it unlikely to be the same, as in this story. It was a throne enclosed and guarded from a distant place, so it is unlikely that it would appear before her in this condition.

The important point, brothers, is that from her answer we take her intelligence in two respects:

First: she answered with a reply that matched the question. That is one.

Second: she answered with a reply that matched the situation, since affirming it outright would be hasty, and denying it would be slow, and it was possible that it was it.

﴿She said, "It is as if it were it."﴾ *Kaʾanna* is for comparison.

*Student:* "There is no comparison in her words?"

*Shaykh:* No. He says, "She confused them," meaning she concealed it from them. He did not say, "She compared it."

Then he said: (*Sulayman said, when he saw her knowledge and understanding:* ﴿"And we were given knowledge before her, and we were Muslims."﴾)

The connection of this sentence to what came before is that Sulayman wanted to speak about the blessings of knowledge that God had bestowed on them. Knowledge includes religious knowledge, and it includes knowledge of the rules and foundations of kingship, and similar things. That is, when the chiefs of his people saw her intelligence, her knowledge, her caution, and her firmness, they regarded it as a great matter. So Sulayman ﷺ wanted to remind them of something greater than that: the knowledge and Islam that God Most High had given them earlier. ﴿"And we were given knowledge before her, and we were Muslims."﴾

Some exegetes hold that his words ﴿"we were given knowledge before her"﴾ are the woman's speech. That is, "It is as if it were it, and we were given knowledge." They take the matter as connected, so that ﴿"before her"﴾ means "before this matter," meaning that we had knowledge before this affair, so do not be surprised at our knowledge of this, for we had knowledge earlier. But this possibility, though mentioned, is weak. The correct view is that this is Sulayman's speech, peace be upon him, in which he speaks of God Most High's blessing upon him and his people before the knowledge of this woman.

*Student:* "There must be (...) the verb of saying (...)."

*Shaykh:* Where?

*Student:* From ﴿"Is your throne like this?"﴾?

*Shaykh:* (...) No, it is not determined. From his words ﴿"And we were given"﴾, because one of his soldiers may have said it. Then after the viewing takes place, he says: ﴿"And we were given knowledge before her."﴾

*Student:* (...)?

*Shaykh:* It is permissible (...) upon her (...).

He said: ﴿And what she used to worship besides God hindered her﴾ from worshipping God.

﴿And what she used to worship besides God hindered her﴾. So the *mā* (ما) in ﴿مَا كَانَتْ تَعْبُدُ مِنْ دُونِ اللَّهِ﴾ is grammatically the subject: that which she used to worship besides God hindered her. It is possible that *mā* is a verbal-noun particle (*maṣdariyyah*), meaning "her worshipping besides God hindered her." But although that is permissible in the language, it has no place here, so this *mā* is a relative pronoun (*ism mawṣūl*).

His words ﴿"what she used to worship"﴾: what was it that she used to worship besides God?

*Student:* The sun.

*Shaykh:* The sun. The returning pronoun for the relative *mā* is omitted. The estimate is: what she used to worship besides God.

*Ṣadda* (صد) means "turned away." The connection of this to what came before is this: it is said that if this woman had such intelligence and such knowledge, then why did she not worship God, when it was clear that worship belongs to God alone?

He explains that what turned her away from worshipping God was that from the beginning of her life she was occupied with worshipping other than God, because she was from a disbelieving people. She grew up in a disbelieving environment and was occupied with worshipping the created instead of the Creator. So although this woman was intelligent, understanding, cautious, and guarded, she turned away from worshipping God despite its clarity and manifestness, because of her preoccupation with falsehood. The soul must be occupied either with truth or with falsehood, and it must be earning: either earning what is unlawful or what is lawful. If it takes what it has no right to, it is earning unlawfully; if it takes what it has a right to, it is earning lawfully.

So we say: the connection of her words to ﴿"And what she used to worship besides God hindered her"﴾ is that it is like an answer to an implied question. What is the implied question? Why did she not worship God? So it is said: what turned her away from worshipping God was what she used to worship besides God, and she was from a disbelieving people. She grew up from the beginning in a disbelieving environment. The Prophet ﷺ has informed us that: *"Every child is born upon the fitrah (natural disposition), and then his parents make him a Jew, or a Christian, or a Magian."*[[Agreed upon. Al-Bukhari (1385) and Muslim (2658/22), from Abu Hurayrah.]]

﴿And what she used to worship besides God hindered her﴾. It is also said that the subject of *ṣaddahā* (صدها) refers to Sulayman, meaning that Sulayman prevented her from what she used to worship besides God, that is, prevented her from it because of the great kingdom she saw that Sulayman, peace be upon him, possessed. But the first reading is more fitting to the context, namely that *mā kānat taʿbud* is the subject. Still, there is no harm in mentioning the second possibility, since upon reflection it may turn out to be correct.

God Most High said: ﴿"Indeed, she was from a disbelieving people."﴾ That is, her environment from the time she grew up was one whose people disbelieved in God, Glorified and Exalted, worshipping the sun. Therefore she was occupied with worshipping other than God instead of worshipping God.

What benefits are in this sentence will come, God willing.

(﴿It was said to her﴾ also, ﴿"Enter the palace (*ṣarḥ*)."﴾) The speaker, as we have said, is unspecified: either Sulayman or someone else.

The author says about this *ṣarḥ*: (*It is a surface of clear white glass, beneath which is flowing sweet water, in which there are fish, which Sulayman had made, when it was said to him that her shins and feet were like the feet of a donkey.*)

As for his saying that it is (*a surface of white glass*), this is correct: a surface of white glass. The basic meaning of *ṣarḥ* is a tall building, as Pharaoh said to Haman: ﴿"Build me a tower, that I may reach the means."﴾ [Ghafir 36]. But the word is also applied to a surface, even if it is not high. This is a description of a glass surface with water beneath it.

The author says: (*that it is flowing*). He derived the flowing from God's words ﴿"she thought it was a body of water"﴾, because *lujjah* (لُجَّة) refers to the moving waves of the sea. Every moving thing is called *lujjah*, and from it comes *lajjah*, meaning the repetition and rising of voices. So the author apparently took the flowing from ﴿"she thought it was a body of water"﴾, since otherwise nothing in the verse indicates flowing.

As for his saying (*in which there are fish*), this is not a condition. It is not a requirement that there be fish in it, because a *lujjah* may or may not contain fish, and it may contain distant fish that are not seen.

Likewise his saying (*it is sweet water*): there is no evidence that it is sweet or salt. We do not know. The important point is that it is water, as the following will show.

*Student:* (...)?

*Shaykh:* No, because sweet water may contain fish, God willing.

*Student:* (...)?

*Shaykh:* Correct.

*Student:* (...)?

*Shaykh:* No, and it can remain in it, even this, but it does not live a full life. Unless, as the brothers said, there are fish specific to salt water, which is not sufficient.

In any case, all of this is unnecessary, even if someone said that there is no water beneath it.

If someone said that this glass gives the appearance of water, for example because of ribs or something in it, this would not be far-fetched, because it is not necessary that there be water beneath it. It is not determined. In any case, it is not determined. But if we concede, and say that ﴿"she thought it was a body of water"﴾ means that she saw clear glass and thought it was the sea, then that is what it means.

As for his saying (*when it was said to him that her shins and feet were like the feet of a donkey*): they say that when the jinn saw that Sulayman had been attracted to this woman, and he intended to marry her, they envied her. So they told him that her feet and shins were the feet and shins of an animal, and they put her down after a donkey, because it is uglier. This is not correct.

The purpose of this palace was to test the woman too. When it was said, ﴿"Enter the palace"﴾, if she really thought it was a body of water, if she was timid, would she enter or not? She would not enter at all. If she was heedless, she would enter with her clothes trailing. If she was resolute and brave, she would enter and lift her clothes from her shins. She entered and lifted her clothes from her shins.

Then, by her intelligence, she knew that she had not been honored, and that she was told, "Enter the palace," when she would be entering a deep sea that would drown her. So she knew that the most that could be in it was that it would reach her knees or something like that, and that it could not be a deep sea. Why? Because she was told it as an honor: ﴿"Enter the palace."﴾

So the point is that this is also a second test of her intelligence, resolve, and courage. As for the claim that her leg was a donkey's leg, this is clearly a lie, and the basic fact is that she was a woman like the daughters of Adam, with nothing of that in her.

*Student:* (...)?

*Shaykh:* We do not know about the law of those before us (...).

He said: (﴿When she saw it, she thought it was a body of water﴾ of water, ﴿and she uncovered her shins﴾). There is no doubt that this indicates her resolve, strength, and courage, because a stranger who encounters such a situation might say, "I do not know; perhaps they are deceiving me, and I may get wet in it and die." But she was strong and resolute as well. She went forward to enter, but with caution against harm, by lifting her clothes from her shins.

Regarding lifting from the shins, Ibrahim [the commentator] says that it may be derived from this that it is permissible for a woman to show her shins. We say: first, this is not derived from it, because here she did it out of necessity. A woman uncovering her shins out of necessity is not objectionable, even in our law. If a woman needs to uncover her shins in such a situation, there is no fault in it, because what is forbidden as a means of prohibition is permitted by necessity, as is established in the science of legal theory (*ʿilm al-uṣūl*). What is prohibited as a means is permitted by needs. For this reason it is permissible to look at the private parts for the slightest need. They even said it is permissible for someone to shave the pubic area of one who does not know how to shave his own, and this will inevitably expose the pubic area so that it can be shaved.

The summary is that if the law of Sulayman permitted such a thing, then there is no proof in it. If it did not permit it, it does not contradict our law either, because need calls for it here.

(﴿And she uncovered her shins﴾ to wade into it, and Sulayman was on his throne at the head of the palace, and he saw her shins and feet as beautiful.) Now the man was reassured, reassured, but she was not as the author said. Was the purpose of this that it be clear to Sulayman whether her leg was a donkey's leg or a human leg?

No. The purpose was to know by this her intelligence, insight, and courage. Whatever meaning this image indicates that relates to the woman, Sulayman, peace be upon him, intends it.

*Student:* (...)?

*Shaykh:* It will certainly come.

(﴿He said﴾ to her, ﴿"It is a palace paved smooth﴾ smoothed, ﴿of glass"﴾ that is, of crystal.)

This sentence also indicates that, along with testing her and examining her, it was intended to display the greatness of Sulayman's kingdom, just as bringing the throne served this purpose.

﴿He said, "It is a palace paved smooth of glass."﴾ Two things become clear from this. The first is the greatness of Sulayman's kingdom, since glass was made for him so that it would look like the deep sea. Second, it points out that this woman, although intelligent, wise, and resolute, could be deceived about a matter, or not? Because she thought this glass was a body of water, when it was not. So there is a kind of showing of her weakness too, since she supposed the matter to be other than what it was.

Among the benefits of these verses that will come, God willing...

*Student:* (...) "palace paved smooth of glass," that there is no water in it?

*Shaykh:* (...) It is not to be ruled out, because the presence of water beneath it, as I said, is not necessary.

﴿He said, "It is a palace paved smooth of glass."﴾ Then she knew her place, and she knew Sulayman's station.

As for his saying (*and he invited her to Islam*), there is nothing in the verse that indicates this. Rather, the apparent meaning is that what she witnessed compelled her to submit, because she saw matters: among them the bringing of her throne, and among them this great palace paved smooth of glass.

*Student:* (...)?

*Shaykh:* She is the one who said ﴿"It is as if it were it."﴾

Also among them: Sulayman, peace be upon him, informed her of his greatness and power, since this is a palace paved smooth of glass and not water. Then she acknowledged it, (*and she said:* ﴿"My Lord, I have wronged myself"﴾ by worshipping other than You).

Worshipping other than God is among the greatest wrongs. God Most High said about Luqman when he said to his son: ﴿"O my son, do not associate anything with God. Indeed, association is a great wrong."﴾ [Luqman 13]. This is because the greatest wrong is to assert yourself over one whose right is clearer and more manifest, and there is nothing clearer and more manifest than God's right over His servants. For this reason shirk is the greatest of wrongs.

When you dispute with a person while you know that the right is his and not yours, you are considered a wrongdoer. When the matter is unclear to you, so that you judge eighty percent that it is his and twenty percent that it is yours, this wrong is lighter than the first. When it is fifty percent yours and fifty percent his, it is lighter than the second. When you judge thirty percent his and seventy percent yours, it is lighter, and so on.

Commentary of Ibn 'Uthaymin (Tafsir al-Quran al-Karim) on surah 27, verses 41–44 (part 2 of 3):

So the point is that wrongdoing becomes uglier and more shameful in proportion to how clear the truth is and how plainly it has been made known. The most evident and clearest of rights is the worship of Allah, Glorified and Exalted. So the greatest wrong is associating partners with Allah, that you associate anyone with Allah. This is why she said: ﴿My Lord, I have wronged myself﴾.

So, the self is a trust (amanah) in your hands. You must strive for it in what is good for it. You must strive for your self in what is good for it. If you presume to take what is not yours, you have wronged yourself. If you neglect what is obligatory upon you, you have wronged yourself. And if you cannot dispose of your body as you wish, how can you dispose of your actions as you wish?

If a person said to someone: "I will give you my finger. Cut off my finger and put it (...) in place of the missing finger on your hand. Is that permissible?"
* Student: It is not permissible.
* Shaykh: It is not permissible. If he said: "I will gouge out my eye and put it in your eye that cannot see, is that permissible?"
* Student: No, it is not permissible.
* Shaykh: It is not permissible. If this is impossible in a body whose end is annihilation, how can it be in actions upon which the happiness of the servant depends? So it is not permissible for you to dispose of your actions in ways that harm yourself. If you do, you are a wrongdoer.

She said: ﴿And I have submitted with Solomon to Allah, Lord of the worlds﴾ (﴿I have submitted﴾ being ﴿with Solomon﴾ [i.e., in the state of being with Solomon]).

The author indicated, by estimating the word "being" (kā'inah), that the adverbial phrase in her saying ﴿with Solomon﴾ is in the position of a circumstantial clause (ḥāl). That is: "I have submitted, being with Solomon, to whom? To Allah, Lord of the worlds." Is she considered a Muslim here or not?
* Student: Yes (...).
* Shaykh: Yes. If a man says "I have submitted (aslamtu)," even if he does not say "I bear witness that there is no god but Allah and that Muhammad is the Messenger of Allah," he has become a Muslim. ﴿The Bedouins say, "We have believed." Say, "You have not believed, but say, 'We have submitted'"﴾ [al-Hujurat 14]. When a person expresses an act by the verb that indicates it, he is judged by it. This is why if someone says to a person, "I swear to you that you will do such-and-such," it becomes an oath, even if he did not say "by Allah." Or "I swear I will not do such-and-such," it becomes an oath even if he did not say "by Allah," because this is the act itself.
If he says "I have submitted," it becomes Islam, even if he does not say "I bear witness that there is no god but Allah and that Muhammad is the Messenger of Allah."
* Student: (...).
* Shaykh: It is commonly used. So we say: ﴿And I have submitted with Solomon to Allah, Lord of the worlds﴾ contains the fact that she submitted completely, since she affirmed the divinity of Allah in her saying ﴿to Allah﴾, and the general lordship in her saying ﴿Lord of the worlds﴾.

The author said: (And he wanted to marry her, but he disliked the hair on her shins, so the devils made depilatory cream (nūrah) for her, and she removed it.) By Allah, the truth is that this is a problematic matter.
* Student: (...)?
* Shaykh: (...) the devils made depilatory cream for him. Depilatory cream removes hair. It is said that the first to have depilatory cream made was the shin of Balqis, by Solomon's command, since the devils made it for him. All of this is false.

The speech of Allah must be kept free of such things. Our position toward such scholars is that we ask Allah to pardon them and forgive them, because putting such matters into the speech of Allah is one of the things by which a person disparages the speech of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic. Most of these reports came, as Ibn Kathir said in this passage, from two men: Ka'b al-Ahbar and Wahb ibn Munabbih. They introduced much of the Israelite narratives (isra'iliyyat) into the interpretation of Allah's speech and other matters that they transmitted. We ask Allah to pardon them.

He said: (Then she removed it, and he married her and loved her, and he kept her in her kingdom. He would visit her once a month and stay with her for three days.) The residence of a man who marries a previously married woman (...).

We have mentioned, in his saying ﴿Disguise her throne for her﴾, the benefit of testing: a person testing another to know his understanding and intelligence, like what happened here.

And the Exalted's saying: ﴿So when she came, it was said, "Is your throne like this?" She said, "It is as if it were it. And we were given knowledge before her, and we were Muslims."﴾
* What is derived from it: tawriya (speaking with a double meaning, a double-entendre), which is that a person shows something other than what he intends. Their saying ﴿Is it like this?﴾ is tawriya, because the reality is that the throne before them was hers. The question's form would have required them to say: "Is this your throne?" But they used the expression of tawriya to avoid the matter directly, because if they had said outright that it was her throne, she might have rushed to say no, since she considered it unlikely that it could have arrived in this period while guarded and locked up. So it was said to her: "Is your throne like this?"
And her saying ﴿It is as if it were it﴾ indicates that the answer should match the question, for she said ﴿as if﴾ by way of comparison, and did not say "it is it."
* It also indicates the intelligence of this woman and her caution against what might be a mistake. If she had said "No," it might have been it. If she had said "Yes," it might have been another. So she said ﴿It is as if it were it﴾, choosing this for the two reasons we mentioned at the time of the tafsir.
* It also indicates that a person should speak of the blessings of Allah, Blessed and Exalted, upon him, based on her saying ﴿And we were given knowledge before her, and we were Muslims﴾. The correct view is that this sentence is from whose speech? From the speech of Solomon. Although some propose the possibility that it is from her speech, the correct view is that it is from Solomon's speech.
* Student: (...)?
* Shaykh: No. Allah does not describe Himself as "Muslim." ﴿And we were given knowledge﴾; He did not say "We gave."

﴿And what she used to worship besides Allah had averted her; indeed, she was from a disbelieving people﴾.
* What is derived from this sentence: a person must occupy himself. Or not? The self must be occupied, either with truth or with falsehood. This woman occupied herself with falsehood instead of truth. It has been said among wise sayings: "If you do not occupy yourself with truth, it will occupy you with falsehood."
It is also said: "Time is like a sword; if you do not cut it, it will cut you." This is correct. In the authentic hadith, the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "Each of you is a earner (ḥārith), and each of you is an aspirant (hammām)." [[The author of Tamyiz al-Tayyib min al-Khabith, p. 117, said: it is not a hadith, and close to it is: "The truest of names are Ḥārith and Hammām."]] So a person must have aspiration and must act, but either toward good or toward something else.
﴿And what she used to worship besides Allah had averted her﴾.
* It also indicates that the environment has influence, based on His saying ﴿indeed, she was from a disbelieving people﴾. These people influenced her, so she became a disbeliever who worshipped other than Allah.
* It also contains a warning against associating with evil people, based on His saying ﴿indeed, she was from a disbelieving people﴾. Even if they are your relatives, you should not befriend them. If they have a right over you by kinship, give them their due right, but do not be intimate or companionable with them. The Prophet (ﷺ) said, as is transmitted: "A person is upon the religion of his close friend," and it is a good (ḥasan) hadith: "Let each of you look at whom he befriends." [[Narrated by Abu Dawud (4833), al-Tirmidhi (2378), and Ahmad (8028), and the wording is his, from the hadith of Abu Hurayrah.]] "A person is upon the religion of his close friend; so let each of you look at whom he befriends." This is something that occurs, and history and the previous hadith attest to it.
* Student: Is the environment an excuse for a person?
* Shaykh: It is not an excuse. The obligation upon a person is to leave this environment. This is why emigration (hijrah) was made obligatory upon whoever was able to emigrate. But when the Messenger says: "Then his parents make him a Jew, or a Christian, or a Magian," he is informing, and information does not imply permissibility. The Prophet (peace be upon him) said: "You will surely follow the ways of those before you." [[Agreed upon; al-Bukhari (7320) and Muslim (2669) from Abu Sa'id.]] This is a report. Does its meaning mean that it is permissible for us to do it? He also informed: "By Allah, Allah will surely complete this matter until a woman traveler (ẓa'īnah) goes from Sana'a to Hadramawt." [[Narrated by al-Bukhari (3595) from 'Adi ibn Hatim, similarly.]] Does that mean it is permissible for a woman to travel without a mahram? No. So what the Prophet (peace be upon him) informed of, that which occurs, does not imply permissibility.

﴿It was said to her, "Enter the palace." And when she saw it, she thought it was a body of water and uncovered her shins﴾, to the end.
* It indicates the greatness of Solomon's kingdom and Allah's subjugation of things to him. At that time, as far as we know, there were no furnaces that melt glass in which a person does as he wishes. But there is no doubt that glass existed. It may have been extracted from the sea by the devils, or there may have been smelting works and furnaces suited to their condition. This is why Allah said of the devils that they ﴿make for him whatever he wills of sanctuaries, statues, bowls like water-troughs, and fixed cooking pots﴾ [Saba 13]. ﴿Jifan﴾ is the plural of jafnah, which is a large bowl.
﴿Like al-jawab﴾. What is al-jawab?
* Student: The jabiyah.
* Shaykh: It is the plural of jabiyah, which is a cistern (birkah), meaning a large one.
﴿And fixed cooking pots﴾ means: they are not moved because of their size and greatness.
So the summary is that this indicates the greatness of Solomon's kingdom, since jinn and humans were subjugated to him to make for him whatever he willed.
* It also indicates the permissibility of testing a person, as already mentioned.
This story contains several tests, based on His saying ﴿Enter the palace﴾, to see whether she would be fearful and not enter, or would take a risk and enter without caution, or what she would do. The woman, because of her intelligence, entered but with caution and wariness. She uncovered her shins, meaning she lifted her garment until the shins became visible.
* It also indicates that from ancient times, a woman's adornment is concealment. His saying ﴿and she uncovered her shins﴾ indicates that the default is that she was covered, and that is so, unlike the man. The Prophet (ﷺ) said: "The lower garment of the believer is above half his shin," or he said: "to half his shin." [[Narrated by al-Nasa'i in al-Kubra (9626) from Abu Hurayrah, similarly.]] I have forgotten the wording. Now the matter has become reversed among many Muslims, unfortunately. Men's garments have become trailing, and women's garments have become short. This goes against the natural disposition (fitrah) upon which Allah created people.
* It also indicates that sight can deceive, and that what is perceived by the senses is not exactly the reality one hundred percent. Based on His saying ﴿she thought it﴾ [i.e., "thought it a body of water"], since in reality it is a palace paved with smooth glass, and you look at it with the eye, yet you think it is a body of water. This shows that what is perceived by the senses can be mistaken. Is that not so? A person may see a moving thing as still, a still thing as moving, white as black, and a man as a woman. Indeed, something may appear in his sight that has no reality. The same applies to hearing. From this we know that testimonies, reports of news, and other things can all contain error and are not infallible one hundred percent. However, there is no doubt that whenever reports converge and multiply, it indicates the matter is confirmed. But the possibility of error cannot be ruled out, however strong the observer or hearer is and however trustworthy, because error is a risk in what one sees or what one hears. Even in touch: you may touch a thing and think it soft or smooth, and vice versa. A farmer touches a rough thing and thinks it smooth, and a delicate person touches something very simply rough and finds it like thorns.
So the summary is that even in sensory matters error can occur. So what about intellectual matters? They are more so and greater. From this we know human weakness and that he is in dire need of knowledge of the Shari'ah and revelation, however far he reaches. He is still in need of this.
* Student: (...) Are the senses among the certainties?
* Shaykh: Yes.
* Student: (...) Can it become an error?
* Shaykh: No, it is not that. That is doubt. It is among the certainties, but when considered through thought and reason it is sound in such matters. It is only illusion (wahm) that can enter into them.
* It also indicates, in His saying ﴿Indeed, it is a palace paved with glass﴾, that speech should be emphasized in its proper place. He did not say "this is a palace." He said "indeed it is a palace," and "indeed" (inna) is for emphasis. The emphasis here is appropriate, because although she was not denying it, her state was like that of one who denies, since she thought it was a body of water and uncovered her shins.
* It also indicates, in His saying ﴿She said, "My Lord, I have wronged myself"﴾, that Allah, Blessed and Exalted, may grant a person what necessitates his submission, and may even facilitate for him the causes that necessitate his Islam with great ease. According to the story, we did not find that this woman was invited, pressed, or shown her error, except in His saying at the beginning of the story: ﴿Do not be arrogant toward me, and come to me in submission﴾. But when she witnessed what she witnessed of Solomon's greatness and power, she knew that she had to submit. So likewise, when Allah facilitates for a servant what guides him, the matter becomes easy for him. And when it is not facilitated for him, every obstacle prevents him from being guided, even if it is not a strong obstacle.
* It also indicates that the woman believed in Solomon. She did not submit absolutely, because she said ﴿And I have submitted with Solomon﴾, and this indicates she believed in him, since "with" (ma'a) denotes accompaniment. So she was among his believing companions.
* Student: (...)?
* Shaykh: This last one? (...) She did not believe absolutely. That is, she did not say "I have submitted to Allah only," but she explicitly declared that she was a follower of Solomon.
* Student: (...)?
* Shaykh: I say this because of her saying ﴿with Solomon﴾. That is, for example, she did not believe in another prophet or another law. She believed in Solomon's law, so she was among his people, even though she was in Sheba in Yemen and Solomon was in al-Sham.

And in this there is an indication in His saying ﴿I have wronged myself﴾. It indicates that sins are a wrong to the self, and the reason for this has already been mentioned. A person is entrusted with his self in terms of conduct and course, entrusted with his self in terms of his disposal of his wealth, and entrusted with his self in terms of his disposal of his body. This is why he was forbidden to squander wealth, and forbidden to kill the self: ﴿And do not kill yourselves﴾ [al-Nisa' 29], ﴿And do not throw yourselves into destruction with your own hands﴾ [al-Baqarah 195]. He was commanded to seek treatment: "Seek treatment, but do not seek treatment with what is unlawful" [[Narrated by Abu Dawud (3874) from Abu al-Darda'.]]. He was commanded to eat, drink, dress, and protect himself from heat and from cold. All of this is for the preservation of the self, which is a trust with him. So a person is not free to dispose of his body as he wishes, or of his conduct as he wishes, or of his wealth as he wishes. No, he is restricted.
* Student: (...) is it the commanding self (al-ammārah)?
* Shaykh: Yes.
* Student: And here the agent is attributed.
* Shaykh: Yes, indeed. This is because a human has two selves. It has been said there are three selves: the commanding (ammārah), the tranquil (muṭma'innah), and the self-reproaching (lawwāmah). The correct view is that the self-reproaching is an attribute of the two. But there is the commanding self, which orders evil and forbids good, and there is the tranquil self, which orders good. When I wronged my self, the tranquil self says it.
* In this verse there is also an affirmation of the general lordship of Allah, based on His saying ﴿Lord of the worlds﴾. No one has the general, all-encompassing lordship except Allah, the Mighty and Majestic. A person may be a lord of his household, a lord of his animal, or a lord of his slave, as in the authentic hadith: "That a slave-girl gives birth to her master, and that you see the barefoot, naked ones..." [[Agreed upon; al-Bukhari (50) and Muslim (9) from Abu Hurayrah.]]
It has already been explained to us in the tafsir that what the author mentioned of these Israelite narratives is not obligatory to believe. Rather, whatever of them contradicts the Qur'an or is unbefitting the station of a prophet must be rejected. Whatever of them neither contradicts nor conflicts with what is befitting a prophet is neither affirmed nor denied.
* Student: And it is not written down?
* Shaykh: Yes? And it is not written down. It should not be written in the tafsir, because if it is included in the tafsir, its meaning is that it has been affirmed, since it has been made an interpretation of Allah's speech.

﴿And We had certainly sent to Thamud their brother Ṣāliḥ﴾ [al-Naml 45].
* Student: Regarding Balqis, how did she submit so quickly when she saw his wealth?

Shaykh: She saw the greatness of Sulayman and his soldiers, and she recalled his letter in which he said: ﴿Do not exalt yourselves against me, and come to me in submission﴾. She realized that this man would inevitably either bring you to submission or pass judgment against you.

Student: (...)?

Shaykh: But she did submit.

Student: (...)?

Shaykh: We see this as well-known, but we do not adopt it. The apparent meaning is that it is among the matters that are neither to be affirmed as true nor denied as false. However, there is no harm in it, since it is widely circulated, so there is no objection to it.

**Commentary of Ibn ʿUthaymin (Tafsir al-Quran al-Karim) on Surah 27, verses 41–44 (part 1 of 3):**

﴿When she came, it was said﴾ to her, ﴿"Is your throne like this?"﴾ That is, "Is your throne like this?" ﴿She said, "It is as if it were it."﴾ That is, she recognised it.

﴿When she came﴾ means: to Sulayman. When she looked at the throne, it was said to her, ﴿"Is your throne like this?"﴾ The speaker is either Sulayman or one of his soldiers, and this is not specified, because the intended meaning is the content of the statement, not who said it.

As for his words, ﴿"Is your throne like this?"﴾, the interrogative here is genuine, and it is meant as a request for information. The *hāʾ* (هاء) is for alerting (*al-tanbīh*), and the *kāf* (كاف) is a prepositional particle that intervenes between the *hāʾ* of alerting and the demonstrative noun. The *hāʾ* of alerting normally attaches to the demonstrative noun, but the *kāf* comes between them because a preposition is directly attached to what it governs. This is specific to the *kāf*. If you use any other preposition, you cannot separate it from the demonstrative. For example, if you say, "Ālihādhā ḥaḍarta?" (ألهذا حضرت؟, "Did you come for this?"), you cannot say "Ahlādhā ḥaḍarta" (أهلذا حضرت). It is not correct. In other words, the *hāʾ* of alerting can be separated from the demonstrative only by the *kāf*, and by no other preposition.

So we say: in ﴿أَهَكَذَا عَرْشُكِ﴾, the prepositional phrase (*al-jār wa-l-majrūr*) is a fronted predicate (*khabar muqaddam*), and ﴿عَرْشُكِ﴾ is a postponed subject (*mubtadaʾ muʾakhkhar*). Is fronting the predicate here optional or obligatory? It is obligatory, because of the interrogative, which requires that it come first.

Note that they did not say, "Is this your throne?" Rather they said, "Is your throne like this?" That is, "Is your throne like this?" She answered in the same form as the question she was asked, saying: ﴿"It is as if it were it."﴾ *Kaʾanna* (كأن) is for comparison. She did not say "It is it," nor did she negate it. The reason is that it resembled her throne in its essence but differed from it in its attributes, because it had been altered. This was part of her intelligence: since it occurred to her that it was her throne, but its attributes had changed, she said, "It is as if it were it." Her answer matched the question.

The author took an unusual approach here. He said: (*"That is, she recognised it, and she confused them just as they had confused her, since it was not said, 'Is this your throne?' If it had been, she would have said, 'Yes.'"*)

We do not know whether she would have said "Yes" or "It is as if it were it." Her answer matches the question and also matches the situation. It matches the question because she was asked, "Is it like this?", meaning, "Is it like this?", so the answer was "It is as if it were it." It matches the situation because the woman saw that the throne had been altered, so she did not affirm it or deny it outright. If one looks at the basic form of the throne, it is it. If one looks at its attributes, it is not it. Therefore her answer was extremely good, and it contains no comparison, contrary to what the author said. There is no comparison here.

If they had said, "Is this your throne?", we would not know whether she would say "Yes" or "It is as if it were it." The author's assertion that she would say "Yes" is not correct, because this woman was very intelligent. When a person is in such a situation, does he affirm that what he sees is what he knew before? He does not affirm it outright. Rather, the requirement of caution and prudence is to say, what would he say?

*Student:* "*Kaʾannahu*" ("it is as if it were").

*Shaykh:* ﴿"It is as if it were it."﴾ This is what caution requires, especially with the indications that make it unlikely to be the same, as in this story. It was a throne enclosed and guarded from a distant place, so it is unlikely that it would appear before her in this condition.

The important point, brothers, is that from her answer we take her intelligence in two respects:

First: she answered with a reply that matched the question. That is one.

Second: she answered with a reply that matched the situation, since affirming it outright would be hasty, and denying it would be slow, and it was possible that it was it.

﴿She said, "It is as if it were it."﴾ *Kaʾanna* is for comparison.

*Student:* "There is no comparison in her words?"

*Shaykh:* No. He says, "She confused them," meaning she concealed it from them. He did not say, "She compared it."

Then he said: (*Sulayman said, when he saw her knowledge and understanding:* ﴿"And we were given knowledge before her, and we were Muslims."﴾)

The connection of this sentence to what came before is that Sulayman wanted to speak about the blessings of knowledge that God had bestowed on them. Knowledge includes religious knowledge, and it includes knowledge of the rules and foundations of kingship, and similar things. That is, when the chiefs of his people saw her intelligence, her knowledge, her caution, and her firmness, they regarded it as a great matter. So Sulayman ﷺ wanted to remind them of something greater than that: the knowledge and Islam that God Most High had given them earlier. ﴿"And we were given knowledge before her, and we were Muslims."﴾

Some exegetes hold that his words ﴿"we were given knowledge before her"﴾ are the woman's speech. That is, "It is as if it were it, and we were given knowledge." They take the matter as connected, so that ﴿"before her"﴾ means "before this matter," meaning that we had knowledge before this affair, so do not be surprised at our knowledge of this, for we had knowledge earlier. But this possibility, though mentioned, is weak. The correct view is that this is Sulayman's speech, peace be upon him, in which he speaks of God Most High's blessing upon him and his people before the knowledge of this woman.

*Student:* "There must be (...) the verb of saying (...)."

*Shaykh:* Where?

*Student:* From ﴿"Is your throne like this?"﴾?

*Shaykh:* (...) No, it is not determined. From his words ﴿"And we were given"﴾, because one of his soldiers may have said it. Then after the viewing takes place, he says: ﴿"And we were given knowledge before her."﴾

*Student:* (...)?

*Shaykh:* It is permissible (...) upon her (...).

He said: ﴿And what she used to worship besides God hindered her﴾ from worshipping God.

﴿And what she used to worship besides God hindered her﴾. So the *mā* (ما) in ﴿مَا كَانَتْ تَعْبُدُ مِنْ دُونِ اللَّهِ﴾ is grammatically the subject: that which she used to worship besides God hindered her. It is possible that *mā* is a verbal-noun particle (*maṣdariyyah*), meaning "her worshipping besides God hindered her." But although that is permissible in the language, it has no place here, so this *mā* is a relative pronoun (*ism mawṣūl*).

His words ﴿"what she used to worship"﴾: what was it that she used to worship besides God?

*Student:* The sun.

*Shaykh:* The sun. The returning pronoun for the relative *mā* is omitted. The estimate is: what she used to worship besides God.

*Ṣadda* (صد) means "turned away." The connection of this to what came before is this: it is said that if this woman had such intelligence and such knowledge, then why did she not worship God, when it was clear that worship belongs to God alone?

He explains that what turned her away from worshipping God was that from the beginning of her life she was occupied with worshipping other than God, because she was from a disbelieving people. She grew up in a disbelieving environment and was occupied with worshipping the created instead of the Creator. So although this woman was intelligent, understanding, cautious, and guarded, she turned away from worshipping God despite its clarity and manifestness, because of her preoccupation with falsehood. The soul must be occupied either with truth or with falsehood, and it must be earning: either earning what is unlawful or what is lawful. If it takes what it has no right to, it is earning unlawfully; if it takes what it has a right to, it is earning lawfully.

So we say: the connection of her words to ﴿"And what she used to worship besides God hindered her"﴾ is that it is like an answer to an implied question. What is the implied question? Why did she not worship God? So it is said: what turned her away from worshipping God was what she used to worship besides God, and she was from a disbelieving people. She grew up from the beginning in a disbelieving environment. The Prophet ﷺ has informed us that: *"Every child is born upon the fitrah (natural disposition), and then his parents make him a Jew, or a Christian, or a Magian."*[[Agreed upon. Al-Bukhari (1385) and Muslim (2658/22), from Abu Hurayrah.]]

﴿And what she used to worship besides God hindered her﴾. It is also said that the subject of *ṣaddahā* (صدها) refers to Sulayman, meaning that Sulayman prevented her from what she used to worship besides God, that is, prevented her from it because of the great kingdom she saw that Sulayman, peace be upon him, possessed. But the first reading is more fitting to the context, namely that *mā kānat taʿbud* is the subject. Still, there is no harm in mentioning the second possibility, since upon reflection it may turn out to be correct.

God Most High said: ﴿"Indeed, she was from a disbelieving people."﴾ That is, her environment from the time she grew up was one whose people disbelieved in God, Glorified and Exalted, worshipping the sun. Therefore she was occupied with worshipping other than God instead of worshipping God.

What benefits are in this sentence will come, God willing.

(﴿It was said to her﴾ also, ﴿"Enter the palace (*ṣarḥ*)."﴾) The speaker, as we have said, is unspecified: either Sulayman or someone else.

The author says about this *ṣarḥ*: (*It is a surface of clear white glass, beneath which is flowing sweet water, in which there are fish, which Sulayman had made, when it was said to him that her shins and feet were like the feet of a donkey.*)

As for his saying that it is (*a surface of white glass*), this is correct: a surface of white glass. The basic meaning of *ṣarḥ* is a tall building, as Pharaoh said to Haman: ﴿"Build me a tower, that I may reach the means."﴾ [Ghafir 36]. But the word is also applied to a surface, even if it is not high. This is a description of a glass surface with water beneath it.

The author says: (*that it is flowing*). He derived the flowing from God's words ﴿"she thought it was a body of water"﴾, because *lujjah* (لُجَّة) refers to the moving waves of the sea. Every moving thing is called *lujjah*, and from it comes *lajjah*, meaning the repetition and rising of voices. So the author apparently took the flowing from ﴿"she thought it was a body of water"﴾, since otherwise nothing in the verse indicates flowing.

As for his saying (*in which there are fish*), this is not a condition. It is not a requirement that there be fish in it, because a *lujjah* may or may not contain fish, and it may contain distant fish that are not seen.

Likewise his saying (*it is sweet water*): there is no evidence that it is sweet or salt. We do not know. The important point is that it is water, as the following will show.

*Student:* (...)?

*Shaykh:* No, because sweet water may contain fish, God willing.

*Student:* (...)?

*Shaykh:* Correct.

*Student:* (...)?

*Shaykh:* No, and it can remain in it, even this, but it does not live a full life. Unless, as the brothers said, there are fish specific to salt water, which is not sufficient.

In any case, all of this is unnecessary, even if someone said that there is no water beneath it.

If someone said that this glass gives the appearance of water, for example because of ribs or something in it, this would not be far-fetched, because it is not necessary that there be water beneath it. It is not determined. In any case, it is not determined. But if we concede, and say that ﴿"she thought it was a body of water"﴾ means that she saw clear glass and thought it was the sea, then that is what it means.

As for his saying (*when it was said to him that her shins and feet were like the feet of a donkey*): they say that when the jinn saw that Sulayman had been attracted to this woman, and he intended to marry her, they envied her. So they told him that her feet and shins were the feet and shins of an animal, and they put her down after a donkey, because it is uglier. This is not correct.

The purpose of this palace was to test the woman too. When it was said, ﴿"Enter the palace"﴾, if she really thought it was a body of water, if she was timid, would she enter or not? She would not enter at all. If she was heedless, she would enter with her clothes trailing. If she was resolute and brave, she would enter and lift her clothes from her shins. She entered and lifted her clothes from her shins.

Then, by her intelligence, she knew that she had not been honored, and that she was told, "Enter the palace," when she would be entering a deep sea that would drown her. So she knew that the most that could be in it was that it would reach her knees or something like that, and that it could not be a deep sea. Why? Because she was told it as an honor: ﴿"Enter the palace."﴾

So the point is that this is also a second test of her intelligence, resolve, and courage. As for the claim that her leg was a donkey's leg, this is clearly a lie, and the basic fact is that she was a woman like the daughters of Adam, with nothing of that in her.

*Student:* (...)?

*Shaykh:* We do not know about the law of those before us (...).

He said: (﴿When she saw it, she thought it was a body of water﴾ of water, ﴿and she uncovered her shins﴾). There is no doubt that this indicates her resolve, strength, and courage, because a stranger who encounters such a situation might say, "I do not know; perhaps they are deceiving me, and I may get wet in it and die." But she was strong and resolute as well. She went forward to enter, but with caution against harm, by lifting her clothes from her shins.

Regarding lifting from the shins, Ibrahim [the commentator] says that it may be derived from this that it is permissible for a woman to show her shins. We say: first, this is not derived from it, because here she did it out of necessity. A woman uncovering her shins out of necessity is not objectionable, even in our law. If a woman needs to uncover her shins in such a situation, there is no fault in it, because what is forbidden as a means of prohibition is permitted by necessity, as is established in the science of legal theory (*ʿilm al-uṣūl*). What is prohibited as a means is permitted by needs. For this reason it is permissible to look at the private parts for the slightest need. They even said it is permissible for someone to shave the pubic area of one who does not know how to shave his own, and this will inevitably expose the pubic area so that it can be shaved.

The summary is that if the law of Sulayman permitted such a thing, then there is no proof in it. If it did not permit it, it does not contradict our law either, because need calls for it here.

(﴿And she uncovered her shins﴾ to wade into it, and Sulayman was on his throne at the head of the palace, and he saw her shins and feet as beautiful.) Now the man was reassured, reassured, but she was not as the author said. Was the purpose of this that it be clear to Sulayman whether her leg was a donkey's leg or a human leg?

No. The purpose was to know by this her intelligence, insight, and courage. Whatever meaning this image indicates that relates to the woman, Sulayman, peace be upon him, intends it.

*Student:* (...)?

*Shaykh:* It will certainly come.

(﴿He said﴾ to her, ﴿"It is a palace paved smooth﴾ smoothed, ﴿of glass"﴾ that is, of crystal.)

This sentence also indicates that, along with testing her and examining her, it was intended to display the greatness of Sulayman's kingdom, just as bringing the throne served this purpose.

﴿He said, "It is a palace paved smooth of glass."﴾ Two things become clear from this. The first is the greatness of Sulayman's kingdom, since glass was made for him so that it would look like the deep sea. Second, it points out that this woman, although intelligent, wise, and resolute, could be deceived about a matter, or not? Because she thought this glass was a body of water, when it was not. So there is a kind of showing of her weakness too, since she supposed the matter to be other than what it was.

Among the benefits of these verses that will come, God willing...

*Student:* (...) "palace paved smooth of glass," that there is no water in it?

*Shaykh:* (...) It is not to be ruled out, because the presence of water beneath it, as I said, is not necessary.

﴿He said, "It is a palace paved smooth of glass."﴾ Then she knew her place, and she knew Sulayman's station.

As for his saying (*and he invited her to Islam*), there is nothing in the verse that indicates this. Rather, the apparent meaning is that what she witnessed compelled her to submit, because she saw matters: among them the bringing of her throne, and among them this great palace paved smooth of glass.

*Student:* (...)?

*Shaykh:* She is the one who said ﴿"It is as if it were it."﴾

Also among them: Sulayman, peace be upon him, informed her of his greatness and power, since this is a palace paved smooth of glass and not water. Then she acknowledged it, (*and she said:* ﴿"My Lord, I have wronged myself"﴾ by worshipping other than You).

Worshipping other than God is among the greatest wrongs. God Most High said about Luqman when he said to his son: ﴿"O my son, do not associate anything with God. Indeed, association is a great wrong."﴾ [Luqman 13]. This is because the greatest wrong is to assert yourself over one whose right is clearer and more manifest, and there is nothing clearer and more manifest than God's right over His servants. For this reason shirk is the greatest of wrongs.

When you dispute with a person while you know that the right is his and not yours, you are considered a wrongdoer. When the matter is unclear to you, so that you judge eighty percent that it is his and twenty percent that it is yours, this wrong is lighter than the first. When it is fifty percent yours and fifty percent his, it is lighter than the second. When you judge thirty percent his and seventy percent yours, it is lighter, and so on.

Commentary of Ibn 'Uthaymin (Tafsir al-Quran al-Karim) on surah 27, verses 41–44 (part 2 of 3):

So the point is that wrongdoing becomes uglier and more shameful in proportion to how clear the truth is and how plainly it has been made known. The most evident and clearest of rights is the worship of Allah, Glorified and Exalted. So the greatest wrong is associating partners with Allah, that you associate anyone with Allah. This is why she said: ﴿My Lord, I have wronged myself﴾.

So, the self is a trust (amanah) in your hands. You must strive for it in what is good for it. You must strive for your self in what is good for it. If you presume to take what is not yours, you have wronged yourself. If you neglect what is obligatory upon you, you have wronged yourself. And if you cannot dispose of your body as you wish, how can you dispose of your actions as you wish?

If a person said to someone: "I will give you my finger. Cut off my finger and put it (...) in place of the missing finger on your hand. Is that permissible?"
* Student: It is not permissible.
* Shaykh: It is not permissible. If he said: "I will gouge out my eye and put it in your eye that cannot see, is that permissible?"
* Student: No, it is not permissible.
* Shaykh: It is not permissible. If this is impossible in a body whose end is annihilation, how can it be in actions upon which the happiness of the servant depends? So it is not permissible for you to dispose of your actions in ways that harm yourself. If you do, you are a wrongdoer.

She said: ﴿And I have submitted with Solomon to Allah, Lord of the worlds﴾ (﴿I have submitted﴾ being ﴿with Solomon﴾ [i.e., in the state of being with Solomon]).

The author indicated, by estimating the word "being" (kā'inah), that the adverbial phrase in her saying ﴿with Solomon﴾ is in the position of a circumstantial clause (ḥāl). That is: "I have submitted, being with Solomon, to whom? To Allah, Lord of the worlds." Is she considered a Muslim here or not?
* Student: Yes (...).
* Shaykh: Yes. If a man says "I have submitted (aslamtu)," even if he does not say "I bear witness that there is no god but Allah and that Muhammad is the Messenger of Allah," he has become a Muslim. ﴿The Bedouins say, "We have believed." Say, "You have not believed, but say, 'We have submitted'"﴾ [al-Hujurat 14]. When a person expresses an act by the verb that indicates it, he is judged by it. This is why if someone says to a person, "I swear to you that you will do such-and-such," it becomes an oath, even if he did not say "by Allah." Or "I swear I will not do such-and-such," it becomes an oath even if he did not say "by Allah," because this is the act itself.
If he says "I have submitted," it becomes Islam, even if he does not say "I bear witness that there is no god but Allah and that Muhammad is the Messenger of Allah."
* Student: (...).
* Shaykh: It is commonly used. So we say: ﴿And I have submitted with Solomon to Allah, Lord of the worlds﴾ contains the fact that she submitted completely, since she affirmed the divinity of Allah in her saying ﴿to Allah﴾, and the general lordship in her saying ﴿Lord of the worlds﴾.

The author said: (And he wanted to marry her, but he disliked the hair on her shins, so the devils made depilatory cream (nūrah) for her, and she removed it.) By Allah, the truth is that this is a problematic matter.
* Student: (...)?
* Shaykh: (...) the devils made depilatory cream for him. Depilatory cream removes hair. It is said that the first to have depilatory cream made was the shin of Balqis, by Solomon's command, since the devils made it for him. All of this is false.

The speech of Allah must be kept free of such things. Our position toward such scholars is that we ask Allah to pardon them and forgive them, because putting such matters into the speech of Allah is one of the things by which a person disparages the speech of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic. Most of these reports came, as Ibn Kathir said in this passage, from two men: Ka'b al-Ahbar and Wahb ibn Munabbih. They introduced much of the Israelite narratives (isra'iliyyat) into the interpretation of Allah's speech and other matters that they transmitted. We ask Allah to pardon them.

He said: (Then she removed it, and he married her and loved her, and he kept her in her kingdom. He would visit her once a month and stay with her for three days.) The residence of a man who marries a previously married woman (...).

We have mentioned, in his saying ﴿Disguise her throne for her﴾, the benefit of testing: a person testing another to know his understanding and intelligence, like what happened here.

And the Exalted's saying: ﴿So when she came, it was said, "Is your throne like this?" She said, "It is as if it were it. And we were given knowledge before her, and we were Muslims."﴾
* What is derived from it: tawriya (speaking with a double meaning, a double-entendre), which is that a person shows something other than what he intends. Their saying ﴿Is it like this?﴾ is tawriya, because the reality is that the throne before them was hers. The question's form would have required them to say: "Is this your throne?" But they used the expression of tawriya to avoid the matter directly, because if they had said outright that it was her throne, she might have rushed to say no, since she considered it unlikely that it could have arrived in this period while guarded and locked up. So it was said to her: "Is your throne like this?"
And her saying ﴿It is as if it were it﴾ indicates that the answer should match the question, for she said ﴿as if﴾ by way of comparison, and did not say "it is it."
* It also indicates the intelligence of this woman and her caution against what might be a mistake. If she had said "No," it might have been it. If she had said "Yes," it might have been another. So she said ﴿It is as if it were it﴾, choosing this for the two reasons we mentioned at the time of the tafsir.
* It also indicates that a person should speak of the blessings of Allah, Blessed and Exalted, upon him, based on her saying ﴿And we were given knowledge before her, and we were Muslims﴾. The correct view is that this sentence is from whose speech? From the speech of Solomon. Although some propose the possibility that it is from her speech, the correct view is that it is from Solomon's speech.
* Student: (...)?
* Shaykh: No. Allah does not describe Himself as "Muslim." ﴿And we were given knowledge﴾; He did not say "We gave."

﴿And what she used to worship besides Allah had averted her; indeed, she was from a disbelieving people﴾.
* What is derived from this sentence: a person must occupy himself. Or not? The self must be occupied, either with truth or with falsehood. This woman occupied herself with falsehood instead of truth. It has been said among wise sayings: "If you do not occupy yourself with truth, it will occupy you with falsehood."
It is also said: "Time is like a sword; if you do not cut it, it will cut you." This is correct. In the authentic hadith, the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "Each of you is a earner (ḥārith), and each of you is an aspirant (hammām)." [[The author of Tamyiz al-Tayyib min al-Khabith, p. 117, said: it is not a hadith, and close to it is: "The truest of names are Ḥārith and Hammām."]] So a person must have aspiration and must act, but either toward good or toward something else.
﴿And what she used to worship besides Allah had averted her﴾.
* It also indicates that the environment has influence, based on His saying ﴿indeed, she was from a disbelieving people﴾. These people influenced her, so she became a disbeliever who worshipped other than Allah.
* It also contains a warning against associating with evil people, based on His saying ﴿indeed, she was from a disbelieving people﴾. Even if they are your relatives, you should not befriend them. If they have a right over you by kinship, give them their due right, but do not be intimate or companionable with them. The Prophet (ﷺ) said, as is transmitted: "A person is upon the religion of his close friend," and it is a good (ḥasan) hadith: "Let each of you look at whom he befriends." [[Narrated by Abu Dawud (4833), al-Tirmidhi (2378), and Ahmad (8028), and the wording is his, from the hadith of Abu Hurayrah.]] "A person is upon the religion of his close friend; so let each of you look at whom he befriends." This is something that occurs, and history and the previous hadith attest to it.
* Student: Is the environment an excuse for a person?
* Shaykh: It is not an excuse. The obligation upon a person is to leave this environment. This is why emigration (hijrah) was made obligatory upon whoever was able to emigrate. But when the Messenger says: "Then his parents make him a Jew, or a Christian, or a Magian," he is informing, and information does not imply permissibility. The Prophet (peace be upon him) said: "You will surely follow the ways of those before you." [[Agreed upon; al-Bukhari (7320) and Muslim (2669) from Abu Sa'id.]] This is a report. Does its meaning mean that it is permissible for us to do it? He also informed: "By Allah, Allah will surely complete this matter until a woman traveler (ẓa'īnah) goes from Sana'a to Hadramawt." [[Narrated by al-Bukhari (3595) from 'Adi ibn Hatim, similarly.]] Does that mean it is permissible for a woman to travel without a mahram? No. So what the Prophet (peace be upon him) informed of, that which occurs, does not imply permissibility.

﴿It was said to her, "Enter the palace." And when she saw it, she thought it was a body of water and uncovered her shins﴾, to the end.
* It indicates the greatness of Solomon's kingdom and Allah's subjugation of things to him. At that time, as far as we know, there were no furnaces that melt glass in which a person does as he wishes. But there is no doubt that glass existed. It may have been extracted from the sea by the devils, or there may have been smelting works and furnaces suited to their condition. This is why Allah said of the devils that they ﴿make for him whatever he wills of sanctuaries, statues, bowls like water-troughs, and fixed cooking pots﴾ [Saba 13]. ﴿Jifan﴾ is the plural of jafnah, which is a large bowl.
﴿Like al-jawab﴾. What is al-jawab?
* Student: The jabiyah.
* Shaykh: It is the plural of jabiyah, which is a cistern (birkah), meaning a large one.
﴿And fixed cooking pots﴾ means: they are not moved because of their size and greatness.
So the summary is that this indicates the greatness of Solomon's kingdom, since jinn and humans were subjugated to him to make for him whatever he willed.
* It also indicates the permissibility of testing a person, as already mentioned.
This story contains several tests, based on His saying ﴿Enter the palace﴾, to see whether she would be fearful and not enter, or would take a risk and enter without caution, or what she would do. The woman, because of her intelligence, entered but with caution and wariness. She uncovered her shins, meaning she lifted her garment until the shins became visible.
* It also indicates that from ancient times, a woman's adornment is concealment. His saying ﴿and she uncovered her shins﴾ indicates that the default is that she was covered, and that is so, unlike the man. The Prophet (ﷺ) said: "The lower garment of the believer is above half his shin," or he said: "to half his shin." [[Narrated by al-Nasa'i in al-Kubra (9626) from Abu Hurayrah, similarly.]] I have forgotten the wording. Now the matter has become reversed among many Muslims, unfortunately. Men's garments have become trailing, and women's garments have become short. This goes against the natural disposition (fitrah) upon which Allah created people.
* It also indicates that sight can deceive, and that what is perceived by the senses is not exactly the reality one hundred percent.
