That is, for example, a head of state who enacts a system he knows contradicts the Shari'ah, but believes it is better than the Shari'ah and more beneficial for creation. He did not judge by it personally, but he enacted it and left people to judge by it. We say: this is a disbeliever in a disbelief that removes one from the religion.

Student: Is rebellion against him permitted?

Shaykh: Rebellion against him is obligatory, unless he is perhaps still one who interprets. He may say: no, this does not contradict the Shari'ah. For example, some scholars, may Allah guide us and them, open doors for the rulers, and even deceive them by saying: worldly matters have nothing to do with the Shari'ah, because the Messenger, peace and blessings be upon him, said: "You are more knowledgeable about the affairs of your world," regarding pollination. So they deceive the rulers, saying for example: banks are permitted, because they are part of the modern economic system, and the Shari'ah has no say in them. Insurance funds are permitted and there is nothing wrong with them, because these are economic matters to which one returns according to what the age requires; the Shari'ah has no say in them (...).

Most rulers may be ignorant of this matter and think it is correct, so it becomes confused for them. But when we know, and make them understand, and explain the truth to them, and say: "You are more knowledgeable about the affairs of your world" regarding work and craft: the craftsman knows how to make the pot, but the Messenger may not know that. The farmer knows how to sow, but the Messenger may not know that. But the rulings on the affairs of our world, who knows them best?

Student: Allah, Glorified and Exalted.

Shaykh: Yes, the Shari'ah. So distinguish between actions and rulings. I now know, for example, that this thing is forbidden in manufacturing, agriculture, or the like. But do I know how to make it? I know that car manufacturing is among the good and desirable matters because of the benefit in it. But do I know how to make a car?

I say to the disbelieving polytheist, the atheist, the wicked Communist: you are more knowledgeable about the affairs of your world, correct or not? But he is not more knowledgeable than me about the ruling on this thing. Is it clear?

So the Messenger's saying: "You are more knowledgeable about the affairs of your world" means: you know whether this pollination benefits or does not benefit, because you have experienced and understood it. But I give you a legal ruling that everything beneficial to creation and containing benefit for creation is among the matters desired by the Shari'ah, because the basis of the laws was revealed only for the reform of creation.

Student: What is reported from the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, in matters of medicine, what (...)? Because if we said the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, was not a physician?

Shaykh: No, we say: no, but through revelation he perceives this matter. Either he perceived it through experience, and when he perceives it through experience and reports it, it is known. If he did not perceive it through revelation, then for example: he mentioned that healing is in three things. Honey is known through revelation: ﴿In it is healing for people﴾ [an-Nahl 69]. Cupping and cauterization: it is possible in my view, and in the view of others, that he received this from revelation, and we do not know this. It is possible that he knew it from experience and it was established for him.

Nevertheless, we also say: since the Messenger, peace and blessings be upon him, affirmed it, we affirm it, because it was established by the Messenger's statement, and experiments also testify to it.

Student: So the basic principle is that we receive from him and do not say this is not from ... (...), except what is established, as in pollination.

Shaykh: No, like pollination and other things, (...). For example, the making of doors, buildings and such things, the Messenger, peace and blessings be upon him, did not know them, if he had practiced them. Therefore, if the Messenger, peace and blessings be upon him, had palm trees in Makkah and practiced this thing, or practiced it (...) with it, the Messenger would not have known about it.

Student: (...).

Shaykh: He would not have known about it, because when he first came to Madinah he said: "By Allah, I do not think this pollination benefits anything," but he did not even say: do not pollinate. However, the Companions, because of their weariness from pollination, when the Messenger, peace and blessings be upon him, said this, rejoiced and said: then we will not pollinate. Leave this pollination.

Student: (...) Is there another example of this pollination (...)?

Shaykh: We do not know, but we now know that the Messenger's saying: "You are more knowledgeable about the affairs of your world" applies to matters that occur through practice, and the Messenger did not know about them.

Student: Okay, (...) occurs through practice?

Shaykh: It occurs through practice. The Messenger reported things he received from revelation, and things that may be from revelation or from experience, and he reported them.

Student: So the things established in medicine through practice, were not (...) about them?

Shaykh: (...)?

Student: I mean, the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, may...

Shaykh: He may not have known about them, and they are beneficial now. For example, penicillin injections were not known to the Messenger.

Student: No, I mean (...) you mentioned, medical matters that (...), some of them may be through practice as you mentioned.

Shaykh: What the Messenger reported may be through practice, and may be through other than practice. For example: "Mushrooms are from al-Manna, and its water is a cure for the eye." Is this revelation or not?

Student: The basic principle is that it is revelation.

Shaykh: This particular one may well be revelation, because it is obscure. But the matter of cupping and cauterization is a known and recognized matter among people, so a person may conclude that the Messenger knew it from experience, and a person may say: this is revelation from Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, which He revealed to him.

Student: Is what is known through experience definitely beneficial?

Shaykh: If the Messenger ruled it, although the Messenger, notice, says: "If there is healing in anything, it is in three," he did not affirm it definitively, because a person may not be healed by these three.

Student: So his first statement was not from experience (...)?

Shaykh: That is why he changed his ruling, because he had neither revelation nor experience, peace and blessings be upon him.

Student: So it was merely his opinion.

Shaykh: It was an opinion from him. He said: "I think that this does not benefit anything." But as I told you: when the Companions heard this statement they rejoiced at it, and said: then we are relieved of the burden. Since this was the Prophet's, peace and blessings be upon him, assumption, they left it, and the palm trees deteriorated.

Student: Yes, but it may confuse some people. They say: just as he was not a pollinator, he was also not a physician (...) the reports that were narrated?

Shaykh: No, that is not correct. The Messenger did not affirm it definitively. He did not say: there is nothing in it, nor did he affirm something that is not beneficial. Furthermore, this is a matter, praise be to Allah, known to every believer, and he can defend against anyone who wants to raise a doubt about this matter, saying: the Messenger did not affirm it definitively.

Second: even if the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, had affirmed this matter definitively, he affirmed it only as a presumption, and a person may affirm something as a presumption. The Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, approved of one who affirmed, indeed of one who swore on the basis of presumption.

Student: O Shaykh (...), modern physicians work on (...), for example they say: does the hadith come into conflict with what has appeared of the types of (...)?

Shaykh: We say: this is not correct. First: they now believe (...). But the means now differ, (...) and cauterization with electricity and such things. These are known now and used, and they believe in them. And as the Messenger said: "Indeed, strength is archery." It is not now archery in the sense of bows, but shooting with the available instruments. And cauterization also with available instruments. It is not necessary that it be so. And they now, in some matters, resort to Arab medicine. I recall that (...) always says that the patient goes to be treated with Arab medicine, and is healed by Allah's permission.

Student: So they are not influenced by Muslims, but if a patient came (...) I mean..?

**Sheikh:** In fact, some people deny the means or instrument by which cauterization (*al-kayy*) is performed, or the practice of some who cauterize with iron. I will mention, for example, some women to whom a child is brought (...) on his head, then (...) a cauterization, and on his back, for every vertebra of the spine, five [cauterizations].

**Student:** One by one.

**Sheikh:** Yes. The doctors, I mean, know about this thing and deny it, so that such cases do not occur (...). Then, when the Messenger (ﷺ) mentioned these things, he did not say that they are absolutely necessary. Something better than them may take their place.

**Student:** (...).

**Sheikh:** Yes, but the meaning (...) is not correct, because he himself cauterized Sa'd ibn Mu'adh (may Allah be pleased with him)[[Narrated by Muslim (2208/75) from the hadith of Jabir.]].

**Student:** (...).

**Sheikh:** They present (...) on Sunday.

**Student:** (...)?

**Sheikh:** No, it is read (...). If it is without an excuse, the person is punished.

**Student:** (...).

**Sheikh:** Muhammad Isma'il has a hadith (...).

**Student:** I saw it (...), but I did not find the words (...).

**Sheikh:** (...) this, you (...).

**Student:** It does not contradict, I will answer him.

**Sheikh:** (...).

**Student:** But, I mean (...).

**Sheikh:** Yes. If you do not find what (...), then "Allah does not burden a soul beyond its capacity."

**Student:** I found Ibn Hibban and al-Hakim, the chains of transmission.

**Sheikh:** Yes.

**Student:** But I searched the statements of the scholars about it, and I found nothing except the agreement of al-Dhahabi with al-Hakim.

**Sheikh:** The main thing: may Allah bless you. Write (...). We do not want more than this.

If the imam is reached after the recitation of al-Fatiha, is it obligatory upon him (...)?

**Student:** (...).

**Sheikh:** The words of Sheikh al-Islam?

**Student:** (...).

**Sheikh:** (...) *al-Muhadhdhab*, the *Sharh al-Muhadhdhab*, because the Shafi'is hold that the recitation is obligatory in all cases.

**Student:** I researched it.

**Sheikh:** You researched *Sharh al-Muhadhdhab*?

**Student:** No, I researched in the books of the Shafi'is.

**Sheikh:** No, it is the comprehensive book for them, like *al-Mughni* for us, *Sharh al-Muhadhdhab*.

* * *

He said: ﴿There were in the city nine men who spread corruption in the land and did not reform﴾. ﴿They said﴾, that is, these nine said to one another, ﴿"Swear to one another by Allah"﴾, meaning: some of them asked others to make a covenant regarding this matter, to bind themselves by oath to attack Salih and his family by night. The meaning of *al-bayat* (a night attack) is to inflict punishment upon them at night.

So here they swore, may Allah protect us, this wicked oath to attack Salih and his family by night. Therefore He said: ﴿"We will surely attack him and his family by night"﴾ [An-Naml 49]. The *lam* in His saying ﴿"la-nubayyitannahu"﴾ is the *lam* of the answer to the oath, and the *nun* is for emphasis. They emphasized this action with the oath, the *lam* and the *nun*.

The author says: (with *nun* and *ta'*, and the second *ta'* vowelled with a *damma*). Is this what you have?

With the *nun*, (...) ﴿"la-nubayyitannahu"﴾, and with the second *ta'*: if we make it with the *ta'*, then it requires the second *ta'* to take a *damma*, ﴿"la-tubayyitunnahu"﴾. As for ﴿"la-nubayyitannahu"﴾, it remains with a *fatha*.

﴿"We will surely attack him and his family"﴾, that is, those who believed in him: we will kill them by night. This is the explanation of *al-bayat*. By "family" is meant his followers, as the author said. However, this may be disputed, and it is said that what is meant is his immediate family, that is, the people of his house, because they are the ones who usually stay with him in the house. Generally, a person at night is not with anyone in his house except his immediate family.

Then after that, ﴿"We will surely say to his heir"﴾ (with *nun* and *ta'*, and the second *lam* vowelled with a *damma*). When is the second *lam* vowelled with a *damma*? When it becomes (...) ﴿"la-taqulunnahu"﴾. As for with the *nun*, it has a *fatha* on the *lam*: ﴿"la-naqulannahu"﴾. That is: after we attack him and kill him, when his heir rises to seek vengeance for him, we will say to him:

(﴿"to his heir"﴾, that is, the heir of his blood.) And who is the heir of the blood? In our Islamic jurisprudence, the heirs of blood are the inheritors, by fixed share or by agnatic relation. Some say that the agnates alone are the heirs of blood, because they are the ones who pay the *diyah* (blood money) on his behalf, whereas the holders of fixed shares are not among the heirs of blood. The correct view is generality: the heirs of blood are the inheritors, by fixed share or by agnation, and even the wife and the mother are among his heirs.

(﴿"We did not witness"﴾, that is, we were not present; ﴿"the destruction of his family"﴾ with a *damma* and a *fatha* on the *mim*.) ﴿"muhlika"﴾ and ﴿"mahlaka"﴾. The author did not mention the third reading, which is ﴿"mahliki"﴾. So the readings are three: *fatha* on the *mim* and *kasra* on the *lam*; *fatha* on the *mim* and *fatha* on the *lam*; and *damma* on the *mim* and *fatha* on the *lam*. The last two are the ones the author mentioned: ﴿"muhlika ahlihi"﴾ and ﴿"mahlaka ahlihi"﴾. He says: (that is, their destruction or their perishing), according to the two readings.

﴿"Muhlak"﴾ means destruction, because ﴿"muhlak"﴾ is from the quadriliteral (*ahlaka*), and ﴿"mahlak"﴾ is from the triliteral (*halaka*). Therefore we say: if the verb is triliteral, its *mim* verbal noun takes the pattern (*mafal*): (*halaka, mahlak*), (*qama, maqam*).

If the verb is quadriliteral, its *mim* verbal noun takes the pattern of the passive participle. You say: (*muhlak*) from (*ahlaka*), and you say: (*muqam*) from (*aqama*).

*Qama fina maqama fulan* (he stood in the place of so-and-so), as Abu Hayyan said about Ibn Taymiyyah:

*Qama Ibn Taymiyyah fi nasri shir'atina* ∗∗∗ *maqama sayyidi Taymin idh 'asat Mudar*

*Qama maqam*, but when you say: *aqama fi hadha al-makan muqam fulan*, with a *damma* on the *mim*, you do not say *maqam*. Is this understood?

This is a known rule in grammar: the *mim* verbal noun of a quadriliteral verb is on the pattern of the passive participle, and of a triliteral verb it is on the pattern (*mafal*) or (*mafil*), like ﴿"mahlik"﴾.

﴿"The destruction of his family"﴾ (so we do not know who killed them). Is this denial correct or false?

* **Students:** False.

* **Sheikh:** Since they were the ones who killed him, their saying ﴿"We did not witness the destruction of his family"﴾ is false. But there is an equivocation (*tawriya*, a statement with a double meaning) in it, because they say: we did not witness it, but we did it. The witness did not do it. Therefore they said: ﴿"and indeed we are truthful"﴾.

Is the clause ﴿"and indeed we are truthful"﴾ part of what they say in defence of themselves, or is it an affirmation of their saying ﴿"We did not witness the destruction of his family"﴾, meaning that they did not say it in defence of themselves? It allows both meanings.

﴿"Then we will surely say to his heir, 'We did not witness the destruction of his family, and indeed we are truthful.'"﴾ Is ﴿"and indeed we are truthful"﴾ part of what they say to the heir, to emphasize the denial? "We did not witness it, and we have not lied to you; indeed we are truthful that we did not witness it." This is one aspect. Or the meaning is: ﴿"Then we will surely say to his heir, 'We did not witness the destruction of his family'"﴾, and "be assured, brothers," they say to one another, "indeed we are truthful that we did not witness it"?

Both are possible. The commentators mentioned two possibilities. One of them: they say it as part of their defence of themselves to the heir, and in that case the clause ﴿"and indeed we are truthful"﴾ is an affirmation of their saying ﴿"We did not witness the destruction of his family"﴾ (...), ﴿"We did not witness"﴾, and ﴿"and indeed we are truthful"﴾, so we have not informed you of a lie.

Or the meaning is: ﴿"Then we will surely say to his heir, 'We did not witness the destruction of his family'"﴾, and when we say this, we are truthful, because we did not witness the destruction, but we destroyed them ourselves. We are not witnesses, but doers.

* **Student:** (...)?

* **Sheikh:** Yes, but the truth is that the doer is not the witness. And this is (...) an equivocation (...), an equivocation, or is it known that whoever does an act has witnessed it? Rather, it is more emphatic.

* **Student:** And whoever kills the Prophet, the believers (...) is it enough for them that (...) for what is greater?

* **Sheikh:** No. They make light of the matter for one another, so that there is no hesitation in their hearts. Or is it not known that the one who kills witnesses it? But to make the matter easy for some of them, some of them prepare others.

In summary: these people, may Allah protect us, intended this forbidden deed, and it is deceit (*makr*), because it is an attack upon Salih and his family from where they do not perceive it, since the night is the place of tranquillity and calm. When someone attacks someone else, that becomes treachery and deceit.

For this reason, even in the war against the disbelievers, the scholars differed: is it permitted to attack the disbelievers by night, or not? Some scholars forbade the night attack and said: it is not possible to kill the disbelievers while they are heedless and asleep. Others permitted it. The matter needs a careful investigation.

The summary is that we say: this is treachery and deceit, that these people come to Salih and his family at night and attack them. Therefore Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, says: ﴿"And they plotted a plot"﴾ [An-Naml 50]: they plotted in this matter a plot. ﴿"A plot"﴾ is indefinite (*nakira*), and sometimes one of the purposes of indefiniteness is glorification: that is, they plotted a great plot.

Some have explained *makr* (deceit) as seeking by hidden means to bring about the destruction of the opponent. So it occurs by hidden means to bring about the destruction of the opponent, because apparent means are not called *makr*; rather, they are hidden means.

Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, said in response to that: ﴿"And We plotted a plot"﴾, that is, greater than their plot: a plot greater than their plot.

The author said: (that is, We requited them by hastening their punishment). So he explained *makr* as requital. The correct view is that *makr* is more severe than requital, because it is a requital from where the one who is requited does not expect it. But the author, may Allah have mercy on him, wanted to remove the attribute of *makr* from Allah, the Glorified and Exalted, so he explained it as requital.

According to the People of the Sunnah and the Community (*Ahl al-Sunnah wal-Jama'ah*), the correct position is that *makr* may not be interpreted as requital in every case, and that its attribution to Allah in its proper place is not forbidden. *Makr* in its proper place is praiseworthy; is it praiseworthy or not? It is praiseworthy. In an improper place it is blameworthy. So the plotting against these plotters is praise, a great praise.

Therefore the correct view on this question, held by the People of the Sunnah and the Community, is that Allah, the Exalted, is described with *makr* but not absolutely. So it is not said: Allah is a plotter, because the absolute form includes the attribute of blame. Rather it is said: He is a plotter against those who plot, or against those who deserve the plot, and then it is an attribute of praise.

Attributes are divided into three categories. The first: attributes that are good in every case, which are affirmed of Allah in an absolute manner, such as hearing, sight, knowledge, life, power, and similar things.

The second: attributes of deficiency in every case, or attributes of evil in every case. Allah is exempted from these in every case, such as injustice, weariness, ignorance, blindness, death, illness, hunger, thirst, and similar things. Allah is exempted from these in every case, and also begetting, being a helper or minister, and having a partner, and what is similar to that, Allah is exempted from them in every case.

The third: attributes with two aspects, which are praise in one situation and blame in another situation. These are not attributed to Allah absolutely, nor are they negated of Him absolutely, such as plotting, deceit, mockery, derision, and similar things. Allah is not described by them in every case, nor are they negated of Him in every case. Rather, He is described by them where they are perfection, and they are negated of Him where they are deficiency.

Allah, the Exalted, said: ﴿"So they mock them; Allah mocks them"﴾ [At-Tawbah 79]. He, the Exalted, said: ﴿"Allah mocks them and extends them"﴾ [Al-Baqarah 15]. He, the Exalted, said: ﴿"They deceive Allah, but He is the One who deceives them"﴾ [An-Nisa' 142]. He, the Exalted, said: ﴿"They plot, and Allah plots"﴾ [Al-Anfal 30].

﴿"And they plotted a plot, and We plotted a plot, while they did not perceive"﴾, that is, they do not perceive the outcome of their plotting, or whether what they intended will be accomplished. And they do not perceive how Allah plots against them. They perceive neither this nor that: neither the result of their plotting nor the plotting of Allah against them. This is because they, may Allah protect us, persist in error, and generally the one who persists in error becomes blind and does not see, and it is called error. Therefore He said: ﴿"while they did not perceive"﴾. The clause in His saying ﴿"and they do not perceive"﴾: what is its place in i'rab (grammatical analysis)?

* **Student:** A circumstantial clause (*hal*).

* **Sheikh:** A circumstantial clause from where?

* **Student:** From the *waw* (of the plural).

* **Sheikh:** From the *waw* in (*makaru*, "they plotted"), or from the omitted pronoun in His saying ﴿"a plot"﴾, meaning: against them, while they did not perceive?

* **Student:** (...) indicates an opposing plot (...) the hidden one at night?

* **Sheikh:** No, it is by hidden means, and it may be perceived.

He said: ﴿"while they did not perceive"﴾ [50]. ﴿"So see how was the outcome of their plotting"﴾. ﴿"See"﴾: the address is first to the Prophet (ﷺ), or to whoever is fit to be addressed; that is: see, O addressee, or see, O Muhammad, who is the head of this nation, its leader and its imam, so his address is also an address to the nation.

﴿"So see how was the outcome of their plotting"﴾: (*kayfa*) here is an interrogative noun, suspending the verb ﴿"see"﴾ from action. Therefore we say its place is accusative as the predicate of (*kana*) placed first, and the clause (*kana*) with its subject and predicate is in the accusative position as the object of ﴿"see"﴾.

﴿"So see how was the outcome of their plotting"﴾: *al-'aqibah* is what follows a thing; that is: see what follows their plotting in the matter.

﴿"That We destroyed them"﴾, that is, We annihilated them. In your copies, is it with a *fatha* on the hamza or a *kasra*?

There are two readings: with a *fatha* on the hamza, ﴿"annaa dammarnahum"﴾, and with a *kasra*, ﴿"innaa dammarnahum"﴾.

As for the *kasra*, it is like His saying, the Exalted: ﴿"So how was My punishment and warning? Indeed, We sent upon them one blast"﴾ [Al-Qamar 30–31]. So according to the reading with the *kasra*, it is a new clause explaining this outcome: ﴿"So see how was the outcome of their plotting"﴾.

Now the mind is eager for this outcome, and the new clause is brought as an explanation of it: indeed We destroyed them and their people entirely.

As for the reading with the *fatha*, it is an explanation of the outcome, a substitute for it: ﴿"See how was the outcome of their plotting"﴾, that We ﴿"destroyed them"﴾; or it is in the predicate of an omitted subject, the estimate being: it is ﴿"that We destroyed them and their people entirely"﴾.

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿"We destroyed them"﴾. The author says: (we destroyed them), from destruction (*tadmir*), which is more emphatic than destruction (*ihlak*), because *tadmir* suggests the severity and magnitude of this destruction. And it is so, for the people of Salih were seized, may Allah protect us, by two things: a blast and a quake. They were shouted at, and the earth shook with them until their building collapsed upon them, and their hearts were torn within their bodies. May Allah grant us well-being. Allah, the Exalted, said: ﴿"Indeed, We sent upon them one blast, and they became like the crumbled dry stalks of one who builds a pen for livestock"﴾ [Al-Qamar 31], like crumbled dry stalks (...), may Allah protect us.

So this (...) is a great outcome of this disobedience, rebellion and plotting that they intended against the Prophet (ﷺ).

His saying: ﴿"We destroyed them and their people"﴾, even though the people did not participate in this crime. But this is the evil consequence of sins: that when Allah, the Glorified and Exalted, punishes someone for them, He includes everyone, although their people deserved punishment, since they were disbelievers who denied. But the hastening of punishment linked to this cause, which is the plotting of these men against Salih, may not be deserved by their people, yet, may Allah protect us, the punishment of these men encompassed them.

Allah, the Blessed and Exalted, has mentioned in other verses in more detail that their prophet Salih said to them: ﴿"Enjoy yourselves in your homes for three days"﴾ [Hud 65]. So they enjoyed themselves and remained for three days, then after that Allah, the Exalted, seized them with this blast and quake.

His saying: ﴿"all"﴾ (*ajma'in*): what is its place in i'rab?

* **Student:** Emphasis (*tawkid*).

* **Sheikh:** Emphasis of the pronoun in His saying ﴿"and their people"﴾? No, it is not for the pronoun; it is for His saying ﴿"and their people"﴾, for the people. That is: none of them remained except those who believed in Salih, peace be upon him.

The author's statement: (by the cry of Gabriel, or by the Angels pelting them with stones which they see and they do not see them).

As for his saying: (by the cry of Gabriel), this may be acceptable, because Allah, the Exalted, says: ﴿"Indeed, We sent upon them one blast"﴾ [Al-Qamar 31]. This blast is either from Allah, or from Gabriel, or from another of the angels. The important point is that they were destroyed by a blast.

Commentary of Ibn 'Uthaymin (Tafsir al-Quran al-Karim) on surah 27, verses 47–50 (part 4 of 6):

As for his statement, "(or by the stoning of the angels)," I do not know of any basis for this. It has been said that when the people came to Salih, Allah the Exalted commanded the angels to guard him. So when they came, they found the angels guarding him, and the angels began to pelt them with stones. But this has no foundation. If it does not come from an infallible source (ma'sum), it is not accepted. Moreover, it is not fitting that the angels should pelt with stones as if they were humans.

Rather, we say that what Allah destroyed these people and their folk with was the Cry (al-sayha) and the Quake (al-rajfa), as mentioned in the Qur'an. We do not go beyond the Qur'an in this matter, because Allah the Exalted says in Surah Ibrahim: ﴿None knows them except Allah﴾ [Ibrahim 9]. Since these matters are among the things known only to Allah, we do not go beyond what Allah has said about them, except for what has been reported from the Prophet (ﷺ) through an acceptable chain of transmission (sanad).

* Student: They reached his house?
* Shaykh: According to the author's opinion, they reached his house.
* Student: So the cave closed in on them.
* Shaykh: Some scholars have mentioned that when they went out, they were struck by rain, and they said: "Let us take refuge in a cave from this rain." When they took refuge in it, the cave closed in on them and they perished. As for their people, they kept searching for them and looking around, but they did not find them, so they returned to their homes. Then Salih came out to them and said: ﴿Enjoy yourselves in your homes for three days﴾ [Hud 65]. They said that this is what (...); because these people entered the cave seeking safety, but death awaited them in that cave.

This story, in this form, is also not something I have found established by a chain of transmission from the Prophet (peace be upon him). Therefore, the better approach is to say that Allah plotted against them, destroyed them and their people, and it is not important for us to know how they were destroyed. What matters is that we know they were destroyed completely, because of what they intended against the Prophet (ﷺ) and because of their disbelief.

* Student: I think this means that the people of Salih did not set a time (...) for ﴿Enjoy yourselves in your homes for three days﴾ (...), for example, their houses and the punishment (...)?
* Shaykh: It does not necessarily follow, because Allah did not mention that He destroyed them on that night.
* Student: (...).
* Shaykh: That they were prevented from this (...), then fear was cast into their hearts. This too we do not know. Or they came but could not get into his house, because it was locked and secured. The main point is this (...): what happened is that they did not carry out what they intended. ﴿That We destroyed them and their people entirely﴾.

Allah the Exalted says: ﴿So those are their houses, empty (khawiyah)﴾ [al-Naml 52]. Meaning: empty. Its grammatical status is that of a circumstantial accusative (hal), and the element governing it is the meaning of the demonstrative.

In ﴿So those are their houses﴾, is the referent known or not? It is known and specific, because the houses of Thamud still exist today and can be seen. But, as Allah said, they are ﴿khawiyah﴾, meaning empty, according to the author's opinion. It has also been said: khawiyah means collapsed and ruined, as Allah says: ﴿Or like the one who passed by a town while it was in ruins upon its roofs﴾ [al-Baqarah 259], meaning: collapsed.

This meaning is more eloquent, because interpreting khawi as ruined and no longer standing is more appropriate and more forceful. Houses may be empty while still inhabited, but when they are khawiyah in the sense of destroyed and collapsed, they are empty. So the destruction of the houses necessarily implies their emptiness, but their emptiness does not necessarily imply their destruction. In reality they were destroyed, because that great quake must have destroyed them.

* Student: (...)?
* Shaykh: Yes, but they did not remain in their former state; rather, they are destroyed.

Then the author said: its accusative status is like the accusative of khawiyah as a circumstantial accusative. From where?

* Student: (...).
* Shaykh: No. It is a circumstantial clause (hal) from "houses": their houses in the state of being empty. But where is the governing element of the circumstantial? Because the governing element must be either a verb or a noun with the meaning of a verb. The author said: "the governing element in it is the meaning of the demonstrative." Because (tilka, "those") means "I point to." So the demonstrative contains an implied verb and a meaningful particle. That is: "I point to their houses as empty."

He said: "﴿Because of what they did wrong﴾ (because of their wrongdoing)." The bi' here indicates cause, and (ma) is maṣdariyyah (the "verbal-noun ma"). The author, may Allah have mercy on him, converted the verb into a verbal noun, indicating that (ma) is maṣdariyyah; that is, what follows it is turned into a verbal noun. Meaning: because of their wrongdoing, not that we wronged them. Rather, they were the ones who wronged themselves.

Then the author explained this wrongdoing as disbelief, saying: "(that is, their disbelief)." This is because every disbelief is a wrong, but not every wrong is disbelief. For this reason the scholars said: we praise Allah the Exalted for saying: ﴿And the disbelievers are the wrongdoers﴾ [al-Baqarah 254], and He did not say: "the wrongdoers are the disbelievers." If He had said "the wrongdoers are the disbelievers," it would mean that every wrongdoer is a disbeliever. But He said: "the disbelievers are the wrongdoers," because every disbeliever is a wrongdoer. ﴿Indeed, associating others with Allah is a great wrong﴾ [Luqman 13].

Is there evidence for the author's interpretation of wrongdoing here as disbelief? Yes, there is evidence, because their action and their denial of their messenger was disbelief. So interpreting wrongdoing here by something more specific is supported by evidence.

﴿Indeed in that is a sign for a people who know﴾ [al-Naml 52]. ﴿Indeed in that﴾: the referent is the whole story according to the correct view, not merely a single thing, but the whole story.

(﴿A sign﴾: a lesson. ﴿For a people who know﴾: Our power, so that they may take heed.)

Restricting ﴿know﴾ to knowledge of power is not accepted, because what is meant is more general than knowledge of Allah's power. Rather, they know Allah's power and His wisdom, and what happened to the nations is all included in this, because one who does not know what to learn from will not benefit. But the one who knows is the one who learns a lesson.

In this there is clear encouragement to know the reports of earlier nations and to learn about them, because through them a person takes admonition.

Likewise, reports of events occurring in a person's own time also should be taken as a source of admonition and lesson. The benefits contained in the words ﴿Indeed in that is a sign for a people who know﴾ will come, Allah willing.

* Student: He said: (...) What is meant by His words ﴿for a people who know﴾ (...), they know the ways in which the proofs indicate?
* Shaykh: There is no benefit in that, but this may happen. However, it is not limited to that (...).
* Student: (...)?
* Shaykh: No, because "they know the proofs" (...). In any case, this is part of knowledge.

(﴿And We saved those who believed﴾ in Salih, who were four thousand, ﴿and they used to fear Allah﴾: they feared shirk.)

﴿We saved﴾: that is, We protected them. Salvation (al-injā') means protection. We saved them from what? From this destruction that Allah mentioned, and from the punishment. ﴿We saved those who believed﴾.

The author's statement "in Salih" is open to question. The correct view is "believed in Allah," so as to include Salih and those with him, as Allah says in Surah Hud: ﴿We saved Salih and those who believed with him, by a mercy from Us﴾ [Hud 66]. So the correct view is that it is belief in Allah. Indeed, we say that Salih, peace be upon him, was obligated to believe in himself as a messenger. For this reason the Messenger (ﷺ) used to affirm his own messengership, saying in his prayer: "I bear witness that there is no god but Allah, and I bear witness that Muhammad is His servant and messenger" [agreed upon; al-Bukhari (1202), Muslim (402/55), from the hadith of 'Abd Allah ibn Mas'ud]. He meant himself. And sometimes, when the matter happened in accordance with what he said, he would say: "I bear witness that there is no god but Allah, and that I am the messenger of Allah" [al-Bukhari (2484), from the hadith of Salamah ibn al-Akwa'].

The main point is that the Messenger himself is obligated to bear witness to his own messengership, that he is the messenger of Allah and believes in what has been revealed to him. Likewise others, all the more so.

As for the author's statement "they were four thousand," where is the register that counted them? There is no evidence for it. Most likely the believers were fewer than that in this case. The Prophet (ﷺ) said: "I saw the prophet with a group, and the prophet with a man or two men, and the prophet with no one with him. Then a dark mass was shown to him, and he thought it was his nation. But they said: This is Musa and his people" [agreed upon; al-Bukhari (5752), Muslim (220/374), from the hadith of Ibn 'Abbas]. The main point is that estimating them at four thousand, or forty men, or four million, or more or less, requires evidence.

This is also among the superfluous (fudul) matters of knowledge, which a person should not trouble himself with, because it has no benefit. What has benefit, Allah will certainly relate to us.

A similar example of this inquiry is: what color was the dog of the People of the Cave? What was its name? How big was it? These have no benefits. Where was the cave they were in? In what place? All these are peripheral issues.

Likewise, what occurs in the hadith in the Sunnah: a man said to the Prophet (ﷺ)... You find some commentators giving it complete attention: "Who said this?" This in reality has no purpose. Although we may benefit that if it is a virtue, it is a merit for that man if he is known. But is this necessary for the ruling or for the indication? No. It is among the superfluous matters of knowledge.

Similarly here: how many were with Salih? Four thousand or four million? It does not matter. The main point is that everyone who was characterized by faith, Allah the Exalted saved them from this general punishment.

﴿And We saved those who believed and used to fear Allah﴾. The author says: "(they feared shirk)." But if he had said "they feared sins," or simply "they feared Allah," that would have been better, because faith and piety (taqwa) together mean faith and righteous deeds. This is because righteous deeds, when mentioned alone, are part of piety. But when piety is paired with righteousness (birr) and the like, piety refers to avoiding sins and righteousness refers to acts of obedience.

Then Allah the Exalted said: ﴿And Lot﴾. The author said: "(in the accusative, governed by a 'remember' (udhkur) implied before it)," meaning: and remember, O Muhammad, Lot.

It is mentioned after Salih, and it is always mentioned after Salih, because the cities of Salih and the villages of the people of Lot are not far from one another, and they were not unknown to people at the time of the Prophet (ﷺ).

Then he said: "(﴿And Lot﴾ is in the accusative, governed by an implied 'remember' before it, and ﴿when he said to his people﴾ is a substitute for it)."

If we parse ﴿when he said﴾ as a substitute for "Lot," then the implied meaning is: "And remember when Lot said to his people."

"(﴿When he said to his people, 'Do you commit lewdness﴾: that is, sodomy.)" The hamzah here is an interrogative particle for what?

* Student: For seeking information (al-isti'lam).
* Shaykh: Seeking information? No? Because he knows, but it is for rebuke and denunciation. I would add to that: astonishment, or making others astonished. Meaning: how is it that you commit lewdness?! So it is for rebuke, denunciation and astonishment.

As for his words ﴿the lewdness (al-fahisha)﴾: the definite article (al-) indicates comprehensiveness of the category in meaning, not in individual instances. The meaning is that this is the greatest lewdness of its kind. It is greater than fornication (zina), because Allah says: ﴿And do not approach fornication; indeed, it is an indecency﴾ [al-Isra 32], an indecency among indecencies. Here He says ﴿the lewdness﴾.

It is also greater than marrying those who are forbidden (dhawat al-mahram), because Allah says: ﴿And do not marry those whom your fathers married, except what has already passed. Indeed, it was an indecency and hatred, and an evil way﴾ [al-Nisa 22]. Marrying forbidden women is greater than fornication, because Allah described them with three attributes: indecency, hatred, and an evil way. He described fornication with two attributes: indecency and an evil way, ﴿Indeed, it was an indecency and an evil way﴾ [al-Isra 32]. For this reason, the correct view is that whoever commits fornication with his close relatives (mahram) is to be executed, even if he was not acting by choice, because this is greater, may Allah protect us, than fornication.

Likewise sodomy: the correct view is that its perpetrator is to be executed, as long as he is an adult and sane, even if he is not married.

"(﴿Do you commit lewdness﴾: that is, sodomy, ﴿while you see﴾: that is, some of you see others, engrossed in sin)," and we seek refuge in Allah.

Meaning: more vile than donkeys, where one sees another doing it to the other. For this reason He said: ﴿And you commit in your gatherings what is evil﴾ [al-'Ankabut 29]. When they gather, may Allah protect us, they mount one another like donkeys. We ask Allah for safety.

* Student: (...) naked?
* Shaykh: But do they do it?
* Student: They do this (...) in Britain (...).
* Shaykh: Foolishness.
* Student: And it is legal.
* Shaykh: And it is legal.

His words ﴿while you see﴾ come from sight with the eye. It has also been said that it is from sight with the heart, meaning: while you see its ugliness and understand it. Every person with sound natural disposition (fitrah) dislikes this kind, because how could one mount the same kind of thing being mounted? (...).

Moreover, that place is not a place for this desire, because it is a place polluted with filth and is not a place of pleasure. It is ugly by natural disposition and also by sense perception.

We say: if we interpreted seeing here as sensory seeing with the eye and inner seeing with the heart, that would be permissible.

In reality, the abomination of this matter in the heart is something known by natural disposition. That they commit it while seeing one another is even more severe and greater.

(﴿Indeed, you﴾, with the two hamzas made clear and the second softened, and with an alif inserted between them in both ways.)

So the recitation becomes four variants.

﴿Indeed, you come to men with desire﴾ is an explanation of His words ﴿the lewdness﴾.

Note here that the interrogative is for affirmation (taqrir), but the sentence that is recited with the interrogative has been emphasized with what? With "inna" and the lam: ﴿Indeed, you come﴾. This is like the brothers of Yusuf saying to Yusuf: ﴿Are you indeed Yusuf?﴾ [Yusuf 90], meaning: do you affirm that you are Yusuf and emphasize it? He said: ﴿I am Yusuf﴾, and in his answer to them there is humiliation of them, because they asked him to affirm that he was Yusuf: ﴿Are you indeed Yusuf?﴾. He did not say "Indeed I am Yusuf," but said ﴿I am Yusuf﴾, dropping the emphasis as a sign of contempt for them.

So the conclusion, I say again: when an emphasis follows the interrogative, it does not remove it from the meaning of interrogation. Rather, it is as if the questioner asks the one questioned to affirm the sentence. For this reason He said to them, but in this matter the interrogative is for affirmation, we affirm with emphasis: ﴿Indeed, you come to men with desire, instead of women﴾ [al-Naml 55]. ﴿With desire (shahwatan)﴾ may be a verbal noun in the position of a circumstantial, and it may be an object of purpose, meaning: for the sake of desire.

In any case, there is rebuke in that they come to men out of desire while they are not worthy of it, and on the other hand that they leave what is for desire: ﴿instead of women﴾, who are the place of desire. Thus they have done wrong in what they did and in what they left. For this reason He said to them in another verse: ﴿And you leave what your Lord created for you of your spouses﴾ [al-Shu'ara 166]. This is more eloquent, meaning: if the matter were restricted, this way would be the only one left.

It would be better, but here there are permitted and lawful paths, in accordance with natural disposition, that you abandon and go toward this instead. Like one who leaves the lawful slaughtered meat and eats carrion, and like one who leaves valid trade and goes to usury, saying: ﴿Trade is only like usury﴾ [al-Baqarah 275]. The conclusion is that (...) becomes more ugly when it has lawful alternatives of good deeds. When it has lawful alternatives, it becomes more ugly. For this reason He said to them: ﴿Indeed, you come to men with desire﴾. If He had limited Himself to this: ﴿Indeed, you come to men with desire, instead of women. Rather, you are a people who are ignorant﴾ [al-Naml 55], the rebuke and blame would be established.

﴿They said, "We have taken an omen from you"﴾ [al-Naml 47]. The benefits?

* Student: The last thing we took was yes, ﴿They said, "We have taken an omen from you"﴾. The last thing we said was: the affirmation of wisdom and cause (...).
* Shaykh: Like that? Did we mention this? Did we mention that hastening toward evil happens either by requesting it or by the acts that cause it? Did we mention this?
* Student: At the beginning of the explanation we have: ﴿They said, "We have taken an omen from you"﴾.
* Shaykh: Allah the Exalted said: ﴿They said, "We have taken an omen from you and from those with you." He said, "Your omen is with Allah; rather, you are a people being tested"﴾ [al-Naml 47].

Commentary of Ibn 'Uthaymin (Tafsir al-Quran al-Karim) on surah 27, verses 47–50 (part 5 of 6):

* This verse shows the method of those who denied the messengers: they resort to likening (tashbih) and obscuring (tamwih). When they were struck by drought and famine, they said: ﴿We have taken an omen from you and from those with you﴾, even though this matter comes from Allah, the Exalted, and not from the causes of the Prophet. Likewise, people of falsehood liken and confuse others with such matters.
* This shows that the calamities that befall a person come only from Allah, the Exalted. This is shown by His saying: ﴿Your omen is with Allah﴾. This does not contradict His saying: ﴿And whatever affliction befalls you is for what your hands have earned﴾ [al-Shura 30], nor His saying: ﴿Corruption has appeared on the land and the sea﴾ [al-Rum 41]. The attribution of these matters to Allah is an attribution of creation and bringing into being, while their attribution to the created is an attribution of causation. They are attributed to people as a thing is attributed to its cause, and attributed to Allah, the Exalted, as a created thing is attributed to its Creator.
By this, the difficulty in many verses that appear to conflict on this subject is resolved.
* This shows that it is wise to answer falsehood with truth without remaining silent. This is shown by His saying in reply to them: ﴿He said: Your omen is with Allah﴾. He does not remain silent about falsehood, but refutes it and exposes it. This is the benefit.
* The fourth benefit: the response should be of the same kind as the statement. Here, they took an omen from Salih and those with him, so he explained that their ill omen and misfortune were due to their own deeds. But he said: ﴿Your omen﴾, meaning the wording is like the wording. Therefore the answer should be like the statement, and the one responding should be careful even about the wording.
* Fifth: whoever refutes another or nullifies his statement should bring a point that cannot be disputed. Had Salih (peace be upon him) said: "This drought is not from me, and I did not bring about its cause," or something similar, there would have been room for argument and counter-argument. Rather, the one responding should choose the answer after which there is nothing more to say.
A parallel to this is Abraham's debate with the one who argued with him about his Lord: ﴿He said: I give life and cause death. Abraham said: Indeed, Allah brings the sun from the east, so bring it from the west﴾ [al-Baqarah 258]. He did not say "No, you do not give life and cause death." Instead he said: "You kill one who does not deserve to be killed and spare one who deserves to be killed, and this is not giving life or causing death," even though that is the truth. But that would have led to dispute, so he brought a point that could not be disputed and that he could not argue against. Thus the one who disbelieved was silenced (buhita).
Likewise, when a person is debated by someone, he should choose answers that do not lead to conflict and argument, because if they lead to conflict and argument, falsehood may prevail over truth through lengthy argument, evasion and circling. Rather, he should bring something that cannot be disputed. This is one of the etiquettes of debate, and even those who discuss these matters hold that among the etiquettes of debate is to adopt what cannot be contested.
* The sixth benefit: His saying ﴿Rather, you are a people being tested﴾ is evidence that Allah may bring about matters that become a cause of trial for some people. Or not? When Salih came and the drought came, it was in reality a trial for some people, since some people would say, for example, that this is one of the consequences of this message. It would have been a cause of trial were it not for Allah's protection, may He be blessed and exalted. This always happens in Allah's decreed (qadari) and legislated (shar'i) acts.
In the legislated sphere: ﴿O you who have believed, Allah will surely test you with something of game that your hands and spears can reach, so that Allah may make evident who fears Him in the unseen﴾ [al-Ma'idah 94]. Allah forbade hunting to those in the state of ihram, and then He sent to the Companions (may Allah be pleased with them) game that their hands and spears could reach. A man could catch it with his hand without difficulty, or with his spear, not even needing a bow.
﴿So that Allah may make evident who fears Him in the unseen﴾: they feared Him in the unseen. Allah also tested the people of Musa with fish that came to them on their Sabbath, legislatively forbidden to them to hunt, and on the days they did not observe the Sabbath the fish did not come to them. But they were not grateful, and they deceived and resorted to trickery. They would set nets for the fish on Friday, the fish would come and get caught in them on Saturday, and on Sunday they would come and take them, saying: "We did not hunt on Saturday." So Allah turned them into apes: ﴿So We said to them: Be apes, despised﴾ [al-Baqarah 65].
In summary, I say: Allah may test a person with legislated and decreed trials, in order to know who fears Him in the unseen, and who is patient and who is not.
Sometimes a person is also tested with calamities: ﴿And among the people is he who worships Allah on an edge; if good befalls him, he is content with it, but if a trial strikes him, he turns back on his face﴾ [al-Hajj 11]. Some people worship Allah on a foundation, not on an edge. If good befalls them, they are content with it and thankful for it; if a trial strikes them, they are patient until they get through it. Is this clear? And His saying here, ﴿Rather, you are a people being tested﴾, indicates this.
* Student: There, Sheikh (...) the verses that (...) because the prophets are given signs that show (...). So if these trials of famine or (...) come, would they be a counterpart to them?
* The Sheikh: No, they do not contradict them. This is a trial, because he (peace be upon him) made clear that the cause was from them, since the message was not brought to witness against them; they were struck because they had denied. Just as Quraysh were struck by the Prophet's ﷺ supplication against them (...). He did not say: "My sign is that Allah will afflict you with famine." Even if he had said: "My sign is that Allah will afflict you with famine," and it happened, it would become a sign.
* Also in it is His saying: ﴿And there were in the city nine men who spread corruption in the land and did not reform﴾ [al-Naml 48]. This contains the principle of gangs, which still exists until now. These nine men spread corruption in the land and did not reform, and the matter continues to this day and beyond. Allah knows best that it will remain, because people of evil have methods they devise to impose their evil on others.
* This also shows that corruption and reform can coexist. This is shown by His saying: ﴿They spread corruption﴾ and ﴿and do not reform﴾. Had it been impossible for them to coexist, His saying ﴿and do not reform﴾ would have no benefit, since the absence of reform would be understood from the affirmation of corruption if they could not coexist. These are two benefits.
* In it: the affirmation that corruption and reform may coexist in one person.
* From this we also take: that disbelief and faith may coexist in one person, since faith is reform and disbelief is corruption. Likewise, wickedness (fusuq) and obedience may coexist. Two groups of people disagreed on this:
* Student: (...).
* The Sheikh: And the Murji'ah.
The Murji'ah said: it is not possible. When a person is a believer, all his states are good, and he is not punished for a sin nor blamed for it. The Khawarij and the Mu'tazilah said the opposite: it is not possible for disbelief and faith to coexist, or wickedness and obedience. Rather, whoever commits what necessitates wickedness becomes a disbeliever, and whoever commits what necessitates disbelief becomes a disbeliever, according to the view of the Khawarij; or he leaves faith and occupies a position between faith and disbelief, according to the view of the Mu'tazilah.
There is no doubt that the souls, reality and reason indicate the opposite of what they said, because the coexistence of this and that is a known, existing matter.
* Student: That is, (...) the man by majority, meaning: (...) coexist in the heart of a man, and the man is by majority (...) that he be a believer (...) faith.
* The Sheikh: No. We say: he is a believer with deficient faith. We do not apply to him absolute faith, even if, for example, ten percent of him is good. He must have deficient faith. Whoever does not have faith in his faith is a sinner by his major sin. For example, if a person backbites another person, this is one of the major sins that diminishes faith. Yet he prays, fasts, pays zakah, performs Hajj and does all the voluntary acts. We do not give him the description of absolute faith. Rather, we say: a believer by his faith, a sinner by his major sin; or a believer with deficient faith.
* Student: Sheikh, His saying: ﴿They spread corruption in the land and do not reform﴾ (...) like the saying of the Companion: "We were commanded to be silent" (...) speech, meaning that the description is realized by one of them, and the second (...).
* The Sheikh: No, and may Allah bless you. Silence and speech are contradictory, but corruption and reform are opposites. They can coexist, so that a thing may have both benefit and harm: ﴿Say: In both there is great sin and some benefit for people﴾ [al-Baqarah 219]. But this, silence and speech, is contradictory: one of them cannot exist without the absence of the other.
* The third benefit: sins are among the causes of corruption in the land. This is shown by His saying: ﴿They spread corruption﴾. These people did not demolish houses, drown crops, or burn markets, but they did things that were a cause of corruption: moral corruption (fasad ma'nawi), which is corruption of character and conduct, and material corruption (fasad hissi), since material corruption follows moral corruption.
﴿They said: Swear to one another by Allah that we will surely attack him and his family by night, then we will say to his heir: We did not witness the destruction of his family, and indeed we are truthful﴾ [al-Naml 49].
* From this noble verse we derive, first: prudence (hazm), and prudence may be in good or in evil, is that a group should bind itself by covenant and commit to the path it follows, so that they do not scatter and disagree. From where is this taken? ﴿They said: Swear to one another by Allah that we will surely attack him﴾. They did not each go their separate way; they first agreed on planning the scheme and then on carrying it out.
So it is derived from this: it is prudent for a group to unite and agree on a pact that binds them together, so that the execution is unified.
This method is still followed until now. You know that the document on which Quraysh agreed to boycott Banu Hashim: was it broken by one man? No. Rather, the man who wanted to break it went to so-and-so and so-and-so, and began gathering people around him until they agreed to break it and prevailed in carrying out their plan.
In summary, when a person wants to undertake a matter and proceed on a course, he should bring together people who will help him, and bind himself to them by covenant and commitment. If it is good, then it is good; if it is evil, then Allah will deal with them.
Here: ﴿They swore to one another﴾, was it for good or for evil?
* Students: For evil.
* The Sheikh: Yes indeed, for evil, among the greatest evils.
* In it is evidence for the principle of assassinations (ightiyalat), from His saying: ﴿We will surely attack him and his family﴾, because tabyit is assassination. Assassination means killing by surprise (ghirra). For this reason, the sound opinion among scholars is that in ghayla (killing by treachery) the heirs of the victim have no option, and the killer must be executed in every case, even if they pardon him. This is the view of Malik and the preference of Shaykh al-Islam Ibn Taymiyyah, because it cannot be guarded against, and it is corruption in the land. This is not contradicted by the Messenger's saying (peace be upon him): «Whoever has a slain relative has the choice of the two options»[[Agreed upon; al-Bukhari (2434) and Muslim (1355/447) from Abu Hurayrah.]], because his saying «Whoever has a slain relative» refers to private rights, whereas assassination falls under public rights: one comes to a person in safety and kills him.
* Student: (...).
* The Sheikh: No. The killer's act, if he is aggressive, is to be killed (...). But the important point is that it may be guarded against: the victim can guard himself by fleeing, by defending himself, or similar means (...). But if he comes to him while he is sleeping, for example, or comes to him in his house while he is unaware, this cannot be guarded against, and it is corruption. Because if he comes while he knows, he can guard himself by fleeing, by defending himself, by crying out to those around him, and similar things.
Our statement is not that it is on (...), because, as I said, usually he is not killed (...). Rather, the discussion concerns killing the victim by surprise, and this is the killing of ghayla. These people agreed upon this ugly, shameful deed, but they did not carry out what they intended, and they did not succeed in executing what they wanted, because they schemed, and Allah schemes, and Allah is the best of schemers.
* Student: (...) indicates (...) the principle of assassinations (...) Allah, the Exalted, mentioned (...) and that is the prohibition of assassination.
* The Sheikh: No. What I mean is that assassination existed even in the earlier times. This does not mean that it is a permissible principle (...). It exists and still exists. In general, for most matters, whether good or evil, you will find that their origin existed among earlier nations.
* Student: Muslims may not follow this method with enemies.
* The Sheikh: If they follow it with us, we follow it with them: ﴿And if you punish, then punish with the like of what you were punished with﴾ [al-Nahl 126].
* In it is evidence in His saying: ﴿We will surely attack him and his family by night, then we will say to his heir: We did not witness the destruction of his family﴾: evidence for denial, the denial of the claimant. This matter is clear: the one who commits an evil does not mind denying his act. In other words, whoever kills finds it easy to deny the killing, is that not so? Whoever kills finds it easy to deny the killing, because killing is greater than denying it. This is why they said: ﴿Then we will say to his heir: We did not witness the destruction of his family﴾.
* The fourth benefit in it: the burden of proof is on the claimant and the oath is on the one who denies. Why? Because if this statement did not clear them, it would not have been valid for them to agree on using it as an argument. Do you understand? They would kill him and say: ﴿We did not witness the destruction of his family﴾. They agreed on this.
This shows that the denial by which the defendant is protected is valid. Its reasoning is that if it did not clear them, agreeing on it would have been of no use to them, because if they had said "We did not witness his destruction," he would have said, "You are the killers." This is also evidence that the burden of proof is on the claimant and the oath is on the one who denies.
So if a person claims that this man killed his father, we say to him: Bring proof. If he does not bring proof, his right is not established, because the burden of proof is on the claimant and the oath is on the one who denies. But is this absolute?
The well-known position of the school is that it is absolute: even if the defendant in a killing is the most wicked of people and the victim is the best of people, and likewise the claimant, his word is not accepted, based on the general statement of the Messenger (peace be upon him): «The burden of proof is on the claimant, and the oath is on the one who denies»[[Narrated by al-Daraqutni (3191) from Abdullah ibn Amr ibn al-As. The second part of the hadith is agreed upon: al-Bukhari (2514) and Muslim (1711) from Ibn Abbas, with the wording: that the Prophet (ﷺ) ruled that the oath is upon the defendant.]].
Shaykh al-Islam Ibn Taymiyyah (may Allah have mercy on him) held that his word is accepted, but the qasama (oath procedure of the heirs) applies if this man is known for wickedness and the victim is known for truthfulness and uprightness, as well as his heirs. He said: this is a circumstantial indicator that overcomes the presumption of the claimant's truthfulness, and so the qasama applies in it. What the Shaykh said is not far from the truth.
Likewise, the second matter is the reverse. If a person killed someone and said: "Yes, I killed him, but the man attacked me and I could not repel him except by killing him. So what should I do?"
The school's position is that his statement is not accepted and he is killed. Do you understand? A person is accused of murder and says: "Yes, I am the killer, but I killed him in self-defense, because the man was trying to kill me." We say to him: Bring proof that he attacked you, or we will kill you. He says: It is impossible to have proof, because he did not attack me in front of people; if he had known there was anyone around, he would not have attacked.
We say: Then we will kill you, and on the Day of Resurrection you will dispute before Allah. This is the school's position. The Shaykh here chose that the word of the one known for truthfulness is accepted. So if this man is upright (this killer who says "I killed him in self-defense") and the victim is known for wickedness and aggression against people, then his word is accepted, but he must swear an oath to confirm his statement.

The view the Shaykh (Ibn Taymiyyah) held is the correct one, and it is not possible to act except by it, nor to act contrary to it. As for his saying, "We will kill him, and he will receive his reckoning before Allah," this is open to examination.

Now, even if there is an indication that proves the man's truthfulness other than the question of the state being such-and-such, for example if one finds the slain man in his house, meaning in the killer's house, a man who entered upon me in the house to kill me or to violate the sanctity of my family, and I find that it cannot be repelled except by killing him, he says: yes, even so, because it is possible that he intended to kill him.

* Student: There is a doubt that averts (...)

* Shaykh: What is it?

* Student: That he was in his house.

* Shaykh: Yes indeed, they say yes, in his house.

* Student: "Avert the prescribed penalties (hudud) by doubts."

* Shaykh: But he says: I have now killed deliberately, there is no doubt (...) that he was an aggressor. He says: That he was in his house does not indicate what he said, because it is possible that he (...) He says: Come in, come into our place, we will show you, and he enters so that (...). This problem: the matter is only consistent with what Shaykh al-Islam Ibn Taymiyyah chose.

Now, the discussion on his saying, ﴿مَا شَهِدْنَا مَهْلِكَ أَهْلِهِ﴾ ("We did not witness the destruction of his family"), indicates that the one who denies is accepted in his statement unless the claimant brings evidence.

* In this verse, ﴿وَمَكَرُوا مَكْرًا وَمَكَرْنَا مَكْرًا وَهُمْ لا يَشْعُرُونَ﴾ ("And they plotted a plot, and We plotted a plot, while they were not aware") [an-Naml 50], there is proof of the greatness of Allah, glorified and exalted, and that He is greater in plotting than those who plot against Him and against His messengers.
These people intended to plot against His messenger, but Allah, exalted is He, plotted against them with something greater.

* It also contains proof that Allah, exalted is He, may be described with plotting, but not in an absolute sense; rather in a restricted sense. It may be said, for example: He is a plotter against His enemies, or against those who deserve plotting, or the like, which makes plotting an attribute of perfection; for plotting is not an attribute of perfection in an absolute sense, nor an attribute of imperfection in an absolute sense.

* In this there is proof that Allah, glorified and exalted, may plot against the servant while he is unaware of His plotting.
Among this (Allah's plotting against the servant while he is unaware) is His leading him on gradually through blessings, where He showers him with favors while he wages war against Allah through disobedience.
Among His plotting is His confusing the ruling for him, so that the ruling is confused for him until he thinks falsehood to be truth, and so persists in it. Hence the transmitted supplication: "O Allah, show us the truth as truth and grant us the ability to follow it, and show us falsehood as falsehood and grant us the ability to avoid it" [mentioned by Ibn Kathir in his tafsir (1/571)]. A person may have a doubt, meaning he does not know the truth, or a desire, meaning he does not want the truth and wants something else.

Regarding His saying: ﴿فَانظُرْ كَيْفَ كَانَ عَاقِبَةُ مَكْرِهِمْ أَنَّا دَمَّرْنَاهُمْ وَقَوْمَهُمْ أَجْمَعِينَ﴾ ("So see how was the outcome of their plotting: that We destroyed them and their people, all of them") [an-Naml 51].

* The verse contains benefits. First: the exhortation to take lessons, from His saying ﴿فَانظُرْ﴾ ("see"). Seeing may be with the heart, called the sight of insight (nazar al-basirah), and may be with the eye, called the sight of vision (nazar al-basar). Both are desired when they lead to what is desired. But if it does not lead to what is desired, rather leads to the opposite, such as one who takes lessons and gains insight, then uses this sight as a means to slander the wisdom of Allah, glorified and exalted, or to describe Allah as unjust, or the like, as occurs from some atheists, then the harm of this is great, and we seek refuge in Allah. But whoever looks in order to take a lesson, who looks with the eye of reason and justice, indeed both are necessary: reason and justice. For without reason a person does not know, and without justice he wrongs.

In any case, this verse is proof that a person should look and reflect upon matters, especially the matters of deniers.

* It also contains proof that when warning, it is appropriate to use the harshest and most impactful words; from His saying ﴿دَمَّرْنَاهُمْ﴾ ("We destroyed them"), and He did not say "We caused them to perish" (ahlaknahum), for destruction (tadmir) has a greater effect on the soul, and the soul recoils from it more. Hence He said: ﴿أَنَّا دَمَّرْنَاهُمْ﴾.

* The verse also contains proof that punishments come about through a person's own deeds, since He made this destruction the outcome of their plotting. This is also indicated by Allah's saying: ﴿وَلَوْ أَنَّ أَهْلَ الْقُرَى آمَنُوا وَاتَّقَوْا لَفَتَحْنَا عَلَيْهِمْ بَرَكَاتٍ مِنَ السَّمَاءِ وَالأَرْضِ وَلَكِنْ كَذَّبُوا فَأَخَذْنَاهُمْ بِمَا كَانُوا يَكْسِبُونَ﴾ ("And had the people of the towns believed and been mindful of Allah, We would have opened upon them blessings from the heaven and the earth; but they denied, so We seized them for what they used to earn") [al-A'raf 96].
And He said, specifically regarding the People of the Book: ﴿وَلَوْ أَنَّ أَهْلَ الْكِتَابِ آمَنُوا وَاتَّقَوْا لَكَفَّرْنَا عَنْهُمْ سَيِّئَاتِهِمْ وَلَأَدْخَلْنَاهُمْ جَنَّاتِ النَّعِيمِ (٦٥) وَلَوْ أَنَّهُمْ أَقَامُوا التَّوْرَاةَ وَالْإِنْجِيلَ وَمَا أُنْزِلَ إِلَيْهِمْ مِنْ رَبِّهِمْ لَأَكَلُوا مِنْ فَوْقِهِمْ وَمِنْ تَحْتِ أَرْجُلِهِمْ﴾ ("And if the People of the Book had believed and been mindful, We would have removed from them their misdeeds and admitted them into Gardens of Bliss. And if they had upheld the Torah and the Gospel and what was revealed to them from their Lord, they would have eaten from above them and from beneath their feet") [al-Ma'idah 65-66]. ﴿مِنْ فَوْقِهِمْ﴾ ("from above them") means from the long-hanging fruits, and ﴿وَمِنْ تَحْتِ أَرْجُلِهِمْ﴾ ("from beneath their feet") means from the crops beneath the earth.

Also in His saying: ﴿أَنَّا دَمَّرْنَاهُمْ وَقَوْمَهُمْ أَجْمَعِينَ﴾.

* In this is proof that punishment encompasses all, but, as the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "People will be resurrected according to their deeds" [Ibn Majah (4229), from the hadith of Abu Hurayrah with the wording: "People will only be resurrected according to their intentions"]. Punishment may encompass, but people are resurrected according to their deeds. This is observed, whether the punishment is from Allah, that is, from His act, or from the acts of servants: Allah empowers some of His servants over others, so this tyrant destroys the righteous and the wicked alike, but on the Day of Resurrection people will be raised according to their deeds and intentions. Or Allah sends down a calamity from Him, such as floods, winds, and others, which destroy the righteous and the wicked alike, but on the Day of Resurrection they will be raised according to their intentions.

This is so, and Allah knows best the wisdom in it, in order that people may be upright in obedience to Allah's command. For if I know that the calamity will encompass all, will I strive to remove the evil that causes the punishment or not? But if we know that the punishment affects only the doer, enjoining good and forbidding evil would not be upright. Is it not so?

Therefore, a person's fear of the sins of others should be like his fear of his own sins, for the punishment is one: when it descends it encompasses all. Indeed, sins, glory be to Allah, are like smoke: it overcomes whoever inhales it, even if it is not in his house. Hence the sins of people today have affected even the distant good people among them. If you asked the people of goodness, "Do you find in your hearts what you used to find years ago of turning to Allah, humility, submission, and love of good?" they would answer: "No."

Let us leave aside the people who died thirty or more years ago; it is known that they were spared this trial. But even those present now, their hearts thirty years ago were far more righteous than today, though their state is the same. You find a person who is, for example, an imam in his mosque, who did not turn to the world nor occupy himself with it, you find a person who, for example, is with his family and does not attend to anyone else, and yet hearts have been affected; for sins are corruptions, whatever they may be.

But despite this, Allah may bring a great volcano that dissolves these things. Allah will raise up for the Islamic nation a victorious, manifest group that will change all of this. Hence there must be action; stagnation does not benefit, stagnation offers no safety at all. There must be action, but upon a straight guidance and with profound wisdom; for what harms the callers to Allah now is one of two things: either ignorance or foolishness. That is, either they lack clear, firm knowledge, so you find them prohibiting what Allah has permitted and obligating what Allah has not obligated, is it clear? As occurs among some of the brothers who are strict in matters, prohibiting what Allah has permitted or obligating what Allah has not obligated, and this is a great corruption. Or they have foolishness, meaning they lack wisdom in calling to Allah, so they are hasty and harsh, or slow where it is not appropriate; in the first case a violent reaction arises from those being called, and in the second, the called persist in a way that makes the callers lose the opportunity. Therefore knowledge and wisdom are necessary: ﴿ادْعُ إِلَى سَبِيلِ رَبِّكَ بِالْحِكْمَةِ وَالْمَوْعِظَةِ الْحَسَنَةِ وَجَادِلْهُمْ بِالَّتِي هِيَ أَحْسَنُ﴾ ("Invite to the way of your Lord with wisdom and good instruction, and argue with them in the best manner") [an-Nahl 125].

Commentary of Ibn 'Uthaymin (Tafsir al-Quran al-Karim) on surah 27, verse 47–50 (part 1 of 6):

The Shaykh: The answer: When he urged them to seek forgiveness and explained to them its good results, their answer was: ﴿They said: "We see an omen of ill in you and those with you."﴾ [An-Naml 47] I seek refuge in Allah. This is the answer; that is to say: you have brought us no benefit, rather you have become a bad omen for us, you and your followers. This is the condition of those who consider people of goodness to be an omen of ill. Allah, blessed and exalted, may test people. For example, it may happen that along with the arrival of good, or at the same time, some calamities or some things disliked by people occur, so that this becomes a trial and a test.

Perhaps, for example, a man of knowledge and worship may stay in a house and then that house catches fire. This is a trial and an examination from Allah, glorified and exalted. The people of evil rejoice and gloat, saying: "O Allah! Look at the causes of misfortune! The house burned when this man came!" Allah, Exalted, may test people: ﴿And We test you with evil and with good as a trial.﴾ [Al-Anbiya' 35]

These people say: "Because of the coming of Salih and the sin of his people, Allah, blessed and exalted, punished them with drought, famine and the disappearance of water." So they said: "You, O Salih, and those with you have brought us nothing good; you have brought us only drought, famine and the disappearance of water," and so they considered him an omen of ill.

And ﴿qalu ittayyarna bika﴾ originally is: tatayyarna. The taa' was assimilated into the taa' (ta') of the ta-ya, and this assimilation is contrary to the rule, since assimilation normally occurs between a sakin and a mutaharrik, whereas this is between two mutaharrik letters. So the taa' was assimilated into the ta' (the emphatic ta'), and when the taa' was assimilated into the ta', the first of the two letters became sakin. Note also that after the assimilation the taa' was changed into a ta'; and a sakin cannot be begun with, so a hamzat al-wasl was brought in to facilitate pronouncing it. This is why the author said: "and the hamzat al-wasl (the connecting hamza) was brought in." For what? To facilitate pronouncing the sakin.

The meaning of ﴿ittayyarna﴾ is: we considered it an omen of ill (tashā'amna), from ash-shu'm, and ash-shu'm means anticipating evil from something seen, heard, a time or a condition. This is why they said that at-tatayyur (augury/divination by omens) is derived from at-tayr (the bird).

In the pre-Islamic period they used to take omens from birds; they would send them off, and they had rules for this omen-taking: if it went to the right they took it as good omen, if to the left they considered it ill omen, if it went forward they would repeat (the sending), I think, a second time, and if it went backward they considered it a greater ill omen. So they had rules for this; therefore this ill-omen-taking was called tatayyur, derived from where? From at-tayr (the bird), because most of the Arabs' omen-taking was by it.

So they say: ﴿ittayyarna bika﴾, that is: we considered it an omen of ill, and your coming was an ill omen for us, you and your followers.

So what is at-tatayyur? It is considering something an omen of ill from something seen, heard, a time, a place or a condition. This is at-tatayyur. At-tatayyur is: considering an omen of ill from what? (...)

* Students: From something seen.
* The Shaykh: From something seen, or heard, or a time, or a place, or a condition; this is considering an omen of ill.
From something seen: a person sees something and takes it as an omen of ill. Suppose, for example, that he wanted to travel, and then he met a person he dislikes; he dislikes this man, so he says: "That's it, we're returning." What is this?
* A student: From something seen.
* The Shaykh: From something seen.
Or he intended to travel, and when he went out he heard a man say: "So-and-so son of so-and-so has died," and he said: "That's it, we're returning." Is this ill-omen-taking?
* Students: From something heard.
* The Shaykh: From something heard.
Or a time: he considers a day of the days ill-omened, Wednesday, Thursday, or a month of the months, such as the month of Shawwal. The Arabs considered the month of Shawwal ill-omened for marriages, saying: whoever marries in the month of Shawwal will not succeed.
(...) Marriages in the month of Shawwal are many, but 'A'isha refuted this by fact, saying: "The Messenger of Allah, peace and blessings be upon him, married her in Shawwal and consummated the marriage with her in Shawwal, so which of you was more favoured by the Messenger of Allah ﷺ?" [Narrated by Muslim (1423/73) from the hadith of 'A'isha.] So, if we want to practise omen-taking and seeking good omens, we should correct ourselves: we should?
* A student: Seek good omen.
* The Shaykh: We seek good omen in the month of Shawwal, but nevertheless we do not seek good omen from time nor take omen from it; good and evil are in the hand of Allah, glorified and exalted.
Some people consider a place ill-omened; you find, for example, that he comes and sits in this place (...), and says: "That's it, we've stood up; we cannot sit in this place."
Or he takes omen from a condition; the condition of a person, for example. Taking omen from a condition is also tatayyur, which is not permitted. A person may, for example, do a deed and it turns against him at the start, or he intends to do something tomorrow, and before tomorrow comes he has some fatigue and incapacity, so he takes an ill omen and changes course because of these conditions that befall him. We say: all of this is not permitted. If you have resolved, then put your trust in Allah. "O Allah, there is no omen except Your omen, no good except Your good, and there is no god other than You." [Narrated by Ahmad (7045), and at-Tabarani in al-Mu'jam al-Kabir (38) from the hadith of 'Abdullah ibn 'Amr.]
