* Shaykh: "The third benefit? Hm?"
* Student: "(...)."
* Shaykh: "No, there is more in it."
* Student: "(...)."

* * *

In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful. ﴿Ta-Sin. These are the verses of the Qur'an, and of a clear Book.﴾ [An-Naml 1], and so on to the end.

He says: this is "Sūrat an-Naml" (the Chapter of the Ant), and it was named so because of the mention of the ant in it. Naming the chapters happens for even a slight connection. For this reason Sūrat al-Baqarah was named after the cow (baqarah) mentioned in it. There is no objection to a chapter having several names for several reasons.

As for his statement that it is Makkan: the correct view regarding the Makkan and the Madinan is that the distinction between them is that whatever was revealed before the Hijrah is Makkan, and whatever was revealed after it is Madinan.

It is also said: the Makkan is what was revealed in Makkah, and the Madinan is what was revealed in Madinah. And it is said: the Makkan is what contains mention of the foundations (uṣūl), the foundations of Islam or of faith, and the Madinan is what contains mention of the branches (furū').

On the first view the criterion is time; on the second it is place; on the third it is subject matter.

But what the verifying scholars hold is that whatever came after the Hijrah is Madinan, and whatever came before it is Makkan. They have mentioned for this, in the principles of tafsir (uṣūl at-tafsīr), rules to which one refers.

As for the basmalah, its discussion has already been given several times, and we explained that the best way to estimate it is as a fitting verb that comes later.

That it be a verb, because that is the basic form of governing words (ʿawāmil). That it come later, for two benefits: the blessing of putting the name of Allah first, and the second, conveying exclusivity, i.e., "in the name of Allah" and not in the name of anyone else.

And that it be fitting, because it is more specific than the general. As for a verb, we said: because it is the basic form of governing words, and it is also more indicative of being newly originated (ḥudūth).

In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful. The estimate: "In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful, I recite." You may also estimate: "I recite in the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful," or: "My recitation is in the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful," or "In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful is my recitation."

But what we mentioned first is the more preferred. Shaykh al-Islam Ibn Taymiyyah pointed to its preference in the statement of the Messenger (ﷺ): "Whoever has not slaughtered, let him slaughter in the name of Allah." [Agreed upon by al-Bukhari (985) and Muslim (1960/1) from Jundub ibn Sufyan.] He mentioned it as a verb, and did not say: "Let his slaughter be..." He said: "let him slaughter in the name of Allah."

When He said: Allah the Exalted said: (﴿Ta-Sin﴾ — Allah knows best what He means by it.)

This is the path taken by the author and a group of scholars: regarding these letters of the alphabet found at the beginnings of some chapters, our position is to say: Allah knows best what He means by them.

It was previously stated in the nighttime tafsir lesson that the preferred view is that these letters are alphabetic, and that, by the requirement that the Qur'an is in clear Arabic, they have no meaning. We mentioned that this has been narrated from Mujahid, and that they are alphabetic letters with which Allah began, having no meaning. On this basis we affirm that they have no meaning, since they have no meaning. But they have a purpose: that this Qur'an, which left these eloquent and articulate people unable to match it, is made only from these alphabetic letters out of which their own speech is composed. That is, He did not bring new letters. For example, they might say: "By Allah, we do not know these letters!" He brought the same letters they speak with.

This is supported by the fact that every set of alphabetic letters is followed by mention of the Qur'an, except in two or similar chapters. These two chapters, such as ﴿Alif-Lam-Mim. Do people think they will be left alone?﴾ [Al-'Ankabut 1-2] and ﴿Alif-Lam-Mim. The Romans have been defeated﴾ [Ar-Rum 1-2], contain what indicates the Qur'an, such as the reports in His statement: ﴿The Romans have been defeated in the nearest land, but after their defeat they will overcome﴾ [Ar-Rum 2-3], and this is one of the characteristics of revelation.

And ﴿Do people think they will be left alone, saying "We believe" and not be tested?﴾ [Al-'Ankabut 2] also contains reports about those who passed before: ﴿We certainly tested those before them﴾ [Al-'Ankabut 3], and so on.

As for what the later deviating scholars claimed, that these letters indicate a miracle of the type of counting and calculation, they claimed that these alphabetic letters have their counterparts in the chapter that opens with them, and the total of this is divisible by nineteen. They claim this is the greatest proof that the Qur'an is the speech of Allah. They argue for this by saying that the first verse revealed, according to their claim, is the basmalah, and that it consists of nineteen letters, and that this is the meaning of His statement: ﴿Over it are nineteen﴾ [Al-Muddaththir 30], and that this nineteen is these letters. All of this is, may Allah protect us, false, does not hold together, is self-contradictory, and is not consistent. But they rejoiced in this computer that produced for them the number of letters and showed that their total is divisible.

We say: it is not impossible that Allah the Exalted intended this. It is not impossible. But we do not affirm that Allah intended this. Here there is a difference between affirming that this is a sign in the Qur'an, and saying: we do not say this.

First: because there is no miracle in this. Humans may hear a sermon, for example, or speech whose letters, when counted, divide by this number or by any number they like, and this is not a miracle.

Then, the basmalah is not the first thing revealed of the Qur'an. The first revealed was ﴿Read in the name of your Lord who created﴾ [Al-'Alaq 1]. Then, the letters of the basmalah are not, as they claim, nineteen, because the Qur'an was revealed to be recited or written? 

* Students: "Recited."
* Shaykh: "Recited. Its letters, as recited, are not so. Writing, as you know, is a craft. Perhaps, if it were assumed that writing in the time of the Messenger (ﷺ) and the time of the caliphs was not in this form, it could be otherwise, could it not? It could. Now there are some writing systems in some languages that make a vowel a letter, make one letter two, or abbreviate, making two letters one. The conclusion is that the Qur'an was not revealed in writing but was revealed to be recited, and there is no proof in that."

So we say: "Allah knows best what He means by it." This is one of the opinions on the matter.

The second view: they are symbols for specific things, as the later scholars held, or as some mention, that they are an indication of wars and battles that will occur at the end of time, and similar things.

The third view: it is said that they have no meaning. If it is objected, "How do we affirm that?" The answer is: this Qur'an was revealed in the language of the Arabs, and the language of the Arabs does not give these letters a meaning. But if we say they have no meaning, they have a purpose that appears, and Allah knows best, that He intended by them that.

He said: (﴿Ta-Sin﴾, that is: these verses; ﴿the verses of the Qur'an﴾: verses from it; ﴿and of a clear Book﴾: one that manifests truth from falsehood. He joined it with an added attribute: it is ﴿guidance﴾, that is, guiding from error.)

﴿Taka āyātu al-Qur'ān (these are the verses of the Qur'an)﴾: is the referent (al-mushār ilayhi) before or after?

* Student: "After."
* Shaykh: "The referent comes after and not before. This is one of the cases where the demonstrative refers to something that is later in both wording and rank, and this is permissible when evidence indicates it."

His statement ﴿āyātu al-Qur'ān (verses of the Qur'an)﴾ — he says: "verses from it." The author resorted to saying "verses from it" because if we took the apparent meaning of the verse ﴿verses of the Qur'an﴾, it would confine the Qur'an to these verses, would it not? ﴿These are the verses of the Qur'an﴾, meaning: this that he points to. It is known that this is not all the verses of the Qur'an, but only part of them.

It is permissible, for example, to keep the verse on its apparent meaning without any need for interpretation, and to say: ﴿These are the verses of the Qur'an﴾, where a part of a kind is pointed to with the demonstrative of the whole kind, as when you say, for example: "this is the human being," pointing to one man, or "this person," pointing to one man.

So the meaning is that pointing to part of a kind with the whole kind is valid and does not need interpretation, as the author said.

His statement ﴿wa-kitābin mubīn (and of a clear Book)﴾: he says "joined with an added attribute: it is guidance." Joined to what? ﴿kitābin﴾.

* Student: "To ﴿āyāt﴾."
* Shaykh: "To ﴿āyāt﴾, is that so? Is this statement correct?"
* Student: "It is correct: 'āyāt' is not written with a mark (...)."
* Another student: "﴿āyāt﴾ is nominative, ﴿kitābin﴾ is genitive..."
* Shaykh: "Yes, ﴿kitābin﴾ is genitive. So it is joined to ﴿al-Qur'ān﴾: ﴿These are the verses of the Qur'an, and [the verses] of a clear Book.﴾"

He described this Qur'an as both Qur'an and Book because it is recited and written. It is written in the Preserved Tablet, it is recited by tongues, and it is written in the mushafs too. Its writing precedes and follows it, but is its recitation later or earlier?

* Students: "Later."
* Shaykh: "Later, because after Allah spoke it and Jibril brought it down: ﴿Indeed, upon Us is its collection and its recitation. So when We recite it, follow its recitation﴾ [Al-Qiyamah 17-18]. Is 'Qur'an' a derived noun or a verbal noun?"
* Student: "Derived."
* Another student: "A verbal noun."
* Shaykh: "A verbal noun, because it is like al-ghufrān and ash-shukrān. It is a verbal noun of (qara'a, yaqra'u), meaning 'recited'."

It is also said that it means "gathering," because the letters qāf and rā' indicate gathering, and from this comes qaryah (village), because it is a gathering place of people.

In reality the Qur'an combines both attributes: it is recited, and it is also gathered.

As for His statement ﴿Kitāb (Book)﴾, it is the form fi'āl in the sense of maf'ūl, that is, written. The form fi'āl in the sense of maf'ūl occurs often in Arabic, like binā' meaning mabnī (built), ghirās meaning maghrūs (planted), and firāsh meaning mafrūsh (spread), and its examples are many.

It was named "Kitāb" for what we pointed to earlier.

His statement ﴿mubīn (clear)﴾: that is, manifesting truth from falsehood. The word mubīn: its verb is?

* Student: "Abāna."
* Shaykh: "Abāna. And abāna can be intransitive and transitive: it comes meaning 'made manifest', and it comes meaning 'became clear' (bāna)."

For this reason you will find the exegete sometimes explain mubīn as bayyin (clear), and in that explanation is it intransitive or transitive?

* Student: "Intransitive."
* Shaykh: "Intransitive. And sometimes he explains it as 'manifesting' (muzhir), in which case it is transitive. ﴿And indeed they were before that in clear error﴾ [Ali 'Imran 164]: what does mubīn mean?"
* Student: "Clear."
* Shaykh: "That is, clear: 'in clear error', so it is from intransitive abāna."

As for a verse like this, that the Qur'an is mubīn, it means "manifesting." Does its being manifesting entail that it is itself clear?

* Student: "Yes."
* Shaykh: "Yes, it entails it. Or we say that it is the use of a homonym (mushtarak) in two meanings, and the correct view is that this is permissible. This has passed with us before: is it permissible to use a homonym in two meanings? And we have already understood the homonym: it is a word whose form is one but whose meanings are many. This is the mushtarak, and it is so named because its meanings are shared in one word."

Commentary of Ibn 'Uthaymin (Tafsir al-Quran al-Karim) on surah 27, verse 56–64 (part 3 of 4):

The correct position regarding the mushtarak (homonym, a word with two meanings) is that it is permissible to use it in two meanings, on one condition or two conditions, which we mentioned two nights ago. And what are they? That there is no contradiction between the two meanings, and that the word is capable of bearing both of them. If it cannot bear them, or if there is a contradiction between them, then it is necessary that one of them be the intended meaning.

Here, for example, if we say that (مُبِين, mubin) is derived from (أَبَان, abana) intransitive, and from (أبان) transitive, is that permissible or not? It is permissible, even though this is a homonym. But when it is used in both meanings, it is used in a manner in which there is no contradiction. The Qur'an is clear (bayyin), and the Qur'an also makes things manifest (muzhir). In this case, is the indication of (mubin) that the Qur'an is clear a denotation of correspondence (dalalat al-mutabaqa) or a denotation of implication (dalalat al-iltizam)?

* Student: A denotation of correspondence.

* The Shaykh: A denotation of correspondence. If we take (mubin) as used in both meanings, then the denotation is one of correspondence. But if we say that (mubin) means (muzhir, making manifest), then its indication that it is clear falls under the denotation of implication.

﴿وَكِتَابٍ مُبِينٍ﴾ (and a clear Book): clear, making manifest the truth from falsehood. Is it general, or is it specific to what the Qur'an was revealed with?

Allah the Exalted says: ﴿وَنَزَّلْنَا عَلَيْكَ الْكِتَابَ تِبْيَانًا لِكُلِّ شَيْءٍ﴾ [An-Nahl 89] ("And We have sent down to you the Book as an exposition of all things"), and it is general over everything. But clarification may be a clarification of a thing in detail, and it may be a clarification of its causes and its methods, and you walk in them.

So the Qur'an in reality is an exposition of all things. Even in matters other than the legislative matters, it clarifies them, but it does not clarify their details, because those other matters are subject to time, place, people's understanding and their capacity. Rather, it mentions the causes and the methods, and you apply them yourself.

Hence, if someone says: How is this statement correct from you, when we do not see in the Qur'an the number of rak'ahs of prayer, nor do we see that they are five prayers, nor do we see the nisab (minimum thresholds) of zakat, nor the quantities (...) in it? So what is the answer?

* Student: We say: the Qur'an, Allah the Exalted says, as Ibn Mas'ud said: ﴿وَمَا آتَاكُمُ الرَّسُولُ فَخُذُوهُ وَمَا نَهَاكُمْ عَنْهُ فَانْتَهُوا﴾ [Al-Hashr 7] ("And whatever the Messenger gives you, take it; and whatever he forbids you, refrain from it"), so the verse includes what the Messenger clarified. Then also His saying: ﴿وَنَزَّلْنَا عَلَيْكَ الْكِتَابَ﴾ [An-Nahl 89], ﴿هُوَ الَّذِي أَنْزَلَ عَلَيْكَ الْكِتَابَ﴾ [Ali 'Imran 7], ﴿لِتُبَيِّنَ لِلنَّاسِ مَا نُزِّلَ إِلَيْهِمْ﴾ [An-Nahl 44], meaning...

* The Shaykh: ﴿وَأَنزَلْنَا إِلَيْكَ الذِّكْرَ لِتُبَيِّنَ لِلنَّاسِ مَا نُزِّلَ إِلَيْهِمْ﴾.

So the Qur'an indicates this through clarifying its cause and its method. So now we have the way of knowing this matter, which is what the Messenger (ﷺ) explained in the Sunnah, and this the Qur'an clarified. It is not necessary that the Qur'an must write down every detail. ﴿مَنْ يُطِعِ الرَّسُولَ فَقَدْ أَطَاعَ اللَّهَ﴾ [An-Nisa' 80] ("Whoever obeys the Messenger has obeyed Allah").

As for Ibn Mas'ud, whom the brother referred to, in the story of cursing the woman who plucks her eyebrows (al-naamisa) and the one who has them plucked (al-mutanammisa): a woman came to him and said: "We do not find this in the Book of Allah." He said: "Yes, it is in the Book of Allah," and then he recited this verse to her.[[Narrated by Ahmad in al-Musnad (3945), and al-Tabarani in al-Mu'jam al-Kabir (9466), from Ibn Mas'ud.]]

The summary is that the Qur'an is clarifying of all things, but the clarification may be detailed, and this exists in some matters, as in the inheritance shares, for example, in the divorces. You will find nothing deviates from this except very few issues, and yet their clarification is present upon reflection, isn't it?

That is, the detail of the fara'id (obligatory inheritance shares) is a detail from which nothing deviates, except one issue, which is the grandmother (al-jadda). It is not mentioned in the Qur'an, but the Sunnah brought it. As for everything else, even the disputed issues such as al-mushtarakah and al-'Umariyyatayn, we find that they exist in the Qur'an, and like the grandfather and the siblings, we find their clarification exists in the Qur'an, but it requires reflection.

Allah the Exalted said: (﴿وَكِتَابٍ مُبِينٍ﴾ making manifest the truth from falsehood; it is conjoined with the addition of an attribute, it is ﴿هُدًى﴾).

"With the addition of an attribute": where is the attribute?

* Student: ﴿مُبِينٍ﴾.

* The Shaykh: ﴿مُبِينٍ﴾.

Then he said: (it is ﴿هُدًى﴾). The author supplied (it is) to show us the i'rab (grammatical analysis) of (hudan), so according to his supposition, (hudan) is the predicate of an omitted subject. The estimate: it is (﴿هُدًى﴾, i.e., guiding one from misguidance).

It is well known that (hudan, هدى) is a verbal noun (masdar), and that (hadin, هادٍ) is an active participle (ism fa'il). So the author here explained the masdar with the active participle, and in his explanation there is consideration, because it is better to keep the masdar in its original form, for two reasons:

The first reason: converting the active participle into a masdar is more emphatic. When you say: "So-and-so is 'adl (justice)," and "So-and-so is 'adil (just)," which of them is more emphatic?

* The students: 'Adl.

* The Shaykh: 'Adl is more emphatic, meaning it is as if he is the very essence of justice, but ('adil) is characterized by justice that exists in something else. There is no doubt that the masdar is more emphatic.

The second reason in this verse: that making it hudan means that the Qur'an itself is guidance by which a person is guided. It is like the knowledge that a person follows until he reaches its goal, just as Allah the Exalted named it light: ﴿وَأَنزَلْنَا إِلَيْكُمْ نُورًا مُبِينًا﴾ [An-Nisa' 174].

So we say: (hudan) must remain as it is, that is, a masdar, and it is more emphatic than converting it into an active participle. And the second is that it is a masdar because the Qur'an itself is guidance; it is not a guide, rather it is guidance by which one is guided, just as He said: ﴿وَأَنزَلْنَا إِلَيْكُمْ نُورًا مُبِينًا﴾.

* * *

And the saying of Allah the Exalted: ﴿هُدًى وَبُشْرَى لِلْمُؤْمِنِينَ﴾ [An-Naml 2] ("a guidance and good tidings for the believers"). (Bushra) also means glad tidings (bisharah), but for whom? (﴿لِلْمُؤْمِنِينَ﴾, those who affirm it, with Paradise.)

His words "with Paradise": we will mention this later.

His words ﴿لِلْمُؤْمِنِينَ﴾ mean: those who affirm it. Mere affirmation is not sufficient here. Rather, the faith mentioned in the Qur'an necessarily involves acceptance and submission along with affirmation. As for mere affirmation, it is not sufficient. The evidence that mere affirmation is not enough is that Abu Talib affirmed what the Messenger (ﷺ) brought, and he said:

They certainly know that our son is not a liar among us, and he is not concerned with the words of falsehoods.
And I know that the religion of Muhammad is of the best of the religions of mankind, our religion.
Were it not for blame, or fear of disgrace, you would have seen me gracious with it, clear (mubinan).

So he did not accept and did not submit, and he was not a believer. Therefore, wherever faith is found in the Book of Allah, what is meant is affirmation that necessarily entails acceptance and submission. It is not mere affirmation.

So, for believers who affirm it, who accept it, and who submit to its rulings, this is necessary.

His saying ﴿هُدًى وَبُشْرَى﴾ is for those ﴿لِلْمُؤْمِنِينَ﴾. From this it is derived that whenever faith is perfected in the servant, his guidance by the Qur'an is perfected, isn't it? Because when a thing is linked to an attribute, it increases with the increase of that attribute and decreases with its decrease. When a ruling is linked to an attribute, that attribute increases the ruling with its increase and decreases it with its decrease. This is well known even in the perceptible realm: you find that a thing linked to something increases with its increase and decreases with its decrease.

So we say: whenever a person's faith increases, his guidance by the Qur'an increases. And the saying of Allah the Exalted indicates this: ﴿وَإِذَا مَا أُنزِلَتْ سُورَةٌ فَمِنْهُمْ مَنْ يَقُولُ أَيُّكُمْ زَادَتْهُ هَذِهِ إِيمَانًا فَأَمَّا الَّذِينَ آمَنُوا فَزَادَتْهُمْ إِيمَانًا وَهُمْ يَسْتَبْشِرُونَ﴾ [At-Tawbah 124] ("And when a surah is revealed, among them are those who say, 'Which of you has had this increase its faith?' As for those who believed, it has increased them in faith, and they rejoice.")

Also indicating this is the saying of Allah the Exalted: ﴿فَبِمَا نَقْضِهِمْ مِيثَاقَهُمْ لَعَنَّاهُمْ وَجَعَلْنَا قُلُوبَهُمْ قَاسِيَةً يُحَرِّفُونَ الْكَلِمَ عَنْ مَوَاضِعِهِ وَنَسُوا حَظًّا مِمَّا ذُكِّرُوا بِهِ﴾ [Al-Ma'idah 13] ("So for their breaking of their covenant, We cursed them and made their hearts hard; they distort words from their places and have forgotten a portion of what they were reminded of").

And also ﴿بُشْرَى لِلْمُؤْمِنِينَ﴾: bushra is the report of what gladdens, and it may be applied to the report of what distresses, but with an indicator.

Here he says: glad tidings of Paradise.

But the correct view is that it is glad tidings of what is more general: of Paradise, of honour and dignity, and of victory. Allah the Exalted said: ﴿وَأُخْرَى تُحِبُّونَهَا نَصْرٌ مِنَ اللَّهِ وَفَتْحٌ قَرِيبٌ﴾ [As-Saff 13] ("and another you love: help from Allah and an imminent victory"), after He mentioned Paradise for the believers, then He said: ﴿وَبَشِّرِ الْمُؤْمِنِينَ﴾ ("and give good tidings to the believers"), meaning: give them glad tidings of what they have in Paradise, and give them glad tidings of the victory they have in this world.

Every human being by his natural disposition loves to triumph over his enemy, does he not? And loves to have honour and dignity. This cannot happen except through faith. The more we increase in faith, the more we triumph over our enemy, and the more we slacken in faith, the more we are forsaken. ﴿إِنَّ اللَّهَ لا يُغَيِّرُ مَا بِقَوْمٍ حَتَّى يُغَيِّرُوا مَا بِأَنفُسِهِمْ﴾ [Ar-Ra'd 11] ("Indeed, Allah does not change the condition of a people until they change what is in themselves"). And if you want evidence of this, look at those who trumpet Arab nationalism: since when have they been trumpeting it?

* Student: Since the beginning of the century.

* The Shaykh: Yes, I think since the beginning of the century, meaning for a long time, and this call reaches its peak in deception, yet they only increase in backwardness and weakness, because it is not based on faith. But when the signs of the call to Islam and Islamic solidarity appeared, what happened?

They tried with all they could to eliminate this, not only from the disbelieving states, but even from the states that claim to be Muslim while being Arab, and they began saying: this is a reactionary call, and so on. Finally, those who stood up for it and called to it were eliminated. In sum: if we now want to return to honour, dignity and victory, that will not be achieved except through faith.

Someone may say: How can we triumph through faith over atomic and hydrogen bombs?

* Student: We have the strength of Allah the Exalted, and we prepare with strength as Allah commanded us.

* The Shaykh: Yes. We say: if we take the moral strength, and if material strength is available to us, well and good; otherwise the divine strength comes. So for us, for example, preparation is part of faith, but if we are unable to prepare, then the role of divine victory comes, and it nullifies what these enemies possess of strength. Allah, blessed and exalted, is over all things capable. Do weather changes affect their weapons, or not? Thunderbolts destroy them, earthquakes swallow them and their people, and all of this is in the hand of Allah, Mighty and Majestic.

A man who went last year to Afghanistan to fight with them told me, and he is a young man who graduated from America, but he insisted (and I think I have related his story to you) that he insisted on striving. He said: "I cannot die without jihad." He persisted against his mother and father, and they referred the matter to Allah the Exalted and then to me to judge between them. They said: "Do not go." He said: "No, I want to go." They said: "Do not go, you have not performed Hajj, you have not fulfilled the obligation." He said: "No, I want to go, and I commit to you that I will return in Dhu al-Hijjah and perform Hajj."

In short, after he broke his fast in Ramadan last year, he went. An eyewitness says, with the scarcity of equipment they have, even medicines: they have no medicines except old, spoiled medicines, which the companies sell to them and deceive them. But he says: I saw with my own eyes, they were building a mosque for Friday prayer where they gather. He says: the Russians are keen, on Friday, to come to this mosque to destroy it. He says they place people around the areas to guard the mosque and its surroundings.

So the bombs came, he says, and struck at the mosque, they wanted the mosque, but he says: they all failed to strike the mosque, and they struck those around it and did not reach it. Glory be to Allah the Mighty!

He says: only one flew off, it flew at one of the soldiers and killed him, and the rest, he says: no, they simply went out as if nothing had happened at all. And this is one of the signs of Allah the Exalted.

In sum, we say: victory, that is to say, we must know that it is not relied upon material strength alone. There is something behind it.

For this reason, Allah Mighty and Majestic says: ﴿وَلَيَنْصُرَنَّ اللَّهُ مَنْ يَنْصُرُهُ إِنَّ اللَّهَ لَقَوِيٌّ عَزِيزٌ (٤٠) الَّذِينَ إِنْ مَكَّنَّاهُمْ فِي الْأَرْضِ أَقَامُوا الصَّلَاةَ وَآتَوُا الزَّكَاةَ وَأَمَرُوا بِالْمَعْرُوفِ وَنَهَوْا عَنِ الْمُنْكَر﴾ [Al-Hajj 40–41] ("Allah will surely support those who support Him. Indeed, Allah is Strong and Mighty. Those who, if We give them power in the land, establish prayer, give zakat, enjoin what is right and forbid what is wrong") — four attributes.

Someone may say: what do we have to do with victory alongside these attributes, against bombs and other things? But He concluded the verse with His saying: ﴿وَلِلَّهِ عَاقِبَةُ الأُمُورِ﴾ [Al-Hajj 41] ("and to Allah belongs the outcome of matters"). These are not sensory matters; the outcome belongs to Allah Mighty and Majestic, and He, the Exalted, alternates the days among those who disobey and oppose.

* Student: Or one of the leaders may embrace faith and grant the Muslims strength?

* The Shaykh: Yes, correct. Perhaps this may happen. In any case, do not consider it unlikely. But we, in reality, consider victory unlikely because of our deeds; we do not have the resources that would entitle us to win.

So then: ﴿وَبُشْرَى لِلْمُؤْمِنِينَ﴾ refers to Paradise, as the author said, or to what is more general?

* Students: What is more general.

* The Shaykh: What is the evidence?

* Student: His saying in Surah As-Saff.

* The Shaykh: In Surah As-Saff: ﴿تُؤْمِنُونَ بِاللَّهِ وَرَسُولِهِ وَتُجَاهِدُونَ فِي سَبِيلِ اللَّهِ بِأَمْوَالِكُمْ وَأَنْفُسِكُمْ ذَلِكُمْ خَيْرٌ لَكُمْ إِنْ كُنْتُمْ تَعْلَمُونَ (١١) يَغْفِرْ لَكُمْ ذُنُوبَكُمْ وَيُدْخِلْكُمْ﴾ [As-Saff 11–12] ("You believe in Allah and His Messenger and strive in the cause of Allah with your wealth and your lives. That is better for you, if you only knew. He will forgive you your sins and admit you into gardens..."),

then He said: ﴿وَأُخْرَى تُحِبُّونَهَا نَصْرٌ مِنَ اللَّهِ وَفَتْحٌ قَرِيبٌ﴾, then He said: ﴿وَبَشِّرِ الْمُؤْمِنِينَ﴾ [As-Saff 13].

* * *

Then Allah the Exalted said: ﴿الَّذِينَ يُقِيمُونَ الصَّلاةَ﴾ [An-Naml 3] ("who establish prayer"): they perform it in its proper form. To establish (aqama) a thing is to bring it upright, and prayer is not upright unless it is performed in its proper form.

The establishment of prayer, as you know, is of two kinds: one kind which is indispensable, namely performing the pillars, obligatory acts and conditions; and another kind which is in its complete form, namely performing the complementary sunan and other things.

("﴿الَّذِينَ يُقِيمُونَ الصَّلاةَ﴾: they perform it in its proper form; ﴿وَيُؤْتُونَ﴾: they give; ﴿الزَّكَاةَ﴾") and so on to the end.

His saying ﴿يُقِيمُونَ الصَّلاةَ﴾: is the intended meaning the obligatory prayer or the voluntary one?

* Student: The obligatory one.

* Another student: General.

* The Shaykh: Yes, general, because it is not permissible for a person to perform a sunnah, for example, in a manner that contradicts the obligatory completeness. If someone said: "I perform the voluntary sunnah, but I do not recite al-Fatihah," is that permissible?

* Student: No.

* The Shaykh: It is not permissible. We say: now it is obligatory for you to recite al-Fatihah. If he said: "I do not bow, I do not prostrate," this is impossible.

So the verse on prayer is general: establishing it in both the obligatory and the voluntary.

His saying ﴿يُؤْتُونَ الزَّكَاةَ﴾: it did not specify the second object of ﴿يُؤْتُونَ﴾, but it is known. What is the estimate? They give zakat to its deserving recipients. Allah, blessed and exalted, has clarified the recipients of zakat in Surah Bara'ah (At-Tawbah) with a clear and detailed explanation.

His saying ﴿يُؤْتُونَ الزَّكَاةَ﴾: zakat does not need definition for you, since you know it. It was called zakat because it purifies the person: ﴿خُذْ مِنْ أَمْوَالِهِمْ صَدَقَةً تُطَهِّرُهُمْ وَتُزَكِّيهِمْ بِهَا﴾ [At-Tawbah 103] ("Take from their wealth a charity by which you purify them and cause them to grow").

His saying ﴿وَيُؤْتُونَ الزَّكَاةَ﴾ is a praise of those who give zakat. And the surah, as we have seen, is Meccan. So does that mean zakat was obligated in Mecca or in Medina?

The known position among the scholars is that it was obligated in Medina. But the correct view is that it was obligated in Mecca, while the determination of its amounts and the explanation of the wealth on which it is due in detail took place in Medina. This is the correct view, and it is the one by which the evidences are reconciled.

His saying ﴿وَهُمْ بِالآخِرَةِ هُمْ يُوقِنُونَ﴾.

* Student: The estimate is that prayer was clarified and zakat was clarified after it. Is this not a matter of delaying the explanation of rulings?

* The Shaykh: No. This is a matter of voluntary practice.

* The student: It clarifies zakat?

**Commentary of Ibn ʿUthaymin (Tafsir al-Quran al-Karim) on Surah 27, verses 56–64 (part 4 of 4):**

* The Shaykh: He explains zakat (obligatory almsgiving), and left it entrusted to the individual to give whatever he wishes, so that souls would become accustomed to it. Then after that, the specific obligation that Allah, the Exalted, intended is imposed on them.
* The student: That is, a person used to choose it.
* The Shaykh: Yes, he chooses what he gives. Yes, indeed. This is like other matters that developed in stages. Prayer was made obligatory as two rak'ahs, then the prayer of travel was confirmed, and it was increased for residence. Zakat was likewise first made obligatory by the individual's choice, then it was specified. Fasting was made obligatory by way of option, then it was determined. As for Hajj, what I know is that it was made obligatory only once. But the reason for that is that it came in the ninth or tenth year, after faith had settled in the hearts. So there is no need for souls to be brought gradually from one stage to another.
* A student: The saying of Ibn ʿAbbas: "The first prayer to be made obligatory was four rak'ahs"?[[Recorded by Muslim (685/5) from the hadith of Mujahid, from Ibn ʿAbbas.]]
* The Shaykh: It is not authentic. Even if this was his statement, the hadith of ʿAʾishah is explicit that the first prayer made obligatory was two rak'ahs.
* The student: It is an authentic hadith.
* The Shaykh: But this is more authentic than it. I do not know of anyone who says this from Ibn ʿAbbas. Even if Ibn ʿAbbas said it, the hadith of ʿAʾishah is more authentic.
* The student: Among the scholars, someone like Ibn Hajar reconciled the two hadiths, saying that ʿAʾishah mentioned the first (...), and Ibn ʿAbbas mentioned what people settled upon. It is as if the first obligation was four, then it was made obligatory as two, and it was increased in ...
* The Shaykh: You mean it was made obligatory twice?
* The student: Yes.
* The Shaykh: The hadith of ʿAʾishah is explicit and authentic: "The first thing made obligatory was two rak'ahs."[[Agreed upon; al-Bukhari (1090) and Muslim (685/3).]] So according to this reconciliation, the meaning is that it was first made obligatory as four, then it was made obligatory as two, then it was divided into residence and travel?
* A student: Is it permissible to introduce rulings gradually to one who embraces Islam?
* The Shaykh: It appears to me that it is permissible, and that he be commanded with the more important first, then the next. Just as the Messenger of Allah ﷺ commanded Muʿadh ibn Jabal, even though the rulings were established. He said: "The first thing you call them to is the testimony that there is no god but Allah and that Muhammad is the Messenger of Allah. Then the establishment of prayer. Then the giving of zakat."[[Recorded by Muslim (19/29) from the hadith of Muʿadh ibn Jabal.]] Even though all of these were obligatory. And fasting and Hajj are also obligatory.

* * *

He said: (﴿And they, in the Hereafter, they are certain﴾: they know it through reasoning. And "they" was repeated because it was separated from the predicate.)

The phrase ﴿وَهُمْ﴾ is the subject, ﴿يُوقِنُونَ﴾ is its predicate, and ﴿بِالآخِرَةِ﴾ is attached to (yuqinun).

However, the word (hum) was repeated a second time. Is this for emphasis, ﴿وَهُمْ بِالآخِرَةِ هُمْ يُوقِنُونَ﴾, meaning: they are the very ones who are certain, to the exclusion of others? Or is it, as the author said, for separating it from the predicate, the separator being the phrase ﴿بِالآخِرَةِ﴾?

Both possibilities are valid. It may also be that the intended meaning is all of them. Allah, the Exalted, has made clear that they are the people of certainty, since He repeated the pronoun twice. It was also repeated twice so that the separation between the predicate and the subject would be lengthened by the intervening phrase.

As for certainty (iqan), the author says: (they know it through reasoning). He said "through reasoning" because certainty (yaqin) is more specific than knowledge (ʿilm). Certainty means knowledge that does not admit doubt. It is the highest degree of knowledge, and this is achieved only through reasoning, that is, through clear and convincing proofs. For this reason, the author explained certainty as knowledge of things by way of reasoning.

As for ﴿بِالآخِرَةِ هُمْ يُوقِنُونَ﴾, does "the Hereafter" mean only that people will be resurrected? No. Everything that Allah, the Exalted, has informed about concerning that Day, or that His Messenger has informed about, is included in "the Hereafter."

Indeed, Shaykh al-Islam (may Allah have mercy on him) says that belief in the Last Day includes everything the Prophet ﷺ informed about that will occur after death.

Accordingly, "the Hereafter" refers to what comes after this world. It includes the punishment of the grave, the bliss of the grave, the scales on the Day of Resurrection, the Pool of the Messenger ﷺ, and what has been mentioned.

Has anything of faith remained? For he mentioned establishing prayer, giving zakat, and certainty about the Hereafter.

* A student: Belief in Allah.
* Another student: Belief in the messengers.
* The Shaykh: No. We have mentioned that belief in Allah includes belief in the messengers, includes belief in the books, and indeed includes belief in the Last Day and belief in the angels.
* A student: Belief in divine decree (qadar).
* The Shaykh: Belief in divine decree is part of belief in Allah, because decree is the decree of Allah, the Exalted. But there remain fasting and Hajj, which are among the pillars of Islam.

The answer to this is that the surah is Meccan, and fasting and Hajj were not made obligatory in Mecca, by consensus. Fasting was made obligatory in the second year (after the Hijrah), and Hajj was made obligatory in the ninth or tenth year, according to the preferred opinion. Therefore, there is no difficulty in the verse on this point.

* It is derived from this that when a person believes in the revealed laws, he is complete in faith, even if he did not live to see the later obligations. Those Companions who died before fasting was made obligatory had complete Islam. Indeed, a man may believe and die before he has prayed a single prayer, and he is thereby complete in faith. That is, his own faith is complete, although others who lived to fulfill more are more complete than him. Yet regarding him it is not said that his faith is deficient in a way that harms it.

* * *

(﴿Indeed, those who do not believe in the Hereafter, We have made their deeds appealing to them﴾ [An-Nur 4] the ugly ones, by installing desire, until they saw them as good, ﴿so they wander bewildered﴾: they are confused in them, because of their ugliness in Our sight.)

﴿إِنَّ الَّذِينَ لا يُؤْمِنُونَ بِالآخِرَةِ﴾: that is, they do not affirm it. Do we say it this way?

* A student: They do not affirm, which implies..
* The Shaykh: If they do not affirm it, it is known that they will neither accept nor submit. For whoever does not affirm cannot accept or submit. Alright, what if they affirm it but do not accept and do not submit? Same thing.

So: ﴿لا يُؤْمِنُونَ بِالآخِرَةِ﴾ includes negation of affirmation, negation of acceptance, and negation of submission. I think you know the difference between acceptance and submission?

For example, I accept that this matter is obligatory and I believe it is obligatory, but I do not act on it. What is it that is missing?

* The students: Submission.
* The Shaykh: Submission. As for non-acceptance, it rejects this, and this is not obligatory for him, and he does not acknowledge that it is obligatory. As for (...), it is absolute denial.

﴿الَّذِينَ لَا يُؤْمِنُونَ بِالْآخِرَةِ زَيَّنَّا لَهُمْ أَعْمَالهمْ﴾.

* A student: The difference between them.
* The Shaykh: Affirmation and acceptance. Affirmation: that he affirms that this is true but does not accept it. He says: Yes, this man brought the truth, but I do not accept it. Acceptance: it generally applies to beliefs. Submission applies to outward actions, such as the actions of the limbs.

﴿زَيَّنَّا لَهُمْ﴾: this clause, ﴿زَيَّنَّا﴾, is the predicate of (inna), and it indicates that the cause of the beautifying is their not believing in the Hereafter, and that Allah, the Exalted, did not make these deeds appealing to them except because of their disbelief. ﴿فَلَمَّا زَاغُوا أَزَاغَ اللَّهُ قُلُوبَهُمْ﴾ (...).

[The author's words have been abridged due to their great length.]

Commentary of Ibn 'Uthaymin (Tafsir al-Quran al-Karim) on surah 27, verse 56–64 (part 1 of 4):

﴿So the answer of his people was only that they said: "Expel the family of Lot from your town."﴾ [al-Naml: 56].
﴿Jawab⁠⁠ (answer)⁠⁠ is the fronted predicate (khabar) of kana, and ﴿an qalu⁠⁠ (that they said)⁠⁠ is its postponed subject (ism).
This sentence is restrictive (lil-hasr). That is: the answer of his people was not that they submitted, nor that they took a passive stance toward his call, such that they held back from accepting or from opposing it. Rather, the answer of his people, we seek refuge with Allah, was resort to force and violence. ﴿Illa an qalu⁠⁠ (except that they said)⁠⁠ means: some of them said to others.
﴿Akhrij/ Akhrijuu ali Lut min qaryatikum (Expel the family of Lot from your town)⁠⁠: the subject of ﴿akhrijuu⁠⁠ refers to the people of authority and influence (ahl al-hall wa al-'aqd) in the town.
As for His saying ﴿ali Lut min qaryatikum⁠⁠ (the family of Lot from your town)⁠⁠: they used this expression to indicate that Lot is not one of them, but is an alien, a newcomer settled upon their land, and therefore he must be kept away from them. For Lot, as is well known, was sent to the people of Sodom, and he was not one of them. Hence He said: ﴿Akhrijuu ali Lut⁠⁠ (expel the family of Lot), meaning: those who came and arrived among you and are not of you ﴿min qaryatikum⁠⁠ (from your town). They did not say "from the town," but said ﴿min qaryatikum⁠⁠ (from your town) in order to incite the expulsion of him.
﴿Min qaryatikum⁠⁠ (from your town) is an incitement to expel him. That is, it is as if they were saying: "This is your town, and this man has come newly to it, and wants to oppose you and stand against you. Expel him; the town is yours, not his."
﴿Akhrijuu ali Lut min qaryatikum⁠⁠ (Expel the family of Lot from your town). The explanation of the benefit in this will come, Allah willing; for some people, when they become impatient with reforming callers, say: "Get out, this is not your ... ," or "Do not speak in this mosque, it is not your mosque," or the like.
﴿Min qaryatikum innahum unasun yatatahharun⁠⁠ (from your town; indeed they are people who purify themselves)⁠⁠: this sentence is a justification (ta'lil) for the ruling that precedes it, namely the command to expel: "Expel them, why? Because they are people who purify themselves (from the backsides of men)." Thus they made the cause of punishment something that is among the causes for lifting punishment, for such purity is a good quality that calls for praise and commendation, namely the good thing for which the one who purifies himself is praised. But these people reversed it, because they, we seek refuge with Allah, are either deviants who know the truth and did not act upon it, or misguided ones who have strayed from the truth and become blind to it. We ask Allah for well-being.
The more likely case is that they are deviants, because it is well known among humankind that human nature recoils from this and no one accepts it.
His saying ﴿innahum unasun yatatahharun⁠⁠ (indeed they are people who purify themselves): did they mean the reality, that this act is filthy and these people want to purify themselves from it? Or did they mean that they purify themselves in their own claim, and that this act is not impure, but these people want to purify themselves from it?
The latter is closer, because it is the requirement of their state. The requirement of their state is that they regarded this evil as normal, and this indecency as trivial, so they clung to it.
Their saying ﴿innahum unasun yatatahharun⁠⁠: ﴿unasun⁠⁠ (people) is indefinite (nakira), and the indefinite is unknown, and all of this is for the purpose of distancing themselves from him and inciting his expulsion.
Allah, Mighty and Majestic, said: ﴿So We saved him and his family⁠⁠. When they resolved to expel him, Allah, exalted is He, commanded him to leave by Allah's command. The angels came to him and commanded him to travel by night with his family, except his wife, who was among those who remained behind. So he set out by Allah's command. When he had gone far from the town, Allah destroyed the people of the town at dawn: ﴿Indeed, their appointed time is the morning. Is not the morning near?⁠⁠ [Hud: 81]. So Allah sent upon them stones of sijjil, and He made its uppermost part its lowest. Hence He said: ﴿So We saved him and his family, except his wife⁠⁠ [al-Naml: 57]. Is the interrogative (istifham) connected (muttasil) or disconnected (munqati')?
* Student: Disconnected.
* Shaykh: Why?
* Student: (...).
* Shaykh: (...) what kind (...).
* Student: (...) of other than its kind.
* Shaykh: And here?
* Student: No, of its kind.
* Shaykh: Then it is connected: ﴿So We saved him and his family, except his wife⁠⁠.
In this is evidence that the wife is among the family, because a person lives with her and takes refuge in her, and she likewise with him. So the wife is among a person's family, just as his relatives, his children and his parents are also among the family: ﴿So We saved him and his family, except his wife; We decreed her to be among those who remain behind⁠⁠ [al-Naml: 57]. That is: We ordained and decreed for her, and therefore he said: (We made her, by Our decree, ﴿among those who remain behind⁠⁠, the ones left in the punishment). Al-ghabir means the remaining one, so the meaning is that she remained and he did not take her along, so she was, we seek refuge with Allah, among the destroyed.
﴿Except his wife; We decreed her to be among those who remain behind⁠⁠. This is the meaning of His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Allah sets forth an example for those who disbelieve: the wife of Noah and the wife of Lot. They were under two of Our righteous servants, but they betrayed them⁠⁠ [al-Tahrim: 10]. This betrayal was not a betrayal of chastity and honour, but a betrayal of disbelief, because they both showed that they were believers while they were not, and by this they became betrayers.

He said: ﴿Except his wife; We decreed her to be among those who remain behind⁠⁠ (﴿And We rained upon them a rain⁠⁠, which is the stones of sijjil that destroyed them. ﴿Evil is the rain⁠⁠ (fa-sa'a: how evil) ﴿of those who were warned⁠⁠ [al-Naml: 58], their rain being a punishment).
﴿Wa amtarna 'alayhim matara⁠⁠ (And We rained upon them a rain): in this is evidence that rain is not specific to water, but everything that is pelted from above is called matar (rain). Hence He said: ﴿amtarna 'alayhim matara⁠⁠. The rain that befell them, as the author said, was the stones of sijjil, as Allah said in another verse: ﴿And We rained upon it⁠⁠ [Hud: 82], and in another verse: ﴿And We rained upon them stones of baked clay⁠⁠ [al-Hijr: 74].
These stones destroyed them and made the upper part of the town its lower part, meaning that they collapsed upon them until its upper part became its lower part; that is, when a building collapses, its top becomes its bottom. This is the apparent meaning. As for what is narrated, that Gabriel lifted them from the lowest depths of the earth and ascended with them until the people of heaven heard the barking of their dogs and the braying of their donkeys, and then overturned it, there is no evidence for it, neither from the Book of Allah nor from the Sunnah of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ. The more likely is that when these stones struck their town, its upper part became its lower part; the building collapsed, so its top became its bottom.
(﴿Fa-sa'a⁠⁠ (evil) means "bi'sa" (how evil)): so "sa'a" is a past-tense verb stripped of time reference, used to express dispraise (inshā' al-dhamm), like "husna" (it was good) at times: ﴿and how good were those as companions⁠⁠ [al-Nisa: 69]; this is a verb expressing praise. ﴿Sa'a matar al-mundhirin⁠⁠ (evil is the rain of those who were warned) is likewise a verb expressing dispraise.
He said: (﴿matar al-mundhirin⁠⁠ (the rain of those who were warned), their rain being a punishment). Why did he say "their rain"? Because sa'a is like bi'sa: it seeks a subject (fa'il) and it seeks a subject of the predicate (mubtada'); the one specified by the dispraise is the omitted subject.
So we say in its parsing: sa'a is a past-tense verb, matar is its subject, and it is in construct with al-mundhirin, and the one specified by the dispraise is omitted, its estimate being: "their rain": ﴿fa-sa'a matar al-mundhirin⁠⁠ (evil is the rain of those who were warned), their rain.
This specified item sometimes comes first, and sometimes in its place comes an accusative noun that is made a specifier (tamyiz) in place of this specified item.

Then He said: ﴿Say: "All praise is for Allah"⁠⁠ [al-Naml: 59]. (﴿Say⁠⁠, O Muhammad: ﴿All praise is for Allah⁠⁠ for the destruction of the disbelievers among the earlier nations).
﴿Qul al-hamdu lillah⁠⁠ (Say: all praise is for Allah): the command is addressed to the Prophet ﷺ, or to anyone among the rational beings to whom it can be addressed.
His saying ﴿al-hamdu lillah⁠⁠ (all praise is for Allah) here is unrestricted as to what is praised for, so it is more general than what the author said. Although the context requires what the author said, it must be taken in its generality, and among what is praised is the destruction of the disbelievers, because it indicates His justice in seizing those people, and His bounty toward the prophets and believers, in that He seized their enemies.
But we say: ﴿al-hamdu lillah⁠⁠ is general: He is praised for His complete attributes and His finest actions. All His actions are good and all His attributes are perfect, so He is praised for this and for that, and the destruction of the disbelieving nations is among what He is praised for. This is the secret of why Allah, exalted is He, did not say: "Say: all praise is for Allah for this," but said ﴿Say: all praise is for Allah⁠⁠, so that Allah, blessed and exalted, is praised in every state. Among what He is praised for is the destruction of those who denied the messengers.
(﴿And peace be upon His servants whom He has chosen⁠⁠, meaning: ) this object was supplied by the author.
﴿And peace be upon His servants whom He has chosen⁠⁠: is this included within what is said, that is: "Say: all praise is for Allah, and say: peace be upon His servants whom He has chosen," so that a person is commanded to praise Allah and to invoke peace upon the servants of Allah whom He has chosen, by praying for them, based on His saying ﴿And peace be upon His servants whom He has chosen⁠⁠? Or is it an independent sentence, a report from Allah, glorified and exalted, that He granted peace to those whom He chose and saved?
There is a possibility for both, but which of them is closer to the context?
* Student: It is said that it is praise of Allah and peace together, in contrast to the disbelievers: praise of Allah for the destruction of the disbelievers (...).
* Shaykh: Indeed there is a possibility; neither of the two possibilities is preferred in my view, because each has a basis: a person is commanded to praise Allah and commanded to greet the servants of Allah.
Likewise, Allah, blessed and exalted, is praised for the perfection of His attributes, and then His report that He granted peace to these people is also something for which He is praised, because removing afflictions is like bringing blessings.
* And there is a benefit in this: that the servants whom Allah chose have been granted peace, so the punishment that befell those disbelievers does not reach them, and Allah, exalted is He, is praised for both: for the destruction of the disbelievers and for granting peace to His chosen servants.
His saying ﴿alladhi istafa⁠⁠ (whom He has chosen) means: chose. ﴿alladhina istafa⁠⁠: that is, He chose them. Allah, blessed and exalted, creates what He wills and chooses what He creates and selects it. Among what He chose from the children of Adam: He chose the prophets, as Allah, exalted is He, said: ﴿And indeed they are with Us among the chosen⁠⁠ [Sad: 47]. He also chose the believers, for the believers are chosen in comparison to the disbelievers, and the prophets are the elite of piety.
Selection, like other attributes that vary according to what the servant has done of the causes of selection, is such that the more a person worships Allah and the more he exalts Allah, glorified and exalted is He, the greater his selection.
(﴿Allah⁠⁠ with the two hamzas realized) ﴿A-Allah⁠⁠ (with the second changed to an alif) ﴿Aallah⁠⁠ (and eased) ﴿Aallah⁠⁠ (with an alif inserted between the eased and the other, and omitted).
* Student: (...).
* Shaykh: Realizing the two hamzas, changing the second to an alif; these two are clear.
* Student: And what is the first?
* Shaykh: Realizing the two hamzas, ﴿A-Allah⁠⁠. Changing the second to an alif is our well-known reading ﴿Aallah⁠⁠.
Easing has two forms: an alif may be inserted between them, between the hamza and the eased one, or omitted, so the readings are now four.
* Student: So the first is realizing the two hamzas, the fourth is easing both hamzas without a madd.
* Shaykh: The third reading is easing the second hamza, but with or without an alif. So the readings are now four, clear?
Then He said: ﴿Aallahu khayrun⁠⁠ (﴿khayrun⁠⁠ for those who worship Him, ﴿ama yushrikun⁠⁠ with ta' and ya', that is: the people of Mecca associate with Him deities that are better for those who worship them).
His saying ﴿Aallahu khayrun⁠⁠ (Is Allah better?): the author restricted its goodness to those who worship Him, but the correct view is that it is absolute goodness for those who worship Him, and this implies beneficence, and it implies His perfection, and this implies majesty and greatness.
So here we do not say: ﴿Allah is better⁠⁠ for those who worship Him only, but ﴿Allah is better⁠⁠ in all His attributes and in His beneficence and giving, because the verse is unrestricted, so its unrestrictedness must be maintained. And its unrestrictedness is more complete than its restriction, because for example this may be good for someone who deals with him, but it does not contain absolute goodness.
We say: this man deals with a person, and when he deals with him he gives him more than he deserves, but in his other attributes he is wretched; and another comes who is good and excellent in his other attributes, but when this man deals with him, perhaps he does not give him what he deserves. So the first is better for him than the second, and yet he is deficient.
So the author's saying "better for those who worship Him" is open to question: first, it is a restriction of the unrestricted without evidence. Second, this restriction does not imply superiority. Therefore it must be said: ﴿Allah is better⁠⁠ in everything, in His attributes, and in His reward and recompense for those who worship Him.
﴿Ama yushrikun⁠⁠ (or what they associate): meaning: or those whom they associate with Allah, such as idols and others? The answer: rather Allah is better. Hence when you recite something like this, you should say: "Rather, Allah."
This equation does not imply comparison or equality, for two things may be preferred over one another while the second party lacks them, as Allah, exalted is He, said: ﴿The companions of the Garden on that Day are better in resting place and finer in resort⁠⁠ [al-Furqan: 24], although there is no good in the resting place of the Fire and no fine resort in it. Rather they prefer between two opposites, so it is said, for example: "Winter is harsher than summer," or they say more eloquently: "Winter is colder than summer," although summer contains no coldness.
The conclusion is that this does not imply equality or parity; but does it imply deficiency? We say: yes, it implies deficiency, because it suggests participation, except in the context of condescension (al-tanazzul), so in that case it does not imply deficiency.
The poet says:
Do you not see that the sword's worth is diminished
When it is said: "The sword is sharper than the staff"?
But in condescension it does not indicate deficiency. These idols that are associated with Allah are those whose worshippers wish them to benefit them in bringing benefit or averting harm.
So we say to them: which is better, your idols or Allah? By way of condescension toward the opponent, because these people claim that their deities have some goodness; so it is said to them: ﴿Allah is better, or what they associate⁠⁠, meaning according to your claim, even though there is no goodness in them at all.
His saying ﴿ama yushrikun⁠⁠ (or what they associate): is "am" here connected or disconnected?
* Student: Connected.
* Another student: Masdariyya for a relative noun.
* Shaykh: No, it is not a relative noun; "am alladhi yushrikun" (or what they associate) means the equation is between two entities, not between two meanings.
* Student: Connected.
* Shaykh: Connected. What is the difference between connected and disconnected, so that I can judge it?
* Student: The disconnected (...).
* Shaykh: And other?
* Student: (...).
* Shaykh: Connected means: it is between equals, while disconnected is between disparates. That is the difference.
That is, the second is disconnected from the first, and that one is connected to it. When it is between equals, it is called connected.
There is also another, verbal difference: the connected is preceded by the interrogative hamza: "Is Zayd standing, or 'Amr?" In it the counterpart is mentioned, and the hamza precedes it, actually or implicitly. As for the disconnected, it is not mentioned between equals, nor does it require them, and it is not preceded by a hamza.
Here, the hamza precedes it: ﴿Aallahu khayrun⁠⁠, and it is also between equals: ﴿Aallahu khayrun, am ma yushrikun⁠⁠.

(with the ta' and the ya'), meaning: ﴿أَمَّا تُشْرِكُونَ﴾ ("or what you associate") or ﴿أَمَّا يُشْرِكُونَ﴾ ("or what they associate"). The author says: "(with the ta' and the ya', i.e., the people of Makkah are meant by it)." What comes next?

* Student: "(Are the gods better for their worshippers?) (...)."
* Shaykh: "(Is it the gods that are better for their worshippers? ﴿أَمَّنْ خَلَقَ السَّمَوَاتِ﴾ [Or He who created the heavens]). The author has estimated it again, a second time. What do you have?"
* Student: "The gods."
* Shaykh: "No, it is with a madd (elongation): ﴿آلآلهة﴾ [Are the gods]."
* Student: "It agrees with the verification (...)."
* Shaykh: "(Are the gods better for their worshippers, or He who created the heavens and the earth, and sent down water for you from the sky, and with it We caused to grow gardens of delight, whose trees you could never have made grow? Is there a god along with Allah?) and so on to the end."

There is an iltifat (shift of grammatical person) from the third person to the first person in ﴿فَأَنْبَتْنَا﴾. The author's statement, "Are the gods better, or Allah?", is clear, and on this reading ﴿أَمْ﴾ is also a connecting ﴿أم﴾ (muttasilah) with ﴿أَمَّنْ خَلَقَ﴾.

The verb ﴿خَلَقَ﴾ here means "brought into existence with measure (taqdir)", because creation (khalq) must be preceded by measuring, while ījād (bringing into existence) is more general. A person may bring a thing into existence without measuring it, but khalq necessarily involves measure.

As for ﴿أَمَّنْ خَلَقَ السَّمَوَاتِ وَالأَرْضَ﴾: some say that "the heavens" is not a direct object (maf'ūl bihi) but a maf'ūl muṭlaq (absolute object), because a direct object requires that what the verb acts upon exist before the action. Here the heavens did not exist before their creation. On this view, one says it is a maf'ūl and does not say "bihi". However, in reality this is one of the philosophical positions that has no real meaning, because "khalaqa" means "he brought the heavens into existence". The action falls upon the bringing into existence, and although the heavens did not exist before being brought into existence, the people who say a direct object must precede the verb are mistaken.

(I struck (zaydan) — Zayd precedes the striking. (I ate the food) — the food precedes the eating. (I made the food) — I transformed it from one state into another, and again the food precedes the making.)

But does the creation of the heavens (...) precede the creation? No. Therefore do not say "direct object", since the doer's action did not fall upon them, for they came into existence only by the doer's action. What do I say? It is simply the first object (maf'ūl awwal), with no bi, fī, ma' or li, because the objects (mafā'īl) are five, as you know: an object not transitive by a particle, and objects transitive by bi', fī, lām, or ma'. These are the objects.

But we say: in truth this is a forced interpretation (tamahhul), because the meaning of khalaqa indicates bringing into existence, and bringing into existence precedes the existent, since existence is attained by it. So there is no need for this forced interpretation. (...) "the heavens" is a direct object (...). We do not delete it.

* Student: "If the object (...)."
* Shaykh: "The absolute object is like: I struck a striking. They call this an absolute object. It is not transitive by bi', and not (...)."
* Student: "(...) it is like this."
* Shaykh: "It is like this, even if it does not match the verb exactly. That is, the absolute object is of the same meaning as the verb."

He says: ﴿أَمَّنْ خَلَقَ السَّمَوَاتِ وَالأَرْضَ﴾. The heavens are mentioned in the singular and the plural many times in the Qur'an, while the earth is mentioned only in the singular, except where Allah says: ﴿اللَّهُ الَّذِي خَلَقَ سَبْعَ سَمَوَاتٍ وَمِنَ الأَرْضِ مِثْلَهُنَّ﴾ [At-Talaq 12: Allah is He who created seven heavens and of the earth their like]. Otherwise the rest of the verses, even in this verse, mention it only in the singular, and He did not say "and of the earths their like". But it came in the Sunnah in the plural, and it was explained that there are seven.

﴿وَأَنزَلَ لَكُمْ مِنَ السَّمَاءِ مَاءً﴾: is "māʾ" here a maf'ūl or a maf'ūl bihi?

In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful. ﴿Ta-Sin. These are the verses of the Qur'an, and of a clear Book.﴾ [An-Naml 1], and so on to the end.

He says: this is "Sūrat an-Naml" (the Chapter of the Ant), and it was named so because of the mention of the ant in it. Naming the chapters happens for even a slight connection. For this reason Sūrat al-Baqarah was named after the cow (baqarah) mentioned in it. There is no objection to a chapter having several names for several reasons.

As for his statement that it is Makkan: the correct view regarding the Makkan and the Madinan is that the distinction between them is that whatever was revealed before the Hijrah is Makkan, and whatever was revealed after it is Madinan.

It is also said: the Makkan is what was revealed in Makkah, and the Madinan is what was revealed in Madinah. And it is said: the Makkan is what contains mention of the foundations (uṣūl), the foundations of Islam or of faith, and the Madinan is what contains mention of the branches (furū').

On the first view the criterion is time; on the second it is place; on the third it is subject matter.

But what the verifying scholars hold is that whatever came after the Hijrah is Madinan, and whatever came before it is Makkan. They have mentioned for this, in the principles of tafsir (uṣūl at-tafsīr), rules to which one refers.

As for the basmalah, its discussion has already been given several times, and we explained that the best way to estimate it is as a fitting verb that comes later.

That it be a verb, because that is the basic form of governing words (ʿawāmil). That it come later, for two benefits: the blessing of putting the name of Allah first, and the second, conveying exclusivity, i.e., "in the name of Allah" and not in the name of anyone else.

And that it be fitting, because it is more specific than the general. As for a verb, we said: because it is the basic form of governing words, and it is also more indicative of being newly originated (ḥudūth).

In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful. The estimate: "In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful, I recite." You may also estimate: "I recite in the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful," or: "My recitation is in the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful," or "In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful is my recitation."

But what we mentioned first is the more preferred. Shaykh al-Islam Ibn Taymiyyah pointed to its preference in the statement of the Messenger (ﷺ): "Whoever has not slaughtered, let him slaughter in the name of Allah." [Agreed upon by al-Bukhari (985) and Muslim (1960/1) from Jundub ibn Sufyan.] He mentioned it as a verb, and did not say: "Let his slaughter be..." He said: "let him slaughter in the name of Allah."

When He said: Allah the Exalted said: (﴿Ta-Sin﴾ — Allah knows best what He means by it.)

This is the path taken by the author and a group of scholars: regarding these letters of the alphabet found at the beginnings of some chapters, our position is to say: Allah knows best what He means by them.

It was previously stated in the nighttime tafsir lesson that the preferred view is that these letters are alphabetic, and that, by the requirement that the Qur'an is in clear Arabic, they have no meaning. We mentioned that this has been narrated from Mujahid, and that they are alphabetic letters with which Allah began, having no meaning. On this basis we affirm that they have no meaning, since they have no meaning. But they have a purpose: that this Qur'an, which left these eloquent and articulate people unable to match it, is made only from these alphabetic letters out of which their own speech is composed. That is, He did not bring new letters. For example, they might say: "By Allah, we do not know these letters!" He brought the same letters they speak with.

This is supported by the fact that every set of alphabetic letters is followed by mention of the Qur'an, except in two or similar chapters. These two chapters, such as ﴿Alif-Lam-Mim. Do people think they will be left alone?﴾ [Al-'Ankabut 1-2] and ﴿Alif-Lam-Mim. The Romans have been defeated﴾ [Ar-Rum 1-2], contain what indicates the Qur'an, such as the reports in His statement: ﴿The Romans have been defeated in the nearest land, but after their defeat they will overcome﴾ [Ar-Rum 2-3], and this is one of the characteristics of revelation.

And ﴿Do people think they will be left alone, saying "We believe" and not be tested?﴾ [Al-'Ankabut 2] also contains reports about those who passed before: ﴿We certainly tested those before them﴾ [Al-'Ankabut 3], and so on.

As for what the later deviating scholars claimed, that these letters indicate a miracle of the type of counting and calculation, they claimed that these alphabetic letters have their counterparts in the chapter that opens with them, and the total of this is divisible by nineteen. They claim this is the greatest proof that the Qur'an is the speech of Allah. They argue for this by saying that the first verse revealed, according to their claim, is the basmalah, and that it consists of nineteen letters, and that this is the meaning of His statement: ﴿Over it are nineteen﴾ [Al-Muddaththir 30], and that this nineteen is these letters. All of this is, may Allah protect us, false, does not hold together, is self-contradictory, and is not consistent. But they rejoiced in this computer that produced for them the number of letters and showed that their total is divisible.

We say: it is not impossible that Allah the Exalted intended this. It is not impossible. But we do not affirm that Allah intended this. Here there is a difference between affirming that this is a sign in the Qur'an, and saying: we do not say this.

First: because there is no miracle in this. Humans may hear a sermon, for example, or speech whose letters, when counted, divide by this number or by any number they like, and this is not a miracle.

Then, the basmalah is not the first thing revealed of the Qur'an. The first revealed was ﴿Read in the name of your Lord who created﴾ [Al-'Alaq 1]. Then, the letters of the basmalah are not, as they claim, nineteen, because the Qur'an was revealed to be recited or written? 

* Students: "Recited."
* Shaykh: "Recited. Its letters, as recited, are not so. Writing, as you know, is a craft. Perhaps, if it were assumed that writing in the time of the Messenger (ﷺ) and the time of the caliphs was not in this form, it could be otherwise, could it not? It could. Now there are some writing systems in some languages that make a vowel a letter, make one letter two, or abbreviate, making two letters one. The conclusion is that the Qur'an was not revealed in writing but was revealed to be recited, and there is no proof in that."

So we say: "Allah knows best what He means by it." This is one of the opinions on the matter.

The second view: they are symbols for specific things, as the later scholars held, or as some mention, that they are an indication of wars and battles that will occur at the end of time, and similar things.

The third view: it is said that they have no meaning. If it is objected, "How do we affirm that?" The answer is: this Qur'an was revealed in the language of the Arabs, and the language of the Arabs does not give these letters a meaning. But if we say they have no meaning, they have a purpose that appears, and Allah knows best, that He intended by them that.

He said: (﴿Ta-Sin﴾, that is: these verses; ﴿the verses of the Qur'an﴾: verses from it; ﴿and of a clear Book﴾: one that manifests truth from falsehood. He joined it with an added attribute: it is ﴿guidance﴾, that is, guiding from error.)

﴿Taka āyātu al-Qur'ān (these are the verses of the Qur'an)﴾: is the referent (al-mushār ilayhi) before or after?

* Student: "After."
* Shaykh: "The referent comes after and not before. This is one of the cases where the demonstrative refers to something that is later in both wording and rank, and this is permissible when evidence indicates it."

His statement ﴿āyātu al-Qur'ān (verses of the Qur'an)﴾ — he says: "verses from it." The author resorted to saying "verses from it" because if we took the apparent meaning of the verse ﴿verses of the Qur'an﴾, it would confine the Qur'an to these verses, would it not? ﴿These are the verses of the Qur'an﴾, meaning: this that he points to. It is known that this is not all the verses of the Qur'an, but only part of them.

It is permissible, for example, to keep the verse on its apparent meaning without any need for interpretation, and to say: ﴿These are the verses of the Qur'an﴾, where a part of a kind is pointed to with the demonstrative of the whole kind, as when you say, for example: "this is the human being," pointing to one man, or "this person," pointing to one man.

So the meaning is that pointing to part of a kind with the whole kind is valid and does not need interpretation, as the author said.

His statement ﴿wa-kitābin mubīn (and of a clear Book)﴾: he says "joined with an added attribute: it is guidance." Joined to what? ﴿kitābin﴾.

* Student: "To ﴿āyāt﴾."
* Shaykh: "To ﴿āyāt﴾, is that so? Is this statement correct?"
* Student: "It is correct: 'āyāt' is not written with a mark (...)."
* Another student: "﴿āyāt﴾ is nominative, ﴿kitābin﴾ is genitive..."
* Shaykh: "Yes, ﴿kitābin﴾ is genitive. So it is joined to ﴿al-Qur'ān﴾: ﴿These are the verses of the Qur'an, and [the verses] of a clear Book.﴾"

He described this Qur'an as both Qur'an and Book because it is recited and written. It is written in the Preserved Tablet, it is recited by tongues, and it is written in the mushafs too. Its writing precedes and follows it, but is its recitation later or earlier?

* Students: "Later."
* Shaykh: "Later, because after Allah spoke it and Jibril brought it down: ﴿Indeed, upon Us is its collection and its recitation. So when We recite it, follow its recitation﴾ [Al-Qiyamah 17-18]. Is 'Qur'an' a derived noun or a verbal noun?"
* Student: "Derived."
* Another student: "A verbal noun."
* Shaykh: "A verbal noun, because it is like al-ghufrān and ash-shukrān. It is a verbal noun of (qara'a, yaqra'u), meaning 'recited'."

It is also said that it means "gathering," because the letters qāf and rā' indicate gathering, and from this comes qaryah (village), because it is a gathering place of people.

In reality the Qur'an combines both attributes: it is recited, and it is also gathered.

As for His statement ﴿Kitāb (Book)﴾, it is the form fi'āl in the sense of maf'ūl, that is, written. The form fi'āl in the sense of maf'ūl occurs often in Arabic, like binā' meaning mabnī (built), ghirās meaning maghrūs (planted), and firāsh meaning mafrūsh (spread), and its examples are many.

It was named "Kitāb" for what we pointed to earlier.

His statement ﴿mubīn (clear)﴾: that is, manifesting truth from falsehood. The word mubīn: its verb is?

* Student: "Abāna."
* Shaykh: "Abāna. And abāna can be intransitive and transitive: it comes meaning 'made manifest', and it comes meaning 'became clear' (bāna)."

For this reason you will find the exegete sometimes explain mubīn as bayyin (clear), and in that explanation is it intransitive or transitive?

* Student: "Intransitive."
* Shaykh: "Intransitive. And sometimes he explains it as 'manifesting' (muzhir), in which case it is transitive. ﴿And indeed they were before that in clear error﴾ [Ali 'Imran 164]: what does mubīn mean?"
* Student: "Clear."
* Shaykh: "That is, clear: 'in clear error', so it is from intransitive abāna."

As for a verse like this, that the Qur'an is mubīn, it means "manifesting." Does its being manifesting entail that it is itself clear?

* Student: "Yes."
* Shaykh: "Yes, it entails it. Or we say that it is the use of a homonym (mushtarak) in two meanings, and the correct view is that this is permissible. This has passed with us before: is it permissible to use a homonym in two meanings? And we have already understood the homonym: it is a word whose form is one but whose meanings are many. This is the mushtarak, and it is so named because its meanings are shared in one word."

Commentary of Ibn 'Uthaymin (Tafsir al-Quran al-Karim) on surah 27, verse 56–64 (part 3 of 4):

The correct position regarding the mushtarak (homonym, a word with two meanings) is that it is permissible to use it in two meanings, on one condition or two conditions, which we mentioned two nights ago. And what are they? That there is no contradiction between the two meanings, and that the word is capable of bearing both of them. If it cannot bear them, or if there is a contradiction between them, then it is necessary that one of them be the intended meaning.

Here, for example, if we say that (مُبِين, mubin) is derived from (أَبَان, abana) intransitive, and from (أبان) transitive, is that permissible or not? It is permissible, even though this is a homonym. But when it is used in both meanings, it is used in a manner in which there is no contradiction. The Qur'an is clear (bayyin), and the Qur'an also makes things manifest (muzhir). In this case, is the indication of (mubin) that the Qur'an is clear a denotation of correspondence (dalalat al-mutabaqa) or a denotation of implication (dalalat al-iltizam)?

* Student: A denotation of correspondence.

* The Shaykh: A denotation of correspondence. If we take (mubin) as used in both meanings, then the denotation is one of correspondence. But if we say that (mubin) means (muzhir, making manifest), then its indication that it is clear falls under the denotation of implication.

﴿وَكِتَابٍ مُبِينٍ﴾ (and a clear Book): clear, making manifest the truth from falsehood. Is it general, or is it specific to what the Qur'an was revealed with?

Allah the Exalted says: ﴿وَنَزَّلْنَا عَلَيْكَ الْكِتَابَ تِبْيَانًا لِكُلِّ شَيْءٍ﴾ [An-Nahl 89] ("And We have sent down to you the Book as an exposition of all things"), and it is general over everything. But clarification may be a clarification of a thing in detail, and it may be a clarification of its causes and its methods, and you walk in them.

So the Qur'an in reality is an exposition of all things. Even in matters other than the legislative matters, it clarifies them, but it does not clarify their details, because those other matters are subject to time, place, people's understanding and their capacity. Rather, it mentions the causes and the methods, and you apply them yourself.

Hence, if someone says: How is this statement correct from you, when we do not see in the Qur'an the number of rak'ahs of prayer, nor do we see that they are five prayers, nor do we see the nisab (minimum thresholds) of zakat, nor the quantities (...) in it? So what is the answer?

* Student: We say: the Qur'an, Allah the Exalted says, as Ibn Mas'ud said: ﴿وَمَا آتَاكُمُ الرَّسُولُ فَخُذُوهُ وَمَا نَهَاكُمْ عَنْهُ فَانْتَهُوا﴾ [Al-Hashr 7] ("And whatever the Messenger gives you, take it; and whatever he forbids you, refrain from it"), so the verse includes what the Messenger clarified. Then also His saying: ﴿وَنَزَّلْنَا عَلَيْكَ الْكِتَابَ﴾ [An-Nahl 89], ﴿هُوَ الَّذِي أَنْزَلَ عَلَيْكَ الْكِتَابَ﴾ [Ali 'Imran 7], ﴿لِتُبَيِّنَ لِلنَّاسِ مَا نُزِّلَ إِلَيْهِمْ﴾ [An-Nahl 44], meaning...

* The Shaykh: ﴿وَأَنزَلْنَا إِلَيْكَ الذِّكْرَ لِتُبَيِّنَ لِلنَّاسِ مَا نُزِّلَ إِلَيْهِمْ﴾.

So the Qur'an indicates this through clarifying its cause and its method. So now we have the way of knowing this matter, which is what the Messenger (ﷺ) explained in the Sunnah, and this the Qur'an clarified. It is not necessary that the Qur'an must write down every detail. ﴿مَنْ يُطِعِ الرَّسُولَ فَقَدْ أَطَاعَ اللَّهَ﴾ [An-Nisa' 80] ("Whoever obeys the Messenger has obeyed Allah").

As for Ibn Mas'ud, whom the brother referred to, in the story of cursing the woman who plucks her eyebrows (al-naamisa) and the one who has them plucked (al-mutanammisa): a woman came to him and said: "We do not find this in the Book of Allah." He said: "Yes, it is in the Book of Allah," and then he recited this verse to her.[[Narrated by Ahmad in al-Musnad (3945), and al-Tabarani in al-Mu'jam al-Kabir (9466), from Ibn Mas'ud.]]

The summary is that the Qur'an is clarifying of all things, but the clarification may be detailed, and this exists in some matters, as in the inheritance shares, for example, in the divorces. You will find nothing deviates from this except very few issues, and yet their clarification is present upon reflection, isn't it?

That is, the detail of the fara'id (obligatory inheritance shares) is a detail from which nothing deviates, except one issue, which is the grandmother (al-jadda). It is not mentioned in the Qur'an, but the Sunnah brought it. As for everything else, even the disputed issues such as al-mushtarakah and al-'Umariyyatayn, we find that they exist in the Qur'an, and like the grandfather and the siblings, we find their clarification exists in the Qur'an, but it requires reflection.

Allah the Exalted said: (﴿وَكِتَابٍ مُبِينٍ﴾ making manifest the truth from falsehood; it is conjoined with the addition of an attribute, it is ﴿هُدًى﴾).

"With the addition of an attribute": where is the attribute?

* Student: ﴿مُبِينٍ﴾.

* The Shaykh: ﴿مُبِينٍ﴾.

Then he said: (it is ﴿هُدًى﴾). The author supplied (it is) to show us the i'rab (grammatical analysis) of (hudan), so according to his supposition, (hudan) is the predicate of an omitted subject. The estimate: it is (﴿هُدًى﴾, i.e., guiding one from misguidance).

It is well known that (hudan, هدى) is a verbal noun (masdar), and that (hadin, هادٍ) is an active participle (ism fa'il). So the author here explained the masdar with the active participle, and in his explanation there is consideration, because it is better to keep the masdar in its original form, for two reasons:

The first reason: converting the active participle into a masdar is more emphatic. When you say: "So-and-so is 'adl (justice)," and "So-and-so is 'adil (just)," which of them is more emphatic?

* The students: 'Adl.
