For this reason, people come from other lands saying: "We do not know how to perform wudu', we do not know how to pray, and we do not know the prayer times," and yet it is written on their identity papers that they are Muslim.

The third category: the Muslim who is not a believer. This is common in our lands: they are Muslims, but they are not believers.

The evidence for this is that the deeds or the morals that are tied to faith are found lacking in many of these people. "None of you believes until he loves for his brother what he loves for himself." Is this found in abundance?

* A student: It is rare.

* The Shaykh: It is scarce. "Whoever cheats is not of us"[[Narrated by Muslim (102 / 164) and al-Tirmidhi (1315) from Abu Hurayrah, and the wording is al-Tirmidhi's.]]. Is the absence of cheating found in abundance? It is scarce. "A man does not believe whose neighbor is not safe from his evil"[[Narrated by al-Bukhari (6016) from Abu Shurayh.]], scarce. Proceed on this basis. "The slanderer will not enter Paradise." Is slander found in abundance? So the point is that faith among Muslims today is scarce, Islam is abundant, and mere submission is more abundant still.

* A student: He will not enter Paradise (...).

* The Shaykh: Yes, indeed, he enters Paradise, because the Muslim in the legal sense, though faith has not entered his heart, his final destiny is Paradise, but he does not enter it immediately... He has sins, and either he will be punished for them, or he will be pardoned.

* The student: What is the difference (...)?

* The Shaykh: The difference between them is that the Muslim has faith, whereas the hypocrite (munafiq) has no faith at all. The hypocrite's heart is empty of faith, and we seek refuge in Allah.

* The student: Is he (the Muslim) of higher rank, O Shaykh?

* The Shaykh: The mustaslim is higher than the hypocrite, yes, because the mustaslim genuinely has, in relation to Islam, something real, but he lacks what the Muslim has, who implements the laws. He is generally ignorant.

* A student: (...).

* The Shaykh: Yes, meaning that he (...) submitted, he realizes Islam.

* The thirteenth benefit: His saying ﴿Our signs﴾ indicates that the signs are many, not one. They are divided into what? Two types: cosmic signs (kawniyyah) and legal signs (shar'iyyah). What the messengers brought and what the scriptures revealed are legal signs, and what events indicate, or what consists of events, is among the cosmic signs. Allah the Exalted said: ﴿And among His signs are the night and the day, and the sun and the moon﴾ [Fussilat 37]. What are these?

* Students: Cosmic.

* The Shaykh: Cosmic. And He, the Exalted, said: ﴿And when Our clear signs are recited to them, those who disbelieve say of the truth when it has come to them, "This is obvious magic"﴾ [al-Ahqaf 7]. These are the legal signs.

The reason they are called signs is that they point to Allah. We do not say "they point to their Creator" meaning the legal ones; they point to Allah.

The cosmic signs point to the Creator in terms of power, wisdom, and sovereignty, and other meanings of lordship. The legal signs point to the One who sent them down in terms of justice and reform, because all the laws, not only the law of Islam which was brought by Muhammad, all of them fight corruption and establish righteousness. But our law is distinguished from others in that it takes into account the general public interests (...).

Commentary of Ibn 'Uthaymin (Tafsir al-Quran al-Karim) on surah 27, verse 76–81 (part 1 of 5):

Then Allah the Exalted said: (﴿Indeed, this Quran relates to the Children of Israel﴾, those present in the time of our Prophet, ﴿most of that about which they differ﴾ [An-Naml 76]. That is: by clarifying what they mentioned in its correct form, which would end their disagreement if they acted upon it and submitted).

﴿Indeed, this Quran relates﴾: ﴿this Quran﴾ means the one revealed to the Prophet ﷺ.

The word "Quran" (qur'an) may be either a verbal noun in the sense of a passive participle, or an active participle.

The first meaning: qur'an is a verbal noun in the sense of the passive participle, because it is read (maqru'), that is, it is recited. It is also maqru' from qar' meaning gathering. So it is gathered and it is recited, in the sense of gathering and recitation.

As for it being a verbal noun: the pattern fu'lan comes as a verbal noun, like al-ghufran (forgiveness) and ash-shukran (gratitude). So it is in reality a verbal noun in the sense of the passive participle, or an absolute verbal noun, like al-ghufran and ash-shukran.

(...) It is an active participle, in the sense that it comprises the rulings of the earlier books (...). This is a third aspect: that qur'an means "comprehensive", and Allah the Exalted has mentioned that the Quran is a guardian (muhaymin) over the earlier books.

As for His saying: ﴿relates to the Children of Israel﴾, al-qass means speaking about a thing; speaking about a thing is qass. So this Quran ﴿relates to the Children of Israel﴾ those present in the time of the Messenger, peace be upon him. What does it relate to them? ﴿most of that about which they differ﴾, and examples of this will come, God willing.

He said: ﴿relates to the Children of Israel﴾. ﴿Children of Israel﴾: are the males among them or the females as well?
* Students: (...).
* The Shaykh: Yes. Because when "sons" refers to a tribe, it includes males and females; and when it does not refer to a tribe, it is specific to males. So if someone says, for example: this is an endowment for the sons of Muhammad, Muhammad being a person, this is an endowment for the sons of Muhammad; who is it specific to?
* Students: The males.
* The Shaykh: The males. But if the whole tribe is called the sons of Muhammad, it is for males and females. Banu Tamim: if a person endows for the Banu Tamim at the time when Tamim existed before they became a tribe, at the time of the forefather, who is Tamim, it is specific to males; and after they became a tribe, it is general to males and females. So here, is Banu Isra'il meant as the tribe or not? Yes, the tribe, so it includes male and female.

Israel is Ya'qub ibn Ishaq ibn Ibrahim. So they are cousins of the Arabs, because the father of the Arabs is Isma'il ibn Ibrahim, and their father is Ya'qub ibn Ishaq ibn Ibrahim; that is, their grandfather Ishaq, who is the brother of Isma'il. These people are attributed to their father. And Isra'il means "servant of Allah" ('abd Allah).

Some people today say: how can we name the Jewish state Israel? How can it be named after Israel? What is the answer?

The answer is that this is an attribution to their father. Do we not call the Arabs Quraysh? Attributed to whom? To their forefather Quraysh. We do not say "Banu Quraysh"; we say Quraysh. So here the tribe is named after its father. Although there is no doubt that the more fitting thing is to name them by what Allah named them, namely Banu Isra'il. Moreover, we also doubt that these present-day Jews are from the Children of Israel; we do not know, perhaps they are from Europe and other lands that are not of the Children of Israel.

But in any case, just as the Arabs today consider Arabness to be by the Arabic language, and say: whoever speaks Arabic is an Arab, even if his origin is non-Arab, those people likewise say: whoever speaks Hebrew is an Israeli, even if he is not of the Children of Israel. For this reason we now affirm that the group now called Jews are not all from the Children of Israel; rather they are attributed to those people on the basis that the common link between them is language.

﴿relates to the Children of Israel most of that about which they differ﴾: ﴿most of that which﴾: He did not say "all that which"; He said ﴿most of that about which they differ﴾. So what is excluded by "most"? What is excluded by "most"?
* A student: The minority.
* The Shaykh: The minority is excluded. That is because the Quran relates to them only what has benefit; as for what has no benefit, it does not relate it. For the Quran, as you know, is guidance, and everything in it has meaning and purpose. So a thing with no benefit in it is not related to them, even if they differed about it. For example, they differed about the color of the dog of the People of the Cave; is there any added benefit in it? There is no benefit. Likewise they differed about many things of this kind which the Quran did not relate. The cow they were commanded to slaughter: they differed about whose it was, and it was said: it belonged to a man who was dutiful to his son, and it was said: it belonged to an old man, and many other things were said. But is there any benefit in this? No, there is no benefit in it. So ﴿most of that about which they differ﴾: that which has benefit in mentioning it, this Quran relates, so that it may judge between them.
﴿relates to the Children of Israel most of that about which they differ﴾: for what purpose does it relate that?

So that they would believe in the Quran; because when this Quran comes relating to them what preceded of what they did, and the Prophet ﷺ was known not to have studied the Torah nor to have studied with the Jews, it becomes known that what he brought is true. This is the wisdom in His saying: ﴿relates to the Children of Israel﴾, although this narration is for the Children of Israel and for others; but the Children of Israel have knowledge of the Book that the Arabs do not have, so it was made clear to them in order to establish the proof against them.
* A student: (...).
* The Shaykh: It is establishing the proof against them, because they know what the Arabs do not know.
* The student: (...).
* The Shaykh: Yes; because they have their book and they know. So when this Quran comes down judging between them and relating to them what they used to differ about, this shows that it is true.
* A student: The stories (al-qasas) (...).
* The Shaykh: Al-qasas is a verbal noun, and qasas is a verbal noun, and al-qisas is the plural of qissa.
* The student: (...).
* The Shaykh: (...) in the sense of the plural of qissa. It is only suitable in the sense of qass. ﴿We relate to you the best of stories﴾ [Yusuf 3].
* The student: (...).
* The Shaykh: ﴿And He is Allah in the heavens and on the earth﴾ [Al-An'am 3].
* The student: ﴿And He is Allah in the heavens and on the earth; He knows your secret and your open﴾ (...).
* The Shaykh: (...).
(...) ﴿Indeed, this Quran relates to the Children of Israel most of that about which they differ﴾.

He said: ﴿most of that about which they differ﴾, meaning: not all of it. And what it relates to them is what had benefit for them and for others. Among that is what it related to them concerning Jesus; for Jesus, as you know, was differed about by the Children of Israel: some denied him and rejected him and claimed his mother was an adulteress, and killed him; and some exaggerated about him and said he is the son of God, or that he is God. Likewise their disagreement about the Sabbath and other matters which Allah related to us in the Quran. So the Quran related most of that about which they differ, and what has no benefit in relating, it left out.

* * *

Allah the Exalted said: (﴿And indeed it﴾ -that is, the Quran- ﴿is guidance﴾ from misguidance ﴿and mercy for the believers﴾ [An-Naml 77] from punishment).

﴿Indeed it is guidance﴾: this sentence is emphasized with "indeed" (inna) and the lam, ﴿indeed it is guidance﴾. Guidance (huda) means indication; the Quran is guidance, that is, an indication, but only the believers benefit from it, as He restricted it in His saying: ﴿for the believers﴾.

His saying: ﴿and mercy﴾: that is, a cause of it, a cause of mercy; because when a person is guided by it, he attains the mercy of Allah the Glorified and Exalted, so it is a mercy, but for the believers. The restriction to the believers is because they are the ones who benefit from it.

Allah has mentioned in the Quran that it is guidance for the worlds, and that it is guidance for the believers and the God-fearing. The reconciliation between them is that in the general case it means: indicative and a place of indication; and in the restricted case: no one benefits from it and is granted success in being guided by it except those to whom it is restricted. Is this verse of the unrestricted or the restricted?
* A student: Of the restricted.
* Another student: The restricted.
* The Shaykh: (...).
* The student: ﴿for the believers﴾.
* The Shaykh: ﴿for the believers﴾, yes indeed.

So ﴿guidance﴾ is this knowledge, and ﴿mercy﴾ is action and success, because it is the cause of mercy.

* * *

(﴿Indeed your Lord will judge between them﴾, as with others, on the Day of Resurrection, ﴿by His judgment﴾, that is His justice, ﴿and He is the Mighty﴾, the Overpowering, ﴿the Knowing﴾ [An-Naml 78] of what He judges, so no one can oppose Him, just as the disbelievers opposed His prophets in this world).

He said: ﴿Indeed your Lord will judge between them﴾, that is, between the Children of Israel, because the context concerns them; for this reason He said: ﴿most of that about which they differ﴾, and those who differ need someone to judge between them as to who is correct. So Allah judged between them in this world, and He will judge between them on the Day of Resurrection. By what did He judge between them in this world? By what He revealed in the Quran, as is derived from His saying: ﴿Indeed, this Quran relates to the Children of Israel﴾. And He will judge between them on the Day of Resurrection with the just judgment: ﴿Indeed your Lord will judge between them by His judgment﴾.

The author's words: (﴿will judge between them﴾, as with others, on the Day of Resurrection): it is not necessarily the case that this judgment is on the Day of Resurrection; it may also be in this world, for judgment occurs on the Day of Resurrection and also occurs in this world. He has judged between them in this world by what He revealed in His Book, and He distinguished those who are upon truth from those who are upon falsehood among the Children of Israel, and this is a kind of judgment. On the Day of Resurrection He will judge between them with a judgment that results in reward; reward is either by punishment or by beneficence.

The upshot is that the saying of Allah, Mighty and Majestic: ﴿Indeed your Lord will judge between them﴾ does not necessarily mean the Day of Resurrection as the author restricted it; for judgment that occurs in the Hereafter also occurs in this world.

The author's words: (as with others) indicate that judgment on the Day of Resurrection is not only between the Children of Israel but between them and others. This is undoubted, and there is no need to supply it; since the context is about the Children of Israel, "others" should not be inserted into this verse, for if you insert "as with others", it becomes like an interjection upon the Quran, meaning that the situation requires it but it was not explained. So we say: there is no need to supply "as with others"; rather He judges between them, and this verse here does not address general judgment; general judgment is derived from other verses.

﴿By His judgment﴾: that is, by His justice. Here He attributed the judgment to Allah the Glorified and Exalted for two reasons:
The first: it is a judgment that includes justice. The second: it is a judgment that cannot be reversed, unlike the judgment of others, which is subject to defect from two sides: it may be unjust, and it may be unenforced. As for the judgment of Allah, it includes both: justice, and the second?
* Students: That it is not reversed.
* The Shaykh: That it is not reversed; rather it must be carried out.

﴿Indeed your Lord will judge by His judgment﴾: (that is, by His justice). This is a part or aspect of what is indicated by His saying: ﴿by His judgment﴾, since it indicates the two matters we mentioned.

﴿by His judgment and He is the Mighty, the Knowing﴾. ﴿The Mighty﴾: the author says: (the Overpowering).
* Student: (...).
* The Shaykh: This you already see (...).
* The student: (...).
* The Shaykh: No (...).

﴿The Mighty﴾: he says: (the Overpowering). It has already passed with us in the explanation of the Beautiful Names that "the Mighty" has three meanings. What are they?
* A student: The might of subjugation and the might of...
* The Shaykh: of decree.
* A student: Of decree, and the might of inaccessibility.
* The Shaykh: And the might of inaccessibility; and that "the Mighty" means the one who is exempt from every deficiency, to whom no deficiency reaches, and that He is overpowering, and that He is of great power. The author and others often interpret "the Mighty" as "the Overpowering", because it is its most apparent meaning, and because it sometimes occurs in a context that requires that overpowering be more specific to Him than to others.

﴿Indeed your Lord will judge between them by His judgment, and He is the Mighty, the Knowing﴾ (by what He judges).

These two matters are among the conditions of judgment; for whoever judges without knowledge, his judgment suffers from defect, does it not? And whoever judges without might, his judgment also suffers from defect.

The first, which is the absence of knowledge, causes a defect in the judgment in hitting the correct outcome, because one who judges without knowledge hits the correct outcome only by coincidence.

The second: overpowering. If might is lacking, a defect occurs in the judgment, not in terms of correctness, but in terms of enforcement; for if one lacks might and issues a ruling, it may be opposed, so He said: ﴿and He is the Mighty, the Knowing﴾ to make both matters clear.

If someone says: why is "the Mighty" placed before "the Knowing", when knowledge precedes in the logical order, since one knows, then judges, then enforces?

We say: because the context here requires showing the strength of Allah's judgment, and that this judgment must be enforced because it proceeds from the Mighty. And what did we say about the purpose of "the Mighty, the Knowing"?
* A student: Where?
* The Shaykh: I mean, the wisdom in His ending: ﴿Indeed your Lord will judge between them by His judgment, and He is the Mighty, the Knowing﴾?
* A student: With "the Knowing" (...) without knowledge, (...) his judgment is by coincidence.
* The Shaykh: His hitting the correct outcome is by...
* The student: His hitting it is by coincidence.
* The Shaykh: Yes.
* The student: And if he is knowing but without might, his judgment is not enforced (...).
* The Shaykh: Then the defect becomes a defect in judgment in the loss of both this and that (...). So the defect now, in judgment, is either from the loss of knowledge or from the loss of might. In the loss of knowledge, the defect occurs in correctness, because the ignorant one who judges hits the right outcome by coincidence. And in the loss of might? A defect in enforcement; because the weak one who lacks might is not enforced. Therefore judgment requires both of the two qualities, might and knowledge.

We raised an objection: placing "the Mighty" before "the Knowing", although might relates to enforcement, and enforcement comes after judgment, whereas knowledge relates to judgment, and judgment precedes enforcement. So what is the wisdom in placing might before knowledge here?

We said: because the context requires it, the context of enforcement and decree; so it was appropriate to place might before knowledge.

﴿And He is the Mighty, the Knowing﴾. He said: (so no one can oppose Him, just as the disbelievers opposed His prophets in this world).

Judgment in this world, as the author said, is opposed. What is meant is the legislative judgment, which is opposed; as for the cosmic judgment, it cannot be opposed, neither in this world nor in the Hereafter; no one can oppose Allah. Legislative judgment can be opposed in this world, as is common, indeed most people oppose the legislative judgment in this world; for among the children of Adam, nine hundred and ninety-nine out of every thousand all oppose the legislative judgment, and only one in a thousand conforms to it. (...).
* A student: (...) is there evidence for it?
* The Shaykh: Yes, there is evidence: the hadith of Adam, that Allah calls to him on the Day of Resurrection and says: "O Adam!" He says: "Here I am, at Your service and pleasure!" He says: "Bring out from your offspring a group for the Fire." He says: "What is the group for the Fire?" He says: "Out of every thousand, nine hundred and ninety-nine; and one for Paradise, and these are for the Fire."[[Agreed upon; al-Bukhari (3348) and Muslim (222/379), from the hadith of Abu Sa'id al-Khudri.]] This is the text.

Ibn al-Qayyim says in the Nuniyya:
O commodity of the Most Merciful, none attains it
among a thousand except one, not two.
Yes indeed, is that clear?

* * *

He said: ﴿So rely upon Allah﴾ [An-Naml 79]: (﴿So rely upon Allah﴾, trust in Him ﴿Indeed you are upon the clear truth﴾, that is, the manifest religion, so the outcome is yours with victory over the disbelievers).

Commentary of Ibn 'Uthaymin (Tafsir al-Quran al-Karim) on surah 27, verses 76–81 (part 2 of 5):

﴿So rely upon Allah﴾: The address is to the Prophet ﷺ, and the command here is obligatory. Reliance (tawakkul) is half of the religion. Allah the Exalted says: ﴿So worship Him and rely upon Him﴾ [Hud 123], and He says: ﴿You alone we worship, and You alone we ask for help﴾ [al-Fatihah 5]. There is no seeking of help except with reliance. For this reason they say: the religion is worship and tawakkul. Worship is what a person does; tawakkul is what he relies upon Allah with, relying upon Allah, glorified and exalted is He.

Here the author said: (﴿Rely upon Allah﴾: trust in Him). Others have explained it as: tawakkul and reliance upon Allah together with trust (thiqah). So there must be both reliance and trust, and through both tawakkul is realised. For you may rely upon someone without trusting him. For example, you rely upon a person to buy something for you, yet you do not trust him. Or you may trust a person in his honesty, but not rely upon him because of his weakness. The first is either because of his weakness or his treachery.

As for Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, it is obligatory for you to rely upon Him while trusting in Him. Tawakkul cannot be realised except this way. So tawakkul upon Allah is: relying upon Him together with trust in Him. Both things are necessary: reliance and trust.

The command to rely upon Allah does not contradict taking the means (al-asbab). Taking valid means that have real effects on their results is part of it. The Messenger ﷺ was without doubt the leader of those who rely upon Allah, yet he would still take the means by which benefits are obtained and harms are averted. He ate, drank and dressed, and he also took what protects against harm. Indeed, at Uhud he wore two coats of mail [[Abu Dawud (2590) from the hadith of al-Sa'ib ibn Yazid from a man, and Ibn Majah (2806) from the hadith of al-Sa'ib ibn Yazid.]], meaning he wore two coats of armour. All of this strengthens the means by which harms are averted.

So reliance upon Allah does not mean that you do not take the means to success. Rather, take the means, while relying upon Allah, glorified and exalted is He, and trusting Him that this means will benefit you. A group of people from Yemen once performed Hajj without provisions and said: "We are performing Hajj, and we are the ones who rely upon Allah." What was said to them? It was said to them: "You are the ones who depend on others (mutawakkilun)," meaning those who neglect the means.

So there is a difference between tawakkul and tawakkul's counterfeit, tawakkul (sic: tawakkul versus tawakkul-in-name). The person who wants things to come to him without taking their means is a mutawakkil in this false sense, and he has no intellect. Even intellect he lacks. Do animals, insects and others take the means or not? They take the means, even though the One who provided for them and undertook their provision is Allah, glorified and exalted is He: ﴿There is no creature on earth but that its provision is upon Allah﴾ [Hud 6]. Yet you find them taking the means.

Indeed, the Messenger ﷺ said: «If you were to rely upon Allah with the reliance due to Him, He would provide for you as He provides for the birds: they go out hungry in the morning and return full at evening» [[al-Tirmidhi (2344) and Ibn Majah (4164) from the hadith of Umar ibn al-Khattab.]]. He did not say: they stay in their nests and their provision comes to them. He said: «They go out» (taghdu), meaning they go off in the morning, «hungry» (khimasan), meaning empty-bellied, «and return» (tarhu) at the end of the day, «full» (bitanan), their bellies filled.

So the person who truly relies upon Allah is the one who takes the beneficial means.

As for means that do not benefit, taking them is a kind of shirk. Whoever takes a means that is not beneficial, meaning one whose benefit is not shown by sense perception (hiss) or by the Sharia, has committed a kind of shirk. For this reason, amulets (tama'im), incantations (ta'awwudhat), and tiwalah (love charms), and similar things that people claim work when they do not work, the Prophet ﷺ made them shirk [[Abu Dawud (3883) and Ibn Majah (3530) from the hadith of Abdullah ibn Mas'ud, with the wording: «Indeed, incantations, amulets and tiwalah are shirk.»]]. We state this principle: whoever takes a means that is not beneficial, meaning its benefit is not indicated by the Sharia or by sense perception, or, if you prefer, by the Sharia or by divine decree (qadar), then he is a mushrik. How is he a mushrik? What is the basis of his being a mushrik?

He has affirmed a means which Allah did not make a means. Thus he has become a partner with Allah in His decree, because the one who decrees the means and makes things means is Allah. This belongs to Allah. So when you say: this is a means, and it is not a means, you have associated (ashraktu) with Allah and made yourself a partner with Allah, glorified and exalted is He.

* Student: Your saying, "(...) for the obligation" — is this command for obligation?
* Shaykh: Yes, for obligation or recommendation. What is at the level of sufficiency is obligatory, and what exceeds it is recommended.
* Student: (...) takes a forbidden means.
* Shaykh: Yes.
* Student: Meaning he takes a forbidden means (...). Is that considered shirk?
* Shaykh: No, that is not considered shirk, because this means is sensory. Being a means of provision is a sensory matter, but it is forbidden by the Sharia.
Now, for example: the one who deals in riba (usury), has he taken a means that by decree achieves profit for him?
* Student: Yes.
* Shaykh: I ask you: the usurer has taken a means that, by decree, yields profit for him. A person known (...) takes twelve. Is this a means of profit or not? But is it a legal means or a decreed means?
* Student: (...).
* Shaykh: Decreed or not? What do you say?
* Students: (...).
* Shaykh: Decreed. Allah did not permit it by the Sharia, but when it occurs we know that He permitted it by decree. This is not a kind of shirk. It is not shirk, because it is a decreed means. It is only forbidden because it is prohibited by the Sharia.
* Student: O Shaykh (...), regarding the saying of Allah, the Exalted: ﴿And He is the Mighty, the All-Knowing﴾. No one can oppose Him, but the ruling He issued is not one that someone can oppose.
* Shaykh: No, His intent is in all His rulings.
* Student: Shaykh, here the ruling, for example, is in the Hereafter.
* Shaykh: It applies to the Hereafter and to this world, according to the correct view. The verse is general: in the Hereafter and in this world.
* Student: (...) the context of the verse, it is about the Hereafter and this world (...) the context of the verse.
* Shaykh: The context of the verse, what is the context of the verse? ﴿Indeed, this Qur'an narrates to the Children of Israel most of that over which they differ. And indeed, it is guidance and mercy for the believers. Indeed, your Lord will judge between them by His ruling, and He is the Mighty, the All-Knowing﴾ [al-Naml 76–78]. Among the things Allah related to us in the Qur'an is that He judged between the Children of Israel. The Children of Israel differed over matters, for example their differences concerning the Messiah, peace be upon him, and other things. Allah judged between them by the Qur'an. The ruling that results in reward and recompense will be on the Day of Resurrection. So the ruling here, in this world, is that by which truth is distinguished from falsehood. As for the Hereafter, it is what brings about reward or punishment.
* Student: O Shaykh, is it correct to say: some people rely (a'timad) upon you to accomplish this work?
* Shaykh: Yes, there is no objection, because reliance upon real means is permissible, provided one believes that it is a means and not independently effective.
* Student: O Shaykh (...) the Children of Israel after (...) how (...)?
* Shaykh: No, He judges between them by saying that these are correct and these are mistaken. He explains that the Jews erred, and the Christians also erred, and the moderate Christians were correct.
* Student: The common people's saying: "Wakkala Allah."
* Shaykh: "Wakkala Allah."
* Students: (...) "Wakkala Allah."
* Shaykh: Apparently, the meaning of "Wakkala Allah" for them is: rely upon Allah. It does not mean: make Allah your deputy (wakil). Or the meaning of "make Allah your deputy" is that Allah becomes a witness over you, or does it imply that my management of your affairs is like Allah's management of your affairs? Without doubt, that is not what is intended.
* Student: (...) "Tawakkalt 'ala Allah."
* Shaykh: Yes, if they mean "rely upon Allah," meaning: rely upon Allah and make Him your trustee (wakil) over me. Now, if we want to look at the apparent wording: "I am to you in the position of Allah." The common people do not mean this at all. They do not mean this, not at all. They mean "Wakkala Allah," meaning: make Him a witness over me. Yes. Or the meaning of "wakkala" is: rely upon Allah.
* Student: (...).
* Shaykh: (...) "'ala Allah" has no problem. This is correct and good. Also "Allah wakkalaka" (Allah has made you His deputy) has no problem.
* Student: (...).
* Shaykh: And "ittakil 'alayhi" (rely upon Him) has no problem.
* Student: What the reports indicate of (...).
* Shaykh: No, because Allah is without doubt the one who appoints (wakkala), and whatever happens happens by Allah's decree. What has occurred does not need (...) Allah's decree. "Allah wakkalaka" means He has made you His deputy, in the wording you spoke, for example.
* Student: (...).
* Shaykh: There is no problem, on condition that it is truly something in which one can be relied upon (...).

So, what is tawakkul upon Allah? It is reliance upon Allah together with trust in Him. It is not mere reliance, but reliance with trust. Trust is not complete without hope (raja'). Then we have said that tawakkul does not contradict taking the means that Allah has made means, by Sharia or by decree.

﴿So rely upon Allah. Indeed, you are upon the clear truth﴾ (i.e., the evident religion).

The commentator (al-Mu'allaq) explained ﴿the truth﴾ as the religion, and ﴿clear﴾ as evident (bayyin).

This is not good, because is there not truth and falsehood within religion? Is that not so? For this reason He said: ﴿That He may make it prevail over all religion﴾ [al-Tawbah 33], and this refers to false religion. The religion of truth prevails over all religion, meaning over false religion. So the author's explanation of al-Haqq (the truth) as the religion is without doubt deficient. Rather, al-Haqq here means that which is established by the truthfulness of its reports and the justice of its rulings. This is the meaning of al-Haqq: it is established, through the truthfulness of its reports and the justice of its rulings.

As for His saying al-Mubin (the clear), the author explained it as bayyin. In this, did he take (abana) as transitive or intransitive?
* Student: Transitive.
* Shaykh: No, intransitive. He took it as intransitive, because (bana yabynu fahuwa bayn) and (abana yubinu fahuwa mubin).

Could it not be here in the sense of muzhir (one who makes manifest)?
Answer: No. Bayyin is more appropriate here than muzhir. This truth is clear and manifest.

In His saying: ﴿Indeed, you are upon the clear truth﴾ there is a confirmation of the Messenger ﷺ, that he remain upon what he is upon, relying upon Allah, blessed and exalted is He. For when a person knows that he is upon the truth, he stands firm and his feet become steady. If he is doubtful or hesitant, he does not stand firm. So He commanded him to rely upon Him, and He showed him that what he was upon of this religion is truth, clear and evident.

The turning away of these people from it, the turning away of those who turn away, does it detract from its being clear?
* Student: No.
* Shaykh: It does not detract, because the affliction does not come from the Qur'an. The affliction comes from them. For this reason He followed it with His saying: ﴿Indeed, you cannot make the dead hear, nor can you make the deaf hear the call﴾, to the end of the verse [al-Naml 80].

So, in summary: Allah commanded His Prophet to rely upon Allah, and He explained to him the state he was in, and that this religion is what? And that this religion is the clear truth: ﴿Indeed, you are upon the clear truth﴾.

Then, glorified and exalted is He, explained that the turning away of those who turn away from it is not due to a deficiency in the explanation and manifestation of this religion, but due to a deficiency in those who turn away. Because the religion, in relation to them, did not meet a suitable locus (mahall). You know that when a matter does not meet a suitable locus, it does not take effect. When it does not meet a receptive locus, it does not take hold. A person may recite a verse over a sick person and he is cured, and recite it over another sick person with the same illness and he is not cured, because the first patient is receptive and believes in its effect, while the second does not believe in its effect, so it does not benefit him. In matters there must be receptivity, meaning a locus that accepts the thing. If it does not accept it, then it cannot suit it. This applies to legal matters, and likewise to matters of decree. If we were to implant a heart into a person and his body rejected it, would it remain? It does not remain; he dies. Or if we implanted a kidney into a person and his body rejected it, it would not remain; it would rot and he would die. So every thing must have a locus that is receptive to it. If it does not accept it, there is no place for it. Those who turned away from the Qur'an, this does not mean there is a deficiency in the Qur'an. The Qur'an is true, clear and evident, but the affliction comes from them.

Allah the Exalted said: ﴿Indeed, you﴾, meaning: (the clear religion. So the final outcome is yours, with victory over the disbelievers. Then He struck examples for them with the dead, the deaf and the blind, and said: ﴿Indeed, you cannot make the dead hear﴾).
* Student: It is derived from the verse that the dead do not hear.
* Shaykh: We have not yet reached it. We have not reached it now, nor have we reached the benefits.

He says: (He struck for them examples with the dead, the deaf and the blind, and said: ﴿Indeed, you cannot make the dead hear﴾). This is an example, as the author said, because the Messenger ﷺ did not go out to the graveyards calling the people of the graves, so that it could be said to him: ﴿Indeed, you cannot make the dead hear﴾. Rather, he called the living. The living divided into two groups regarding this call:

One group accepted it and was reassured by it. Such a person is alive, and for this reason Allah said in the Qur'an: ﴿That it may warn whoever is alive and the word may take effect against the disbelievers﴾ [Ya-Sin 70]. Against whom? Against the dead?
* Student: ﴿Against the disbelievers﴾.
* Shaykh: ﴿Against the disbelievers.﴾ This shows that the meaning of life here is life of the heart, the life of faith, not physical life. Because contrasting one thing with another clarifies its meaning. ﴿That it may warn whoever is alive﴾: physical life?
* Students: No, the heart.
* Shaykh: No. If it were physical life, He would have said: "and the word may take effect against the dead." But He said: ﴿against the disbelievers﴾. From this we learn that every instance of life in such a context means life of the heart, not life of the body.
* Student: (...).
* Shaykh: Yes.

﴿Indeed, you cannot make the dead hear﴾: ﴿the dead﴾ is the plural of dead (mayyit), and what is meant here is the dead of heart. Or we may say that what is meant is the dead of body, and it is then a comparison: those whom you call and who do not believe are like the dead. If you came to a dead person and said: "O so-and-so, worship Allah, believe in the Messenger, peace be upon him, and fear Allah," would he benefit? He would not benefit, like a stone that does not benefit. There is no doubt that the Messenger, peace be upon him, established the truth against those thrown into the well of Badr, and said to them: «Have you found what your Lord promised to be true? For I have found what my Lord promised me to be true» and he said: «You are not better at hearing what I say than they are» [[Muslim (2874/77) from the hadith of Anas ibn Malik. The hadith is agreed upon: al-Bukhari (3976) and Muslim (2875/78) from the hadith of Abu Talha, with a similar meaning.]]. But this was by way of rebuke, not by way of invitation, because these people, however the case, could not answer a call in that state. For this reason, the disbeliever does not benefit, in terms of reward, from what he hears at his grave of recitation or remembrance.

By this we know the innovation of those who introduced recitation at graves or upon graves, thinking that the dead benefit from it. We say: the benefit of reward is not possible for him. As for the benefit of lightening punishment, this may perhaps help, but since it has not been reported, it is an innovation. Otherwise, they claim that this lightens the punishment because the Messenger said concerning the two palm fronds: «Perhaps it will be lightened for them as long as they have not dried out» [[Agreed upon: al-Bukhari (218) and Muslim (292/111) from the hadith of Abdullah ibn Abbas.]], and they said: the reason for that is that before drying they glorify Allah, so the punishment is lightened for him because he glorifies Allah at his grave. But this is not correct. So ﴿you cannot make the dead hear﴾ may mean the dead of hearts, in which case the verse contains no comparison. Or it may mean the dead of bodies, in which case these people are compared to the dead.
* Student: (...) I read the Qur'an (...) he is punished by it, if he acted upon it (...), and if he did not act (...).
* Shaykh: I did not know this, I do not think (...).

He said: ﴿And you cannot make the deaf hear the call﴾.
﴿And you cannot make the deaf hear﴾, or (the deaf)?
* Student: (...).
* Shaykh: ﴿And you cannot make the deaf hear﴾.
* Student: (...).
* Shaykh: Where is the subject (fa'il) of ﴿tusmi'﴾ (you make hear)?
* Student: You.
* Another student: A hidden pronoun.
* Shaykh: Obligatory.
* Student: Yes.
* Shaykh: Obligatory. ﴿And you cannot make the deaf hear the call﴾: so ﴿the deaf﴾ is the first object, and ﴿the call﴾ is the second object.

Commentary of Ibn 'Uthaymin (Tafsir al-Quran al-Karim) on surah 27, verses 76–81 (part 3 of 5):

﴿And you cannot make the deaf hear the call﴾. That is, you cannot make the deaf, who do not hear, hear your call. The intended meaning of "call" here is "request." It does not mean calling upon Allah. If you called a deaf person and said, "O so-and-so, O so-and-so," would he hear or not?
* Student: He would not hear.
* Shaykh: He would not hear. On this point, in (...) ﴿you cannot make the deaf hear the call﴾ refers to calling upon Allah. That is, if you call them, they do not hear, or "call" means their request. Yes, their request. The meaning is that if you call them, they do not hear you. Allah the Exalted says: ﴿Do not make the calling of the Messenger among yourselves like your calling of one another﴾ [al-Nur: 63]. That is, your calling him and his calling you. It includes both meanings according to the correct view.
The meaning is that this is ﴿you cannot make the deaf hear the call﴾.
Also: when they become deaf, if they are deaf and turn away, backs turned, this is more eloquent. A deaf person who faces you may perhaps understand speech from the movement of the lips, or not? But if he turns his back, he is never [reachable]. Even if cannons are fired behind him, he will not hear. This is why He said: ﴿And you cannot make the deaf hear the call when they turn their backs and flee﴾. This is the utmost in remoteness, in being beyond hearing. Allah, blessed and exalted, describes these people. In reality, their state is like the state of these deaf people who turn their backs, or not? Because these people turn away from the truth and are unwilling to accept it. Therefore this comparison with them is the most eloquent possible. They are deaf and do not hear, and in addition they do not turn toward it. For a deaf person who faces you, as you said, may perhaps grasp something from you, or not? But if he has his back turned, there is no hope or expectation.
The author's words: ﴿the deaf the call when﴾ say: there are two readings in it (with the two hamzas realized fully). How do I recite it?
* Student: ﴿the call when﴾.
* Shaykh: ﴿the call when﴾.
Or (softening the second [hamza] to be between it and the yā'), that is, you soften the second hamza so that it is between a hamza and a yā', such as: ﴿al-du'ā' idhā﴾. Leave it: it is neither a pure yā' nor a pure hamza.
﴿when they turn their backs and flee﴾. ﴿They turn their backs﴾: turning away (tawallī) is the same as turning one's back (idbār). On this basis, ﴿turning their backs﴾ is a ḥāl (circumstantial accusative, describing the state of the subject) that is emphatic of the verb (al-'āmil) or of the doer of the state (ṣāḥib al-ḥāl)? Of the verb (...) turned; because turning away itself is turning one's back. Similar to His saying: ﴿And do not act corruptly on the earth, causing corruption﴾ [al-Baqara: 60]. ﴿Causing corruption﴾ is a ḥāl from the waw (the plural subject), and it is emphatic of what? Of the verb, because 'ath' is corruption. Here, ﴿when they turn their backs and flee﴾ is a ḥāl from the doer, but it is not emphatic of the doer. The emphasis of the doer would come with the word ajma'īn (all of them), in which case the waw indicates plurality. If it came with the word ajma'īn, it would be emphatic. But it came with the word ﴿mudbirīn﴾ [fleeing], so it is emphatic of what? Of the verb ﴿they turn﴾. Thus this is in reality two emphases: turning away and turning one's back. Or not? Even though turning away is turning one's back, a person who turns away may still have hope and expectation; he turns away while holding his burden in his house. But if he has turned his back? (...) Bodily and heart-based turning back. And he is deaf. Here there are three barriers to acceptance or to hearing: deafness, turning away, and turning one's back, ﴿when they turn their backs and flee﴾.
﴿And you cannot guide the blind away from their error﴾ [al-Rum: 53]. Yes.
* Student: ﴿And you cannot make the deaf hear﴾ (...) ﴿you cannot make the dead hear﴾ (...).
* Shaykh: No, this one is correct; this is closer. It does not have the function of simile and comparison. That is, He compares them to a deaf man who has turned his back.
* Student: (...).
* Shaykh: (...).
* Student: Yes indeed (...).
* Shaykh: ﴿they turn their backs and flee﴾ is acceptable in any case. But here, as a closer comparison, or may we say that they are deaf, and hearing is negated from them because its benefit is negated? Here, hearing is negated from them because its benefit is negated, and a thing may be negated because its benefit is negated: ﴿O you who believe, obey Allah and His Messenger, and do not turn away from him while you hear. And do not be like those who say, "We hear," while they do not hear﴾ [al-Anfal: 20–21].
Then He said: ﴿And you cannot guide the blind away from their error﴾. ﴿And you cannot guide the blind﴾, with a kasra (bi-hādi)?
* Student: Yes.
* Shaykh: Yes. This has a grammatical problem. He said ﴿bi-hādi al-'umy﴾. Is ﴿bi-hādi﴾ not an active participle (ism fā'il)?
* Student: (...).
* Shaykh: And the active participle operates like the verb, and here it did not put al-'umy in the accusative.
* Student: By annexation (iḍāfa).
* Shaykh: By annexation. So it is annexed to its object in meaning, and it is not like His saying: ﴿And if not for Allah's repelling people﴾ [al-Baqara: 251], because ﴿Allah's repelling﴾ is annexed to its doer. Here it is annexed to its object.
The second problem: His saying ﴿al-'umy﴾ with a kasra. We said that when a noun is defective (manqūṣ), it only shows a fatḥa? (...) The fatḥa? And here a kasra appeared on the yā'?
* Student: Plural.
* Shaykh: Yes (...) the plural? (...) It is a plural. There is no difference between a plural and a non-plural. Is this like the defective noun?
* Student: (...) ﴿hādi al-'umy﴾ is with a sukūn.
* Shaykh: Yes, indeed. Then it is not defective. This is not defective, because a defective noun is every inflected noun whose last letter is a necessary yā', preceded by what?
* Student: (...).
* Shaykh: With a kasra on what precedes it, and this one has a sukūn on what precedes it. Clear? Therefore it is not defective.
﴿bi-hādi al-'umy﴾: plural of a'mā (blind).
﴿'an ḍalālatihim﴾. His saying ﴿'an ḍalālatihim﴾: does it depend on al-'umy or on ﴿bi-hādi﴾? ﴿Bi-hādi﴾ without doubt.
Some of them said: it depends on al-'umy, and this 'an is for transgression (mujāwaza), like His saying: ﴿And we will not leave our gods on account of your word﴾ [Hud: 53]. That is, they are blind because of their error. But this is not correct.
Rather, ﴿'an ḍalālatihim﴾ depends on ﴿bi-hādi﴾, and hādi means "one who turns away," because guidance includes two matters: turning away from error and what else?
* Student: And indicating (the way) (...).
* Shaykh: And indicating the truth. So He says: you are not one who turns these people away from their error toward the truth. Why?
(﴿in﴾ [meaning: not] you make hear [with understanding and acceptance] except those who believe in Our signs, the Qur'an, and they are Muslims, submitting sincerely to Allah in His Oneness.)
His saying: You do not make hear except those who believe. ﴿In﴾ means: not.
We have mentioned to you before that ﴿in﴾ comes for several purposes. Does it come?
* Student: For the conditional.
* Shaykh: It comes as a conditional. And what else?
* Student: (...) negative.
* Shaykh: And it comes as a negative.
* Student: After (illa) [except].
* Shaykh: When it occurs after (illā) for emphasis, and it is the lightened form of the heavy (in) [i.e., inna]. The fourth?
* Student: It is extra (zā'ida).
* Shaykh: It is extra, so it is extra.
The extra one, as in His saying:
Banū Ghudāna, you are not gold, nor refined silver, but you are only potsherds.
His saying (mā in antum): that is, mā antum [you are not].
Yes, and for this Ibn Mālik said:
The operation of laysa is given to (mā) without (in), while the negation remains, and [the condition of] order is maintained.
The operation of (mā) without (in): he means the extra (in), and it is exemplified by this verse:
Banū Ghudāna, you are not gold, nor refined silver, but you are only potsherds.
* Student: (...).
* Shaykh: No, this is a lightened form of (inna), this inna is lightened (...) except. Yes, fine.
He says: in...
﴿And when the word comes due against them, We will bring forth for them a creature from the earth, which will speak to them, that the people were not certain of Our signs﴾ [al-Naml: 82].
Before we speak about this, we derive from what came before, from His saying: ﴿Indeed, this Qur'an relates to the Children of Israel most of that over which they differ﴾ [al-Naml: 76], whatever Allah wills of benefits.
* First: From this verse are the benefits: that the Qur'an is speech, since He says ﴿relates﴾, and relating is speech. So the Qur'an is speech, and it is known that the Qur'an was sent down from Allah, so it is speech of Allah the Exalted, as the context of the verses indicates: ﴿Indeed, your Lord will judge between them by His judgment﴾ [al-Naml: 78], in this speech which is related to them.
* The second benefit: It is permissible to single out a group among those addressed in order to establish proof against them. The Qur'an relates to the Children of Israel and others, but the Children of Israel are given particular attention here, because the subject concerns them.
* The third benefit: One should give attention to what is more important or important, and leave what has no benefit, by His saying: ﴿most of that over which they differ﴾. He did not relate all that they differ over, and among what they differ over is what has no benefit in mentioning or no reason to mention. A person should pay attention to this matter by limiting himself to what is important or most important, and leaving what has no benefit, because it is a waste of time and lengthening speech without benefit. Among this is what is found in many tafsirs: they mention disagreements about matters which in reality are one. For example, you find that they mention the disagreement from Mujāhid, Muqātil, 'Alqama, Ibn Mas'ūd, and Ibn 'Abbās, while the difference between them is only in wording. For example: ﴿And your Lord has decreed that you worship none but Him﴾ [al-Isra': 23]. He says: some scholars said: qaḍā (decreed) means waṣṣā (enjoined); some say it means 'ahida (charged); some say it means awjaba (obligated); some say it means alzama (required). There is no need for these, because all four words, for example, indicate one meaning.
Likewise they mention disagreements that have no value, as they mention the disagreement about the dog of the People of the Cave: is it black, or red, or white, and similar things.
Likewise their disagreement about the number of the People of the Cave. Allah the Exalted mentioned the disagreement, refuted two opinions, and affirmed the third. The point is that after mentioning the two opinions and refuting the third, Allah says: ﴿Say, "My Lord is most knowing of their number; none knows them except a few. So do not argue concerning them except with an apparent argument"﴾ [al-Kahf: 22]. That is: do not go deep if someone comes to argue with you about this matter, because there is no benefit in it. A thing that has no benefit, or whose benefit is little and wastes what is more important for you, you should avoid. I wish we would follow this in our whole lives, and fill our time with what is beneficial. But how many times are wasted on us, and how many sayings are said while we waste time on them. The point is that it is taken from this verse that one should give attention to what is more important and leave what has no benefit, by His saying: ﴿most of that over which they differ﴾.
* The fourth benefit: an indication of the disagreement among the Children of Israel: ﴿most of that over which they differ﴾. Is disagreement a mercy or an evil?
* Students: An evil.
* Shaykh: As for the saying, "The difference of opinion within my community is a mercy" [[See the takhrīj of the hadiths in Iḥyā' 'Ulūm al-Dīn (1/106) and Kanz al-'Ummāl (10/136).]], it is a fabricated matter that is not authentic, because Allah says: ﴿And they will not cease to differ, except those on whom your Lord has mercy﴾ [Hud: 118–119]. But if this hadith were authentic, for example, or if some scholars said it, the meaning would be that this disagreement falls within Allah's mercy and His vastness with respect to those who differ; that is, they will not be punished. The meaning is not that causing disagreement among them is from Allah's mercy. Rather, it is from Allah's wisdom. But Allah's mercy encompasses, so it should not be said, for example, that they are punished by this disagreement, or that the one of them who is correct has a reward while the rest are deprived, or similar things.
* Student: (...) The correct view is that they do not speak at ease about this; they are excused (...)?
* Shaykh: No, that is not correct. Some people say this and use this meaning as a means to permit taking dispensations, and say: their disagreement is a mercy, meaning that I may take whichever of the opinions suits me. But it is not like that. If it is said as a saying of the people of knowledge, it is not correct except in the way I said: the meaning is that this disagreement is under Allah's mercy, so no one is punished for it.
* Student: It is possible that (...) what apparently is disagreement (...) scholars until now. So the appearance of disagreement exists. Is it possible that its existence is contrary to a greater benefit?
* Shaykh: Exactly. But wisdom requires it, because the conflict between these opinions makes the truth clearer. For this reason, when a person encounters a statement that has no disagreement, he finds that it does not require evidence, and he does not let himself pass over it. So this conflict among those who differ contains wisdom. Otherwise, if they were all on one opinion, they would undoubtedly be better off, and the verse is explicit on this. So it is taken from this that disagreement is not praiseworthy.
Then Allah the Exalted said: ﴿And indeed, it is guidance and mercy for the believers﴾ [al-Naml: 77].
* From this verse is derived, first: the explanation of the Qur'an's rank and virtue, that it is guidance and mercy (...) in indication, and mercy by acting upon it.
* The second benefit: this guidance and this mercy are attained only by the believers, by His saying: ﴿for the believers﴾.
* The third benefit: there is no contradiction between this verse and His saying, the Exalted, describing the Qur'an: ﴿a guidance for mankind﴾ [al-Baqara: 185], ﴿a guidance for mankind, and clear proofs of guidance and the criterion﴾ [al-Baqara: 185].
The reconciliation: the affirmation here and the affirmation there differ in aspect. There: ﴿a guidance for mankind﴾, meaning a proof for them. It is a proof for all people. But does whoever uses it as evidence benefit from it? No. He may be guided by it, or he may not. Rather, it is itself suitable for the guidance of all mankind.
* The fourth benefit: the benefit of faith. If there were no benefit of faith except this, it would be sufficient. And what is it? Being guided by the Qur'an and attaining mercy through it.
* The fifth benefit: whenever a person is stronger in faith, he is stronger in being guided by the Qur'an. This is derived from a principle that has passed us: that when a ruling is linked to a strong attribute, that ruling becomes strong according to the strength of that attribute, and weakens with the weakness of that attribute. Clear?
Since guidance and mercy are linked to the attribute of faith, whenever this attribute increases, guidance increases and mercy increases. The principle is: when a ruling is linked to an attribute, it increases with its increase and decreases with its decrease.
* Student: The benefit?
* Shaykh: Which one?
* Student: (...).
* Shaykh: The benefit of faith?
* Student: Whenever a person is stronger (...)?
* Shaykh: Whoever is stronger in faith is stronger in being guided.
﴿Indeed, your Lord will judge between them by His judgment, and He is the Exalted in Might, the All-Knowing﴾ [al-Naml: 78].
* From this verse is derived, first: that judgment belongs to Allah alone, by His saying: ﴿Indeed, your Lord will judge between them by His judgment﴾.
* Second: every judgment that is not based on Allah's judgment is false.
* The third benefit: the affirmation of justice for Allah, the Exalted. From where is it taken? From His saying: ﴿by His judgment﴾, for attributing judgment to Allah is evidence that it includes justice.
* The fourth benefit, which is also derived from the tafsir: this judgment includes both legislative judgment and retributive judgment. He judges between them by His legislative judgment in this world, and by His recompense with justice in the Hereafter.
We mentioned in yesterday's lesson two benefits of attributing judgment to Allah. Who knows them? The attribution of judgment to Allah has two benefits.
* Student: (...).
* Shaykh: No, other than this. We said: its attribution to Allah, the Exalted, requires two matters: one of them is justice, and the second is rectification.
That is, since it is a judgment attributed to Allah, the Exalted, and it is known that He is the All-Wise, this judgment must be appropriate and suitable to its place, and every judgment that suits its place is rectification. So this includes justice and rectification.

* **The fifth benefit:** Allah is described with might (ʿizza) and knowledge, in His saying: ﴿And He is the Mighty, the All-Knowing.﴾

* **The sixth benefit:** Combining might with knowledge in this place yields a separate benefit, distinct from what each attribute gives on its own. That is, from their combination there results a meaning: the judgment of Allah, glorified and exalted be He, must certainly be carried out, by His saying ﴿He is the Mighty﴾, and it must certainly be correct and sound, by His saying ﴿the All-Knowing﴾. As we said earlier, the perfection of a judgment lies in knowledge and might: knowledge so that it judges rightly, and might so that what it has judged is enforced.

  The flaw in a judgment comes either from ignorance or from weakness. If the judge is ignorant, he rules incorrectly; if he is weak, he cannot enforce his ruling. Is that right or not?

  So from the combination of these two attributes of Allah, mentioned right after the ruling, we derive the perfection of Allah's judgment, since it is founded on what? On might and knowledge. By might the ruling is enforced, and by knowledge it is correct. Have you understood or not?

* **The seventh benefit:** Mentioning the more specific attributes before the more general ones. "More specific" here means more fitting to the matter at hand. So here He placed might before knowledge, although knowledge precedes it in the logical order. In the logical order, which comes first?

* **A student:** Knowledge comes first, because a person knows and then judges.

* **The Shaykh:** He knows, then judges, then enforces. In the logical order knowledge comes first. But here He mentioned might before knowledge. Why? Because the most important concern in a judgment is that it be enforced, so it was fitting to put what first?

  Might before knowledge. A parallel to this is His saying, concerning the angels, when Abraham's wife ﴿struck her face and said: "An old barren woman!"﴾ (Surah al-Dhariyat 51:29). ﴿They said: "Thus says your Lord; indeed He is the All-Wise, the All-Knowing."﴾ (Surah al-Dhariyat 51:30). They placed wisdom before knowledge, although knowledge comes first, since there is no wisdom without knowledge. But because this was something beyond the usual and surprising, they placed wisdom first, so that it would become clear that this departure from custom was for a wise purpose.

  These are seven benefits from His saying: ﴿Indeed your Lord will judge between them by His judgment, and He is the Mighty, the All-Knowing.﴾ (Surah al-Naml 27:78).

Allah, exalted be He, says: ﴿So put your trust in Allah; indeed you are upon the manifest truth.﴾ (Surah al-Naml 27:79)

* From this verse we derive, first: the obligation of trusting in Allah, by His saying ﴿So put your trust in Allah﴾. The basic meaning of a command is obligation. The meaning of tawakkul (reliance on Allah) was explained earlier in detail.

* **The second benefit:** Through reliance on Allah, glorified and exalted be He, affairs are made easy. The Messenger, peace be upon him, was suffering the obstinacy of the Children of Israel and others, so Allah commanded him to rely on Him. Allah mentioned the benefit of reliance in His saying: ﴿And whoever relies upon Allah, He is sufficient for him.﴾ (Surah al-Talaq 65:3). Thus through relying on Allah affairs become easy, and through a person relying on himself, failure results. ﴿On the day of Hunayn, when your great number impressed you, but it did not avail you at all, and the earth was constricted for you despite its vastness, then you turned back in retreat.﴾ (Surah al-Tawba 9:25). This happened although the Messenger, peace be upon him, was with them, and although they were the best generations and the best people on earth, when they said: "We will not be defeated today because of our small number." This shows that whoever relies on himself to achieve his aim or ward off his harm will be forsaken. Is that clear?

  For this reason Allah commanded His Messenger to rely on Allah in this situation, the situation of dispute and of making the truth clear to the Children of Israel, while the Prophet, peace be upon him, was suffering from that.

* **The third benefit:** Consolation of the Messenger, peace be upon him, by His saying: ﴿indeed you are upon the manifest truth.﴾

* **The fourth benefit:** Allah's testimony that what the Messenger brought is the truth, by His saying: ﴿indeed you are upon the manifest truth.﴾

  * From this benefit we derive another: encouragement to follow the path of the Prophet ﷺ, since it is the truth. Every sensible person chooses truth over falsehood.

* **The fifth benefit:** The virtue of the Prophet ﷺ, since his way is the manifest truth: ﴿indeed you are upon the manifest truth.﴾ This contains a testimony from Allah and a consolation for the Messenger, peace be upon him, and it includes the virtue of the Messenger ﷺ, since the testimony from Allah is that he is upon the manifest truth.

* **The sixth benefit:** Whatever contradicts what the Messenger, peace be upon him, was upon is false. For if we said it is true, it would follow that two contradictories are combined: what the Messenger was upon is true, and this (the contrary) is true. That is impossible, since it contradicts him, and combining two contradictories is impossible. Two contradictory things cannot both be true; one of them must be the truth. For this reason Allah, mighty and majestic, says: ﴿So what is there after the truth but error?﴾ (Surah Yunus 10:32). He also says: ﴿And indeed we or you are upon guidance, or in manifest error.﴾ (Surah Saba 34:24). Is that clear?

  From this we know that everything that contradicts what the Messenger, peace be upon him, was upon is false, and it is in the Fire, as the Messenger ﷺ said: "All of them are in the Fire except one."[^1] If the contradiction is total, it is entirely false. If the contradiction is partial, it contains falsehood to the extent that it contradicts what the Messenger ﷺ was upon.

* **The seventh benefit:** The clear evidence that what the Messenger, peace be upon him, was upon is the truth, with nothing obscure about it, by His saying: ﴿the manifest﴾.

* **The eighth benefit:** Making the truth clear does not necessarily mean it is clear to everyone. Bats are blinded by the daylight. So the fact that the Messenger, peace be upon him, is upon the manifest truth does not mean that no one will turn away from it. For this reason Allah followed it with: ﴿Indeed you cannot make the dead hear﴾ (Surah al-Naml 27:80). That is, do not think that those who turned away did so because you are upon falsehood. Rather, it is because the recipient is not receptive.

  You know that even if a thing is complete, if it finds no receptive place it has no effect. A man has a drawn, extremely sharp sword, and in front of him is a column of solid iron. He is roaring and saying:

  "I am the son of Jala, and the one who climbs the heights..." ........

  And he strikes this solid iron with the sword, wanting to cut it. Will it be cut?

* **Students:** No.

* **The Shaykh:** No, because the place is not receptive. Now the cause exists: a sharp sword, a brave man, a man who strengthens himself, encourages himself, and shouts at this iron column. Of course, when he is in this state he strikes with force, does he not? Or does he not strike?

* **A student:** With force.

* **The Shaykh:** With force. Yet it had no effect, because the place is not receptive. What the Messenger, peace be upon him, was upon of manifest truth is undoubtedly manifest truth, clear and evident. Their failure to hear it is not due to a flaw in it. The cause is present, but the flaw is in the place, which is not receptive to this truth. For this reason how excellent is this expression, or this verse after the one before it: ﴿Indeed you cannot make the dead hear﴾. So do not think that you are not upon the truth; rather, these are the dead. These are eight benefits.

﴿Indeed you cannot make the dead hear, nor can you make the deaf hear the call when they turn their backs in retreat. And you are not a guide for the blind away from their error. You can make hear only those who believe in Our signs, and they are submitting.﴾ (Surah al-Naml 27:80–81)

* From this verse there are benefits. First: the dead, and what is meant by "the dead" here is the dead of heart, or the dead of bodies by way of illustration, do not hear. If the person is dead of heart, it is clear that he does not hear in a way that benefits him. Otherwise he hears in the sense of perception, but it does not benefit him.

* **The second benefit:** Those who say the dead in their graves do not hear use this verse as evidence.

  Scholars have differed on this matter. Some said the dead do hear but do not respond. Others said they do not hear, while accepting what the Sunnah has reported about their hearing, but restricting it to that case, and saying that outside of it the dead do not hear. The Sunnah reported that: "When the dead person is buried and his companions turn away from him, he hears the sound of their sandals."[^2] The Sunnah also reported, from what is established about the Prophet, peace be upon him, that he stood over the people of the well at Badr among the polytheists, and began to rebuke them, saying: "O so-and-so, son of so-and-so! O so-and-so, son of so-and-so!" calling them by their names and their fathers' names: "Have you found what your Lord promised to be true? For I have found what my Lord promised me to be true." It was said to the Messenger, peace be upon him: "Do you speak to people who have decayed?" He said: "You are not more able to hear what I say than they are."[^3]

  Now, was this speech and calling at the time of burial, or at the time of placing the dead person in the grave or handing him over to the Hereafter? It does not require that he hears at all times. Some scholars said he hears at all times, like Shaykh al-Islam Ibn Taymiyya, and they cite the hadith narrated by Ibn ʿAbd al-Barr, which he authenticated: "No one passes by a grave of someone he knew in the world and greets him, except that Allah returns his soul to him, and he returns the greeting."[^4] Some authenticate this hadith, while others weaken it and say it is not sound.

  However, this hadith should not be the mainstay of those who say the dead hear. Rather, we say the dead hear, and we may cite a more authentic hadith than this: what is established from the Prophet, peace be upon him, that he would visit the graveyard and say: "Peace be upon you, people of the abode, from among the believers."[^5]

  Addressing them directly with the greeting indicates that they hear. Otherwise he would say, "Peace be upon the people of the abode from among the believers," not "upon you."

  If someone said this is a matter of vividly picturing them, we reply: vivid imagination does not require approaching them. That is why we say, "Peace be upon you, O Prophet," even though we are far away. And it is not prescribed for us to say now, "Peace be upon you, people of the abode, from among the believers," as if we were present before them. This shows that they hear.

  There remains the question: if they hear, what is the answer to His saying ﴿Indeed you cannot make the dead hear﴾?

  We say: what is meant is the hearing of acceptance, if "the dead" means the dead of hearts, or the hearing by which a response is obtained. The worldly perception of hearing is not what is denied. That is, the dead hearing what a person says is not like the perception of a living person. Rather, it is a hearing whose nature we do not know, and which cannot be answered unless Allah, blessed and exalted be He, wills to revive him and he speaks. This is possible, like the owner of the cow: they struck him with part of it, Allah revived him, he spoke, and then died. But he did not speak, nor did he answer, except after he was given a worldly life, and then Allah caused him to die again.

* **A student:** What is the basis for the indication of hearing in the hadith narrated by Ibn ʿAbd al-Barr?

* **The Shaykh:** His saying: "Except that Allah returns his soul to him, and he returns the greeting."

* **The student:** (...)

* **The Shaykh:** Yes, but whenever someone greets him, he returns the greeting and recognizes him. So he hears.

* **A student:** But it is not specifically about calling (to him).

* **The Shaykh:** No, it is not specifically about calling.

* **A student:** Perhaps he does not greet, but speaks some other speech.

* **The Shaykh:** Alright, and what prevents that? In any case, they do not hear all speech. For example, if you and I passed by a grave while talking, it does not follow that they hear. They hear only the address directed to them, and that does not mean they hear everything. Although the apparent meaning of the jurists' words is that they hear even what is not addressed to them.

* **A student:** Would there be no objection to their hearing speech directed to them only, and if we spoke again they would not hear?

* **The Shaykh:** No, they hear in every case, because if the cause of this hearing is the address, then our address to them…

* **The student:** Is this a matter of revelation (tawqifi), Shaykh?

* **The Shaykh:** It is tawqifi (based on revelation). But since, once they hear an address, they hear it again, what prevents that?

* **A student:** Does this not imply that the soul is taken back after the greeting? Because if it is returned for the sake of the greeting...

* **The Shaykh:** Yes, that is the apparent meaning: once it is returned, when the greeting ends they do not hear. We say: whenever they are addressed, Allah returns their souls to them, and they hear.

  It remains to be said: do they hear without being addressed?

  The apparent meaning of the jurists' words is also that they hear. For this reason they said that the dead is harmed by the committing of wrongdoing in his presence, whether by speech or action. On the view of the jurists, and I do not know what their basis is, they hear even what is not addressed to them. From this it follows also that if a person builds up a grave by placing stones on it, or inscriptions, or other things, the dead person is harmed by it, because this is wrongdoing. Elevating a grave and distinguishing it from other graves is wrongdoing and is not permissible.

  So according to the jurists' statements, the dead person is harmed by that, and the one who wanted to honor his dead has in reality harmed him.

* **A student:** (...) their hearing on Friday, or the Friday prayer...

* **The Shaykh:** This is not correct in any case.

* **The third benefit:** Whoever does not accept the truth is like the deaf person who cannot hear it, by His saying: ﴿nor can you make the deaf hear the call﴾.

* **The fourth benefit:** Senses and organs that are not benefited from are like those that do not exist. The reason: these people have ears and have hearing, but since they did not benefit from it, they became deaf.

* **The fifth benefit:** It shows the severity of these people's aversion to the truth, since they are deaf and turning their backs in retreat, which is the farthest thing from hearing. A deaf person who is facing you may understand from you what he understands from gestures and movements, and benefit from that even though he is deaf. But if he turns away, turning his body away or his heart away, or vice versa, then his hearing becomes even more impossible than if he were deaf while facing you.

  Also, in this there is evidence that a person, may Allah protect us, if he turns his back on the Shariʿa in retreat, may be punished with deafness to hearing the truth, so that no admonition or advice benefits him. This is the usual case. Generally, when a person has no inclination toward the truth, he is deprived of it, even if people speak to him, act, and present proofs, he does not benefit.

  Let us give you an example now: the usurers and those who devise tricks to evade riba. Do they not hear the admonitions? They hear them, but they turn away. They think that what they are doing must be done. For this reason they were not granted success in benefiting from them. They were not granted success, but remained in their error. The reason is that they have no inclination of the kind that would benefit them. So we say this verse shows that when a person turns his back in retreat from the truth, he is not granted success in hearing it.

* **The seventh benefit:** The one who turns away from the truth is like the blind. Here He said: ﴿And you are not a guide for the blind away from their error.﴾

* **The eighth benefit:** The Messenger, peace be upon him, does not possess the power to guide creation. This is shown by His saying: ﴿And you are not a guide for the blind away from their error.﴾ This is not contradicted by His saying: ﴿And indeed you guide to a straight path﴾ (Surah al-Shura 42:52), because affirmed guidance is not the same as negated guidance.

  What is the affirmed guidance?

* **Students:** The guidance of pointing the way.

* **The Shaykh:** The guidance of indication, knowledge, and clarification. The Messenger, peace be upon him, is a teacher and a clarifier, one who points creation to the truth. But granting success to accept it is in the hand of Allah. So the reconciliation between the guidance affirmed for the Messenger ﷺ and the guidance negated from him is this: what is affirmed for the Messenger is the guidance of knowledge and clarification, and what is negated from him is the guidance of granting success and action. He is never able to do that.

---

[^1]: Narrated by Ibn Majah (3993) from the hadith of Anas ibn Malik.
[^2]: Agreed upon; al-Bukhari (1338) and Muslim (2870/70) from the hadith of Anas ibn Malik.
[^3]: Agreed upon; al-Bukhari (3976) and Muslim (2875/78) from the hadith of Abu Talha al-Ansari.
[^4]: Al-Istidhkar (1/185) from the hadith of Ibn ʿAbbas.
[^5]: Narrated by Muslim (975/104) from the hadith of Buraydah al-Aslami.

* It can be inferred from this verse that these people who turned away from the truth have had the paths of goodness closed to them. They are dead of heart: they have not benefited from their hearts. They are deaf of ear: they have not benefited from their ears. They are blind of eye: they have not benefited from their eyes.

Signs are either rational, audible, or visible. The rational ones are located in the heart, and their benefit has been denied to them in His saying: ﴿Indeed, you cannot make the dead hear﴾. The visible ones are perceived by the eye, and their benefit has been denied to them in His saying: ﴿nor are you a guide for the blind﴾. The audible ones are perceived by the ears, and their benefit has been denied to them in His saying: ﴿nor can you make the deaf hear the call﴾. Thus all the avenues through which guidance is attained are, for these people, entirely blocked and closed, and we seek refuge in Allah.

* The ninth or tenth benefit: Those who benefit from the signs that the Messenger brought are the believers in them: ﴿You can only make hear those who believe in Our signs﴾.

* The eleventh: The more a person's faith in the signs of Allah grows, the more he benefits from them, because benefit has been tied to the attribute of faith in them in these verses. Whenever this attribute grows stronger, the benefit grows greater.

* The twelfth benefit: Faith entails Islam, by His saying: ﴿so they are submitting﴾. Does Islam entail faith?

* Students: It does not entail it.

* The Shaykh: It does not entail it. A person may be a Muslim without being a believer. For this reason, it was said that when the Prophet ﷺ was told about a man that he was a believer, he said: «Or [say] a Muslim»[[Agreed upon; al-Bukhari (27) and Muslim (150 / 236), and the wording is his, from the hadith of Sa'd ibn Abi Waqqas.]]. This indicates the difference between faith (iman) and Islam.

Many people today, many Muslims, are Muslims but not believers, and many Muslims are merely submitters (mustaslim) and not Muslims. So Muslims today are either a mustaslim, or a Muslim, or a believer, and the fewest of them are, without doubt, the believers.

The Muslim who is merely a submitter is common in lands other than ours. Most of them are Muslim only in the sense of submitting in name, only in identity papers. For this reason, people come from other lands saying: "We do not know how to perform wudu', we do not know how to pray, and we do not know the prayer times," and yet it is written on their identity papers that they are Muslim.

The third category: the Muslim who is not a believer. This is common in our lands: they are Muslims, but they are not believers.

The evidence for this is that the deeds or the morals that are tied to faith are found lacking in many of these people. "None of you believes until he loves for his brother what he loves for himself." Is this found in abundance?

* A student: It is rare.

* The Shaykh: It is scarce. "Whoever cheats is not of us"[[Narrated by Muslim (102 / 164) and al-Tirmidhi (1315) from Abu Hurayrah, and the wording is al-Tirmidhi's.]]. Is the absence of cheating found in abundance? It is scarce. "A man does not believe whose neighbor is not safe from his evil"[[Narrated by al-Bukhari (6016) from Abu Shurayh.]], scarce. Proceed on this basis. "The slanderer will not enter Paradise." Is slander found in abundance? So the point is that faith among Muslims today is scarce, Islam is abundant, and mere submission is more abundant still.

* A student: He will not enter Paradise (...).

* The Shaykh: Yes, indeed, he enters Paradise, because the Muslim in the legal sense, though faith has not entered his heart, his final destiny is Paradise, but he does not enter it immediately... He has sins, and either he will be punished for them, or he will be pardoned.

* The student: What is the difference (...)?

* The Shaykh: The difference between them is that the Muslim has faith, whereas the hypocrite (munafiq) has no faith at all. The hypocrite's heart is empty of faith, and we seek refuge in Allah.

* The student: Is he (the Muslim) of higher rank, O Shaykh?

* The Shaykh: The mustaslim is higher than the hypocrite, yes, because the mustaslim genuinely has, in relation to Islam, something real, but he lacks what the Muslim has, who implements the laws. He is generally ignorant.

* A student: (...).

* The Shaykh: Yes, meaning that he (...) submitted, he realizes Islam.

* The thirteenth benefit: His saying ﴿Our signs﴾ indicates that the signs are many, not one. They are divided into what? Two types: cosmic signs (kawniyyah) and legal signs (shar'iyyah).
