But these Bedouins had not yet had faith enter their hearts, except that it was near: ﴿and faith has not yet entered your hearts﴾.

So the correct position on this question is: faith is Islam when they are mentioned together, and when they are mentioned separately, each includes the other.

* Student: (...) indicated that faith is the outward deeds.
* The Shaykh: Yes, faith, because it is included within it; when it is paired with Islam, this is explained by that and that by this. But when mentioned alone, it encompasses it.
* Student: (...).
* The Shaykh: Yes, Muslims outwardly.
* Student: Submitting; meaning they do not come with (...).
* The Shaykh: No, because the Messenger intended to explain it by the outward deeds grounded in sincerity, and the outward deeds of the hypocrites are not grounded in sincerity. That is why you find them praying with the people and mentioning Allah, the Exalted, in their prayer, yet they do not remember Allah except a little. The Messenger ﷺ did not distinguish between them and their relatives in inheritance and other matters; he would inherit from some of them and they from him. Shaykh al-Islam Ibn Taymiyyah adopted this view and said: the hypocrite inherits from the believer, and the believer inherits from the hypocrite, and he cited as evidence that the Messenger ﷺ..

What he said is correct, except that we object to it in cases where his hypocrisy is known; that is, if his hypocrisy is known, it is not obligatory that he inherit from a Muslim or a Muslim inherit from him. Allah the Exalted said: ﴿And do not pray over any of them who dies, ever, nor stand at his grave﴾ [at-Tawbah 84].

* Student: In the case of those known to be hypocrites.
* The Shaykh: Among them are people he knows, and among them are people he does not know.

He said: ﴿And to recite the Quran. Whoever is guided, is only guided for his own soul; and whoever strays, say: I am only one of the warners﴾.

* From this verse is derived, first: the obligation of reciting the Quran in both its forms. What are the two forms?
* Students: The verbal and the practical.
* The Shaykh: The verbal and the practical. It is obligatory upon a person to recite the Quran both verbally and practically, whether from the heart's memory or while looking at the text?
* Student: Even while looking.
* The Shaykh: Even while looking.
* The second benefit: the excellence and nobility of the Quran, since he was commanded to recite it.
* The third benefit: the obligation of beautifying the recitation of the Quran, from His saying: ﴿And to recite the Quran﴾.
* The fourth benefit: the obligation upon the Prophet ﷺ to convey the Quran, from His saying: ﴿And I have been commanded to be among the Muslims (91). And to recite the Quran﴾.
* The fifth benefit:..

Ibn 'Uthaymin, Tafsir al-Quran al-Karim, on Surah 27, verses 90–93 (part 1 of 4):

Allah the Exalted says: ﴿Whoever comes with a good deed will have better than it, and they will be safe from the terror of that Day. And whoever comes with an evil deed, their faces will be thrown into the Fire: "Are you recompensed except for what you used to do?"﴾ [An-Naml 90].

﴿Hal tujzawn﴾ (Are you recompensed): meaning "mā tujzawn" (you are not recompensed). The interrogative here is more emphatic than a bare negation, because it indicates negation plus something additional. For example, "mā tujzawna illā mā kuntum ta'malūn" (you are not recompensed except for what you used to do) indicates that they are recompensed only for what they did. But ﴿hal tujzawn﴾ indicates the affirmation of this matter, that a person can only be recompensed for what he did, and it carries both affirmation and rebuke at the same time.

The author said: (It is said to them as a rebuke: ﴿hal﴾, meaning "mā" (not), ﴿tujzawna illā﴾ the recompense of ﴿mā kuntum ta'malūn﴾ (what you used to do) of shirk and sins.)

As for his words, (mā ﴿tujzawn﴾), this has already been discussed.

As for his words, (﴿illā﴾ the recompense of ﴿mā kuntum ta'malūn﴾), is there in it a diversion of the wording from its apparent meaning? How is that?

* Student: (...).
* Shaykh: Yes, (...).
* Student: (...).
* Shaykh: The recompense of "mā kuntum" (what you were). Good, what is the intent?

Because His saying ﴿illā mā kuntum ta'malūn﴾ requires that the deed itself be the recompense, that the deed is the recompense ﴿illā mā kuntum﴾. And it is known that the deed is not the recompense; rather the recompense is one thing and the deed is another. When you hire a person to work for you and then give him his wage, his work is other than his wage. The one who works for Allah, the Exalted, his deed is other than his recompense.

So what is the apparent meaning of the verse ﴿hal tujzawna illā mā kuntum ta'malūn﴾? Is a person recompensed by his deed or not?

Therefore the author found it necessary to supply this omitted element: (﴿illā﴾ the recompense of ﴿illā mā kuntum ta'malūn﴾). But the wording of the verse is more eloquent, because it is a matter of hyperbole in justice, that the recompense is made to be the deed itself, as if the recompense itself were your deed. It is hyperbole in justice: if you want much reward, then do much deed, because your reward is your deed.

As for his words (﴿hal tujzawna illā﴾ the recompense of ﴿mā kuntum ta'malūn﴾), there is also in it awkwardness: "You are not recompensed except the recompense of the deed?" It is known. The word ﴿tujzawn﴾ already conveys recompense, so there is no need for elaboration. Therefore the correct approach is to leave the verse as it is, on its apparent meaning.

What is understood is that what they are given is the recompense, from His saying ﴿hal tujzawn﴾, and expressing the recompense by the deed itself is hyperbole in justice, such that your recompense is your deed.

As for his words (of shirk and sins), this is what the majority of scholars held, and it is the correct view: that the disbeliever is punished for the root of disbelief and also for the sins he committed. So a polytheist who commits adultery, steals and drinks wine is punished for that. He is punished for the root and the branches, and this is what the majority of scholars hold. They cite as evidence the saying of Allah the Exalted: ﴿They will ask one another about the criminals, "What has caused you to enter Saqar?" They will say, "We were not of those who prayed, nor did we used to feed the poor, and we used to engage in vain discourse with those engaged in it, and we used to deny the Day of Judgement"﴾ [Al-Muddaththir 40–46].

Prayer and charity are not among the roots, although the correct view is that prayer is among the roots and whoever abandons it commits disbelief. But charity is not among the roots; even zakat, according to the correct view, its abandoner does not become a disbeliever. Nevertheless, they mentioned it among the causes of their entry into the Fire, and if it had no effect on the recompense it would not have been among the causes. This is evidence that they are punished for the branches of Islam just as they are punished for its roots.

Based on this, they are punished for their sins other than shirk. This is without doubt the perfection of justice, for if a Muslim is punished for them, how much more so a disbeliever?

Would it be a vengeance for the Muslim and a blessing for the disbeliever? No. Rather, even more than that, the disbeliever is punished even for what is permissible for the believer. Allah the Exalted said: ﴿Say: "Who has forbidden the adornment of Allah which He brought forth for His servants, and the good provisions?" Say: "They are for those who believed in the life of this world, purely for them on the Day of Resurrection."﴾ [Al-A'raf 32].

From His saying ﴿purely for them on the Day of Resurrection﴾ it is taken that these things are not pure for non-believers, and that they will be recompensed for them. This is also what sound reasoning requires: how can a person enjoy the blessings of the Creator while disobeying the Creator?

He must punish him. He says: "I did good to you; I fed you, gave you drink, clothed you, housed you, married you, and the like," and so he is punished for this blessing, because it requires gratitude.

He said: (Say to them: ﴿I have only been commanded to worship the Lord of this city﴾ [An-Naml 91]; that is, Makkah, ﴿who﴾) He did not say "allatī" (feminine), why? Because it is an attribute of a masculine noun, ﴿Rabb hādhihi al-baldah alladhī﴾. Therefore you parse ﴿alladhī﴾ as a relative pronoun built on sukūn in a position of nasb, an attribute of the ﴿Rabb﴾.

(﴿Rabb hādhihi al-baldah alladhī ḥarramahā﴾; that is, He made it a sanctuary, secure) Did He make it so by decree (kawnan) or by law (shar'an)?

* Student: (...).
* Shaykh: By law. He made it, by law, a sanctuary, secure.

As for His saying ﴿Lord of this city﴾, attributing lordship to it indicates its excellence, and that Allah, the Exalted, has cared for it and honoured it.

He said: (Blood is not shed in it, a person's), and the hadith: «Blood shall not be shed therein» [agreed upon; al-Bukhari (104) and Muslim (1354 / 446) from the hadith of Abu Shurayh al-'Adawi].

Which is more general, "a person's blood" or "blood"? "Blood" is more general; therefore blood of a person is not shed in it, nor the blood of game. As for livestock such as camels, cattle, sheep and the like, the Sunnah has shown that this is permitted.

As for his words (and no one is wronged in it), this is not specific to Makkah; even outside Makkah it is not permitted for anyone to be wronged there. That is why the hadith does not say "no one is wronged therein" alone; rather the Messenger said: «Blood shall not be shed therein». So it is not one of Makkah's special features that no one is wronged there. It is true that wrongdoing in Makkah is greater than elsewhere: ﴿And whoever intends therein deviation by wrongdoing, We will make him taste a painful punishment﴾ [Al-Hajj 25]. But that wrongdoing elsewhere is permissible, no.

Likewise: (no game is hunted in it).

* Student: (...).
* Shaykh: No, it does not indicate that; because here ﴿man yurid fīhi bi-ilḥād﴾ the letter bāʾ indicates that the verb is implicitly containing the meaning of true determination.

* Student: (...).
* Shaykh: A sin is not multiplied by a place merely in quantity; it is multiplied in quality only. It does not mean that a sin is recompensed with two sins; rather the meaning is that it is greater, and that you should know the difference is in quality: the manner of punishment differs. I may strike this person one blow, and strike another one blow, and this second one is painful while the first is not.

He said: (no game is hunted in it). Is this correct or not? Correct, and elsewhere game is hunted.

(nor is its grass cut): Correct, and elsewhere grass is cut.

* Student: Madinah?

* Shaykh: In Madinah the grass may be cut, yes, it is permitted. Only what is cut without need is forbidden in Madinah; what is needed is permitted. This is the difference between it and Makkah.

(And that is among the blessings upon Quraysh, its people, in that Allah, the Exalted, lifted from their lands the punishment and the widespread strife found in all the lands of the Arabs.)

So His saying ﴿alladhī ḥarramahā﴾ means: He made it a sanctuary, and made it forbidden. What we have said is more general than what the author said, because the author says "He made it a secure sanctuary," then mentioned things; so it is a ḥaram (sacred place) and also ḥarām (forbidden). Ḥaram means it is held sacred, and ḥarām means it is made forbidden.

Therefore whoever intends it, it is prescribed for him, by the consensus of scholars, not to enter it except as a Muslim; and regarding its obligation there is a well-known difference of opinion.

Also, among its sanctity: polytheists do not approach it, or do they? They do not approach the Sacred Mosque, so the whole ḥaram is forbidden to them, because entering the ḥaram is approaching the Sacred Mosque. Thus this was a token of honour for this city.

Yet Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, says: (﴿And to Him belongs﴾ the Exalted ﴿everything﴾, He is its Lord, Creator and Owner.)

The last sentence contains a great benefit: since He said ﴿Lord of this city﴾, one might suppose that His lordship is specific to this city, so He then generalized, saying ﴿and to Him belongs everything﴾.

A parallel to this is His saying: ﴿Not equal among you are those who spent and fought before the victory. Those are greater in rank than those who spent afterward and fought﴾ [Al-Hadid 10]; after it He said: ﴿And to each Allah has promised the best﴾, lest one suppose that this excellence is specific to those, so He clarified that the reward is for all, which is Paradise, even though they are not equal.

Here: ﴿Lord of this city﴾ and ﴿and to Him belongs everything﴾: the lordship of Allah is general to everything, but His lordship over this city is more specific than His general lordship.

* Student: (...).
* Shaykh: No, it is not masculine gender; we mean by "masculine" the wording, not the meaning. One may not say "masculine" about Allah; we say the word is masculine. Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, may not be described by this or that.

He said: ﴿And I have been commanded to be among the Muslims﴾.

﴿Umirtu﴾ (I have been commanded): by whom? ﴿Innamā umirtu an aʿbud﴾ and ﴿wa-umirtu an akūna min al-muslimīn﴾.

Is not worship itself Islam? The answer: Yes, worship is Islam.

But there He said ﴿I have only been commanded to worship the Lord of this city, who has made it sacred﴾, and worship is submission to Him through obedience.

Then He said ﴿And I have been commanded to be among the Muslims﴾, meaning: that I realize this worship through complete submission to the commands of Allah, Blessed and Exalted.

A person may be a worshipper in principle, but complete compliance with all the prescriptions of Islam is derived from His saying ﴿And I have been commanded to be among the Muslims﴾, that is, among those who submit completely to Allah, the Exalted, with no opposition or arrogance in them.

In His saying ﴿an akūna min al-muslimīn﴾ is there evidence that there were Muslims before? Are Jews and Christians Muslims?

* Students: No.

* Shaykh: While their legislations were in force, they were Muslims, or not? But after they were abrogated, if they do not adhere to the abrogating law, they are not Muslims. Islam is the religion with Allah at every time and place, and after the sending of the Messenger, peace be upon him, there is no Islam except by following his law. Otherwise the root of Islam, as you know, is from submission, which is surrender, and this includes every submission to Allah, the Exalted, whether in the era of this nation or before it. Noah, peace be upon him, says: ﴿And I have been commanded to be among the Muslims﴾ [An-Naml 91], just as it was said to the Messenger, peace be upon him. And of Jacob it is said: He said to his sons: ﴿O my sons, indeed Allah has chosen for you this religion, so do not die except while you are Muslims﴾ [Al-Baqarah 132]. And Bilqis said: ﴿I have wronged myself, and I have submitted with Solomon to Allah, Lord of the worlds﴾ [An-Naml 44].

(﴿And I have been commanded to be among the Muslims (91), and to recite the Quran﴾ to you, the recitation of the call to faith ﴿So whoever is guided, is guided only for his own soul﴾; that is, for its sake, for its reward from his guidance is for himself; ﴿and whoever strays﴾ from faith and misses the path of guidance ﴿then say: "I am only among the warners"﴾.)

As for His saying ﴿and to recite the Quran﴾: recitation is divided into two kinds: verbal recitation and meaningful recitation.

The first recitation is reading the Quran; the second recitation is acting upon what the Quran brought, derived from tala al-shay'a yatlūhu, when one follows a thing and becomes its follower.

So the Messenger's saying ﴿and to recite the Quran﴾ includes both: that I recite it by reading, and that I recite it by following. He is commanded to do so; it is as if he says: "I will recite the Quran to you by reading, and I will also recite the Quran by following, and I do not care about your opposition and aversion." This is not only for the Messenger, peace be upon him, but for everyone who follows the Messenger: it is obligatory upon him to recite the Quran verbally, and it is known that reciting al-Fatihah is a pillar of prayer, which is among the pillars of Islam.

Secondly: it is obligatory upon the Muslim to recite the Quran by following, and not to mind whoever opposes him. Had we considered people's feelings and people's minds, religion would not remain religion; rather religion would become custom, accepted if people accept it according to their habits, and not religion if they do not accept it. What is obligatory is that religion be remote from people's customs, meaning that the judgement is the Quran and the Sunnah, not what people are accustomed to in their worships or other things. This is unlike some people today who wish to deceive people regarding what they are upon, even if it is falsehood, and this is not correct; for if we walked upon this matter or this method, Islam would have no life left. Islam would remain dead, and part of it would die in this age, then another age would come and another part would die, and so on until it ends. But when we act by Islam and renew according to what the Book and the Sunnah require, not according to our opinions, that is the true leadership.

As for us remaining silent and burying our heads in the sand, saying: "These people cannot be opposed," or hesitating because some people say: "You have brought a new religion; we have never known this religion before," and the like, this should not prevent a person from speaking the truth.

Therefore His saying ﴿and to recite the Quran﴾ is recitation of wording by which the proof is established against you, and recitation of following, not caring about your opposition and contradiction; and this is what is obligatory upon every Muslim in every place.

But is accommodating people, meaning gradually bringing people along until they take the correct path, permissible or not?

* Students: Permissible.

* Shaykh: Yes indeed. Accommodating the situation gradually is not objectionable. For this reason, what we see is that calling to Allah, the Exalted, with wisdom encompasses this matter, namely bringing people to Islam stage by stage.

Though some people say this applies to the beginning of the call: it is true that Islam developed; prayer came, then zakat, then fasting, then hajj; wine was forbidden in several stages; fasting was made obligatory in several ways.

But we say: just as this is at the origin of the call, or the beginning of the call, it is also at its end. When was Mu'adh sent? In the tenth year after the Hijrah. Yet he said: «Call them first to testifying that there is no god but Allah, then to prayer, then to zakat» [agreed upon; al-Bukhari (1395) and Muslim (19 / 29) from the hadith of 'Abdullah ibn 'Abbas]. So the Messenger arranged this, and did not say: call them to all of them together.

For example, if we see a person absorbed in committing a sin, and we know that if we tell him to abandon it completely, he will not be able, or he will be repelled, then it is fine that we move him away from it little by little, gradually; for this is like treating an illness. An illness cannot be treated all at once; there must be a transition from one thing to another until the disease is fully eradicated.

So this matter returns to the condition of the people, and it does not mean submitting to the condition of the people, for the submission I denied earlier means a person leaves people alone and does not oppose them regarding the truth. This, however, does not leave them alone, but moves them from stage to stage until they become upright. For example, when we want to introduce an act in prayer that is not customary among people, it is wise first to prepare for it with speech, then once people know it and it settles in their souls, we move them to the act afterward. Likewise in other matters beside this one.

The main point: reciting the Quran to people who turn away is something the Messenger, peace be upon him, was commanded, and the whole nation is also commanded with it. The recitation here is both verbal and by following. But the whole matter is that we should not be weak before the existing reality; rather it is obligatory upon us to be in a stronger and firmer stance.

**Student:** Transferring a person from one sin to another sin.

**Shaykh:** To another sin?

**Student:** A lesser one.

**Shaykh:** No, that is not permitted.

**Student:** Gradualness...

**Shaykh:** How? Give an example. If it is of the same kind, perhaps we can say. For instance, suppose a person is afflicted with fornication, may Allah protect us, and we say to him: "My brother, what is wrong with you? The desire you have, you can reduce it through masturbation, for example. That, being of the same kind, is not harmful." But if someone steals, we say: "My brother, leave off theft, drink wine, I will make it appealing to you!" That is not possible.

**Student:** I mean of the same kind of harm.

**Shaykh:** Yes. Being of the same kind means reduction, because if you move him to something else, its first direction generally does not disappear.

**Student:** (...).

**Shaykh:** And the world (...).

**Student:** (...).

**Shaykh:** Yes, the meaning is that even "Take care of yourself" [[Abu Dawud (4341), al-Tirmidhi (3058), with his wording, and Ibn Majah (4014), from the hadith of Abu Tha'labah al-Khushani.]] is not about enjoining good and forbidding evil, because it concerns your own self. But the meaning of "leave them" is: do not be preoccupied with them in a way that keeps you busy from what is obligatory. Some people become so concerned with this matter that they occupy themselves with people to the neglect of themselves. You find such a person may even pray while he feels he is commanding so-and-so, and imagines that he is saying to him, like: "Come on, pray!" This is what is forbidden.

**Student:** (...).

**Shaykh:** ﴿O you who believe, take care of yourselves﴾ [Al-Ma'idah 5:105]. Because some people understand that if a person has corrected himself, he has no duty to correct others. But we say: correcting others is bound up with your correcting yourself. You are commanded to enjoin good and forbid evil, but if they go astray, their straying does not harm you, once you have performed what is obligatory upon you of calling and commanding.

**Student:** (...)?

**Shaykh:** Correct. (...) says? But this gradualness is a path, and that does not mean that when I move him from this to something lighter, I permit him the lighter. Rather, it is a path of gradual progression. So gradualness here does not mean that the ruling is established at the level to which we lowered him, but that we move him from the greatest degree to the lesser, then to abandoning it entirely. His saying, peace and blessings be upon him: "Avoid it" [[Agreed upon: al-Bukhari (7288) and Muslim (1337/130), from the hadith of Abu Hurayrah.]], but what is the path to avoiding it? It is this that we are saying. The path to avoiding it is this that we are saying. Therefore, now when you forbid a person from an evil (...).

That which the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, said concerning it was in Makkah, as shown by His saying: ﴿this city﴾, and the demonstrative here is for what is near. Then His saying: ﴿who has made it sacred﴾ contains a manifestation of the favor of Allah, may He be blessed and exalted, upon the inhabitants of this town, since Allah made this town a sanctuary.

He said: ﴿And to Him belongs everything, and I have been commanded to be among the Muslims﴾, meaning: those who submit to the judgment of Allah. There is no contradiction between this and the worship mentioned before: ﴿to worship the Lord of this city﴾, because worship is one thing, and Islam across the whole Sharia is another thing.

﴿And to recite the Qur'an﴾: a verbal recitation by which the proof is established against you, and a practical application by which it becomes clear that I am not concerned with whoever opposes me in this matter.

His saying: ﴿the Qur'an﴾ is that which was revealed to him, peace and blessings be upon him, and after the recitation of the Qur'an.

(﴿So whoever is guided﴾ to it) Is this how it is in your copies? Is it "guided to it" or "guided by it"?

**Students:** To it.

**Shaykh:** To it? (﴿So whoever is guided﴾ to it).

But according to the author's interpretation, ﴿is guided﴾ becomes in the sense of (submits), because ﴿is guided﴾ is not transitive with *lam*; it is transitive with *ba'* (guided by it). But he has made it include the meaning of submission, so as to encompass guidance of knowledge and guidance of success, the one who is guided and submits to it.

(﴿then he is only guided for his own self﴾; i.e., for its benefit, for the reward of his guidance is for it) Correct. Whoever is guided by this Qur'an and submits to it, for whose benefit is it? Not for Allah, Mighty and Majestic, because Allah is free of need from it. Nor is it for so-and-so or so-and-so, because every soul ﴿has what it earned and bears what it has earned﴾ [Al-Baqarah 2:286].

So it is for himself. And although the caller benefits from it as well, the benefit of one who points to good, like the one who does it, but the basic reward belongs to whom? To the doer. The basic reward belongs to the doer. So it is not said, for example, that the Messenger, peace and blessings be upon him, calls people so that they may be guided and thus has a reward. Rather, his primary intention, peace and blessings be upon him, was benefiting creation, and for this reason He said: ﴿then he is only guided for his own self﴾. Although the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, benefits from their guidance, he is a follower in that.

(﴿So whoever is guided, he is only guided for his own self, and whoever goes astray﴾ from faith and misses the path of guidance, ﴿then say﴾ to him: ﴿I am only one of the warners﴾.)

The author: He supplied for "whoever is guided" the phrase "say to him," and here he supplied "say to him," and the reason is that it is supplied here so that the answer is connected to the condition. Because His saying: ﴿And to recite the Qur'an, so whoever is guided﴾, guided by what? By the Qur'an that I recite.

And here ﴿whoever goes astray﴾: ﴿whoever﴾ is a conditional, and ﴿then say, I am only one of the warners﴾ cannot be the answer to ﴿and whoever goes astray﴾ unless there is a pronoun referring back to it, and for this he supplied it with his statement: (﴿then say﴾ to him ﴿I am only one of the warners﴾).

If someone says: what is the wisdom in omitting it? We say: the wisdom in omitting it is generality; meaning: ﴿then say﴾ to him and to others: ﴿I am only one of the warners﴾.

The meaning is that this sentence, which is a permanent attribute of the Messenger, peace and blessings be upon him, is not specific to whoever goes astray. Rather, whoever goes astray and whoever does not go astray is told: the Messenger, peace and blessings be upon him, is ﴿one of the warners﴾. The meaning of "warner" is one who frightens.

He said: (those who frighten), "so there is upon me only the delivery." His saying: ﴿I am only﴾, ﴿only﴾ is a particle of restriction.

If someone says: this indicates that the Messenger, peace and blessings be upon him, is specific to warning, while Allah says: ﴿Indeed, We have sent you with the truth as a bringer of good news and a warner, and you will not be questioned about the companions of the Blazing Fire﴾ [Al-Baqarah 2:119].

We say: each context has the wording suited to it. Here, who is the addressee?

**Student:** The deniers.

**Shaykh:** A people who deny. So mentioning the aspect of warning concerning them is more fitting than combining it with giving good news.

He said: (And this was before the command to fight). The author, may Allah have mercy on him, often takes this approach regarding verses like this, saying it was before the command to fight, and this implies that the verse is abrogated and not to be acted upon. But this is an extremely weak view. The correct view is that this is said even after the command to fight.

So what is the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, responsible for? He is responsible for warning and delivering the message, not for guidance. And the Messenger, peace and blessings be upon him, would generally or often recite every Friday: ﴿So remind; you are only a reminder. You are not over them a controller﴾ [Al-Ghashiyah 88:21–22], ﴿Indeed, to Us is their return. Then indeed, upon Us is their account﴾ [Al-Ghashiyah 88:25–26]. How could verses like these, which are repeated to the Muslims in their Friday gatherings, be abrogated?

Furthermore, claiming abrogation is not a trivial matter, because what does it mean? It means nullifying the indication of the verse or the hadith, and this involves transgression against Allah, the Exalted, and against His Messenger. Therefore, a person must be extremely cautious about claiming abrogation, and if he cannot reconcile the texts, he should say: ﴿Glory be to You; we have no knowledge except what You have taught us﴾ [Al-Baqarah 2:32]. But the author, may Allah have mercy on him, and many other scholars, when they cannot reconcile, say: this is abrogated.

This approach is not good, not sound, and not correct. Rather, it is dangerous. Ibn al-Qayyim, may Allah have mercy on him, mentioned that abrogated rulings in the Sharia do not exceed ten rulings.

If we followed what the author followed, the abrogated rulings would be dozens, or perhaps reach a hundred, and this is a great error.

So the correct view is that this statement: ﴿then say, I am only one of the warners﴾ is said: until now, and even after the command to fight, he is a warner. But this warning does not require that he not perform what is obligatory upon him of jihad. He says: I am a warner, so I am not responsible for your guidance; your guidance is upon Allah, the Exalted. As for the matter of the command to fight, this is possible even with this statement.

So the correct view on this issue is that the verse is muhkam (clear and firmly established). This and others like it are muhkam, and similar ones are muhkam, and claiming abrogation in them is not permitted, because one of the most important conditions of abrogation, or one of its most important, is the impossibility of reconciliation. If reconciliation is possible, there is no abrogation, because abrogation, as you have heard, is the nullification of the meaning of the verse or the hadith, and this is no trivial matter. A hadith comes, and you wipe it out. The meaning of "wiping" is that we struck it.

**Student:** (...).

**Shaykh:** Yes, it is one of the conditions.

**Student:** Is it a condition that there be an indication showing abrogation (...)?

**Shaykh:** No, that is not a condition. The point is that if reconciliation is impossible and the chronology is known, then the later one abrogates the earlier.

He says: ﴿I am only one of the warners﴾; is it with a *kasrah* or a *fathah*?

**Student:** With a *kasrah*: *mundhirin*.

**Shaykh:** Because it is an active participle: he is *mundhir* (a warner), while people are *mundharun* (warned).

﴿And say: All praise is for Allah﴾ [An-Naml 27:93] is conjoined to His saying: ﴿I have only been commanded﴾, because according to the interpretation of ﴿say﴾, meaning ﴿And say: All praise is for Allah﴾. This sentence is for praising Allah, may He be blessed and exalted. Allah has praised Himself at the beginning of creation, at its end, at the beginning of the revelation of the Qur'an, and in the context of honoring the Messenger, peace and blessings be upon him, in the revelation of the Qur'an, and similar matters.

So here He said: ﴿All praise is for Allah﴾, (...) for it? For the perfection of His attributes and the manifestation of His signs.

Among them is ﴿He will show you His signs, and you will recognize them﴾.

﴿He will show you﴾: showing is more emphatic than explaining, because a thing may be clear while eyes are blind to it, but showing is more emphatic, since everything seen is clear, though not everything clear is seen.

The *sin* in His saying ﴿He will show you﴾ conveys two benefits. The first benefit: the nearness of this matter. The second benefit: its certainty. So it conveys both certainty and nearness.

﴿He will show you His signs﴾: the showing here is visual, and since it is transitive by the *hamzah*, it takes two objects: the first object is the *kaf* (you), and the second object is ﴿His signs﴾.

His saying: ﴿He will show you His signs﴾: Is the intended meaning of Allah's signs here the signs that confirm the truth of what He informed of in the Qur'an, so that they are cosmic signs, or are they more comprehensive than that?

The apparent view is that they are more comprehensive than that: they include the signs that confirm the truth of what He promised His Messenger and threatened those people with, and likewise the legislative signs that demonstrate the perfection of His Sharia.

His saying: ﴿and you will recognize them﴾ is also more emphatic than showing, because a person may be shown something yet not recognize it. Here He said: ﴿and you will recognize them﴾.

So we have explanation, showing, and recognition; the highest of these is recognition, then showing, then explanation.

His saying: ﴿and you will recognize them﴾: the result of this is that the proof is established against you, because when they are shown the signs until they recognize them, the proof is established against them.

The author, may Allah have mercy on him, said: (So Allah showed them on the day of Badr the killing, the captivity, and the angels striking their faces and backs, and Allah hastened them to the Fire). These are among the signs that He showed them. Otherwise, Allah showed them the splitting of the moon before Badr, when they asked the Messenger, peace and blessings be upon him, for a sign, "so he pointed to the moon and it split into two halves," until they witnessed it with their own eyes. They said: "Muhammad has bewitched us, so ask the travelers who come to Makkah whether they witnessed that or not." They asked them, and they informed them that they had witnessed it [[al-Tirmidhi (3289), from the hadith of Jubayr ibn Mut'im. The hadith is originally agreed upon: al-Bukhari (3636) and Muslim (2800/43), from the hadith of Abdullah ibn Mas'ud.]].

A people have denied this sign, the splitting of the moon, among them Muhammad Rashid Rida, and I think his teacher Muhammad Abduh as well. This is a manifest error, may Allah protect us, because the hadiths about it are mass-transmitted (mutawatir), and the Qur'an's allusion to it is clear: ﴿The Hour has drawn near, and the moon has split﴾ [Al-Qamar 54:1].

They distorted the Qur'an, saying: "the moon split" means that the light of truth and the illumination brought by the Messenger, peace and blessings be upon him, became evident. This is without doubt a distortion of the Qur'an and a denial of what has been transmitted by mass narration in the Sunnah. The correct view, about which there is no doubt, and which is part of the creed of Ahl al-Sunnah wal-Jama'ah (the People of the Sunnah and the Community), is that the moon did split.

As for their claim that if it had split, it would have been a worldwide event and would have been recorded in history, because it is a global matter, since the moon is a sign visible on the horizon that everyone sees, and since this state of the moon is strange and outside the ordinary, then the aspirations of people converge on what?

**Student:** On transmitting it.

**Shaykh:** On transmitting it, and it must be mentioned in histories, in the history of India, the Romans, the Persians, and the like.

We say: woe to you, that you make what Allah has informed of a subject of doubt, because these people did not record it. Rather, if they had recorded that it did not occur, we would say: you have lied, and Allah has spoken the truth.

Also, the response to this is: it does not follow that if the moon split and the people of Makkah and those near them saw it, everyone else must see it, because half of the earth's globe could not have seen it, why? Because it was hidden from them. That is one point.

The surrounding towns on the surface of the earth near Makkah may have had it occur in the middle of the night or at the end of the night, or they may have had clouds blocking the view, or similar circumstances. The obstacles to seeing it are many. But what concerns us is not whether they saw it or not, or whether they recorded it in their histories or not.

To deny the Qur'an or mass-transmitted Sunnah on such matters is in reality excessive reliance on reason, or on what they call rationalism. A person should not be purely rationalist, nor purely literalist. Rather, he must have a reason by which he weighs matters, and when the legislative matters are clear, there is no room for reason.

So Allah, the Exalted, showed them signs, among them the splitting of the moon. Among them also: the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, witnessed before all the people that the stone and the tree greeted him with salaam, to the point that he said: "There was a stone in Makkah that used to greet me with salaam; I recognize it" [[Muslim (2277/2), from the hadith of Jabir ibn Samurah.]].

Likewise, among the signs was what happened on the day of Badr. Among the signs there was killing and captivity. Killing of whom?

**Student:** Of the leaders of the disbelievers.

**Shaykh:** Yes, of the leaders of the disbelievers, not their common people: the chieftains of Quraysh. The killing of the chieftains, the enemies of the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, is a sign for him, because that is a victory for him. Had what he said been false, Allah, may He be blessed and exalted, would never have given him victory, because Allah does not grant lasting victory to falsehood over truth. But falsehood may have a momentary surge so that Allah may test the believers, and then the people of falsehood achieve a temporary victory.

Likewise the captivity: were any of them taken captive? Yes, seventy men of them were taken captive and brought to Madinah, and they were also among their nobles who were captured.

The point is that this battle, the Battle of Badr, crushed them completely and humiliated them with extreme humiliation. For this reason Allah named it: ﴿the Day of Criterion﴾ [Al-Anfal 8:41], because Allah distinguished through it between truth and falsehood. And you know that people were waiting to see what would happen. When the Arabs saw that the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, with a small number of three hundred and some men, defeated about a thousand from Quraysh, fully equipped and numerous, they knew that the Messenger's matter would prevail.

Likewise: ﴿the angels strike their faces and their backs﴾ [Al-Anfal 8:50]. Was this mentioned concerning Badr, or concerning the disbelievers in general?

**Student:** All of them (...).

**Shaykh:** ﴿And if you could see when the angels take the souls of those who disbelieved, striking their faces and their backs, [saying]: "Taste the punishment of the burning"﴾.

**Student:** (...).

The Sheikh: Alright, but regarding Badr: was it mentioned that the angels strike their faces and their backs?

The Student: (...).

The Sheikh: ﴿When your Lord revealed to the angels, "I am with you, so strengthen those who have believed. I will cast terror into the hearts of those who disbelieved, so strike [them] upon the necks and strike from them every fingertip."﴾ [al-Anfal 12]. There is nothing in it (...) the faces and the backs. What is in it is that they strike above the necks, meaning their necks are struck, and every fingertip of them is struck, meaning the fingers. This is the apparent meaning.

As for what the author (the one whose commentary this is) went to, I do not know of any sunnah that clarifies this either. The author has a point of view that the angels strike their faces when they advance against the Muslims and strike their backs when they turn away from the Muslims. But since this has not been reported, it is better to limit oneself to what has been reported, which is that Allah said to them: ﴿strike above the necks and strike from them every fingertip﴾. He did not say, "strike their faces and their backs."

Unless someone says: His saying ﴿And if you could see when the angels take those who disbelieved, striking their faces and their backs﴾ includes these, since they are from the disbelievers; at the time of death they strike their faces and their backs. If the author intends by this what the generality of the verse leads to, then it is a valid consideration.

He said: "And Allah hastened them to the Fire." How did He hasten them to the Fire?

The Student: He hastened them to the Fire, because the punishment of the grave (...). When a person dies, he is in the punishment of the grave.

The Sheikh: Meaning, Allah hastened them before the death of the Messenger, peace and blessings be upon him; this matter befell them and they were hastened to the Fire.

He said: "﴿And your Lord is not unaware of what they do﴾ (with the ya' and the ta')", i.e., ﴿what they do﴾ and ﴿what you do﴾ are two canonical recitations. "And He only gives them respite for their time."

His saying: ﴿And your Lord is not unaware of what they do﴾ – this sentence is intended as a warning and a consolation: a warning to these deniers, and a consolation to the Messenger ﷺ.

In it: that among the attributes of Allah is that it is one of the negative attributes. It has already passed with us that negative attributes include two things: negation of the mentioned attribute, and affirmation of the perfection of its opposite. So Allah, exalted is He, is not heedless, due to what? Due to the perfection of His knowledge and His oversight: perfect knowledge and perfect oversight: ﴿And Allah is ever over all things Watchful﴾ [al-Ahzab 52].

The surah has ended and we did not take the benefits of the previous lesson; we will take them now.

First: Allah, blessed and exalted, said: ﴿And whoever comes with an evil deed – their faces will be thrown into the Fire﴾.

- It is derived from it: that the basis of punishment for evil deeds is bringing them on the Day of Resurrection, not merely doing them. A person may do an evil deed and it is expiated, or he repents from it, but the matter rests on the coming (with it).

- The second benefit: affirmation of the punishment of the Fire, from His saying: ﴿their faces will be thrown into the Fire﴾, and we seek refuge in Allah.

- The third benefit: explanation of the severity of the punishment – we seek refuge in Allah – for these people, in that they are thrown on their faces into the Fire, and the face is the most noble of the limbs, and humiliating it is greater than humiliating anything else.

If someone slapped you on your cheek or struck you on your leg, which would be the greater humiliation? The face is more noble, and for this reason being thrown on their faces into the Fire – we seek refuge in Allah – is more severe and more eloquent in humiliation and in punishment.

- The fourth benefit: the perfection of Allah's justice, azza wa jall, from His saying: ﴿Are you recompensed except for what you used to do?﴾, meaning: We did not wrong you; you wronged yourselves, so you did what made you deserve this punishment.

- The fifth benefit: that the punishment of the people of the Fire – we seek refuge in Allah – is both spiritual and physical. Physical, in that their faces are thrown into the Fire; spiritual, in that they are rebuked and reproached: ﴿Are you recompensed except for what you used to do?﴾. Consider what is the state of one who is told such a thing.

You find him, for example, filled with shame, and filled also with regret, saying: "If only I had not done it," "if only, if only." But ﴿how can they reach [repentance] from a place far away?﴾ [Saba 52].

So there is gathered for them – we seek refuge in Allah – both physical punishment and spiritual punishment. Allah, exalted, mentioned in Surat al-Mu'minun that they say: ﴿Our Lord, bring us out of it, and if we return [to disbelief], then indeed we are wrongdoers﴾ [al-Mu'minun 107]. And if they were brought out, they would return to their wrongdoing, as there is no difficulty in this, as Allah, exalted, said: ﴿And if they were returned, they would return to what they were forbidden﴾ [al-An'am 28]. But they say this from the severity of what they find.

So the answer – we seek refuge in Allah – was the greatest answer in humiliation: ﴿Remain in it in humiliation and do not speak to Me﴾ [al-Mu'minun 108]. This is an answer in utmost humiliation, abasement, and disgrace. It has been mentioned that Allah does not speak to them except after a long period, and He speaks to them with this speech that holds no good for them, rather it is despair of every good and every relief. We ask Allah for well-being.

﴿Remain in it and do not speak to Me﴾ means: be driven away, be humbled, and let humiliation and degradation befall you; and in addition, you are not to be spoken to; you are not worthy of being spoken to. We ask Allah for well-being. Thus there is gathered for the people of the Fire both the physical and the spiritual punishment.

﴿Are you recompensed except for what you used to do?﴾

He said: ﴿I have only been commanded to worship the Lord of this city, which He has made sacred and to whom belongs everything. And I have been commanded to be among the Muslims﴾ [an-Naml 91].

- From this verse are benefits. First: the obligation on the Messenger, peace and blessings be upon him, to proclaim what is mentioned, since the implied meaning is: Say, "I have only been commanded," and it is obligatory upon him to announce this so that he may serve as an example in it.

- Second: His saying: ﴿to worship﴾ – the obligation of worship upon the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him.

- The Student: On everyone.

- The Sheikh: No, upon the Prophet ﷺ: ﴿to worship﴾. It is not said that the obligations fall away from the prophets and the saints; rather they are obligatory upon the Prophet ﷺ just as they are obligatory upon others, and it is obligatory upon him, peace and blessings be upon him, to testify that there is no god but Allah and that he is the Messenger of Allah. This is what Islam requires.

- Third: By this we know the falsehood of what the people of those who are claimed to be saints claim, or the followers of those who are claimed to be saints; they said that the saint reaches a level by which the obligation falls from him.

This exists among the Sufis and others; they say: these acts of worship with which we are charged are means to an end, and the end is certainty: ﴿And worship your Lord until there comes to you the certainty﴾ [al-Hijr 99]. So when a person reaches certainty, worship falls from him; prayer is no longer obligatory upon him, nor zakat, nor fasting, nor hajj, and marrying anyone is not forbidden to him; he marries whomever he wishes, of males and females – we seek refuge in Allah – and any number, young or old. Indeed, we now hear about them in Africa: one of them has fifty wives; they count the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, as having fifty wives. Moreover, he does not marry by contract: if he desires a woman, he sends to her father and says: "Give your daughter to me as a wife, I want her as a wife," and no one is able to oppose him, because they claim they have reached a station for which they no longer need obligation.

If the Messenger ﷺ was commanded to worship Allah, then others are all the more so.

The Student: (...).

The Sheikh: Yes, they are (...) the disbelievers, we seek refuge in Allah.

The Student: They make the saint higher than the Prophet?

The Sheikh: If they claim this, it is not correct; this too is a lie.

- Also among the benefits of this verse: the virtues of Makkah, the virtue of Makkah in two respects:
From attributing lordship to it: ﴿Lord of this city﴾, and from Allah, exalted, having made it sacred: ﴿which He has made sacred﴾. So there is in it the virtue of Makkah over all other lands.

It has many virtues; even if there were none but that He singled it out among the pillars of Islam, singling it out for worship among the pillars of Islam: Hajj is a pillar of Islam, and there is no other city in the world to which travel is obligatory at all, nor is there a recommended travel except to Madinah, and what else? And al-Masjid al-Aqsa.

- The fourth benefit: that the One who made Makkah sacred is Allah; from His saying: ﴿which He has made sacred﴾.

If someone says: Does this not conflict with what is established from the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, his saying: "Indeed Ibrahim made Makkah sacred"[[Agreed upon; al-Bukhari (2129) and Muslim (1360 / 454) from the hadith of Abdullah ibn Zayd ibn Asim.]]?

We say: No; because the meaning of his saying "made Makkah sacred" is that he made its sanctity apparent and declared it. Otherwise, who made it sacred? Allah.

For this reason we say, for example, that the Messenger ﷺ made carrion, wine, and pork forbidden; meaning he made their prohibition apparent and declared it, though the One who forbade them is Allah.

The point is that here there is no contradiction between His saying ﴿which He has made sacred﴾ and the Messenger's saying ﷺ: "Indeed Ibrahim made Makkah sacred." The reconciliation is simple and clear.

The Student: And did Allah make Madinah sacred?

The Sheikh: Yes, Allah made it sacred.

- The fifth benefit: that everything belongs to Allah; Makkah and other than it; from His saying: ﴿and to Him belongs everything﴾.

- The sixth benefit: a refutation of the Mu'tazila Qadariyya who say that man is independent in his deeds; for according to their view, some things are removed from Allah's dominion, whereas Allah, exalted, says: ﴿and to Him belongs everything﴾.

- The seventh benefit: the eloquence of the Qur'an; for when He said ﴿Lord of this city﴾, someone might understand that Allah's lordship is specific to this place. To guard against this mistaken understanding, He followed it with ﴿and to Him belongs everything﴾, and this is from the eloquence of the Qur'an.

Does Makkah enter into His saying ﴿and to Him belongs everything﴾?

The Students: Yes.

The Sheikh: Or does it not enter?

This question is disputed among the usulis (scholars of legal theory); that is, when a specific item is mentioned alongside a general one, does explicit mention of it exclude it from the generality?

Then it is mentioned once, but singled out for its nobility, for example, and for the care given to it; or it does not exclude it from the generality, so it is mentioned twice: once in the form of specification and once in the form of generalization. So which is what comes first to the mind?

The Student: (...).

The Sheikh: ﴿The angels and the Spirit descend therein by permission of their Lord﴾ [al-Qadr 4]. And what comes to minds?

The Student: The Spirit is the angels.

The Sheikh: Yes, the Spirit is the angels and Jibril. But what comes to my mind is that when the specific is mentioned after the general or before it, it is not intended to be included in the general.

When you say: "The students came, and Ali."

And he is one of the students; it is known who the students are; you understand that he was excluded from them by being explicitly named, and it is enough honor for him to be singled out from among the general and named in the ruling.

But those others say: it is mentioned twice, once by way of generality and once by way of specificity. But as I think, and as it occurs to me, it is not so. Yes, if the general were mentioned in another place and the specific not mentioned, there is no doubt that it is included in the generality.

The Student: (...).

The Sheikh: Yes, according to the view that when the specific is mentioned, it is a general with a specific exception.

The Student: (...).

The Sheikh: Emphasis.

The Student: (...).

The Sheikh: No, and in any case, whoever says this thinks it is emphasis, but it is not exact emphasis; it is emphasis by generality.

- The ninth benefit: it is not permissible for anyone to rule by other than what Allah has revealed; from His saying: ﴿and to Him belongs everything﴾, because among all things is judgment between the servants, indeed it is among the greatest things. So if that belongs to Allah, then no one may take it on independently; whoever wishes to take it on independently has tried to be a partner with Allah in that, and has placed himself in a station he does not deserve.

So the matter of permitting, forbidding, and obligating belongs to whom? To Allah; because ﴿to Him belongs everything﴾.

The matter of good and bad?

The Student: (...).

The Sheikh: No, the correct view is yes, it belongs to Allah; because we do not know the goodness or badness of some things except through Allah. But reason also has scope in this; therefore: ﴿Do you order the people to righteousness and forget yourselves while you recite the Book? Then will you not reason?﴾ [al-Baqarah 44]. What follows it?

The Students: ﴿Then will you not reason?﴾

The Sheikh: ﴿Then will you not reason?﴾ indicates that reason makes things good and bad, for this is among the bad things.

Do not forbid an ethic while you commit its like; it is a shame upon you when you do it, a grave matter.

So reason makes things good and bad, but it does not obligate or forbid. Obligation and prohibition belong to Allah. As for good and bad, reason makes things good and bad; for this reason Allah refers many matters to reason, which shows that reason may call things good and bad, but some things are not known to be good or bad except through the path of the Sharia.

This is the correct view on this question, the question of rational good and bad, over which a long dispute arose between the People of the Sunnah and the Jama'ah and the People of innovation. Some said: it does not make things good or bad; and strangely, this is the well-known view of the Hanbalis.

Al-Futuhi said in the book Mukhtasar al-Tahrir in the principles of jurisprudence: Reason does not make things good or bad, nor obligate or forbid.

We say: as for his saying that it does not obligate or forbid, this is correct; as for his saying that it does not make things good or bad, this is not correct.

It is narrated from Ibn Mas'ud, may Allah be pleased with him, that he said: "What the Muslims see as good is good with Allah, and what they see as bad is bad with Allah,"[[Narrated by Ahmad in al-Musnad (3600).]] and perhaps the saying of the Messenger ﷺ supports this: "Sin is what troubles your soul, and you dislike that people should see it,"[[Narrated by Muslim (2553 / 15) from the hadith of al-Nawwas ibn Sam'an.]] because this is evidence that a person... but a person whose inner self is pure and whose intention is sincere does not find peace in sin at all. As for the wicked person – you know that the refuse collector is not bothered by refuse, right? But the perfume seller, if he sits next to refuse? He cannot sit.

So the person whose inner self is pure and whose intention is sincere, and whom Allah knows to have good intention, is granted success; you will find that if he does an evil deed without knowing it is evil, his soul is not at ease and it does not settle; for this reason he said: "Righteousness is what the soul is at rest with and the heart is at peace with, and sin is what troubles the self and wavers in the chest."[[Narrated by Ahmad in al-Musnad (18006) from the hadith of Wabisa ibn Ma'bad al-Asadi.]]

But to whom is this addressed? All people? No; it is addressed to the one with a pure heart and sincere faith. As for people immersed in this, they are not addressed with this example.

The Student: (...) meaning reason (...) custom (...).

The Sheikh: No, reason; custom has no role.

The Student: Meaning reason makes good...

The Sheikh: Now custom makes some ugly things good.

The Student: The refuse collector considers refuse good, and the perfume seller does not consider it good.

The Sheikh: No, this is not that he considers it good; perhaps reason considers refuse good if it becomes a way of earning, but his disposition is not at ease with it, because it harms with its smell; custom is not reliable, because custom... people now, and before now, may find good things ugly and ugly things good.

The Student: (...).

The Sheikh: Yes, it is known; even the sincere Muslim; the Messenger said: "What troubles your soul."

- Also among the benefits of the verse: that the Messenger, peace and blessings be upon him, is commanded to be among the Muslims: ﴿and I have been commanded to be among the Muslims﴾.

- The eleventh: that Islam and faith are one thing; because His saying ﴿to be among the Muslims﴾ – there is no doubt that what he was commanded is the highest state, which is faith.

But this question, whether Islam is faith or not, is also a point of contention among the People of the Sunnah and the Jama'ah themselves and the Ash'aris.

The correct view is that it should be said: when "Islam" is used without qualification, it includes faith, and when "faith" is used without qualification, it includes Islam.

Commentary of Ibn 'Uthaymin (Tafsir al-Quran al-Karim) on surah 27, verse 90–93 (part 4 of 4):

But when they are specified and paired together, then faith (īmān) is what settles in the heart, and Islam (islām) is what the limbs carry out, because Islam comes from istislām (submission), which is non-opposition, rather, compliance. Thus the hypocrites who do not show opposition we call Muslims, but we do not call them believers, because faith is absent from their hearts.

Among people there is one in the middle: ﴿The Bedouins say: "We have believed." Say: "You have not believed; rather say, 'We have submitted,' for faith has not yet entered your hearts."﴾ [al-Hujurat 14]. ﴿Lamma yadkhul﴾ (has not yet entered), he did not say "lam yadkhul" (has not entered), to convey that faith is close to entering their hearts, but it has not entered; it is only near. Faith is far from the hypocrites; they shrink from it, and if it drew near to them they would flee from it. But these Bedouins had not yet had faith enter their hearts, except that it was near: ﴿and faith has not yet entered your hearts﴾.

So the correct position on this question is: faith is Islam when they are mentioned together, and when they are mentioned separately, each includes the other.

* Student: (...) indicated that faith is the outward deeds.
* The Shaykh: Yes, faith, because it is included within it; when it is paired with Islam, this is explained by that and that by this. But when mentioned alone, it encompasses it.
* Student: (...).
* The Shaykh: Yes, Muslims outwardly.
* Student: Submitting; meaning they do not come with (...).
* The Shaykh: No, because the Messenger intended to explain it by the outward deeds grounded in sincerity, and the outward deeds of the hypocrites are not grounded in sincerity. That is why you find them praying with the people and mentioning Allah, the Exalted, in their prayer, yet they do not remember Allah except a little. The Messenger ﷺ did not distinguish between them and their relatives in inheritance and other matters; he would inherit from some of them and they from him. Shaykh al-Islam Ibn Taymiyyah adopted this view and said: the hypocrite inherits from the believer, and the believer inherits from the hypocrite, and he cited as evidence that the Messenger ﷺ..

What he said is correct, except that we object to it in cases where his hypocrisy is known; that is, if his hypocrisy is known, it is not obligatory that he inherit from a Muslim or a Muslim inherit from him. Allah the Exalted said: ﴿And do not pray over any of them who dies, ever, nor stand at his grave﴾ [at-Tawbah 84].

* Student: In the case of those known to be hypocrites.
* The Shaykh: Among them are people he knows, and among them are people he does not know.

He said: ﴿And to recite the Quran. Whoever is guided, is only guided for his own soul; and whoever strays, say: I am only one of the warners﴾.

* From this verse is derived, first: the obligation of reciting the Quran in both its forms. What are the two forms?
* Students: The verbal and the practical.
* The Shaykh: The verbal and the practical. It is obligatory upon a person to recite the Quran both verbally and practically, whether from the heart's memory or while looking at the text?
* Student: Even while looking.
* The Shaykh: Even while looking.
* The second benefit: the excellence and nobility of the Quran, since he was commanded to recite it.
* The third benefit: the obligation of beautifying the recitation of the Quran, from His saying: ﴿And to recite the Quran﴾.
* The fourth benefit: the obligation upon the Prophet ﷺ to convey the Quran, from His saying: ﴿And I have been commanded to be among the Muslims (91). And to recite the Quran﴾.
* The fifth benefit:..

Ibn 'Uthaymin, Tafsir al-Quran al-Karim, on Surah 27, verses 90–93 (part 1 of 4):

Allah the Exalted says: ﴿Whoever comes with a good deed will have better than it, and they will be safe from the terror of that Day. And whoever comes with an evil deed, their faces will be thrown into the Fire: "Are you recompensed except for what you used to do?"﴾ [An-Naml 90].

﴿Hal tujzawn﴾ (Are you recompensed): meaning "mā tujzawn" (you are not recompensed). The interrogative here is more emphatic than a bare negation, because it indicates negation plus something additional. For example, "mā tujzawna illā mā kuntum ta'malūn" (you are not recompensed except for what you used to do) indicates that they are recompensed only for what they did. But ﴿hal tujzawn﴾ indicates the affirmation of this matter, that a person can only be recompensed for what he did, and it carries both affirmation and rebuke at the same time.

The author said: (It is said to them as a rebuke: ﴿hal﴾, meaning "mā" (not), ﴿tujzawna illā﴾ the recompense of ﴿mā kuntum ta'malūn﴾ (what you used to do) of shirk and sins.)

As for his words, (mā ﴿tujzawn﴾), this has already been discussed.

As for his words, (﴿illā﴾ the recompense of ﴿mā kuntum ta'malūn﴾), is there in it a diversion of the wording from its apparent meaning? How is that?

* Student: (...).
* Shaykh: Yes, (...).
* Student: (...).
* Shaykh: The recompense of "mā kuntum" (what you were). Good, what is the intent?

Because His saying ﴿illā mā kuntum ta'malūn﴾ requires that the deed itself be the recompense, that the deed is the recompense ﴿illā mā kuntum﴾. And it is known that the deed is not the recompense; rather the recompense is one thing and the deed is another. When you hire a person to work for you and then give him his wage, his work is other than his wage. The one who works for Allah, the Exalted, his deed is other than his recompense.

So what is the apparent meaning of the verse ﴿hal tujzawna illā mā kuntum ta'malūn﴾? Is a person recompensed by his deed or not?

Therefore the author found it necessary to supply this omitted element: (﴿illā﴾ the recompense of ﴿illā mā kuntum ta'malūn﴾). But the wording of the verse is more eloquent, because it is a matter of hyperbole in justice, that the recompense is made to be the deed itself, as if the recompense itself were your deed. It is hyperbole in justice: if you want much reward, then do much deed, because your reward is your deed.

As for his words (﴿hal tujzawna illā﴾ the recompense of ﴿mā kuntum ta'malūn﴾), there is also in it awkwardness: "You are not recompensed except the recompense of the deed?" It is known. The word ﴿tujzawn﴾ already conveys recompense, so there is no need for elaboration. Therefore the correct approach is to leave the verse as it is, on its apparent meaning.

What is understood is that what they are given is the recompense, from His saying ﴿hal tujzawn﴾, and expressing the recompense by the deed itself is hyperbole in justice, such that your recompense is your deed.

As for his words (of shirk and sins), this is what the majority of scholars held, and it is the correct view: that the disbeliever is punished for the root of disbelief and also for the sins he committed. So a polytheist who commits adultery, steals and drinks wine is punished for that. He is punished for the root and the branches, and this is what the majority of scholars hold. They cite as evidence the saying of Allah the Exalted: ﴿They will ask one another about the criminals, "What has caused you to enter Saqar?" They will say, "We were not of those who prayed, nor did we used to feed the poor, and we used to engage in vain discourse with those engaged in it, and we used to deny the Day of Judgement"﴾ [Al-Muddaththir 40–46].

Prayer and charity are not among the roots, although the correct view is that prayer is among the roots and whoever abandons it commits disbelief. But charity is not among the roots; even zakat, according to the correct view, its abandoner does not become a disbeliever. Nevertheless, they mentioned it among the causes of their entry into the Fire, and if it had no effect on the recompense it would not have been among the causes. This is evidence that they are punished for the branches of Islam just as they are punished for its roots.

Based on this, they are punished for their sins other than shirk. This is without doubt the perfection of justice, for if a Muslim is punished for them, how much more so a disbeliever?

Would it be a vengeance for the Muslim and a blessing for the disbeliever? No. Rather, even more than that, the disbeliever is punished even for what is permissible for the believer. Allah the Exalted said: ﴿Say: "Who has forbidden the adornment of Allah which He brought forth for His servants, and the good provisions?" Say: "They are for those who believed in the life of this world, purely for them on the Day of Resurrection."﴾ [Al-A'raf 32].

From His saying ﴿purely for them on the Day of Resurrection﴾ it is taken that these things are not pure for non-believers, and that they will be recompensed for them. This is also what sound reasoning requires: how can a person enjoy the blessings of the Creator while disobeying the Creator?

He must punish him. He says: "I did good to you; I fed you, gave you drink, clothed you, housed you, married you, and the like," and so he is punished for this blessing, because it requires gratitude.

He said: (Say to them: ﴿I have only been commanded to worship the Lord of this city﴾ [An-Naml 91]; that is, Makkah, ﴿who﴾) He did not say "allatī" (feminine), why? Because it is an attribute of a masculine noun, ﴿Rabb hādhihi al-baldah alladhī﴾. Therefore you parse ﴿alladhī﴾ as a relative pronoun built on sukūn in a position of nasb, an attribute of the ﴿Rabb﴾.

(﴿Rabb hādhihi al-baldah alladhī ḥarramahā﴾; that is, He made it a sanctuary, secure) Did He make it so by decree (kawnan) or by law (shar'an)?

* Student: (...).
* Shaykh: By law. He made it, by law, a sanctuary, secure.

As for His saying ﴿Lord of this city﴾, attributing lordship to it indicates its excellence, and that Allah, the Exalted, has cared for it and honoured it.

He said: (Blood is not shed in it, a person's), and the hadith: «Blood shall not be shed therein» [agreed upon; al-Bukhari (104) and Muslim (1354 / 446) from the hadith of Abu Shurayh al-'Adawi].

Which is more general, "a person's blood" or "blood"? "Blood" is more general; therefore blood of a person is not shed in it, nor the blood of game. As for livestock such as camels, cattle, sheep and the like, the Sunnah has shown that this is permitted.

As for his words (and no one is wronged in it), this is not specific to Makkah; even outside Makkah it is not permitted for anyone to be wronged there. That is why the hadith does not say "no one is wronged therein" alone; rather the Messenger said: «Blood shall not be shed therein». So it is not one of Makkah's special features that no one is wronged there. It is true that wrongdoing in Makkah is greater than elsewhere: ﴿And whoever intends therein deviation by wrongdoing, We will make him taste a painful punishment﴾ [Al-Hajj 25]. But that wrongdoing elsewhere is permissible, no.

Likewise: (no game is hunted in it).

* Student: (...).
* Shaykh: No, it does not indicate that; because here ﴿man yurid fīhi bi-ilḥād﴾ the letter bāʾ indicates that the verb is implicitly containing the meaning of true determination.

* Student: (...).
* Shaykh: A sin is not multiplied by a place merely in quantity; it is multiplied in quality only. It does not mean that a sin is recompensed with two sins; rather the meaning is that it is greater, and that you should know the difference is in quality: the manner of punishment differs. I may strike this person one blow, and strike another one blow, and this second one is painful while the first is not.

He said: (no game is hunted in it). Is this correct or not? Correct, and elsewhere game is hunted.

(nor is its grass cut): Correct, and elsewhere grass is cut.

* Student: Madinah?

* Shaykh: In Madinah the grass may be cut, yes, it is permitted. Only what is cut without need is forbidden in Madinah; what is needed is permitted. This is the difference between it and Makkah.

(And that is among the blessings upon Quraysh, its people, in that Allah, the Exalted, lifted from their lands the punishment and the widespread strife found in all the lands of the Arabs.)

So His saying ﴿alladhī ḥarramahā﴾ means: He made it a sanctuary, and made it forbidden. What we have said is more general than what the author said, because the author says "He made it a secure sanctuary," then mentioned things; so it is a ḥaram (sacred place) and also ḥarām (forbidden). Ḥaram means it is held sacred, and ḥarām means it is made forbidden.

Therefore whoever intends it, it is prescribed for him, by the consensus of scholars, not to enter it except as a Muslim; and regarding its obligation there is a well-known difference of opinion.

Also, among its sanctity: polytheists do not approach it, or do they? They do not approach the Sacred Mosque, so the whole ḥaram is forbidden to them, because entering the ḥaram is approaching the Sacred Mosque. Thus this was a token of honour for this city.

Yet Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, says: (﴿And to Him belongs﴾ the Exalted ﴿everything﴾, He is its Lord, Creator and Owner.)

The last sentence contains a great benefit: since He said ﴿Lord of this city﴾, one might suppose that His lordship is specific to this city, so He then generalized, saying ﴿and to Him belongs everything﴾.

A parallel to this is His saying: ﴿Not equal among you are those who spent and fought before the victory. Those are greater in rank than those who spent afterward and fought﴾ [Al-Hadid 10]; after it He said: ﴿And to each Allah has promised the best﴾, lest one suppose that this excellence is specific to those, so He clarified that the reward is for all, which is Paradise, even though they are not equal.

Here: ﴿Lord of this city﴾ and ﴿and to Him belongs everything﴾: the lordship of Allah is general to everything, but His lordship over this city is more specific than His general lordship.

* Student: (...).
* Shaykh: No, it is not masculine gender; we mean by "masculine" the wording, not the meaning. One may not say "masculine" about Allah; we say the word is masculine. Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, may not be described by this or that.

He said: ﴿And I have been commanded to be among the Muslims﴾.

﴿Umirtu﴾ (I have been commanded): by whom? ﴿Innamā umirtu an aʿbud﴾ and ﴿wa-umirtu an akūna min al-muslimīn﴾.

Is not worship itself Islam? The answer: Yes, worship is Islam.

But there He said ﴿I have only been commanded to worship the Lord of this city, who has made it sacred﴾, and worship is submission to Him through obedience.

Then He said ﴿And I have been commanded to be among the Muslims﴾, meaning: that I realize this worship through complete submission to the commands of Allah, Blessed and Exalted.

A person may be a worshipper in principle, but complete compliance with all the prescriptions of Islam is derived from His saying ﴿And I have been commanded to be among the Muslims﴾, that is, among those who submit completely to Allah, the Exalted, with no opposition or arrogance in them.

In His saying ﴿an akūna min al-muslimīn﴾ is there evidence that there were Muslims before? Are Jews and Christians Muslims?

* Students: No.

* Shaykh: While their legislations were in force, they were Muslims, or not? But after they were abrogated, if they do not adhere to the abrogating law, they are not Muslims. Islam is the religion with Allah at every time and place, and after the sending of the Messenger, peace be upon him, there is no Islam except by following his law. Otherwise the root of Islam, as you know, is from submission, which is surrender, and this includes every submission to Allah, the Exalted, whether in the era of this nation or before it. Noah, peace be upon him, says: ﴿And I have been commanded to be among the Muslims﴾ [An-Naml 91], just as it was said to the Messenger, peace be upon him. And of Jacob it is said: He said to his sons: ﴿O my sons, indeed Allah has chosen for you this religion, so do not die except while you are Muslims﴾ [Al-Baqarah 132]. And Bilqis said: ﴿I have wronged myself, and I have submitted with Solomon to Allah, Lord of the worlds﴾ [An-Naml 44].

(﴿And I have been commanded to be among the Muslims (91), and to recite the Quran﴾ to you, the recitation of the call to faith ﴿So whoever is guided, is guided only for his own soul﴾; that is, for its sake, for its reward from his guidance is for himself; ﴿and whoever strays﴾ from faith and misses the path of guidance ﴿then say: "I am only among the warners"﴾.)

As for His saying ﴿and to recite the Quran﴾: recitation is divided into two kinds: verbal recitation and meaningful recitation.

The first recitation is reading the Quran; the second recitation is acting upon what the Quran brought, derived from tala al-shay'a yatlūhu, when one follows a thing and becomes its follower.

So the Messenger's saying ﴿and to recite the Quran﴾ includes both: that I recite it by reading, and that I recite it by following. He is commanded to do so; it is as if he says: "I will recite the Quran to you by reading, and I will also recite the Quran by following, and I do not care about your opposition and aversion." This is not only for the Messenger, peace be upon him, but for everyone who follows the Messenger: it is obligatory upon him to recite the Quran verbally, and it is known that reciting al-Fatihah is a pillar of prayer, which is among the pillars of Islam.

Secondly: it is obligatory upon the Muslim to recite the Quran by following, and not to mind whoever opposes him. Had we considered people's feelings and people's minds, religion would not remain religion; rather religion would become custom, accepted if people accept it according to their habits, and not religion if they do not accept it. What is obligatory is that religion be remote from people's customs, meaning that the judgement is the Quran and the Sunnah, not what people are accustomed to in their worships or other things. This is unlike some people today who wish to deceive people regarding what they are upon, even if it is falsehood, and this is not correct; for if we walked upon this matter or this method, Islam would have no life left. Islam would remain dead, and part of it would die in this age, then another age would come and another part would die, and so on until it ends. But when we act by Islam and renew according to what the Book and the Sunnah require, not according to our opinions, that is the true leadership.

As for us remaining silent and burying our heads in the sand, saying: "These people cannot be opposed," or hesitating because some people say: "You have brought a new religion; we have never known this religion before," and the like, this should not prevent a person from speaking the truth.

Therefore His saying ﴿and to recite the Quran﴾ is recitation of wording by which the proof is established against you, and recitation of following, not caring about your opposition and contradiction; and this is what is obligatory upon every Muslim in every place.

But is accommodating people, meaning gradually bringing people along until they take the correct path, permissible or not?

* Students: Permissible.

* Shaykh: Yes indeed. Accommodating the situation gradually is not objectionable. For this reason, what we see is that calling to Allah, the Exalted, with wisdom encompasses this matter, namely bringing people to Islam stage by stage.

Though some people say this applies to the beginning of the call: it is true that Islam developed; prayer came, then zakat, then fasting, then hajj; wine was forbidden in several stages; fasting was made obligatory in several ways.

But we say: just as this is at the origin of the call, or the beginning of the call, it is also at its end. When was Mu'adh sent? In the tenth year after the Hijrah. Yet he said: «Call them first to testifying that there is no god but Allah, then to prayer, then to zakat» [agreed upon; al-Bukhari (1395) and Muslim (19 / 29) from the hadith of 'Abdullah ibn 'Abbas]. So the Messenger arranged this, and did not say: call them to all of them together.

For example, if we see a person absorbed in committing a sin, and we know that if we tell him to abandon it completely, he will not be able, or he will be repelled, then it is fine that we move him away from it little by little, gradually; for this is like treating an illness. An illness cannot be treated all at once; there must be a transition from one thing to another until the disease is fully eradicated.

So this matter returns to the condition of the people, and it does not mean submitting to the condition of the people, for the submission I denied earlier means a person leaves people alone and does not oppose them regarding the truth. This, however, does not leave them alone, but moves them from stage to stage until they become upright. For example, when we want to introduce an act in prayer that is not customary among people, it is wise first to prepare for it with speech, then once people know it and it settles in their souls, we move them to the act afterward. Likewise in other matters beside this one.

The main point: reciting the Quran to people who turn away is something the Messenger, peace be upon him, was commanded, and the whole nation is also commanded with it. The recitation here is both verbal and by following. But the whole matter is that we should not be weak before the existing reality; rather it is obligatory upon us to be in a stronger and firmer stance.

**Student:** Transferring a person from one sin to another sin.

**Shaykh:** To another sin?

**Student:** A lesser one.

**Shaykh:** No, that is not permitted.

**Student:** Gradualness...

**Shaykh:** How? Give an example. If it is of the same kind, perhaps we can say. For instance, suppose a person is afflicted with fornication, may Allah protect us, and we say to him: "My brother, what is wrong with you? The desire you have, you can reduce it through masturbation, for example. That, being of the same kind, is not harmful." But if someone steals, we say: "My brother, leave off theft, drink wine, I will make it appealing to you!" That is not possible.

**Student:** I mean of the same kind of harm.

**Shaykh:** Yes. Being of the same kind means reduction, because if you move him to something else, its first direction generally does not disappear.
